overview.summary: The Aidi, also known as the Atlas Mountain Dog, is a sturdy guardian breed originating in Morocco. It has a thick, weather-protective coat, an alert outlook and a strong instinct to protect its family and property. It is generally better suited to experienced, active homes that can provide secure space, training and purposeful daily activity.
overview.description: The Aidi is a powerful but agile dog developed in the mountainous regions and plateaus of Morocco. Its dense coat helps protect it from changing outdoor conditions, while its muscular build supports sustained movement over rugged ground. The breed is known for vigilance and a natural tendency to assess unfamiliar people, animals and situations. It can be devoted and affectionate with familiar family members, but its guarding instincts make early socialisation, careful introductions and consistent, humane handling particularly important. An Aidi needs more than a place to sleep: it benefits from regular exercise, mental enrichment and clear boundaries. Individual dogs vary, and breed descriptions should not be treated as a guarantee of temperament.
overview.history: The Aidi has a long association with the Atlas Mountains and surrounding plateaus of North Africa, especially Morocco. It traditionally worked alongside semi-nomadic communities as a guardian of people, camps, belongings and livestock against potential threats. Its historical role was protection rather than herding flocks in the conventional European sheepdog sense. The breed developed in working environments where alertness, hardiness and independent judgement were useful. Detailed claims about particular ancestral crosses or a single precise date of origin are not established here.

grooming.brushing: Brush regularly, increasing frequency when the coat is shedding or collecting debris. Check the dense coat carefully for tangles, burrs and parasites, especially after outdoor activity.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when needed with a dog-appropriate shampoo. Avoid unnecessary frequent bathing, and dry the dense coat thoroughly.
notes: Inspect the skin beneath the thick coat rather than relying on a quick surface check.
Check and trim nails as needed.
Clean the ears when required and seek veterinary advice for persistent redness, odour or discharge.
Maintain routine dental care.
Do not crop ears or dock tails for cosmetic reasons; follow applicable animal-welfare laws and veterinary guidance.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging for an inexperienced handler
tips: Begin reward-based training and household routines early.
Teach reliable recall, leash manners and calm responses to everyday situations.
Use gradual, controlled introductions to unfamiliar people, dogs and environments.
Provide mental enrichment and appropriate tasks rather than relying on physical exercise alone.
Use secure fencing and actively supervise interactions; do not rely on breed reputation as a substitute for training.
Avoid intimidation or harsh punishment, which can undermine trust and make behaviour harder to manage.
training.socialization: Start early and continue throughout adulthood. Introduce people, animals, handling and new environments gradually and positively, while maintaining enough distance for the dog to remain calm. Because the breed has strong guarding instincts, socialisation should teach safe, controlled behaviour rather than force the dog to welcome every stranger.

nutrition.guidelines: Choose a nutritionally complete diet and measure portions rather than feeding by guesswork. Adjust intake according to growth, activity, body condition and life stage. Keep clean drinking water available. Introduce diet changes gradually, and consult a veterinarian for an individual feeding plan, especially during growth, pregnancy, illness or older age.
considerations: Monitor body condition and weight rather than relying on a generic portion estimate.
Avoid feeding immediately around vigorous exercise if the dog is uncomfortable after meals; ask a veterinarian about an appropriate routine.
Keep treats moderate and include them in the overall daily intake.
Do not add supplements or restrictive diets without a specific reason and veterinary guidance.

health.overview: The sources reviewed did not establish a comprehensive, breed-wide inherited-disease profile for the Aidi. A 2022 field study examined 161 Atlas shepherd dogs in the Tiaret region of Algeria and reported positive leishmaniasis results in 110 dogs using at least one of several diagnostic methods. This was a geographically specific study of a particular sample; it should not be interpreted as a global prevalence estimate or proof of a genetic predisposition in the breed. In areas where canine leishmaniasis occurs, ask a local veterinarian about sand-fly exposure, prevention and appropriate testing.
preventiveCare: Arrange routine veterinary examinations and keep vaccinations appropriate to local risks and veterinary advice.
Use parasite prevention suited to the dog's location, lifestyle and exposure.
Maintain a healthy body condition and regular, appropriate activity.
Check the skin, coat, paws, nails and ears during routine handling.
Discuss any persistent change in appetite, weight, movement, energy or behaviour with a veterinarian.
In regions where sand flies and canine leishmaniasis occur, ask a veterinarian about locally appropriate protective measures.
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with dog-safe toothpaste. Introduce handling gradually, and seek veterinary advice about persistent bad breath, gum bleeding, oral pain or difficulty eating.
health.earCare: Inspect the ears routinely and keep them clean and dry when needed. Do not insert cotton swabs deeply into the ear canal. Seek veterinary advice for persistent scratching, odour, discharge or redness.
health.skinCare: Part the dense coat periodically to check the skin for irritation, parasites, wounds or unusual lumps. After outdoor activity, check for burrs and other debris. Persistent itching, hair loss, sores or skin changes warrant veterinary assessment.

notIdealFor: Owners who want a dog that automatically welcomes unfamiliar visitors

funFacts: The Aidi is also known as the Atlas Mountain Dog.
The breed's recognised country of origin is Morocco.
Its traditional role is guarding and protection rather than herding flocks in the conventional European sheepdog sense.
The coat can be fawn, brown or black, with a range of darker overlays, brindling and white markings.
The official FCI standard describes the breed as not subject to a working trial.

faq.question: Where does the Aidi come from?
faq.answer: The Aidi originates in Morocco and is associated with the Atlas Mountains and surrounding plateaus of North Africa.

faq.question: Is the Aidi a herding dog?
faq.answer: Its traditional work is guarding and protecting people, camps, property and livestock. The breed standard distinguishes this role from conventional flock herding.

faq.question: How tall is an Aidi?
faq.answer: The official breed standards give a height range of approximately 52–62 cm at the withers.

faq.question: What coat colours can an Aidi have?
faq.answer: Recognised descriptions include fawn, brown and black. These may appear with brindling, darker overlays or mantles, and white markings that vary in extent.

faq.question: Is the Aidi suitable for a first-time dog owner?
faq.answer: There is no universal yes-or-no answer for every household, but its strong guarding instincts and need for careful socialisation can make it challenging for an inexperienced owner. Learn about guardian-dog behaviour and seek qualified, reward-based training support before choosing one.

faq.question: How much exercise does an Aidi need?
faq.answer: The reviewed standards do not prescribe a daily number of exercise minutes. Plan for regular physical activity and mental enrichment, then adjust the routine to the individual dog's age, health, temperament and fitness.

faq.question: Does the Aidi have known breed-specific health problems?
faq.answer: The sources reviewed do not establish a complete breed-wide inherited-disease profile. One study reported canine leishmaniasis in dogs sampled in a specific region of Algeria; local exposure risk and prevention should be discussed with a veterinarian rather than assumed to apply equally to every Aidi.

overview.summary: The Airedale Terrier is a large, athletic terrier from Yorkshire, England, recognised by its wiry coat, tan head and legs, and dark saddle marking. Intelligent, alert and energetic, it combines a working-dog background with the potential to be an engaging family companion.
overview.description: The Airedale is strongly built without being heavy, with a long head, folded V-shaped ears, a characteristic beard and a dense, wiry double coat. Its traditional black or dark-grizzle saddle contrasts with the tan head, legs and underside. The breed was developed for practical work and retains curiosity, stamina and a strong interest in its surroundings. It generally needs daily activity as well as opportunities to use its mind, so walks alone may not satisfy every individual. Reward-based training, clear routines and suitable games can help channel its energy. Coat maintenance is also important: brushing helps keep the coat free of debris and tangles, while clipping or hand-stripping may be used depending on coat condition and the owner's grooming goals.
overview.history: The Airedale Terrier developed in the Aire valley and surrounding parts of Yorkshire in northern England. Early dogs, sometimes known as Waterside or Working Terriers, were used for hunting and controlling animals such as rats and otters. The breed later demonstrated tracking and other working abilities and served in roles including police and military work. Its versatility helped it become established as both a working dog and a companion. The exact contribution of every early cross is not fully documented, so detailed claims about individual ancestral breeds should be treated cautiously.

training.difficulty: Moderate; intelligence and enthusiasm can support learning, while terrier persistence and high activity can make consistency important.
tips: Use reward-based methods and short, varied training sessions.
Teach a reliable recall and practise it around gradually increasing distractions.
Build impulse control with waits, leave-it exercises and calm greetings.
Offer structured tasks and scent games to engage the dog's problem-solving ability.
Reward calm behaviour as well as active performance.
Use secure areas for running and consider prey drive when near small animals.
Avoid harsh punishment; clear boundaries and consistent reinforcement are more useful.

feedingFrequency.adult: Many adult dogs do well with two measured meals a day. Adjust portions for activity, body condition and individual health needs.

Keep fresh water available, count treats as part of daily intake and make diet changes gradually unless your veterinarian advises otherwise. Seek veterinary guidance for persistent digestive problems, weight changes or suspected food reactions.

Use treats strategically during training and include them in the daily calorie allowance.

health.overview: Airedale Terriers should receive routine veterinary care and screening appropriate to the breed and individual family history. Breed-club screening guidance includes hip evaluation, cardiac examination and kidney-disease screening, with eye examinations and some additional tests listed as optional. Screening can help identify selected risks, but it cannot guarantee that a dog will remain free of inherited or acquired disease.

Cardiac conditions: cardiac examination is included in breed-club screening guidance.
Kidney disease: kidney-disease screening is included in the breed's CHIC-related recommendations.

Autoimmune thyroiditis: thyroid evaluation is listed as an optional screening in the breed-club health statement.
Elbow dysplasia: elbow evaluation is listed as an optional screening in the breed-club health statement.
Skin and coat problems: tangles, trapped debris or poor grooming can contribute to discomfort and may conceal skin irritation.

Ask the breeder for documented screening results and discuss their significance with a veterinarian.
Maintain a healthy body condition and build exercise gradually.
Monitor mobility, appetite, energy, skin and behaviour for changes.
Seek prompt veterinary advice for persistent vomiting, unusual thirst, urinary changes, exercise intolerance or eye discomfort.
Keep grooming and dental care on a regular schedule.

health.earCare: Check the folded ears routinely for redness, odour, discharge or discomfort. Clean only as advised by a veterinarian and seek care if signs of infection appear.

It is recognised as the largest of the terrier breeds.
The breed has worked in varied roles, including tracking and service work.

The traditional coat pattern has a dark saddle with tan on the head, legs and underside.

faq.question: How much exercise does an Airedale Terrier need?
faq.answer: A healthy adult often benefits from around 60–90 minutes of daily activity, adjusted for age, health and temperament. Mix walks with training and mental enrichment rather than relying on exercise alone.

faq.question: Do Airedale Terriers shed?
faq.answer: They can shed loose hair, although the wiry coat may not release hair in the same way as many soft-coated breeds. Regular brushing and appropriate coat maintenance help remove loose undercoat and keep the coat in good condition.

faq.question: Are Airedale Terriers easy to train?
faq.answer: They are intelligent and capable learners, but their energy and terrier persistence mean that training should be consistent, varied and rewarding. Recall, impulse control and calm behaviour are useful skills to practise early.

faq.question: Are Airedale Terriers good with children?
faq.answer: An individual Airedale may live successfully with children when introductions, training and supervision are appropriate. Suitability depends on the dog's temperament and the children's behaviour; supervise interactions and teach children to respect the dog's space.

faq.question: What grooming does an Airedale Terrier need?
faq.answer: Brush several times a week and keep the beard, legs and furnishings clean. Depending on the desired coat texture, the dog may need hand-stripping or clipping. A professional groomer can help choose a suitable routine.

faq.question: What health tests should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Ask for documented hip evaluation, cardiac examination and kidney-disease screening results. The breed-club health statement also lists eye, thyroid and elbow evaluations as optional screenings. Discuss results and any family history with a veterinarian.

faq.question: What colours does an Airedale Terrier have?
faq.answer: The recognised standard colour pattern is black and tan or grizzle and tan, with the darker colour forming a saddle over the body and tan appearing on the head, legs and underside.

faq.question: How long does an Airedale Terrier live?
faq.answer: The American Kennel Club lists an average life expectancy of 11–14 years. Individual lifespan varies with genetics, health, preventive care and living conditions.

overview.summary: The Alpine Dachsbracke is a sturdy, short-legged Austrian scent hound developed for demanding work in mountainous hunting country. It has a strong, elongated body, a dense double coat, pendant ears, and a confident, alert expression. Traditionally, it follows scent trails to locate wounded deer and is also used to hunt hare and fox. Its compact build should not be mistaken for low exercise needs: this is a working hound with a strong nose and a drive to investigate scents. As a companion, it benefits from daily outdoor activity, nose-led enrichment, patient training, and secure handling wherever wildlife or traffic may be present.
overview.description: The Alpine Dachsbracke is a compact but powerfully built hound whose short legs and long body give it a distinctive outline. Its body is muscular and elongated, with strong bone, a broad and deep chest, and firm feet suited to working over challenging terrain. The head is slightly arched through the skull, with a pronounced stop, strong muzzle, dark-brown eyes, and smooth, pendant ears with rounded tips. Its double coat has a dense undercoat beneath a thick outer coat that lies close to the body. Common standard colours are dark deer red, sometimes interspersed with black hairs, or black with clearly defined red-brown markings; a white chest star is permitted. The breed was developed as a practical hunting dog rather than as a purely decorative companion. It can be affectionate and friendly, but its scenting instincts, stamina, and need for meaningful activity should be part of any ownership decision.
overview.history: The Alpine Dachsbracke has a long association with hunting in the Alpine region. Historical accounts describe dogs of similar appearance being used for hunting long before the modern breed was formally recognised. In the late nineteenth century, Crown Prince Rudolf of Habsburg took these hounds on hunting expeditions. Austrian canine organisations recognised the Alpine-Erzgebirge Dachsbracke in 1932; the breed name was later changed to Alpenländische Dachsbracke, and Austria was designated its country of origin. It was subsequently placed in the scent-hound section of the international classification.
overview.originalPurpose: A robust mountain hunting dog used to track wounded deer and to hunt hare and fox by scent.

Active companion for owners able to meet working-hound needs

Likely to investigate interesting scents during walks
Benefits from consistent, reward-based training

exercise.level: Moderate to high. The Alpine Dachsbracke was developed for sustained scent work and outdoor hunting. Provide daily walks, opportunities to sniff, and structured activities matched to the dog's age, fitness, and health. Secure areas are preferable for off-leash activity unless recall is reliable and the location is safe.

Scent trails and beginner nose-work games
Reward-based recall and handler check-in practice
Tracking games in safe, legal environments
Food puzzles and scent-based enrichment
Hikes or outdoor exploration suited to the individual dog's fitness
Short, positive obedience sessions

grooming.level: Low to moderate. The double coat is designed for practical outdoor work, but routine brushing and checks help keep it in good condition.
grooming.brushing: Brush regularly with a suitable grooming brush or mitt to remove loose hair and debris. Increase brushing during heavier shedding periods if needed.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when the dog is dirty or has developed an odour, using a dog-formulated shampoo. Avoid frequent unnecessary bathing that could dry the skin or disrupt coat condition.
notes: Inspect the coat and skin after outdoor activity for ticks, burrs, cuts, and irritation.
Check the pendant ears regularly for redness, odour, discharge, or persistent scratching.
Dry the ears gently if they become wet and ask a veterinarian about recurring ear problems.
Trim nails as needed to maintain comfortable movement.
Brush teeth regularly with dog-safe toothpaste.
Check the paws and pads after walks on rough or rocky ground.

training.difficulty: Moderate. This is a working scent hound, so interesting trails can be more rewarding than handler cues. Use consistent reward-based methods, practise recall in secure places, and give the dog suitable outlets for scenting behaviour.
tips: Start recall and name-response training early, beginning in low-distraction environments.
Reward voluntary check-ins and returning promptly to the handler.
Use scent games to provide a structured outlet for natural tracking behaviour.
Train loose-leash walking before pulling becomes habitual.
Keep sessions positive and short enough to maintain engagement.
Avoid relying on off-leash recall in unsecured areas near roads or wildlife.
Introduce handling for grooming, nail care, and veterinary examinations gradually.
training.socialization: Provide gradual, positive exposure to people, friendly dogs, household sounds, transport, and varied walking environments. Practise calm responses around wildlife and scent distractions while maintaining secure physical control. Keep introductions age-appropriate and do not force interactions when the dog is frightened or overwhelmed.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced dog food appropriate to the dog's life stage, body condition, activity, and health. Working dogs may need different energy intake from less active companions.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Use a complete puppy diet appropriate for growth and follow its feeding guidance. Monitor growth and body condition with veterinary advice rather than increasing portions solely because the puppy seems hungry.
feedingFrequency.adult: Feed measured portions of a complete adult diet and adjust them according to body condition, activity, and health. Account for training treats in the daily allowance.
feedingFrequency.senior: Choose portions and food according to body condition, mobility, dental health, activity, and any medical conditions. Discuss persistent appetite or weight changes with a veterinarian.

nutrition.guidelines: Provide a complete and balanced diet, clean drinking water, and portions suited to the individual dog. Monitor body condition regularly and adjust intake when activity or weight changes. Avoid unbalanced homemade diets and unnecessary supplements; ask a veterinarian for a tailored plan when the dog has medical needs or performs substantial working activity.
considerations: Measure meals and adjust portions to maintain a healthy body condition.
Provide fresh, clean water at all times.
Include training treats in the daily food allowance.
Transition gradually when changing foods where practical.
Avoid giving supplements without a clear need and appropriate veterinary guidance.
Seek veterinary advice for persistent digestive changes, appetite loss, or unexplained weight change.
nutrition.note: The consulted breed standard does not provide a breed-specific weight range or calorie requirement. Feeding quantities should be individualised rather than inferred from the breed name alone.

preventiveCare: Arrange regular veterinary wellness examinations and maintain vaccination and parasite prevention appropriate to local risks.
Monitor body condition, mobility, appetite, drinking, and changes in activity.
Inspect ears, paws, skin, and coat after outdoor work.
Maintain routine dental care and seek veterinary assessment for pain, persistent bad breath, or eating changes.
Use secure leads and fencing in areas where scent-following could lead the dog toward roads or wildlife.
Seek prompt veterinary attention for serious injury, collapse, breathing difficulty, sudden weakness, or other acute concerning signs.
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly using dog-safe toothpaste. Dental chews may provide supplementary help but do not replace brushing or veterinary examinations. Ask a veterinarian about professional dental cleaning if there is significant tartar, persistent bad breath, pain, or a change in eating.
health.earCare: Check the ears regularly for redness, odour, discharge, discomfort, or head shaking. Clean only with a product appropriate for dogs and seek veterinary advice for recurring or painful symptoms.
health.skinCare: Check the coat and skin during grooming and after outdoor activity. Look for ticks, plant material, scratches, rashes, or persistent itching. Seek veterinary advice for sores, unexplained hair loss, or recurring skin irritation.

faq.question: Where does the Alpine Dachsbracke originate?
faq.answer: The Alpine Dachsbracke originates from Austria and is associated with hunting traditions in the Alpine region.

faq.question: How tall is an Alpine Dachsbracke?
faq.answer: The breed standard gives a height at the withers of 34–42 cm. Ideal heights are listed as 37–38 cm for males and 36–37 cm for females.

faq.question: How much does an Alpine Dachsbracke weigh?
faq.answer: The consulted official breed standard does not specify a weight range, so a reliable breed-specific figure cannot be provided from that source.

faq.question: What colours does the Alpine Dachsbracke come in?
faq.answer: Recognised colours include dark deer red, sometimes with lightly interspersed black hairs, and black with clearly defined red-brown markings. A white star on the chest is permitted.

faq.question: What was the Alpine Dachsbracke bred to do?
faq.answer: It was developed as a robust hunting dog, especially for tracking wounded deer and hunting hare and fox by scent.

faq.question: Is the Alpine Dachsbracke easy to train?
faq.answer: Training is usually most effective when it is consistent and rewarding. Because the breed was developed for scent work, recall and attention around interesting trails need deliberate practice.

faq.question: How much exercise does an Alpine Dachsbracke need?
faq.answer: It needs regular outdoor activity and opportunities to use its nose. There is no verified universal daily minute target for every dog, so exercise should be adjusted to age, health, fitness, and behaviour.

faq.question: What health problems are common in the Alpine Dachsbracke?
faq.answer: The sources consulted did not establish a reliable breed-specific list of common conditions or screening tests. Routine veterinary care and individual assessment are more appropriate than assuming a disease list without evidence.

faq.question: How long does an Alpine Dachsbracke live?
faq.answer: A reliable lifespan range was not established from the sources consulted. Individual lifespan depends on many factors, including genetics, health, environment, and care.

overview.summary: The American Cocker Spaniel is a compact sporting dog recognised for its expressive eyes, long feathered ears, and abundant silky coat. Developed in the United States from spaniel stock brought from Britain, it was bred to help hunters find and flush game birds. It is now also kept as a companion, but its coat, ears, weight, and exercise needs require consistent care.
overview.description: The American Cocker Spaniel has a sturdy, balanced body, a rounded head, dark expressive eyes, and long, pendulous ears covered in feathering. Its coat is silky and may be flat or slightly wavy, with longer feathering on the chest, belly, legs, and ears. The breed includes solid-colour and parti-colour varieties. Many individuals enjoy close contact with their families and respond well to patient, reward-based training. The profuse coat can mat easily, and the ears need routine inspection and cleaning as advised by a veterinarian. Regular activity, measured feeding, dental care, and preventive veterinary visits help support a healthy life.
overview.history: The American Cocker Spaniel developed in the United States from Cocker Spaniel stock imported from Britain. American breeders gradually selected for a smaller dog with a more rounded head, shorter muzzle, and more profuse coat than the English type. The two types were shown separately by the American Kennel Club in the 1930s, and the American and English varieties became distinct breeds in the United States in 1946. The American breed retained its sporting heritage while becoming widely established as a companion dog.

activities: Daily walks adjusted to age, fitness, and health
Retrieving games in safe areas
Reward-based obedience practice
Scent games and supervised exploration
Food puzzles and interactive toys
Suitable agility, rally, or other dog sports
Field activities for dogs appropriately trained for hunting work

grooming.brushing: Brush and comb the coat thoroughly every day when it is kept long, paying particular attention to the ears, armpits, chest, belly, legs, and feathering where mats commonly form. Check down to the skin rather than brushing only the surface. A shorter pet trim can reduce, but not eliminate, grooming needs.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when needed using dog-appropriate shampoo and rinse the coat thoroughly. Dry the coat and ear area carefully after bathing or swimming. Ask a veterinarian how to clean the ears safely, and avoid inserting cotton swabs or other objects into the ear canal.
notes: Arrange regular trimming or professional grooming; the interval depends on coat length and condition.
Check the ears frequently for redness, odour, discharge, moisture, or discomfort.
Keep nails at a comfortable length and inspect paws after walks.
Brush teeth with dog-safe toothpaste and arrange routine dental checks.
Check the skin while grooming, especially under dense feathering.
Avoid forceful detangling that pulls or irritates the skin.

training.difficulty: Moderate. Many individuals respond well to calm, consistent, reward-based training.
tips: Use small rewards, praise, and short training sessions.
Teach recall and loose-lead walking early.
Introduce grooming, ear handling, nail care, and tooth brushing gradually.
Reward calm behaviour and provide appropriate outlets for retrieving instincts.
Avoid harsh corrections; use clear cues and consistent routines.
Practise settling alone gradually and avoid leaving a young puppy alone for extended periods.
training.socialization: Introduce the dog gradually and positively to different people, friendly dogs, handling, household sounds, transport, and new environments. Teach children to interact gently and supervise interactions. Socialisation helps build familiarity and confidence but does not guarantee that every dog will enjoy every situation.

climates: Provide fresh water, shade, and a comfortable resting area in warm weather.
Avoid strenuous exercise during the hottest parts of the day.
Keep the coat clean and dry, and check for dampness or irritation beneath the feathering.
Adjust outdoor activity to weather, age, health, and the individual dog's tolerance.
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Individual tolerance varies. Build alone-time skills gradually, provide enrichment, and arrange companionship or suitable care when the dog would otherwise be alone for long periods.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced dog food appropriate for the dog's life stage, body condition, activity, and individual health needs.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Feed several appropriately sized meals according to age, food guidance, and veterinary advice.
feedingFrequency.adult: Many adults do well with two measured meals per day. Adjust portions to body condition, activity, and the food's calorie content.
feedingFrequency.senior: Choose a suitable diet and feeding schedule based on body condition, activity, dental health, and any veterinary recommendations.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure meals rather than feeding by guesswork. Monitor weight and body condition regularly, as excess weight can place additional strain on the joints and affect general health. Keep clean drinking water available, introduce diet changes gradually, and include treats in the daily calorie total. Seek veterinary advice if weight, appetite, digestion, or food tolerance changes persist.
considerations: Monitor body condition and avoid routine overfeeding.
Adjust portions for age, activity, neuter status, and individual metabolism.
Use suitable treat sizes during training and account for them in daily intake.
Do not use supplements or restrictive diets without an appropriate reason and veterinary advice.
Ask a veterinarian about persistent itching, ear problems, digestive signs, or changes in appetite.
nutrition.note: These are general feeding principles, not an individual calorie prescription. The correct diet and portion size depend on the dog's age, condition, activity, and health.

health.overview: Breed health programmes place particular emphasis on hip and eye evaluations. Breed-club health resources also discuss thyroid testing and other inherited-health considerations. Screening can help identify risks in breeding dogs, but it does not guarantee that a dog will remain free of disease. Health concerns should be assessed by a veterinarian rather than inferred from breed alone.
commonConditions: Ear inflammation or infection, a concern for dogs with long, pendulous ears that can retain moisture and debris
Hip dysplasia, for which screening is used in breeding programmes
Eye disorders, including cataracts and progressive retinal atrophy, which are among the conditions considered in eye-health screening
Thyroid dysfunction, which is discussed in breed-club health-monitoring resources
preventiveCare: Maintain routine veterinary examinations and preventive care appropriate to age and local risks.
Keep vaccinations and parasite prevention up to date under veterinary guidance.
Inspect the ears regularly and seek advice for redness, odour, discharge, pain, or repeated head-shaking.
Maintain a healthy body condition and provide regular, age-appropriate activity.
Arrange dental care and monitor the skin and coat during grooming.
Ask the breeder for documented health-screening results and relevant family history.
recommendedScreenings: Hip evaluation through a recognised programme such as OFA or an equivalent organisation
Eye examination by a qualified veterinary ophthalmologist, following current breed-club and veterinary recommendations
Ask a veterinarian or responsible breeder whether thyroid evaluation or additional tests are appropriate for the dog's family line
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste and arrange routine veterinary dental checks. Seek veterinary advice for persistent bad breath, oral pain, bleeding, or difficulty eating.
health.earCare: Inspect the ears frequently, especially after bathing or swimming. Use only a dog-safe ear-cleaning product recommended for the individual dog, and do not insert objects into the ear canal. Redness, odour, discharge, pain, or repeated head-shaking warrants veterinary assessment.
health.skinCare: Check the skin during brushing, particularly beneath the ears and long feathering. Persistent itching, sores, unusual hair loss, or recurring irritation should be assessed by a veterinarian.

People who want a companion for daily walks, play, and training
Owners who can keep the ears, teeth, nails, and skin in good condition
Families willing to teach children gentle handling and supervise interactions
Owners who can provide companionship and gradual alone-time training

funFacts: The name 'Cocker' is associated with the breed's historical use in hunting woodcock.
The American Cocker Spaniel developed separately from the English Cocker Spaniel.
The American breed is known for its abundant coat and distinctive rounded head.
Its coat includes both solid-colour and parti-colour varieties.
Although widely kept as a companion, it retains a sporting background.

faq.question: How big does an American Cocker Spaniel get?
faq.answer: The AKC standard gives ideal adult heights of about 15 inches for males and 14 inches for females, with defined height boundaries used in judging. The figures describe the breed standard rather than the size of every individual dog.

faq.question: How long does an American Cocker Spaniel live?
faq.answer: A commonly cited life-expectancy range is about 10–14 years. Individual lifespan varies with genetics, health, weight, preventive care, and environment.

faq.question: Does an American Cocker Spaniel need a lot of grooming?
faq.answer: Yes. The long, silky coat can tangle and mat, especially around the ears, chest, belly, and legs. Frequent brushing and regular trimming are important.

faq.question: Are American Cocker Spaniels good family dogs?
faq.answer: Many are affectionate and people-oriented, but temperament varies between individuals. Supervise interactions with children and teach gentle handling; no breed description can guarantee that every dog will suit every household.

faq.question: How much exercise does an American Cocker Spaniel need?
faq.answer: Provide daily walks, play, and mental enrichment. The amount of activity should be adapted to the dog's age, health, fitness, and whether it comes from a working or companion line.

faq.question: What health checks should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Ask for documented hip and eye screening results. Discuss the dog's family history and whether additional checks, such as thyroid testing, are appropriate. Screening reduces uncertainty but cannot guarantee a disease-free dog.

faq.question: How should I care for the ears?
faq.answer: Inspect the ears frequently and follow veterinary advice for cleaning. Persistent odour, redness, discharge, pain, or head-shaking can indicate a problem and should be checked by a veterinarian.

faq.question: Can an American Cocker Spaniel live in an apartment?
faq.answer: A dog's suitability depends on exercise, training, noise, companionship, and the individual living arrangement. This record does not assign a universal apartment-suitability rating.

overview.summary: A sleek, racy, and muscular American scent hound bred for speed, stamina, and hot-trailing quarry from dusk to dawn, combining relentless treeing drive and a resonant, carrying bawl with an amiable, pack-friendly nature at home.
overview.description: The American English Coonhound—widely known among hunters simply as the English Coonhound, Redtick Coonhound, or 'English dog'—is a balanced, athletic scent hound built for both speed and all-night endurance. Built on a square to slightly off-square frame with a deep chest reaching the elbows, strong straight forelegs, well-sprung ribs, a broad muscular loin, and catlike well-padded feet, it carries a hard, protective medium-length coat most famously seen in red-and-white ticked ('redtick'), blue-and-white ticked, or tricoloured-with-ticking patterns. Its broad, slightly domed head features a prominent stop, a square muzzle with flews covering the lower jaw in profile, dark-brown eyes set wide apart, and low-set, soft, fine-textured ears that reach nearly to the tip of the nose when drawn forward. In the woods, it is a fast, hot-trailing hunter that drives raccoons and other game into trees and holds them there with a loud, melodious bay or bawl; indoors, a well-exercised hound is sweet-tempered, mellow, and sociable with people and other dogs. Because of its powerful scent drive, tree-climbing agility, and carrying voice, prospective owners must provide a securely fenced yard, leashed or enclosed exercise, patient reward-based training, and a living setting tolerant of vocalisation.
overview.history: Like most American coonhounds (apart from the German-descended Plott Hound), the American English Coonhound descends from English Foxhounds and related British hounds imported to the North American colonies in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Early foundation imports included Robert Brooke's pack brought to Maryland in 1650, Dr. Thomas Walker's hounds imported to Virginia in 1742, and English foxhounds imported by George Washington in 1770. Known in colonial times as 'Virginia Hounds', these dogs were selectively bred by American frontiersmen and Southern hunters to work rougher, more open terrain and to pursue foxes by day and tree-climbing raccoons, opossums, cougars, and bears at night. First formally registered in 1905 under the name English Fox and Coonhound, the population originally encompassed all three major ticked and tricoloured strains until breeders of the Treeing Walker Coonhound broke away as a separate breed in 1945, followed by the Bluetick Coonhound in 1946. Renowned in field competitions—where an English hound named 'Bones', owned by Colonel Leon Robinson, won the inaugural Leafy Oak National Coonhound Field Trial in 1927—the breed entered the Foundation Stock Service in 1995 and achieved full recognition in 2011 (as the 171st recognized breed) under the name American English Coonhound to distinguish it clearly from British foxhounds, making its Westminster debut in 2012.
overview.originalPurpose: Hot-trailing and treeing raccoons by night and running foxes by day across rough terrain, as well as baying larger quarry such as bear and cougar until the hunter arrives.
currentRoles: Night hunts ('nite hunts'), field trials, water races, and lawful coon or big-game hunting
Scent work, nose work, tracking, and trailing competitions
Agility, lure coursing (including FastCAT), dock diving, and canine sports
Active running, hiking, and biking partner (on leash or in secure enclosures)
Affectionate family companion in an active home prepared for its exercise and vocalisation needs

physical.coatType: Hard, dense, protective hound coat of medium length lying close to a lean, muscular frame.
physical.coatLength: Short to medium
coatColors: Red and white ticked (redtick — the most iconic pattern)
Tri-coloured with ticking (black, white, and tan with ticking)

White and lemon (permitted in traditional hunting standards; conformation standards disqualify solid coat colours with less than 10% ticking, tri-coloured coats without ticking, any brindle markings, or albinism)
physical.sheddingLevel: Low to moderate; sheds year-round with heavier seasonal shedding in spring and autumn, easily managed with weekly brushing.
distinctiveFeatures: Strong yet racy, well-conditioned athletic build that is square to slightly off-square (body length from breastbone to rear of thigh equal to or slightly greater than height at the withers, with leg length from elbow to ground approximately half the withers height)

Deep chest reaching to the elbows with well-sprung ribs tapering to the floating ribs, a strong back sloping slightly from withers to hips, a broad muscular loin, and a tight, smooth underline with moderate tuck-up

Broad head of moderate length with a very slightly domed skull, prominent stop forming a right angle with the upper line of the square muzzle, parallel skull and foreface planes, a black nose with well-opened nostrils, and flews covering the lower jaw in profile
Low-set, fine-textured, soft hanging ears that reach nearly to the tip of the nose when drawn forward
Wide-set, dark-brown eyes with tight-fitting lids conveying a kind, pleading hound expression
High- to moderately set, medium-length tail carried gaily with a slight brush (never hooked over the back, plumed, or rat-tailed) that moves side to side at the trot
Straight, well-boned forelegs, balanced hindquarters with muscular thighs, and round, catlike feet set directly under the legs with well-arched toes, deep pads, and strong nails

Adult withers height of 61 to 66 cm (24 to 26 inches) for males and 58.4 to 63.5 cm (23 to 25 inches) for females in primary conformation standards—or 55.9 to 68.6 cm (22 to 27 inches) for males and 53.3 to 63.5 cm (21 to 25 inches) for females in traditional hunting-registry standards—with a typical adult weight of 20.4 to 29.5 kg (45 to 65 pounds; 40 to 70 pounds across veterinary guides)

traits: Pleasant, sweet-tempered, and mellow indoors when exercise needs are met
Sociable, amiable, and pack-oriented with both people and other dogs
High-spirited, tireless, and tenacious on a hot scent trail
Alert and vocal, with a resonant, carrying hound bawl and bay
Confident, agile, and courageous in the field (even capable of climbing into angled trees after quarry)
Independent-minded and stubborn when distracted by wildlife or fresh scent
Attentive watchdog that announces approaching strangers, though too friendly to serve as an aggressive guard dog

exercise.level: Very high. Bred to hunt from dusk to dawn across rough country, this athletic hound requires vigorous daily physical workouts and regular scent-based mental stimulation.
activities: Long, brisk daily leashed walks, trail hikes, jogging, or running alongside a bike
Free running and ball-chasing inside a securely fenced yard
Scent-work games, nose work, tracking, and trailing exercises
Field trials, night hunts ('nite hunts'), water races, and lawful hunting work
Canine sports such as agility, lure coursing, and dock diving or swimming

grooming.brushing: Brush once or twice a week with a rubber grooming mitt or short-hair deshedding tool to remove loose hairs (which are hard and can stick to upholstery) and distribute natural skin oils down the hair shaft for a healthy shine; increase brushing during spring and autumn sheds.
grooming.bathing: Bathe every four to six weeks—or after muddy woodland runs—using a mild, dog-safe shampoo to keep the coat and skin clean and minimize hound odour.
notes: Inspect and gently clean the long, low-hanging ears every week with a veterinarian-recommended ear cleanser to remove excess wax, moisture, and debris.
Dry the ear canals thoroughly after swimming, water races, or bathing.
Trim the strong nails about once a month if they do not wear down naturally.
Check the coat, skin, eyes, and catlike paw pads after field or trail outings for ticks, fleas, burrs, thorns, cuts, or dust irritation.
Brush the teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging for novice owners. While amiable and intelligent at home, the breed's intense scent drive, stubbornness on a trail, and ringing voice require patient, consistent, firm-yet-positive leadership.
tips: Begin early socialization and reward-based training in puppyhood to prevent possessive habits over food or toys.
Keep training sessions short, upbeat, and varied, pairing food rewards and praise with mental and physical outlets.
Never allow an American English Coonhound off-leash in an unfenced or uncontrolled area, as its nose will override recall commands once it strikes a fresh trail.
Ensure backyard fencing is tall, secure, and escape-proof—remembering that these agile hounds are famous for climbing trees and scaling barriers when pursuing quarry.
Provide structured nose-work games and tracking outlets so the dog's natural trailing instincts are satisfied constructively.
Establish household routines early to manage the breed's loud, carrying bawl around neighbours.
training.socialization: Expose puppies early and positively to a wide variety of people, children, other dogs, sights, and sounds, and supervise interactions with cats and small household pets, which can trigger the breed's strong chasing instinct.

climates: Temperate climates
Warm climates with shade, abundant fresh water, and careful monitoring against overheating during summer runs (as high-drive hounds rarely quit on their own)
Cool climates when provided with warm indoor living quarters
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate. As a pack-oriented hound that craves human or canine companionship, an under-exercised dog left isolated for long periods can become bored, frustrated, destructive, and very vocal.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced, high-quality commercial or veterinarian-approved home-prepared diet formulated for the dog's life stage (puppy, adult, or senior) and actual workload.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three to four smaller measured meals per day to support steady growth.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals per day (morning and evening), avoiding a single large daily meal.

nutrition.guidelines: Adjust daily caloric intake to match the dog's age, weight, and real-world activity—an active hunting or running hound requires substantially more calories than a retired or companion dog, and adult coonhounds are prone to gaining excess weight as they age. To help reduce the risk of gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat), divide the daily ration into two or more smaller meals, use a slow-feeder bowl if the dog gulps food, avoid elevated food bowls unless directed by a veterinarian, and restrict vigorous exercise immediately before and after eating. Keep clean, fresh water available at all times.
considerations: Monitor body condition closely and limit high-calorie training treats, as coonhounds easily become overweight when field workload drops.
Feed two smaller daily meals for adults (and three to four for puppies), use slow-feeder bowls, avoid raised bowls, and rest before and after meals to lower bloat (GDV) risk.
Ask your veterinarian whether prophylactic gastropexy ('stomach tacking' surgery) is appropriate for your individual dog.
Watch carefully for dehydration and overheating during warm-weather hunting or running.
Consult a veterinarian before adding joint or coat supplements such as glucosamine, chondroitin, or omega-3 fatty acids.
nutrition.note: While veterinary care guides recommend three to four daily meals for puppies and two daily meals for adults, exact portion sizes and senior meal schedules should be tailored with a veterinarian based on the individual dog's body condition and workload.

health.overview: Bred primarily as a functional, hard-working field hound, the American English Coonhound is generally a hardy breed with a typical lifespan of 11 to 12 years and no formal mandatory national health-testing panel currently established. However, responsible breeders and veterinary guides identify several orthopaedic, ophthalmic, endocrine, otic, and emergency conditions to monitor. These include hip dysplasia, elbow dysplasia, patellar luxation, progressive retinal atrophy (PRA), cataracts, hypothyroidism, recurrent ear infections (otitis externa) associated with long pendulous ears, and life-threatening gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat / GDV) in deep-chested individuals. In addition, hard-charging working hounds require watchful protection against summer overheating and field injuries (such as ticks, burrs, and pad cuts). Conformation standards also disqualify overshot or undershot bites, unilateral or bilateral cryptorchidism, albinism, congenital deafness, and blindness.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia and elbow dysplasia — developmental joint malformations that can cause lameness and osteoarthritis in active hounds; responsible breeders screen breeding stock even though no formal national test mandate is currently published.
Patellar luxation — intermittent dislocation of the kneecap reported in veterinary breed profiles.
Ophthalmic disorders (progressive retinal atrophy [PRA] and cataracts) — inherited or age-related eye conditions that can impair night vision and gradually lead to vision loss.

Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat) — a sudden, life-threatening emergency in large, deep-chested dogs in which the stomach distends with gas and twists on its axis; requires immediate emergency veterinary intervention.
Otitis externa (ear canal infections) — long, low-hanging ears restrict airflow and trap moisture, wax, and woodland debris, predisposing the ear canals to bacterial and yeast overgrowth.
Hypothyroidism — insufficient thyroid hormone production occasionally seen in the breed, causing weight gain, lethargy, dry skin, or coat thinning and managed with daily hormone replacement.
Exertional overheating (heatstroke) and field trauma — high hunting drive can cause hounds to run past exhaustion in warm weather, and brush work exposes them to ticks, thorns, and paw-pad cuts.
preventiveCare: Check and gently clean the long hanging ears every week—and after swimming or wet weather—using a veterinarian-recommended ear cleanser to prevent otitis externa.

Learn the emergency warning signs of bloat (GDV)—distended abdomen, unproductive retching, restlessness, excessive drooling, or collapse—and feed divided meals without vigorous exercise immediately before or after eating.
Monitor body weight and calorie intake throughout adulthood so excess weight does not overload the hips, elbows, and stifles.
Watch closely for signs of overheating during summer exercise or hunting, providing frequent shade and water breaks because driven hounds rarely stop on their own.
Inspect the coat, skin, eyes, and feet after every woodland or trail outing for ticks, fleas, burrs, awns, and cuts.
Discuss family health history and optional orthopaedic, ophthalmic, and thyroid evaluations with the breeder and your veterinarian.
recommendedScreenings: No formal mandatory national pre-breeding health test panel is currently established for the breed.
Hip and elbow radiographic evaluations (voluntarily performed by responsible breeders to screen for hip and elbow dysplasia).
Ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (to screen for progressive retinal atrophy and cataracts).
Routine veterinary wellness assessments, including patellar palpation, bite/dentition and testicular checks, and thyroid blood testing if clinical signs arise.
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste and schedule periodic veterinary oral examinations and professional cleanings. Conformation standards require a close-fitting scissors bite (with an even/level bite also acceptable in traditional hunting standards, while overshot or undershot bites are disqualifications).
health.earCare: Inspect the long, soft, low-hung ears at least once a week for redness, foul odour, head-shaking, or excess wax and debris. Clean gently with a veterinarian-approved ear cleanser and dry thoroughly after baths or swimming.
health.skinCare: Brush the short, hard coat weekly with a rubber grooming mitt to distribute natural skin oils, bathe every four to six weeks or when dirty from the woods, and check the skin, paw pads, and nails after outdoor runs for ticks, fleas, cuts, or rashes.

idealFor: Active runners, hikers, bikers, and outdoor enthusiasts who want an energetic, pack-oriented companion
Coon hunters, field-trial competitors, and handlers interested in scent work, tracking, or canine sports
Families with gentle, respectful children and a securely fenced yard in a rural or low-density setting
Experienced dog owners comfortable with a loud, ringing hound voice and patient, consistent training
Multi-dog households where the hound can enjoy canine pack companionship
notIdealFor: Apartment dwellers, condominium residents, or close urban neighbourhoods with noise-sensitive neighbours
First-time or sedentary dog owners seeking a quiet, low-energy indoor pet
Handlers who expect reliable off-leash recall in unfenced areas around wildlife or scent trails
Households with unsupervised cats, rabbits, or small furry pets that may trigger strong prey drive
Homes where the dog would be left isolated alone for long workdays without exercise

funFacts: Among experienced coon hunters in the American South, the breed is rarely called by its full four-word name—aficionados simply call them 'English dogs' or 'Redtick Coonhounds'.

The everyday English idiom 'barking up the wrong tree' comes directly from night hunting with coonhounds, when a hound bays at the base of an empty tree after a raccoon has leapt to a neighbouring branch.
American English Coonhounds are remarkably agile and are known for their ability to scramble partway up angled tree trunks in pursuit of a treed raccoon.

In 1927, an English Coonhound named 'Bones', owned by Colonel Leon Robinson of Dunkirk, Ohio, won the inaugural Leafy Oak National Coonhound Field Trial—the most famous early coonhound competition in North America.

Both the Treeing Walker Coonhound and the Bluetick Coonhound were originally registered as colour varieties within the English Coonhound population before separating into independent breeds in 1945 and 1946.

To distinguish the breed visually from its cousins—the Bluetick Coonhound and the clear-coated Treeing Walker Coonhound—conformation rules disqualify solid-coloured dogs with less than 10% ticking as well as tricoloured dogs that lack ticking.

A rescue American English Coonhound named Maddie became a viral photography sensation and New York Times bestselling book star in photographer Theron Humphrey's project 'Maddie on Things', balancing calmly on fire hydrants, bicycles, and fence posts across the United States.

faq.question: Why is the breed called both the American English Coonhound and the Redtick Coonhound?
faq.answer: Historically registered in 1905 as the English Fox and Coonhound and later known simply as the English Coonhound (or 'English dog'), the breed had 'American' added to its name upon national recognition in 2011 to clarify that it was developed in the United States rather than Britain. Because red-and-white ticking is its most common and iconic coat pattern, it is also widely nicknamed the Redtick Coonhound.

faq.question: How large does an American English Coonhound get?
faq.answer: Primary conformation standards specify a withers height of 24 to 26 inches (61 to 66 cm) for males and 23 to 25 inches (58.4 to 63.5 cm) for females, while traditional hunting-registry standards allow a slightly broader range of 22 to 27 inches (55.9 to 68.6 cm) for males and 21 to 25 inches (53.3 to 63.5 cm) for females. Adult weight is typically 45 to 65 pounds (20.4 to 29.5 kg), with some veterinary guides noting a range of 40 to 70 pounds in proportion to height.

faq.question: What coat colours and patterns are accepted, and which are disqualified?
faq.answer: Accepted patterns are red and white ticked ('redtick'), blue and white ticked ('bluetick'), tri-coloured with ticking, red and white, and white and black, with white and lemon also permitted in traditional hunting standards. Conformation standards disqualify any brindle markings, albinism, tri-coloured coats without ticking, and solid-coloured coats with less than 10% ticking.

faq.question: How does an American English Coonhound differ from a Bluetick or Treeing Walker Coonhound?
faq.answer: All three descended from the same colonial English Foxhound stock, and both the Treeing Walker (1945) and Bluetick (1946) split from the English Coonhound. Compared with the heavier-boned, cold-trailing Bluetick Coonhound, the American English Coonhound has a leaner, racier build bred for speed on 'hot' (fresh) trails and requires at least 10% ticking if solid-coloured. Compared with the tricoloured Treeing Walker Coonhound—whose white areas are clear and unticked—a tricoloured American English Coonhound must display distinct ticking.

faq.question: How long does an American English Coonhound live?
faq.answer: The typical life expectancy is 11 to 12 years.

faq.question: Is the American English Coonhound a good apartment dog or guard dog?
faq.answer: It is poorly suited to apartment living because of its high daily exercise needs and loud, carrying bay or bawl. While its resonant voice makes it an attentive watchdog that will announce anyone approaching the property, its friendly, sociable nature with people makes it too welcoming to serve as an aggressive guard dog.

faq.question: Can an American English Coonhound be trusted off leash or with small pets?
faq.answer: No. Once its sensitive nose locks onto a fresh wildlife trail, its hunting instinct overrides recall commands. Outside of lawful hunting, the dog should always be exercised on a sturdy leash or inside a securely fenced yard (built high and secure enough to deter climbing), and interactions with cats or small furry pets should be closely supervised.

faq.question: What health concerns and screenings should prospective owners know about?
faq.answer: Although no formal mandatory national health-testing list is currently published for the breed, responsible breeders and veterinarians monitor hip dysplasia, elbow dysplasia, patellar luxation, progressive retinal atrophy (PRA), cataracts, hypothyroidism, recurrent ear infections, summer overheating, and life-threatening bloat (gastric dilatation-volvulus). Prospective buyers should ask breeders about hip, elbow, and eye clearances in the parent dogs.

overview.summary: A sturdy, compact medium-sized northern French scent hound of classic briquet build, prized for its cold-trailing nose on hare, roe deer, and wild boar, its nearly flat hanging ears, and its dark-fawn tricolour coat.
overview.description: The Artois Hound (Chien d'Artois, historically called the Picard or Briquet d'Artois) is a well-constructed, muscular, medium-sized French pack hound built for methodical stamina and scenting precision rather than sheer speed. Standing 53 to 58 cm at the withers (with a ±1 cm tolerance) and weighing 28 to 30 kg on average, it embodies the compact, nearly square 'briquet' format (withers height to body length between 10:10 and 10:11). Its broad, strong, rounded skull with a flattened top and accentuated stop is slightly longer than its straight muzzle (roughly a 10:8 skull-to-muzzle ratio), whose overhanging upper lips give the tip of the foreface a square profile. Unlike Anglo-French hounds with narrower skulls and lower-set curled ears, the Artois Hound is distinguished by wide-set round dark brown eyes with a gentle, melancholic expression and broad, fairly thick, almost flat ears set at eye level and reaching the base of the black nose. Its short, thick, flat coat is always dark-fawn tricolour with a hare- or badger-like shading, a mantle or large patches, and a fawn head sometimes overlaid with black. Renowned as a meticulous 'closer' (rapprocheur) capable of puzzling out cold trails up to six hours old and giving voice in a high-pitched, melodious cry, it is a peaceful, gregarious pack mate and an affectionate, calm companion off duty.
overview.history: Originating in the historic northern French provinces of Artois and Picardy as a smaller descendant of the black Saint-Hubert hound, hounds of Artois are recorded as early as 1394 and 1410 ('valets de chiens d'Artois') in the hunting accounts of the Dukes of Burgundy Philip the Bold and John the Fearless, and in a 1431 chronicle of King Henry VI of England's coronation entry into Paris. Highly prized during the reigns of Henry IV and Louis XIII (who hunted hare, fox, and wild boar with his 'petits chiens d'Artois' between 1608 and 1610, and whose father received a prized pack from Prince Charles-Alexandre de Croÿ in 1609), the breed—also known as the Chien Picard—was celebrated by Jean de Sacquépée, seigneur de Sélincourt, in Le Parfait Chasseur (1683) for trailing a hare that had passed an hour earlier in dry weather. In Manuel de Vénerie Française (1890), Count Jean-Emmanuel Le Couteulx de Canteleu noted that although pure specimens had grown scarce through crossbreeding with Norman and English hounds, the Artois remained one of the finest hare hounds and placed examples in the Paris Jardin d'Acclimatation. Around 1888, Picardy breeder Ernest Levoir at the Château du Plouy in Domqueur (Somme) founded the Rallye-Scardon pack (motto: 'Chasse droit, Briquet d'Artois') to restore the ancestral type without English or heavy Norman blood, while Auguste and Albert Mallart in Barly (Pas-de-Calais) bred a competing line until 1932. In 1930, French hunting authorities dropped the term 'Briquet' in favour of 'Chien d'Artois', and the breed received definitive international recognition on 18 October 1963. Nearly extinct after the Second World War, the breed was rescued in the early 1970s by farmer-hunter André Audréchy of Buigny-lès-Gamaches in the Somme ('du Parc à Biches' kennel), joined around 1975 by Joseph Mancini in the Var and breeder Josette Pilat in Oise ('La Meute Saint-Louis' kennel and 'Piqu'Artois Saint-Louis' pack), leading to the modern standard published in July–November 1996.
overview.originalPurpose: Scent hunting with the gun (chasse à tir) and in small packs (petite vénerie) of 6 to 8 hounds, specializing in cold-trailing and outwitting hare on open plains as well as driving roe deer in woods and flushing or holding wild boar in thickets.
currentRoles: Shooting-pack scent hound (chasse à tir) and small-pack hound (petite vénerie) for wild boar, hare, and roe deer
Cold-trail finder ('rapprocheur') and working-hound field-trial competitor
Active rural companion for hunting households with a spacious enclosure or kennel

physical.coatType: Short, thick, dense, and fairly flat single coat over fairly thick, moderately loose skin, with a few longer, coarser, slightly off-standing hairs ('épiée' / like ears of grain) along the underside of the tail toward the tip.
physical.coatLength: Short
coatColors: Dark-fawn tricolour (fawn, black, and white) with a hare-toned or badger-toned ('poil de lièvre ou de blaireau') shading, carried as a mantle (blanket) or large patches

Fawn head, sometimes with a black overlay ('charbonnée'; bicolour white-and-orange coats without black/badger hair are not accepted, and invasive ticking or mottling on the white areas is a disqualifying fault)
physical.sheddingLevel: Low to moderate; weekly brushing removes dead hairs and field debris.
physical.droolingLevel: Low (despite well-developed upper lips that give the muzzle tip a square profile, the skin is only moderately loose with very little throat dewlap).
distinctiveFeatures: Compact, muscular, nearly square 'briquet' outline (withers height to body length between 10:10 and 10:11, and chest depth equal to half the withers height) built for steady endurance rather than high speed
Strong, broad, rather short skull rounded at the sides and flattened on top (skull width to head length ~5:9) with an inconspicuous occipital peak and an accentuated stop

Straight, moderately elongated muzzle slightly shorter than the skull (muzzle-to-skull ratio ~8:10), with overhanging upper lips giving the muzzle tip a distinct square profile, clean cheeks, a strong black nose with wide nostrils, and a square-set scissor bite
Round, dark brown eyes set well apart and level with the head surface with concealed lower-lid conjunctiva, conveying a soft, melancholic expression
Broad, somewhat thick, almost flat hanging ears set at eye level with rounded tips, reaching the beginning of the nose (a key hallmark distinguishing it from Anglo-French hounds)
Moderately long, powerful neck with very little dewlap, broad well-supported back, slightly arched loin, deep chest reaching the elbows with well-sprung ribs, and full flanks

Strong, fairly long tail carried sickle-fashion (never falling forward over the back) and furnished toward the tip with slightly longer, coarser off-standing hairs like ears of grain ('épiée' / 'espiée')
Strong, vertical, round-boned limbs ending in tight, slightly elongated 'cat-like' feet with tough, compact black pads, and an even, effortless gait

Withers height of 53 to 58 cm with a ±1 cm tolerance (52–59 cm; French breed commentary favours 52–56 cm in males and 48–53 cm in females to preserve true briquet proportions) and average adult weight of 28 to 30 kg across both sexes

traits: Vigorous, hardy, and tireless in the field across plains, woods, and thickets
Exceptionally fine nose ('rapprocheur') capable of unravelling cold trails up to six hours old
Gregarious, peaceful, and non-quarrelsome in a pack (entering the pack from 6 months of age and coexisting peacefully with same-sex hounds)
Balanced, gentle, and affectionate with its handler, actively seeking petting and cuddles
More biddable, cooperative, and easy to lead than many other scent hounds
High-pitched, melodious hunting voice audible from afar (often preceded by soft 'meowing' whimpers when working a cold trail), yet quiet and rarely a nuisance barker off duty
Dislikes being tied or chained and requires space and regular field or outdoor exercise
Never aggressive or timid (aggression or shyness is a disqualifying fault)

exercise.level: High. Bred as an all-terrain endurance hound, it needs long daily country walks or runs, spacious enclosed turnout, and regular scent-tracking or hunting work—and must never be kept tied up.
activities: Small-pack or shooting-party scent hunting (chasse à tir / petite vénerie) on hare, wild boar, or roe deer
Cold-trail tracking, blood trailing, and structured nose-work games
Long, brisk daily country walks or hikes (ideally twice daily) on a leash or long line
Free movement and social interaction with packmates in a spacious, securely fenced rural enclosure
Recall, horn/whistle conditioning, and handler-focus exercises

grooming.brushing: Brush once or twice a week with a rubber hound mitt or soft bristle brush to remove dead hair, dust, and plant debris and keep the short, thick coat clean.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only when dirty or malodorous using a mild, dog-safe shampoo, rinsing thoroughly and drying the coat and hanging ears completely afterward.
notes: Inspect the long, broad, nearly flat hanging ears systematically after every outing in woods or brambles to remove burrs, grass awns, or ticks and check for moisture, redness, or odour.
Examine the short coat, skin, and tough black paw pads after field work for thorns, cuts, or external parasites.
Trim the nails whenever natural wear does not keep them short.
Brush the teeth frequently with dog-specific toothpaste to prevent tartar accumulation.

training.difficulty: Moderate for experienced hound handlers. National breed guidance notes that the Artois Hound is intelligent, gentle, and more obedient and easier to lead than many other scent hounds, though dominant individuals require a 'firm hand in a velvet glove' and early recall training.
tips: Begin recall conditioning and basic obedience early in puppyhood, combining calm firmness with kindness ('an iron hand in a velvet glove') so the dog's natural willingness to please develops.
For working hounds, gentle scent-search initiation can begin at 4 to 5 months of age in a safely enclosed brushy paddock, and young hounds can integrate into an adult pack from 6 months of age.
Never tether or chain an Artois Hound, and always use a leash or secure fencing in open areas where a fresh game trail can override recall.
Provide structured olfactory enrichment—such as laid scent trails or tracking games—if the dog is not actively hunted.
training.socialization: Bred to live and hunt harmoniously in packs—including peacefully with hounds of the same sex—the Artois Hound is naturally dog-sociable. Introduce puppies early and positively to household routines, varied people, children, handling, and rural environments, while supervising around small non-canine pets due to its strong hunting instinct.

livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low when isolated alone. As a deeply gregarious pack hound that loves living with fellow hounds and stays closely attached to its owner, the Artois Hound thrives in a spacious rural enclosure with packmates or attentive human company and does poorly if isolated or tied up.

nutrition.dietType: Complete and balanced, high-quality commercial diet (or a veterinarian-supplemented home-prepared ration with added calcium and vitamins) tailored to life stage, body condition, and seasonal hunting workload.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Two substantial measured meals daily until the dog finishes growing at around 12 months of age.

nutrition.guidelines: Feed a nutritionally complete, balanced industrial diet suited to growth and adult maintenance—or, if feeding a traditional home-prepared ration, supplement with appropriate vitamins and calcium under veterinary guidance. Because the Artois Hound continues growing until about 12 months of age, provide two substantial measured meals per day throughout its first year. In adulthood, increase daily rations during active hunting seasons to match higher energy expenditure, then return to maintenance portions during the off-season so the dog stays lean and muscular around 28 to 30 kg. Keep clean, fresh water available at all times.
considerations: Provide two substantial measured meals daily during the growth period up to 12 months of age.
If using a home-prepared (ménagère) diet rather than complete commercial food, add veterinary-recommended vitamin and calcium supplementation.
Increase energy intake during active hunting seasons and reduce portions in the off-season to prevent excess weight.
Allow rest before and after meals rather than feeding immediately before or after intense field runs.
Monitor body condition regularly so the flanks remain full without obesity.
nutrition.note: While two substantial meals daily during the first year of growth are recommended for puppies, adult and senior meal frequencies and exact calorie targets should be individualized with a veterinarian.

health.overview: A hardy, rustic, and solid working hound (with typical longevity estimates ranging from 10 to 13 or 12 to 14 years), the Artois Hound has no documented breed-specific hereditary disease prevalence profile or mandatory genetic testing panel. Conformation and breeding rules mandate that only functionally and clinically healthy dogs with breed-typical morphology be used for reproduction, and explicitly disqualify any dog exhibiting a detectable disabling hereditary defect, anatomical anomaly, frail limbs, overshot or undershot jaw (prognathism), very light eyes, or behavioural abnormality. As with other active, drop-eared pack hounds worked across fields, woods, and brambles, everyday veterinary care centres on post-outing ear canal hygiene, parasite and infectious-disease prevention, dental care, and field-injury checks.
preventiveCare: Verify that breeding stock is functionally and clinically healthy, free of disqualifying hereditary or anatomical defects, and has a normal scissor bite.
Inspect the long, broad hanging ears, short coat, and black paw pads after every outing in woods, fields, or thickets to remove ticks, grass awns, burrs, or thorns and prevent otitis externa.
Keep vaccinations, deworming, and external parasite prevention strictly up to date—especially for hounds living in packs or working in wildlife areas.
Maintain a lean, athletic body weight (typically 28–30 kg) by adjusting food intake between hunting and rest seasons.
Brush the teeth frequently with dog-safe toothpaste and schedule routine veterinary wellness and oral examinations.
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth frequently with dog-specific toothpaste and have the mouth examined at routine veterinary visits. Conformation rules require a regular scissor bite with the upper incisors closely overlapping the lower incisors and set squarely in the jaws, while overshot or undershot jaws (prognathism) are disqualifying faults.
health.earCare: Inspect the broad, nearly flat hanging ears after every field outing and during weekly brushing for plant debris, parasites, excess wax, redness, or foul odour. Clean only as advised by a veterinarian and dry the ears thoroughly after wet weather.
health.skinCare: Examine the short, dense tricolour coat, fairly thick skin, and compact black paw pads during weekly brushing and after runs through brambles or forest cover for scratches, ticks, burrs, or interdigital foreign bodies.
