funFacts: Records of 'valets de chiens d'Artois' appear as early as 1394 and 1410 in the hunting accounts of the Dukes of Burgundy (Philip the Bold and John the Fearless), and in 1431 a live stag hunt with Artois hounds was staged along the streets of Paris during the coronation entry of young King Henry VI of England.

Formerly called the Picard or Chien Picard, the breed was a favourite of Kings Henry IV and Louis XIII; in 1683, royal huntsman Jean de Sacquépée, seigneur de Sélincourt, marvelled at seeing these hounds puzzle out the trail of a hare that had passed an hour earlier in dry weather.

Around 1888, Picardy breeder Ernest Levoir established the famous 'Rallye-Scardon' pack at the Château du Plouy in the Somme under the rhyming French motto 'Chasse droit, Briquet d'Artois' ('Hunt straight, Briquet of Artois').

Feared extinct after the Second World War, the breed was rescued in the 1970s by Somme farmer André Audréchy (in the very same Gamaches area where seventeenth-century authors had praised Picard hounds), joined by Joseph Mancini and Josette Pilat.

Renowned as a cold-trail specialist ('rapprocheur') able to pick up trails up to six hours old, an Artois Hound often emits high-pitched whimpers—humourously described by breeder Josette Pilat as 'meowing' ('miauler')—when working a cold scent before bursting into full, resonant voice once the trail is hot.

A matched pack of just six to eight tricolour Artois Hounds is traditionally considered sufficient to delight the most demanding huntmaster, and although bred for hare, roughly three-quarters of working Artois Hounds in France today are used on wild boar.

faq.question: Where does the Artois Hound come from, and what are its historical names?
faq.answer: The Artois Hound (officially the Chien d'Artois) originates from the Artois and Picardy regions of northern France. Historically, it was also known as the Picard, Chien Picard, and—until French hunting authorities dropped the term 'Briquet' in 1930—the Briquet d'Artois.

faq.question: What was the Artois Hound bred to do, and how is it used today?
faq.answer: It was bred as a medium-sized 'briquet' scent hound for hunting with the gun (chasse à tir) and in small packs (petite vénerie) of six to eight hounds. Prized for its fine nose and steady endurance as a cold-trail finder ('rapprocheur' capable of following trails up to six hours old), it outwits hare on open plains, drives roe deer through open woods, and flushes or holds wild boar in thickets. Today, roughly three-quarters of working Artois Hounds in France hunt wild boar, and the breed is also appreciated in Greece, Italy, and Spain for hare hunting.

faq.question: How large is an adult Artois Hound?
faq.answer: Conformation rules specify a withers height of 53 to 58 cm (with a ±1 cm tolerance, or 52 to 59 cm) and an average weight of 28 to 30 kg for both males and females. In France, an ideal working height of 52 to 56 cm for males and 48 to 53 cm for females is favoured to preserve the breed's compact, nearly square 'briquet' proportions.

faq.question: How can you tell an Artois Hound apart from an Anglo-Français de Petite Vénerie?
faq.answer: The Artois Hound is more compact and cobby, with a broader, rounded skull flattened on top, a muzzle slightly shorter than the skull (about an 8:10 ratio) squared off at the tip by overhanging upper lips, and broad, thick, almost flat ears set at eye level. By contrast, the Anglo-Français de Petite Vénerie has a narrower skull equal in length to the muzzle (1:1), drier lips, and lower-set, thinner, slightly curled ears.

faq.question: What coat colours are accepted in the Artois Hound?
faq.answer: The short, thick, flat coat must always be dark-fawn tricolour (fawn, black, and white) with a hare-toned or badger-toned shading, carried as a mantle or large patches, with a fawn head that is sometimes overlaid with black ('charbonnée'). Bicolour white-and-orange coats without black/badger hair are not accepted, and heavy ticking or mottling on the white areas is a disqualifying fault.

faq.question: Is the Artois Hound suitable for city or apartment living?
faq.answer: No. This country hunting hound is not suited to urban or apartment living, dislikes confined spaces, and must never be kept tied up. It needs a rural home with a large, securely fenced enclosure or kennel, ideally with canine companions, and long daily country outings.

faq.question: What is the Artois Hound's temperament like with people and other dogs?
faq.answer: Off the hunting field, the Artois Hound is calm, gentle, affectionate, and fond of cuddles, and barks very little at home. It is more obedient and easier to lead than many other scent hounds—making it popular even with novice hare hunters—and is exceptionally sociable and non-quarrelsome with other dogs, integrating into packs from 6 months of age and living peacefully with same-sex kennelmates.

faq.question: Does the Artois Hound have known hereditary diseases or a fixed lifespan?
faq.answer: A breed-specific list of hereditary diseases and a single definitive lifespan range have not been established (so those structured fields are kept empty or null), though typical longevity estimates in France range from 10 to 13 or 12 to 14 years. Breeding rules disqualify any dog with a detectable disabling hereditary defect, anatomical anomaly, or bite malocclusion, and routine care focuses on ear checks after field outings, dental hygiene, parasite prevention, and balanced nutrition.

overview.summary: The Petit Basset Griffon Vendéen is a small, sturdy French scent hound developed to follow rabbits and other small game through rough, thorny country. It combines an energetic, sociable manner with a rough coat, short legs, a longish body, and a keen nose.
overview.description: Often called a PBGV, this breed is built for persistent scent work rather than speed. Its compact frame, strong legs, weather-resistant rough coat, expressive eyebrows and beard, and mobile tail suit outdoor work in dense undergrowth. At home, many PBGVs are cheerful and people-oriented, but their hunting instincts, curiosity, independence, and tendency to use their voice can make them demanding companions. They generally benefit from daily exercise, scent-based activities, patient reward-based training, secure outdoor spaces, and regular coat and ear checks. Individual temperament and health vary; breed descriptions are not guarantees about a particular dog.
overview.history: The breed developed in the Vendée area of western France as a small scent hound able to work over difficult terrain while pursuing rabbits and other small game. It was historically grouped with the larger Grand Basset Griffon Vendéen before a separate standard and more distinct type were developed. Its name describes its size, low-set build, rough coat, and Vendéen origin. The breed is now kept as a companion as well as being used in hunting and dog activities.

health.overview: The breed is generally described as robust, but health information from its parent club reports concerns that owners and breeders should discuss with a veterinarian. These include primary open-angle glaucoma, other eye abnormalities, hip dysplasia, hypothyroidism, epilepsy, and patellar luxation. A breed-level list does not establish how likely an individual dog is to develop any condition, and the available sources do not support ranking these conditions by prevalence.

preventiveCare: Arrange routine veterinary examinations and keep vaccination and parasite prevention appropriate to local risks.
Discuss the breed club's eye-health guidance and relevant family history with the breeder and veterinarian.
Seek prompt veterinary advice for eye pain, cloudiness, sudden vision changes, persistent lameness, seizures, or significant changes in behaviour.
Maintain a healthy body condition and provide age-appropriate exercise.
Keep up with dental hygiene, nail care, coat maintenance, and regular ear checks.
recommendedScreenings: Ask the breeder about primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) DNA testing and the health history of the puppy's relatives.
Discuss periodic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist.
Ask the veterinarian or breeder about hip evaluation and any other screening appropriate to the dog's family history and intended breeding role.
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste and arrange veterinary dental assessment as recommended. Dental disease can affect dogs of any breed.
health.earCare: Check the folded, hair-covered ears routinely for redness, odour, discharge, or persistent scratching. Clean only with an appropriate product and veterinary guidance when needed.
health.skinCare: Inspect the skin while brushing, particularly beneath the rough coat and around the ears and beard. Seek veterinary advice for persistent itching, sores, hair loss, or recurring irritation.

idealFor: Active households that can provide daily walks, scent-based enrichment, and training.
Owners who enjoy an outgoing, playful dog with an independent streak.
People prepared to work patiently on recall and manage scent-driven behaviour.
Households able to provide a secure outdoor area or safe alternatives for exercise.
notIdealFor: People seeking a quiet, low-energy dog with minimal exercise needs.
Owners expecting dependable off-leash recall without sustained training.
Households that cannot tolerate frequent vocalisation.
People who want a very low-maintenance coat and minimal routine care.
Homes where small animals cannot be safely separated or supervised.

funFacts: The breed's name refers to its small size, low-set build, rough coat, and connection with the Vendée region of France.
It was developed to follow scent through brambles and difficult terrain rather than relying on speed alone.
The breed's rough, naturally tousled appearance is part of its recognised type.
Its scenting instincts can make tracking and nose-work games especially engaging activities.

faq.question: Is the Petit Basset Griffon Vendéen a good family dog?
faq.answer: It can be a lively and sociable family companion in a household that provides activity, training, supervision, and enrichment. As with any breed, children should be taught to interact respectfully with dogs and interactions should be supervised.

faq.question: Does this breed need a lot of exercise?
faq.answer: It needs regular daily activity and mental stimulation, especially opportunities to sniff and follow scent. The sources reviewed do not establish a single exercise-minute target suitable for every dog.

faq.question: Can a PBGV be trusted off leash?
faq.answer: Not automatically. Its scent-hound instincts can draw it away from its handler, so recall should be trained gradually and off-leash activity should be limited to secure areas unless the dog is reliably trained in that environment.

faq.question: What grooming does a PBGV need?
faq.answer: Regular brushing and checks for burrs or tangles are useful, along with routine ear, nail, and dental care. The coat should retain its natural rough appearance rather than being heavily sculpted.

faq.question: What health issues should owners ask about?
faq.answer: Ask about primary open-angle glaucoma and the breed club's eye-health recommendations, as well as reported concerns such as hip dysplasia, hypothyroidism, epilepsy, and patellar luxation. A veterinarian can advise which checks are appropriate for an individual dog.

faq.question: How much should an adult PBGV weigh?
faq.answer: The sources reviewed did not establish a reliable sex-specific weight range suitable for this record. Body condition and veterinary advice are more useful for managing an individual dog's weight than relying on an unverified number.

overview.summary: A powerful, elegant, medium-to-large Swiss herding breed with a pure white double coat, erect ears, and a calm, attentive, deeply loyal character suited to active families and versatile canine sports.
overview.description: The Berger Blanc Suisse (White Swiss Shepherd Dog) is a well-muscled, medium-to-large shepherd dog combining athletic power with an elegant, harmonious outline. Slightly rectangular in proportions—with a body length to withers height ratio of 12:10—it features a level, firm topline, a finely sculpted wedge-shaped head, erect triangular ears, and a bushy sabre tail reaching at least to the hock. The weather-resistant double coat is pure white and occurs in two varieties: a dense medium-length coat (Stockhaar) and a longer coat (Langstockhaar) with a distinct neck mane and leg breeches. Lively, attentive, and socially adaptable, it bonds deeply with its household and remains watchful without unprovoked aggression, thriving on daily outdoor activity, positive training, and close human companionship.
overview.history: The breed shares ancestral roots with the German Shepherd Dog, in which white-coated individuals were recorded in the late nineteenth century. After white colouring was struck from European shepherd standards in 1933, white shepherd dogs were preserved and selectively bred in the United States and Canada as an independent population. In the early 1970s, dogs from North America were imported to Switzerland; an American-bred male named Lobo (whelped 5 March 1966) was brought by Agatha Burch and became the foundational progenitor of the Swiss lines. The breed multiplied across Europe and was registered in the Swiss Stud Book appendix from June 1991. Demonstrating eight independent ancestral maternal lines, Switzerland achieved definitive international recognition for the breed in 2011 as its official country of origin.
overview.originalPurpose: Family companion and versatile shepherd dog with aptitude for herding, tracking, and guard work
currentRoles: Family companion and devoted household dog

physical.coatLength: Medium-length or long
coatColors: White with slight pale yellowish or fawn tinting on the ear tips, back, or upper tail

Wedge-shaped, finely chiselled head with parallel skull and muzzle planes and a slight, perceptible stop
High-set, erect triangular ears with slightly rounded tips, carried parallel and facing forward
Almond-shaped brown to dark-brown eyes placed slightly obliquely, with dark eye-rims desirable
Medium-sized nose with black pigmentation desired (snow nose and lighter pigmentation accepted) and dry, tightly closing lips
Two distinct double-coat varieties: medium-length (Stockhaar) and long-coat (Langstockhaar, with distinct neck mane and leg breeches)
Bushy, low-set sabre tail reaching at least to the hock joint, carried low at rest and lifted in action without rising above the topline
Withers height of 58–66 cm for males (approximate weight 30–40 kg) and 53–61 cm for females (approximate weight 25–35 kg)

exercise.level: High. An energetic, athletic shepherd breed that needs daily outdoor exercise, structured activity, and ongoing mental enrichment to stay healthy and contented.

grooming.brushing: Weekly thorough brushing and combing during normal periods; daily brushing during twice-yearly seasonal undercoat blows to remove loose undercoat and prevent matting
grooming.bathing: Occasional baths only as needed; the coat naturally repels dried mud and dirt once dry
notes: Use an undercoat rake or slicker brush to remove loose undercoat hair during seasonal coat blows.
Never shave or clip the double coat, as it insulates against both winter cold and summer heat.
Check and clean the erect ears periodically to keep them free of debris.
Keep toenails trimmed regularly to preserve sound foot structure.
Brush teeth consistently using a canine toothbrush and dog-safe toothpaste.
Examine paw pads and skin folds after hikes and outdoor workouts.

training.difficulty: Moderate. Highly intelligent, biddable, and eager to please, but naturally sensitive and easily discouraged by harsh corrections or raised voices.
tips: Use consistent, reward-based positive reinforcement with treats, enthusiastic praise, and play.
Avoid harsh corrections, shouting, or physical punishment, which can damage trust and cause the dog to become fearful.
Introduce gradual alone-time conditioning early in puppyhood to prevent separation anxiety, as the breed forms an intense attachment to its people.
Manage exercise impact in growing puppies; avoid repetitive high jumps and forced long runs until growth plates have closed.
Provide regular mental enrichment alongside physical exercise to keep its active mind engaged.
training.socialization: Early, comprehensive socialization to varied people, calm dogs, children, household noises, vehicles, and novel environments helps the puppy develop into a confident, socially competent adult.

Cool and temperate climates

livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate. Highly people-oriented and deeply bonded to its family; long, repeated periods of isolation can cause distress or separation-related vocalization and chewing.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality, complete and balanced commercial dog food or veterinarian-supervised diet formulated for medium-to-large active breeds and tailored to life stage (puppy, adult, senior) and activity level
nutrition.guidelines: Provide measured portions of a nutritionally balanced diet suited to the dog's age, weight, and activity level. Large-breed puppies benefit from controlled caloric and mineral intake to prevent overly rapid skeletal growth. Divide daily food into two or more meals and avoid vigorous running or exercise immediately before or after feeding to minimize the risk of gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat).
considerations: Monitor body condition regularly to maintain a lean, athletic frame and prevent excess weight on joints.
Feed a large-breed puppy formula during growth to ensure balanced calcium and phosphorus levels.
Account for training treats within the daily caloric allowance.
Ensure clean, fresh drinking water is available at all times.
Consult a veterinarian to customize portion sizes and nutritional choices.
nutrition.note: Consulted breed standards and kennel-club sources do not mandate fixed daily meal counts across life stages; tailor feeding frequency and portion sizes with a veterinarian or breeder.

health.overview: The Berger Blanc Suisse is fundamentally a robust and athletic breed with an average lifespan of 10 to 14 years. Because it shares ancestral genetic roots with the German Shepherd Dog while having been bred independently for decades, primary health management and pre-breeding screening focus on orthopedic health (hip and elbow dysplasia), hereditary spinal neuropathy (degenerative myelopathy, DM), and the multi-drug resistance 1 (MDR1) gene mutation. Official breed clubs in Switzerland, Europe, and North America mandate or strongly recommend pre-breeding radiographic screening for hip and elbow dysplasia, DNA testing for DM and MDR1, veterinary eye examinations, and cardiac evaluations.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia: a developmental orthopedic malformation evaluated prior to breeding via radiographic scoring; health registry data indicates hips average tighter than ancestral German Shepherd stock
Elbow dysplasia: developmental elbow joint disease (fragmented medial coronoid process, ununited anconeal process, or osteochondritis dissecans), monitored through pre-breeding radiographic clearance

Multi-Drug Resistance 1 (MDR1 / ABCB1 gene mutation): a transport protein defect causing sensitivity and neurotoxicity to certain antiparasitic agents (such as high-dose ivermectin), loperamide, acepromazine, and chemotherapy drugs
Degenerative myelopathy (DM / SOD1 mutation): a late-onset, progressive spinal cord neuropathy causing hind-limb ataxia and weakness in older dogs, monitored via DNA screening

Gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat): an acute, life-threatening emergency in deep-chested dogs where the stomach distends with gas and twists; manageable through divided meals and resting around exercise
Cardiac abnormalities: subaortic stenosis, aortic stenosis, and heart murmurs have been detected in some lines, warranting veterinary cardiac auscultation and optional echocardiography
Ophthalmic and dental conditions: occasional cataracts or eyelid abnormalities, as well as missing premolars (PM1) or bite irregularities evaluated in conformation
preventiveCare: Verify that breeding parents hold documented health clearances for hip and elbow dysplasia, DNA test certificates for MDR1 and DM, and current veterinary eye and cardiac examinations.
Determine the dog's MDR1 status before administering certain prescription drugs, or inform your veterinarian to avoid known neurotoxic medications (such as high-dose ivermectin and loperamide).
Raise puppies on non-slip surfaces and avoid forced high-impact jumping or prolonged stair climbing until growth plates have closed.
Feed multiple smaller meals daily and avoid vigorous running immediately before or after eating to reduce bloat risk.
Maintain a lean body condition and keep vaccinations, dental hygiene, and routine veterinary wellness visits up to date.
recommendedScreenings: Hip dysplasia evaluation (radiographic certification via recognized national or international veterinary scoring schemes prior to breeding)
Elbow dysplasia evaluation (radiographic screening via recognized veterinary scoring schemes prior to breeding)
Multi-Drug Resistance 1 (MDR1 / ABCB1 mutation) DNA test
Degenerative Myelopathy (DM / SOD1 mutation) DNA test
Ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (specialist eye registry scheme)
Basic or advanced cardiac evaluation by a qualified veterinarian or veterinary cardiologist
Optional dentition evaluation and screening for inherited bleeding disorders (Von Willebrand's disease and Hemophilia A)
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth regularly with dog-safe toothpaste and schedule veterinary dental checks. The breed standard calls for a strong, complete scissor bite of 42 teeth set square to the jaws (missing more than two PM1 is a severe fault; over- or undershot bites and wry mouth are disqualifying faults).
health.earCare: Inspect the erect triangular ears regularly for wax accumulation, dirt, redness, or odour, and clean gently only as needed using a veterinarian-approved ear cleaner.
health.skinCare: The dense double coat naturally repels dried dirt and protects the skin. Brush weekly (daily during shedding season) to remove loose undercoat, inspect the skin for parasites, cuts, or hot spots, and never shave the coat for routine convenience.

Owners interested in obedience, rally, agility, tracking, mantrailing, or search-and-rescue training
Handlers who appreciate a sensitive, intelligent companion that responds to gentle, positive reinforcement
Households prepared for regular brushing and heavy twice-yearly seasonal undercoat shedding
Homes where someone is present for much of the day to provide companionship
notIdealFor: Sedentary households unable to provide substantial daily physical exercise and mental engagement
Homes where the dog would be left isolated outdoors, confined in a kennel, or alone for long workdays
Handlers who rely on harsh, forceful, or punitive training methods
People intolerant of dog hair indoors during seasonal coat blows

funFacts: Although the breed's historical roots trace to white-coated herding dogs in North America and Europe, Switzerland proved eight independent breeding lines to become recognized as its official country of origin.
A white male puppy named Lobo, whelped in the United States on 5 March 1966, was imported to Switzerland by Agatha Burch and became the foundational ancestor of the modern European population.
Despite its striking pure white coat, the breed is not an albino; official standards call for dark skin pigmentation with black eye rims, lips, and nose leather.

White coats were originally disqualified from the German Shepherd standard in Europe in 1933, leading North American fanciers to preserve the white lineage before it was reintroduced to Switzerland in the 1970s.

The breed exists in two distinct double-coat varieties—medium-length (Stockhaar) and long-coat (Langstockhaar, featuring an elegant neck mane and bushy tail)—both of which naturally shed dried dirt once dry.
Known for high social competence and versatility, the breed excels across a wide spectrum of canine sports, including agility, mantrailing, obedience, and search-and-rescue.

faq.question: What is a Berger Blanc Suisse?
faq.answer: The Berger Blanc Suisse (White Swiss Shepherd Dog) is a medium-to-large, white-coated herding breed that originated from North American white shepherd bloodlines and was formally developed and recognized in Switzerland as an independent companion and family dog.

faq.question: How big does a Berger Blanc Suisse get?
faq.answer: Conformation standards specify a withers height of 58 to 66 cm (about 23 to 26 inches) and an approximate weight of 30 to 40 kg (66 to 88 pounds) for males, and 53 to 61 cm (about 21 to 24 inches) and an approximate weight of 25 to 35 kg (55 to 77 pounds) for females.

faq.question: How does the Berger Blanc Suisse differ from the German Shepherd?
faq.answer: While sharing ancestral origins, the Berger Blanc Suisse has been recognized as a distinct breed for decades with its own closed studbooks and standard. Conformationally, it requires a pure white coat, a level backline without an exaggerated slope, and more moderate angulation. Temperamentally, it was bred specifically as a gentle, socially adaptable family companion rather than for bite work.

faq.question: What coat varieties does the breed have?
faq.answer: The breed has two accepted double-coat varieties: a dense medium-length coat (Stockhaar) and a long coat (Langstockhaar), the latter featuring a distinct neck mane, leg feathering ('trousers'), and a very bushy tail. Both varieties possess an abundant undercoat.

faq.question: What is the temperament of the Berger Blanc Suisse?
faq.answer: The breed is known for its balanced, attentive, and lively disposition. It is deeply devoted to its family, gentle with children, highly trainable, and alert without unprovoked aggression, though it can be sensitive to harsh handling.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Berger Blanc Suisse need?
faq.answer: As an active and intelligent shepherd breed, it requires substantial daily physical activity—such as brisk walks, hiking, and off-leash running in secure areas—combined with mental enrichment through obedience, agility, or scent tracking.

faq.question: Can a Berger Blanc Suisse live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Yes, provided it receives sufficient daily outdoor exercise, mental stimulation, and close companionship with its family, as it is generally calm and quiet indoors.

faq.question: Does the Berger Blanc Suisse shed a lot?
faq.answer: Yes. The dense double coat sheds moderately year-round and blows its entire undercoat heavily roughly twice a year over several weeks, during which daily brushing is recommended.

faq.question: What health screenings are recommended for breeding dogs?
faq.answer: Parent-club health guidelines recommend radiographic screening for hip and elbow dysplasia, DNA testing for the multi-drug resistance 1 (MDR1) mutation and degenerative myelopathy (DM), veterinary eye examinations, and cardiac evaluations.

faq.question: How long does a Berger Blanc Suisse live?
faq.answer: The average life expectancy is 10 to 14 years when provided with appropriate nutrition, regular exercise, weight management, and preventive veterinary care.

faq.question: Is the Berger Blanc Suisse easy to train?
faq.answer: Yes. The breed is exceptionally intelligent, eager to please, and responsive to positive reinforcement and food rewards. However, because of its sensitive nature, training must be patient and encouraging rather than punitive.

overview.summary: The Bernese Mountain Dog is a large, long-coated Swiss working breed known for its striking black, white and rust markings, steady nature and close bond with its family. Developed for practical farm work, it can be a devoted companion when its size, coat care, exercise and health needs are well managed.
overview.description: Powerful but balanced in build, the Bernese Mountain Dog has a long, dense coat, dark eyes, pendant ears and distinctive tricolour markings. The ground colour is black, with rich rust markings and clear white areas arranged in a characteristic pattern. Historically associated with farms around the Swiss canton of Bern, the breed helped guard property, move cattle and pull loads. Many individuals are affectionate and calm with familiar people, but they are still large, strong dogs that benefit from early training, sensible exercise and thoughtful socialisation. Their thick coat needs regular care, and prospective owners should be prepared for a relatively short expected lifespan compared with many smaller breeds.
overview.history: The Bernese Mountain Dog developed as an all-purpose farm dog in the pre-Alpine and lowland areas around Bern, Switzerland. It was historically known as the Dürrbächler, a name associated with the Dürrbach area where dogs of this type were numerous. Dogs of the breed appeared at shows in the early 1900s, and enthusiasts formed a club in 1907 to promote consistent breeding. The name Bernese Mountain Dog became established as the breed gained recognition beyond its original region.
overview.originalPurpose: Farm guarding, cattle driving, and draft work such as pulling carts or loads.
currentRoles: Therapy or community work for suitable, trained individuals

physical.coatType: Long, dense double coat with a moderately long outer coat and a woolly undercoat.
physical.coatLength: Long, moderately soft, straight or slightly wavy.
coatColors: White markings on the head, chest, feet and tail tip in the characteristic tricolour pattern
physical.sheddingLevel: High, with heavier seasonal shedding.
distinctiveFeatures: Large, strong, well-balanced working-dog build
Long, dense coat with a black, rust and white tricolour pattern
White facial blaze and chest markings are characteristic
Dark brown, almond-shaped eyes
Medium-sized, high-set triangular ears that hang close to the head when relaxed
Broad, deep chest and strong limbs
Bushy tail reaching at least to the hocks
A compact body proportion, with the body slightly longer than the height at the withers

traits: Affectionate and devoted to familiar people
Generally calm and steady when appropriately socialised
Attentive and watchful
Confident in ordinary situations
Often friendly and gentle with family members
May be reserved or composed around unfamiliar people
Intelligent and usually responsive to reward-based training
People-oriented and often happiest when included in family activities

exercise.level: Moderate. Regular daily movement and family activities are important, but exercise should be adjusted for age, health, weather and individual fitness. Growing puppies should not be pushed into strenuous repetitive exercise.
activities: Daily walks at a comfortable pace
Sniffing and exploration in safe areas
Hiking on suitable routes once the dog is physically mature and conditioned
Reward-based obedience and training games
Carting or draft activities with appropriate training and equipment
Low-impact play and enrichment adapted to age and joint health

grooming.level: Moderate to high, especially during seasonal shedding.
grooming.brushing: Brush at least weekly to remove loose hair and help prevent tangles. Brush more frequently during heavy shedding periods, paying attention to areas where the coat can mat, such as behind the ears, around the hindquarters and under the legs.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when needed using a dog-formulated shampoo and rinse the dense coat thoroughly. Make sure the undercoat dries fully, particularly in cool or humid conditions.
notes: Expect substantial hair around the home, with heavier shedding periods during the year.
Check the skin and coat during brushing for mats, irritation, ticks or unusual lumps.
Trim nails regularly and inspect paw pads after outdoor activities.
Check ears for redness, odour, discharge or persistent scratching.
Brush teeth regularly with dog toothpaste and arrange veterinary dental care as needed.
Avoid shaving the double coat for routine cooling; ask a veterinarian or qualified groomer about coat problems or medical exceptions.

training.difficulty: Moderate. The breed is often eager to work with its people, but its large adult size makes early manners, leash skills and calm behaviour especially important.
tips: Start reward-based training and positive socialisation early, before the dog becomes physically powerful.
Teach loose-leash walking, recall, settling and polite greetings in manageable steps.
Avoid harsh corrections; use consistent cues, rewards and short, successful sessions.
Introduce handling for brushing, nail care, ear checks and veterinary examinations gradually.
Manage jumping and pulling before they become difficult habits in a large adult dog.
Keep activity appropriate to growth and health; ask a veterinarian for guidance on strenuous exercise during development.
training.socialization: Introduce puppies and young dogs to people, surfaces, sounds, transport, handling and suitable dogs in a gradual, positive way. Supervise interactions with children because even a friendly large dog can accidentally knock a child over. Give the dog space and reward calm behaviour rather than forcing contact.

climates: Generally better suited to cool or temperate conditions than prolonged hot weather because of the dense double coat.
In hot weather, provide shade, ventilation, fresh water and exercise during cooler periods.
Avoid leaving the dog in a hot vehicle or exposed outdoor space during high temperatures.
Provide a comfortable indoor resting area and monitor the individual dog's comfort in both hot and cold conditions.
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: This is a people-oriented breed. Build time alone gradually, provide a safe resting space and suitable enrichment, and avoid routinely leaving the dog isolated for long periods.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced diet appropriate to the dog's life stage, body condition, activity and veterinary needs. Large-breed puppy food is generally appropriate during growth when recommended for the individual puppy.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Use an age-appropriate complete puppy diet and follow its feeding guidance with veterinary advice. Divide the daily amount into suitable meals for the puppy's age and appetite.
feedingFrequency.adult: Feed measured meals on a consistent schedule and adjust the total amount to maintain a healthy body condition.
feedingFrequency.senior: Choose a diet and feeding routine based on age, activity, body condition and any health conditions, with veterinary advice when needed.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure portions rather than feeding by guesswork, keep fresh water available, and monitor body condition as the dog grows. Avoid excessive calorie intake during growth and adulthood. Make dietary changes gradually and consult a veterinarian for individual calorie targets, persistent weight changes or special dietary needs.
considerations: Account for training treats and chews in the daily calorie intake.
Monitor growth and body condition rather than trying to maximise a puppy's growth rate.
Ask a veterinarian about feeding routines around vigorous exercise, particularly if the dog has digestive or other health concerns.
Do not add supplements or use restrictive diets without an appropriate reason and veterinary guidance.
Keep foods that are unsafe for dogs out of reach.
nutrition.note: These are general canine nutrition recommendations, not a breed-specific veterinary diet or calorie prescription.

health.overview: Bernese Mountain Dogs have several documented breed health concerns, including orthopaedic disease and certain cancers. Hip and elbow dysplasia, some eye and cardiac disorders, degenerative myelopathy and histiocytic sarcoma are among the conditions considered in breed health programmes. These risks do not mean that every dog will develop a condition, and individual risk depends on genetics and other factors. Prospective owners should seek health-test information from responsible breeders and discuss preventive care with a veterinarian.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia
Elbow dysplasia
Histiocytic sarcoma and other cancers reported in the breed
Degenerative myelopathy
Selected cardiac disorders
Selected eye disorders
Gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat), a potentially life-threatening emergency in large dogs
Von Willebrand disease, a bleeding disorder considered in breed health testing
Thyroid disorders
preventiveCare: Arrange routine veterinary examinations and keep vaccinations appropriate to local veterinary guidance.
Discuss breed-relevant health testing and family health history when selecting a puppy or planning breeding.
Maintain a healthy body condition and use age-appropriate exercise to support joint health.
Seek prompt veterinary advice for persistent lameness, unusual lumps, unexplained weight loss, exercise intolerance or changes in behaviour.

Learn the emergency signs of gastric dilatation-volvulus, including a swollen abdomen, repeated unproductive retching, restlessness or sudden weakness, and seek emergency veterinary care if suspected.
Use parasite prevention appropriate to local risks and the dog's activities.
recommendedScreenings: Hip evaluation
Elbow evaluation

Cardiac examination
Degenerative myelopathy DNA testing, interpreted with veterinary or genetic counselling
One additional test as advised by the breed club and veterinarian, such as von Willebrand disease, thyroid evaluation or histiocytic sarcoma risk assessment
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with dog toothpaste. Arrange veterinary dental checks and seek advice for persistent bad breath, gum inflammation, oral pain or difficulty eating.
health.earCare: Check ears regularly for redness, odour, discharge or persistent scratching. Seek veterinary advice if signs of irritation or infection appear.
health.skinCare: Inspect the dense coat and skin during grooming for mats, parasites, irritation or unusual lumps. Contact a veterinarian about persistent skin changes or new or growing masses.

idealFor: Households able to include a large, people-oriented dog in daily family life
Owners prepared for regular brushing and seasonal shedding
People who can provide consistent training and moderate daily activity
Families interested in suitable outdoor activities, obedience or draft work
notIdealFor: Households that cannot accommodate a large adult dog
People who need a low-shedding or very low-grooming breed
Owners who routinely leave a dog alone for long periods
People unable to manage heat exposure or provide appropriate veterinary care
Anyone expecting a long-lived breed without considering its known health risks

funFacts: The breed was historically known as the Dürrbächler, named after an area near Riggisberg in the canton of Bern.
It is one of the four Swiss Mountain Dog breeds and is distinguished by its long coat.
Its original farm duties included guarding, driving cattle and pulling loads.
The breed's characteristic appearance combines a black ground colour with rust and white markings.
Its working background is reflected in activities such as carting, tracking and obedience.

faq.question: Where did the Bernese Mountain Dog originate?
faq.answer: It originated in Switzerland, particularly the farming areas around the canton of Bern, where it was used for practical farm work.

faq.question: How large does a Bernese Mountain Dog get?
faq.answer: The FCI standard gives a height of 64–70 cm for males and 58–66 cm for females. Published weight ranges vary by registry; the figures in this record are converted from an American Kennel Club profile.

faq.question: What colours does a Bernese Mountain Dog have?
faq.answer: The breed has a characteristic tricolour coat: black, with rust markings and white areas on the head, chest, feet and tail tip.

faq.question: How long does a Bernese Mountain Dog live?
faq.answer: The American Kennel Club lists an expected lifespan of 7–10 years. This is a population-level estimate, not a prediction for an individual dog.

faq.question: Does a Bernese Mountain Dog shed a lot?
faq.answer: Yes. Its dense double coat sheds noticeably, with heavier seasonal shedding. Regular brushing and more frequent grooming during shedding periods help manage loose hair and tangles.

faq.question: Is a Bernese Mountain Dog good with children?
faq.answer: Many are affectionate and gentle with family, including children, but temperament varies. Because the breed is large and strong, supervise interactions and teach children how to interact respectfully with dogs.

faq.question: Which health tests are relevant to the breed?
faq.answer: Breed-club guidance includes hip and elbow evaluations, eye and cardiac examinations, and degenerative myelopathy testing. Additional testing may be considered with veterinary guidance. Screening helps inform decisions but cannot guarantee that a dog will remain healthy.

faq.question: Can a Bernese Mountain Dog live in a hot climate?
faq.answer: It can be challenging because the breed has a dense double coat. In warm weather, provide shade, water, good ventilation and exercise during cooler hours, and watch carefully for signs of overheating.

overview.summary: The Black Mouth Cur is a muscular, agile American working dog known for its hunting ability, stamina, loyalty, and protective instincts. It generally suits an active home that can provide purposeful exercise, training, and clear boundaries.
overview.description: This medium-sized, short-coated working dog has a sturdy, athletic build, a broad head, drop ears, and a muzzle that is often darkly pigmented. Coat colours vary and can include shades of red, yellow, fawn, brown, black, buckskin, and brindle. The black muzzle is characteristic but is not present in every accepted colour pattern. Bred for practical work rather than an exaggerated appearance, the Black Mouth Cur is valued for stamina, courage, scenting ability, and versatility. Individual dogs can differ substantially in size, appearance, and working style, particularly across established bloodlines.
overview.history: The breed developed in the southern United States, where families used versatile cur-type dogs for practical work on farms and homesteads. Its precise origin is uncertain: accounts have associated its development with more than one southern state. Historically, these dogs helped track and hunt game and guard people, property, and livestock. The breed was recognised by the United Kennel Club in 1998.

Check the ears routinely and clean only as needed with a suitable veterinary-recommended product.

tips: Begin reward-based training and gentle handling early.

Practise recall on a long line before considering any off-leash activity; use a secure area where necessary.
Provide suitable outlets for scenting, exploring, and problem-solving rather than relying on physical exercise alone.

feedingFrequency.adult: Feed regular measured meals and adjust portions to maintain a healthy body condition.
feedingFrequency.senior: Choose a diet and meal routine appropriate to the dog's age, health, and activity, with veterinary guidance when needed.

faq.question: Is every Black Mouth Cur's muzzle black?
faq.answer: No. Dark muzzle pigmentation is characteristic, but accepted coat colours and markings vary, and not every dog has a solid black mask.

faq.question: Where did the Black Mouth Cur originate?
faq.answer: It developed in the southern United States. Its exact origin is uncertain, and historical accounts differ about the state where it first developed.

faq.question: Is the Black Mouth Cur a good choice for a low-activity home?
faq.answer: Usually not the easiest match. It is a working-type dog that generally benefits from regular physical activity, training, and mental enrichment.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Black Mouth Cur need each day?
faq.answer: A reliable breed-specific minute range is not established in this record. Needs vary with age, health, fitness, and working drive, so build a routine around the individual dog and consult a veterinarian when necessary.

faq.question: Are there confirmed common health problems for this breed?
faq.answer: The sources checked for this profile did not establish a sufficiently reliable list of breed-specific common conditions. Routine preventive veterinary care is still important.

overview.summary: A massive, noble, and powerfully built scent hound originating from the Ardennes of Belgium, world-renowned for its unmatched cold-trail scenting ability, long velvety curling ears, abundant head and neck folds, and gentle, sensitive nature at home.
overview.description: The Bloodhound—officially known in continental Europe as the Chien de Saint-Hubert and historically celebrated as the 'Sleuth Hound'—is the most powerful and substantial of all scent hounds. Built on a harmonious rectangular outline (roughly a 10:9 ratio of body length to withers height, with chest depth equal to half the withers height), it combines heavy, round bone and strong muscle with a solemn, dignified bearing and a free, elastic, slightly rolling trot capable of covering ground effortlessly for hours. Its majestic head—measuring 30 cm (12 inches) or more in adult males and 28 cm (11 inches) or more in females—is narrow relative to its length, crowned by a pronounced occipital peak, and draped in thin, supple skin that falls into deep forehead and cheek ridges and a pronounced double dewlap when the nose is lowered to the ground. Extremely long, low-set, velvety ears curl inward and backward past the tip of the nose, working alongside the loose facial folds to funnel and trap scent particles. Off duty, the Bloodhound is a gentle, placid, and affectionate companion that gets along well with people and other dogs, yet on a trail it becomes single-minded and unstoppable. Prospective owners must be prepared for heavy drooling (including 15-foot 'slobber missiles' when the dog shakes its head), a resonant baying voice, a high physical fence, leashed exercise, and daily cleaning of the ears and facial folds.
overview.history: One of the oldest scent-hunting breeds, the modern Bloodhound traces its primary lineage to the Ardennes forest region of Belgium, where black and black-and-tan pack hounds were bred from the seventh century onward by the monk Hubert (later Bishop of Liège and canonised as Saint Hubert, the patron saint of hunters) and maintained for centuries by monks at the Abbey of Saint-Hubert to hunt wild boar and stag. In 1066, William the Conqueror brought Saint-Hubert hounds—alongside white hounds of similar type known as Talbots—to England, where the breed was recorded by around 1300 and acquired the English name 'Bloodhound', derived from 'blooded hound' (meaning a hound of pure, aristocratic breeding kept carefully recorded) or from its skill in tracking wounded, bleeding game. Along the Anglo-Scottish border through the sixteenth century, these hounds were known as 'sleuth hounds' and were used to track cattle raiders ('reivers'), with law dictating that anyone who barred a sleuth hound on a hot trail was deemed an accomplice. By the seventeenth century, scientist Robert Boyle documented a Bloodhound trailing a quarry seven miles along busy thoroughfares to an upstairs room, and in 1805 the Thrapston Association for the Prevention of Felons in England recorded the first organized law-enforcement use of a Bloodhound to catch poachers and thieves. Exported to North America by the nineteenth century (where the breed was formally registered in 1885 and where trailing evidence from a proven Bloodhound is accepted in courts of law, though historical records also note its misuse in the antebellum American South), North American and continental lines later helped replenish British stock after the breed nearly died out in Britain during the Second World War.
overview.originalPurpose: Trailing large game (such as wild boar and deer) and tracking wounded animals as a leash hound, as well as long-distance human scent-trailing (mantrailing) in law-enforcement and search-and-rescue operations.
currentRoles: Law-enforcement, search-and-rescue, and forensic human mantrailing dog
Leash hound for tracking wounded game and blood-scenting trials
Competitive mantrailing, tracking, and scent-work participant
Active leashed hiking and walking partner

physical.coatType: Short, dense, close-lying, and weatherproof single coat that is quite harsh on the body, very short, soft, and velvety on the head and ears, and slightly longer and coarser (about 5 cm / 2 inches) along the underside of the tapering tail.
physical.coatLength: Short
coatColors: Black and tan (bicolour with either a predominant black mantle or a more limited dorsal black saddle, sometimes interspersed with lighter or badger-coloured hairs)
Liver and tan (bicolour in mantle or saddle pattern with brown/liver nose and lip pigment, sometimes interspersed with lighter or badger-coloured hairs)

Red (unicolour ranging from light red/blond to deep red; across all three colours, a small amount of white on the forechest, toes/feet, and tip of the tail is permissible, whereas widespread white reaching the wrists/hocks or white patches on the muzzle or blaze are disqualifying faults)
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate year-round, with heavier seasonal shedding twice a year in late spring and late autumn.
distinctiveFeatures: Most powerful and massive of all scent hounds, built on a rectangular 10:9 body-length-to-height ratio with a deep, oval chest forming a prominent keel between the forelegs (chest depth equal to half the withers height)

Majestic, narrow, flat-sided head (measuring 3/7 of body length, or at least 30 cm [12 in] in males and 28 cm [11 in] in females) with a very pronounced occipital peak ('cone head'), slight stop, and deep, square-profiled muzzle equal in length to the skull

Abundant, thin, supple skin over the forehead and cheeks that falls into deep pendulous ridges and wrinkles when the head is carried low, blending into long upper lips (hanging about 5 cm below the lower jaw) and a pronounced double dewlap (less marked in females)
Extremely long, thin, velvety ears ('leathers') set at or below eye level, falling in graceful inward- and backward-curling folds that reach well beyond the tip of the nose

Moderate-sized, oval dark brown or hazel eyes (amber to yellow in liver-and-tan or red hounds without a black saddle/mantle) conveying a solemn, wise, and dignified expression; conformation standards emphasize that loose skin and eyelid shape must never obscure vision or allow eyelashes to irritate the cornea
High-set, thick, tapering tail ('stern') furnished with ~5 cm harsher hair underneath and carried high in a graceful sabre/scimitar curve on the move without curling over the back
Elastic, swinging, ground-covering trot with a characteristic slight roll, strong rear drive, and straight, heavy-boned legs ending in compact, well-knuckled cat feet

Adult withers height of 68 cm ideal (64–72 cm with ±4 cm tolerance) for males and 62 cm ideal (58–66 cm with ±4 cm tolerance) for females in international standards—or 63–69 cm (25–27 in, average 66 cm / 26 in) for males and 58–63 cm (23–25 in, average 61 cm / 24 in) in British and American standards—with weights of 46–54 kg (101–119 lbs) for males and 40–48 kg (88–106 lbs) for females internationally (41–50 kg [90–110 lbs] for males and 36–45.5 kg [80–100 lbs] for females in British and American standards, and tall individuals occasionally exceeding 55–60 kg / 120–130+ lbs)

traits: Gentle, placid, and kind-hearted ('nature's gentleman') indoors
Deeply affectionate and strongly bonded to its owner and family
Sociable, courteous, and non-quarrelsome with people, kennelmates, and other dogs
Relentless, single-minded, and independent once locked onto a scent trail
Equally sensitive to praise and correction
Somewhat reserved or shy, yet never aggressive
Stubborn and inclined to test boundaries if not guided with patient consistency
Rarely barks like a guard dog, but communicates with a resonant, melodious bay or howl ('rooooo')
Curious mouth-explorer and counter-surfer capable of reaching standard kitchen tables without lifting its paws

exercise.level: Moderate to high. Despite a laid-back indoor demeanour, the Bloodhound was bred to follow a scent trail for hours and requires daily sustained leashed walks, safe enclosed play, and regular nose-work enrichment.
activities: Long daily walks and hikes on a strong leash and harness where the dog can safely sniff
Mantrailing (human scent trailing), tracking trials, and blood-scenting games
Structured nose work and hidden-scent search games in the yard or home
Supervised play and romping with other dogs in a securely fenced enclosure
Jogging, swimming, or rally/obedience exercises for skeletally mature adult hounds

grooming.brushing: Brush weekly with a rubber grooming mitt, hound glove, or medium-bristle brush to remove dead hair and distribute natural skin oils; increase brushing frequency during spring and autumn coat sheds.
grooming.bathing: Bathe as needed (every few weeks to months, or when smelly) using a mild dog-safe shampoo, rinse thoroughly, and dry all facial, neck, and dewlap folds completely so moisture is never trapped against the skin.
notes: Inspect and wipe the facial wrinkles, lip folds, and neck dewlap daily with a warm damp cloth or pet-safe wipe, then dry thoroughly to prevent moisture, food debris, and skin-fold dermatitis.

Check the long, heavy hanging ears ('leathers') daily—and clean them regularly with a veterinarian-approved ear cleanser—because they dip into food and water bowls, sweep the ground, and trap warmth and moisture.
Keep 'slobber cloths' (towels) handy around the house and when travelling: a head shake can fling ropes of saliva 15 feet across furniture, walls, and clothing.
Check the eyes daily for dust, debris, redness, or irritation from eyelid folds.
Trim toenails regularly and inspect the compact cat feet after outdoor walks.
Brush the teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging. Affectionate and capable of remarkable focus in scent work, yet independent-minded, quick to become set in its ways, and deeply sensitive to harsh handling.
tips: Start puppy socialization and basic obedience classes early so polite leash manners and household rules are established before the dog reaches 40 to 54+ kg.

Be firm, patient, and kind, using positive reinforcement (high-value food rewards and warm praise); Bloodhounds are equally sensitive to kindness and correction and will shut down or resist under harsh methods.
Never trust a Bloodhound off-leash in an unenclosed area—even obedience-titled hounds will ignore recall when they strike a compelling scent and have no road or traffic sense.
Enclose yards with a sturdy 5- to 6-foot (1.5–1.8 m) above-ground fence and guard against digging under the fence line.

Do not rely on electronic ('invisible') underground fences: a Bloodhound's high pain threshold, thick loose neck skin, and intense scent drive allow it to charge right through the shock zone and never return.

Dog-proof counters, tables, and rubbish bins: an adult Bloodhound stands tall enough to rest its chin on a 29-inch dining table with all four feet on the floor and is notorious for swallowing non-food items.
Channel the dog's natural nose into mantrailing or tracking games, which build a strong cooperative bond between handler and hound.
training.socialization: Provide early, calm, positive exposure to varied people, friendly dogs, children, surfaces, and veterinary/grooming handling. Because Bloodhounds are gentle pack hounds that enjoy canine company but are often unaware of their own bulk, supervise interactions with young children (particularly toddlers under 5 years old who can be accidentally knocked over by a wagging tail or playful nudge).

livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate. As pack-oriented hounds that bond closely with their families, Bloodhounds left isolated alone for long periods often become bored, bay loudly enough to disturb neighbours, or chew furniture and household objects.

nutrition.dietType: Complete and balanced, high-quality large-breed dog food (commercial or veterinarian-formulated home-prepared diet) matched to life stage (large-breed puppy, adult, or senior), body condition, and workload.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Several smaller measured meals daily using a large-breed puppy formula to support steady, controlled skeletal growth, adjusted with veterinary guidance.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two to three smaller meals daily rather than a single large meal to help reduce the risk of life-threatening gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat).
feedingFrequency.senior: Two to three smaller daily meals tailored to body condition, mobility, dental health, and veterinary advice.

nutrition.guidelines: Feed measured portions appropriate for a large, deep-chested hound (typically 4 to 8 cups of dry food daily for an 80- to 110-pound adult depending on calorie density, age, and activity level, confirmed with a veterinarian). Divide the daily ration into two or three smaller meals, avoid elevated food bowls unless specifically directed by a veterinarian, and restrict vigorous exercise for at least an hour before and after mealtimes to help minimize gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV) risk. Keep clean, fresh water available at all times (wiping the ears and flews after drinking).
considerations: Feed a dedicated large-breed puppy diet during growth so bone and joint development proceed at a steady pace without excess weight.
Divide daily food into two or three smaller meals and avoid strenuous exercise immediately before or after eating to reduce bloat (GDV) risk.

Discuss prophylactic gastropexy ('stomach tacking' surgery, often performed during spaying or neutering) with your veterinarian, as epidemiological studies rank the Bloodhound among the breeds at highest risk of GDV.
Keep all non-food objects, socks, rocks, corn cobs, and rubbish strictly out of reach; Bloodhounds are notorious for indiscriminate ingestion leading to gastrointestinal foreign-body obstruction.
Monitor body condition score regularly and deduct training treats from the daily food ration so excess weight does not overload the hips and elbows.
Consult a veterinarian before adding joint supplements (such as omega-3 fatty acids, glucosamine, or chondroitin).
nutrition.note: Exact caloric needs vary widely across individuals ranging from 36 to over 54 kg (80 to 130+ lbs) and between working mantrailing hounds and family companions; establish portion sizes and bloat-prevention routines with a veterinarian.

health.overview: The Bloodhound has an average life expectancy of 10 to 12 years, and health priorities centre on risks linked to its large, deep-chested build, heavy bone, abundant skin folds, and long pendulous ears. In both British breed-health surveys and a peer-reviewed UK epidemiological study of 15,881 deceased and 36,006 living pedigree dogs across 165–169 breeds (Evans & Adams, 2010), gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat) and cancer were identified as the two leading causes of mortality, with the Bloodhound ranking among the breeds at greatest risk of both GDV mortality and GDV morbidity. Orthopaedic, cardiac, ocular, and neurological screening data are tracked in North American and British health registries: in cumulative North American orthopaedic registry evaluations through December 2014, 25.4% of 2,941 hip evaluations were graded abnormal (72.6% normal), 14.2% of 1,224 elbow evaluations were abnormal (85.3% normal), 0.7% of 732 cardiac evaluations were abnormal (98.1% normal), 2.7% of 150 patellar evaluations were abnormal (97.3% normal), 5.7% of 159 thyroid panels were abnormal with 19.5% equivocal, and among 311 dogs DNA-tested for degenerative myelopathy (SOD1), 49.5% tested clear/normal, 44.1% carriers, and 6.4% genetically at-risk/affected (figures reflecting tested cohorts rather than random population prevalence). Conformation-related concerns include eyelid abnormalities (entropion, ectropion, prolapsed third-eyelid gland ['cherry eye'], and keratoconjunctivitis sicca ['dry eye']), recurrent otitis externa, and skin-fold dermatitis or atopic dermatitis, though careful selective breeding has reduced severe skin and eyelid exaggerations (reflected in the breed's reclassification from Category 3 to Category 2 in the United Kingdom effective 1 January 2025, alongside a reported breed-average inbreeding coefficient of 10.0%).
commonConditions: Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / gastric torsion / bloat) — a sudden, life-threatening emergency in which the stomach distends with gas and twists on its axis; UK epidemiological research (Evans & Adams, 2010) and breed mortality surveys identify the Bloodhound as one of the breeds at highest risk of GDV morbidity and mortality.

Hip dysplasia and elbow dysplasia — developmental joint malformations causing osteoarthritic pain and lameness; in North American registry statistics, 25.4% of 2,941 tested Bloodhounds showed hip dysplasia and 14.2% of 1,224 showed elbow dysplasia.

Eyelid and ocular surface disorders — entropion (inward-rolling eyelid causing eyelashes to rub the cornea), ectropion (outward-sagging lower lid exposing the conjunctiva), prolapsed gland of the third eyelid ('cherry eye'), and keratoconjunctivitis sicca ('dry eye') linked to loose facial skin and heavy flews.

Recurrent otitis externa (ear canal infections) — the long, heavy, low-set ears ('leathers') restrict airflow and trap moisture, wax, and debris, predisposing the ear canals to bacterial and yeast overgrowth.

Skin-fold dermatitis (intertrigo), atopic dermatitis, and eczema — trapped moisture, saliva, and friction within the deep forehead, cheek, lip, and neck folds can cause bacterial or yeast skin infections.

Gastrointestinal foreign-body ingestion and obstruction — Bloodhounds are notorious for swallowing non-food objects, rocks, clothing, or household items, frequently requiring emergency veterinary intervention.
Neoplasia (cancer) — identified alongside gastric torsion as one of the two leading causes of death in British breed health surveys, a risk shared across many large and giant breeds.

Degenerative myelopathy (DM) — a late-onset (typically 8+ years) progressive spinal cord neuropathy associated with the SOD1 gene; in North American DNA-testing statistics of 311 Bloodhounds, 44.1% were carriers and 6.4% tested genetically at risk.

Congenital cardiac disease, autoimmune thyroiditis (hypothyroidism), and patellar luxation — monitored through pre-breeding cardiac auscultation/echocardiography, thyroid antibody panels, and knee examinations.
preventiveCare: Learn the emergency warning signs of gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV)—distended or tight abdomen, unproductive retching, restlessness, stretching in pain, pale gums, or sudden collapse—and seek immediate emergency veterinary care if suspected.
Feed two to three smaller meals daily rather than one large meal, avoid vigorous exercise before and after eating, and discuss prophylactic gastropexy ('stomach tacking') with your veterinarian.
Inspect and clean the hanging ears and wipe and thoroughly dry the facial, lip, and neck folds daily, especially after drinking, eating, bathing, or swimming.

Verify documented pre-breeding health clearances for both parents before acquiring a puppy, including hip and elbow radiographs, veterinary cardiac evaluation, eye examination, and degenerative myelopathy (SOD1) DNA status (as well as low pedigree inbreeding coefficient).
Keep counters, rubbish bins, laundry, and yard areas clear of swallowable objects to prevent foreign-body intestinal obstructions.
Maintain a lean, well-muscled body condition and avoid over-exercising or jogging growing puppies before skeletal maturity to protect the hips and elbows.
recommendedScreenings: Hip dysplasia radiographic evaluation (core pre-breeding requirement; distraction-index hip evaluation is also used as an optional screening tool).
Elbow dysplasia radiographic evaluation (core pre-breeding requirement).
Cardiac evaluation by a qualified veterinarian—preferably a board-certified veterinary cardiologist or specialist, with echocardiography when indicated (core pre-breeding requirement).

Ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist or accredited eye-scheme examiner (recommended in British breeding guidance and optional in North American health certification).
Degenerative myelopathy (DM / SOD1) DNA test from an approved laboratory (optional pre-breeding test in North American and British health programs).

Patellar luxation veterinary evaluation and laboratory thyroid panel (optional pre-breeding evaluations, alongside permanent microchip or tattoo identification and pedigree inbreeding-coefficient review).
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste and schedule periodic veterinary dental assessments. Conformation standards require strong jaws with complete dentition in a regular scissor bite (a pincer/level bite is also tolerated, whereas overshot, undershot, or wry jaws are disqualifying faults).
health.earCare: Inspect the long, velvety, low-set ears daily for redness, foul odour, excess wax, or discharge, and wipe them clean after meals and drinks. Clean the ear canals routinely—and after every bath or swim—using a veterinarian-approved ear cleanser, drying carefully without inserting cotton swabs deep into the canal.
health.skinCare: Check and wipe the facial wrinkles, hanging flews, and double dewlap daily with a damp cloth or pet-safe facial wipe, then dry every fold thoroughly so trapped saliva or water cannot cause skin-fold dermatitis. Monitor the rest of the short coat for parasites, hot spots, or allergic irritation.

idealFor: Active, patient owners and handlers who enjoy mantrailing, tracking, scent work, and long daily leashed hikes
Households with a securely fenced yard (5 to 6 feet high) and ample indoor space for a 40- to 54+ kg hound
People who are relaxed about housekeeping and comfortable with heavy drooling ('slobber cloths') and daily ear and wrinkle care
Families with children (ideally aged 5 and older, with adult supervision) or multi-dog homes seeking a gentle, pack-friendly companion
Owners financially prepared for the food, preventive gastropexy, and veterinary care costs of a large-to-giant breed
notIdealFor: Fastidious or house-proud owners bothered by ropes of drool on walls, ceilings, furniture, and clothing
Apartment dwellers or densely packed urban neighbourhoods sensitive to deep, resonant baying and howling
Owners seeking reliable off-leash recall in unfenced areas or expecting an Electronic/Invisible fence to contain a scent hound
People who want an aggressive property guard dog rather than a friendly, non-quarrelsome pack hound
Sedentary households or homes where the dog is left isolated alone for long workdays

funFacts: The word 'blood' in Bloodhound does not refer to bloodthirstiness: it derives from 'blooded hound', meaning a hound of pure, aristocratic breeding whose lineage was carefully preserved (along with its historic work tracking wounded game).
So legendary is the breed's nose—estimated to contain roughly 250 to 300 million olfactory receptors—that trailing evidence from a proven Bloodhound is admissible in courts of law.

The Bloodhound's long, velvety ears ('leathers') and loose facial wrinkles are functional scent-tracking tools: as the dog lowers its head, the ears sweep scent particles up from the ground while the skin folds trap them near the nostrils.
In 1805, the Thrapston Association for the Prevention of Felons in England recorded the first organized law-enforcement use of a Bloodhound, acquiring a hound to track down poachers and thieves.

Along the Scottish border up to the late sixteenth century, the Bloodhound was known as the 'sleuth hound' (the origin of the modern word 'sleuth' for a detective), and anyone who refused entry to a sleuth hound pursuing a cattle thief was legally considered an accomplice.

In the seventeenth century, pioneering chemist Robert Boyle documented a trial in which a Bloodhound followed a person's scent trail for seven miles along busy footpaths and located the quarry in an upstairs room.

Standing up to 68–72 cm (27+ inches) at the shoulder, an adult male Bloodhound can rest its chin directly on a standard 29-inch dining table and help itself to dinner without lifting a single paw off the floor.
In 2022, a Bloodhound named Trumpet made dog-show history by winning Best in Show at the 146th Westminster Dog Show—the first Bloodhound ever to take the top prize.

faq.question: Where does the Bloodhound originate, and why is it also called the Chien de Saint-Hubert?
faq.answer: The breed originates from the Ardennes region of Belgium, where black and black-and-tan scent hounds were bred from the seventh century onward by the monk Hubert (later Bishop of Liège and canonised as Saint Hubert, patron saint of hunters) and maintained for centuries at the Abbey of Saint-Hubert. In French-speaking Europe and international standards, the breed is still officially named the Chien de Saint-Hubert.

faq.question: Where do the names 'Bloodhound' and 'Sleuth Hound' come from?
faq.answer: After Saint-Hubert hounds were brought to Britain following the Norman Conquest of 1066, their descendants became known as 'blooded hounds'—meaning hounds of pure, aristocratic blood—as well as hounds used to track wounded, bleeding game. In medieval Scotland and northern England, they were called 'sleuth hounds' (from the Old Norse word slóð, meaning 'trail' or 'track'), which gave English the modern word 'sleuth' for a detective.

faq.question: How big does an adult Bloodhound get?
faq.answer: International conformation standards specify an ideal withers height of 68 cm for males and 62 cm for females, with a tolerance of ±4 cm (64 to 72 cm for males; 58 to 66 cm for females), and typical weights of 46 to 54 kg (101–119 lbs) for males and 40 to 48 kg (88–106 lbs) for females. British and American standards specify a height range of 25 to 27 inches (63–69 cm, average 26 in / 66 cm) for males and 23 to 25 inches (58–63 cm, average 24 in / 61 cm) for females, and weights of 90 to 110 pounds (41–50 kg) for males and 80 to 100 pounds (36–45.5 kg) for females, though large individuals frequently reach 120 to 130+ pounds (54–59+ kg).

faq.question: What coat colours are accepted in the Bloodhound?
faq.answer: Three colours are recognized: black and tan, liver and tan, and solid red. In the bicolour varieties (black and tan or liver and tan), the darker colour may form either a full mantle (where black or liver predominates) or a smaller dorsal saddle with more extensive tan, and darker areas may be interspersed with lighter or badger-coloured hairs. Red dogs range from light golden-blond red to deep red. A small amount of white is permitted on the forechest, toes/feet, and tip of the tail.

faq.question: How long does a Bloodhound typically live?
faq.answer: The average lifespan is 10 to 12 years.

faq.question: Does a Bloodhound drool and make a lot of noise?
faq.answer: Yes to both. Because of its square muzzle, long hanging upper lips (flews), and loose neck folds, the Bloodhound drools heavily—especially after drinking, eating, or sniffing—and a single head shake can fling saliva 15 feet across a room. While Bloodhounds rarely bark like guard dogs, they have a deep, resonant, melodious bay ('rooooo') when excited or on a scent trail.

faq.question: Is a Bloodhound a good family dog or guard dog?
faq.answer: Bloodhounds are gentle, placid, and deeply affectionate with their families and get along well with other dogs and children. Because of their sheer size and wagging tails, interactions with toddlers and children under 5 years old should always be supervised. However, they are terrible guard dogs: they may bay when someone approaches, but their friendly, non-aggressive nature means they are more likely to welcome an intruder than guard property.

faq.question: Can a Bloodhound be let off-leash or kept behind an electronic ('invisible') fence?
faq.answer: No. Once a Bloodhound catches an interesting scent, its tracking instinct overrides recall commands and road awareness—even in obedience-titled dogs. Electronic underground fences are ineffective because the breed's high pain threshold, thick loose neck skin, and scent drive allow it to bolt right through the shock boundary. Always walk a Bloodhound on a leash and enclose yards with a sturdy 5- to 6-foot physical fence.

faq.question: How much daily grooming and ear care does a Bloodhound need?
faq.answer: The short coat needs only a weekly brushing with a hound glove or rubber mitt (more often during spring and autumn sheds), but the ears and facial wrinkles require daily attention. Because the long ears dip into food and water bowls and trap warm moisture, inspect them daily and clean them regularly with a veterinary ear cleanser. Wipe the facial, lip, and neck folds daily with a damp cloth and dry them thoroughly to prevent skin-fold dermatitis.

faq.question: Why is bloat (GDV) such an important concern in Bloodhounds, and how can risk be reduced?
faq.answer: Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV, or gastric torsion/bloat) occurs when the deep, narrow stomach fills with gas and twists, cutting off blood flow. Epidemiological studies in pedigree dogs rank the Bloodhound among the breeds at highest risk of GDV morbidity and mortality. Owners can help reduce risk by feeding two to three smaller meals daily instead of one large meal, avoiding vigorous exercise around mealtimes, avoiding elevated food bowls unless advised by a vet, discussing prophylactic gastropexy ('stomach tacking' surgery) with their veterinarian, and seeking immediate emergency care if abdominal swelling, unproductive retching, or restlessness occurs.

faq.question: What pre-breeding health screenings should I ask a breeder for?
faq.answer: Ask for documented results of the three core pre-breeding evaluations—hip dysplasia radiographs, elbow dysplasia radiographs, and a veterinary cardiac examination (ideally by a veterinary cardiologist)—along with optional screenings such as a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist eye exam, patellar luxation check, thyroid panel, and DNA testing for degenerative myelopathy (SOD1).
