overview.summary: A compact, athletic liver-and-chocolate sporting spaniel from South Carolina, purpose-bred to flush wild turkeys and upland birds and retrieve waterfowl from rivers, marshes, and narrow hunting boats.
overview.description: The Boykin Spaniel is a medium-sized, versatile gun dog developed in the river swamps and bottomland hardwoods of South Carolina. Built to cover rough ground and swim with power and agility, it combines a sturdy, rectangular frame (preferring a two-thirds ribcage to one-third loin ratio) with tightly webbed feet, bright yellow-to-amber or brown eyes, and a flat to moderately curly coat in solid shades of liver or chocolate. The head features parallel skull and muzzle planes of equal length, with the muzzle measuring roughly half the width of the skull and ending in a dark liver nose with wide nostrils. In the field, it works with boundless stamina and a merry, rapid tail action; indoors, it is an affectionate, people-oriented companion that thrives on daily exercise and purposeful engagement.
overview.history: The breed originated shortly after the turn of the twentieth century in South Carolina. Around 1905–1910, a small stray brown spaniel-type male wandered near a Methodist church in Spartanburg, South Carolina, and was taken home by churchgoer Alexander L. White, who named him 'Dumpy.' When Dumpy showed remarkable aptitude for retrieving, White sent him to his hunting partner, Lawrence Whitaker ('Whit') Boykin, in the unincorporated Boykin community near Camden along the Wateree River. Timber and river hunters there used narrow, portable cypress 'section boats' to navigate the Wateree River Swamp and needed a compact dog that could flush wild turkeys and retrieve ducks without rocking the boat. Boykin bred Dumpy to a female sporting dog shipped by rail and selectively incorporated Chesapeake Bay Retriever, English Springer Spaniel, Cocker Spaniel, and American Water Spaniel stock. A dedicated breed society was founded in 1977, opening its studbook in 1979 before closing foundation registration in August 1980. In 1985, the Boykin Spaniel was named the Official State Dog of South Carolina—where September 1 is observed as Boykin Spaniel Day—and gained national registry recognition in 1985 and 2009.
overview.originalPurpose: Flushing wild turkeys and upland game birds and retrieving waterfowl in river swamps, marshes, and flooded timber while riding steadily in small, one-person section boats.
currentRoles: Flushing and retrieving gun dog for waterfowl, wild turkey, dove, and upland game
Retriever and upland hunt-test, field-trial, and dock-diving competitor
Agility, rally, obedience, tracking, and scent-detection participant
Active family companion and outdoor hiking, kayaking, or boating partner

physical.coatType: Flat to slightly wavy or moderately curly medium-length coat with light feathering on the ears, chest, legs, and belly; conformation descriptions note it may appear as a single coat or carry a short, dense, weather-resistant undercoat, and field-hunting lines also permit a short, straight coat without feathering for warm climates.
physical.coatLength: Medium (roughly 1 to 2 inches on the body) with moderate feathering that protects against briars and cold water while remaining 'wash and wear' in the field.
coatColors: Solid dark chocolate (from light to very dark shades; a small white spot on the chest is permitted, and sun-bleached golden highlights are acceptable in field-worked dogs)
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate; sheds lightly year-round with heavier seasonal coat drops in spring and autumn that are readily managed with weekly brushing.
physical.droolingLevel: Low; clean, close-fitting upper lips cover the lower jaw without pendulous flews, producing minimal drooling.
distinctiveFeatures: Compact, rectangular, athletic build sized to ride safely in narrow hunting canoes and cypress section boats
Solid rich liver, brown, or dark chocolate coat paired with a fully pigmented dark liver nose
Wide-set, oval to almond-shaped eyes ranging from brilliant gold or yellow to amber and warm brown (often milky bluish-gold in young puppies before maturing)
Thin, flat, pendulous ears set slightly above or even with the eye line that hang close to the cheeks and reach nearly to the tip of the nose
Round, compact, well-arched webbed feet with thick pads built for strong swimming and marsh traction
Lively, horizontal-to-elevated tail carriage (traditionally docked in some regions or left natural where preferred) with merry action on game
Honorable working scars and broken teeth from field service are explicitly accepted without penalty in conformation judging

traits: Friendly and sociable with people and other dogs
Eager to please and highly biddable
Boundlessly enthusiastic and enduring in the field
Intelligent, curious, and quick to learn
Natural swimmer with strong water-retrieving drive
Affectionate and deeply people-oriented indoors
Alert watchdog that gives a reasonable warning bark without excessive vocalizing
Can become restless or inventive if deprived of daily exercise and human companionship

exercise.level: High. Built to hunt all day every day of the season, the Boykin Spaniel requires at least 60 to 120 minutes of vigorous daily aerobic exercise combined with swimming, retrieving, or scent-based mental work.
activities: Brisk daily walks, trail hikes, and off-leash running in securely fenced areas
Land and water retrieving drills using floating bumpers or dummies
Supervised swimming and dock-diving sessions
Upland flushing, tracking, and nose-work games
Retriever hunt tests, agility, rally, and obedience training
Interactive food puzzles and steadiness/impulse-control drills

grooming.brushing: Brush thoroughly at least once or twice a week with a slicker brush and metal comb to remove loose hair, burrs, and tangles in the ear, leg, chest, and belly feathering. Brush every few days during seasonal coat drops or active field seasons.
grooming.bathing: Rinse with clean fresh water after swimming in marshes, lakes, or brackish water, and bathe up to once a month as needed with a mild dog-safe shampoo so natural coat oils are not stripped. Always dry the coat and ears thoroughly after swimming.
notes: Clean and flush the pendulous ears weekly and dry them after every water session with a veterinarian-approved drying solution to prevent chronic otitis externa.
Many active swimmers and field dogs are given a neat summer trim around the ears, feet, and feathering to speed drying and reduce burr and foxtail collection.
Inspect between the webbed toes, paw pads, and groin after woodland or marsh outings for ticks, briars, and speargrass.
Trim nails regularly and brush the teeth at least two to three times per week with enzymatic canine toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Easy to moderate. Eager to please and highly motivated by retrieving bumpers, praise, and treats, though high bird drive and enthusiasm require consistent recall and steadiness training.
tips: Keep training upbeat, fun, and reward-based; harsh corrections can cause a sensitive, handler-focused spaniel to shut down.
Condition reliable whistle and voice recall early before working off-leash near open water or game.
Practice steadiness and impulse control—such as waiting calmly before a bumper is thrown or before exiting a boat or doorway.
Introduce puppies gradually to water entry, small boats, decoys, and field sounds.
Channel natural mouthiness and retrieving instincts by giving puppies appropriate items to carry and fetch.
training.socialization: Expose puppies early and positively to diverse people, children, other dogs, boats, vehicles, water surfaces, and grooming handling. While young puppies may briefly pause to assess unfamiliar sights, well-socialized adults investigate new environments with confident curiosity.

climates: Specifically developed for the warm, humid wetlands of the southeastern United States, yet adaptable to temperate and cooler climates when properly conditioned and sheltered.
Must live indoors as part of the family household rather than being isolated in an outdoor run or kennel.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced diet formulated for the dog's life stage, body condition, and athletic workload.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Feed three to four measured meals per day during early growth, transitioning to two daily meals by six months of age under veterinary supervision.
feedingFrequency.adult: Feed two measured meals per day, adjusting portion size and caloric density for active hunting seasons versus lighter off-season routines.
feedingFrequency.senior: Feed two measured meals daily tailored to mobility, joint health, metabolic rate, and veterinary recommendations.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure meals carefully to maintain a lean, muscular sporting condition. Keeping excess weight off a Boykin Spaniel is essential because extra mass increases mechanical stress on the hips, patellas, and intervertebral discs. Working dogs retrieving in cold water or covering miles of upland cover require higher fat and protein density than companion pets. Always provide fresh water and factor training treats into the daily calorie budget.
considerations: Maintain a lean body condition score to protect the hips, stifles, and spine.
Feed puppies a balanced growth formula without added calcium or mineral supplements.
Provide frequent small drinks of cool water and rest breaks during warm, humid field sessions.
If recurrent skin itching or ear inflammation develops, consult a veterinarian to evaluate environmental atopy versus dietary sensitivities.
nutrition.note: Daily caloric needs vary substantially with age, ambient temperature, and hunting workload; adjust portions using body-condition scoring and veterinary guidance.

health.overview: The Boykin Spaniel is an energetic sporting breed with a typical life expectancy of 10 to 15 years, supported by well-established pre-breeding orthopedic, ophthalmic, cardiac, and DNA screening protocols. Prospective owners and breeders should distinguish between polygenic structural conditions evaluated by clinical or radiographic examination (such as hip dysplasia, patellar luxation, juvenile cataracts, and pulmonic stenosis) and molecularly characterized mutations tested via cheek-swab DNA panels.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia — a polygenic developmental malformation of the hip joint that represents a primary orthopedic concern in the breed (with roughly one-quarter of radiographically evaluated dogs showing mild to severe dysplasia), making pre-breeding hip screening and lean weight management essential.

Exercise-Induced Collapse (EIC) — an autosomal recessive neuromuscular disorder caused by a missense mutation in the dynamin-1 gene (DNM1 c.767G>T); homozygous affected dogs are normal at rest but can develop hindlimb wobbliness, flaccid paraparesis, and collapse after 5 to 20 minutes of strenuous exercise, particularly in warm weather or high excitement.

Chondrodystrophy and Intervertebral Disc Disease risk (CDDY / IVDD) — caused by a fibroblast growth factor 4 retrogene insertion on chromosome 12 (12-FGF4RG / FGF4L2) that segregates in the breed, acting semi-dominantly to shorten limb length and dominantly to cause premature calcification and degeneration of intervertebral discs (Hansen Type I disc herniation risk).

Collie Eye Anomaly / Choroidal Hypoplasia (CEA/CH) — an autosomal recessive congenital ocular disorder caused by an intronic deletion in the NHEJ1 gene that impairs choroidal vascular development and can lead to retinal detachment or blindness in homozygous dogs.

Inherited cataracts and progressive retinal atrophy (PRA-prcd) — ocular disorders including juvenile cataracts and late-onset photoreceptor degeneration (PRCD gene), managed through annual specialist eye examinations and genetic testing.
Patellar luxation and elbow dysplasia — orthopedic conditions monitored through pre-breeding clinical and radiographic evaluations.

Congenital cardiac disease (including pulmonic stenosis) — narrowing of the pulmonary valve outflow tract or other inherited cardiac anomalies screened via pre-breeding veterinary cardiac auscultation and echocardiography.
Degenerative Myelopathy (DM) — a late-onset (typically after age 7) progressive spinal cord neuropathy associated with an autosomal recessive SOD1 mutation showing incomplete penetrance.

Otitis externa and atopic dermatitis — recurrent ear canal infections favored by wet, feathered pendulous ears after swimming, alongside environmental skin allergies (atopy) documented in some bloodlines.
preventiveCare: Acquire puppies only from breeders who provide documented clearances for both parents covering hips, patellas, annual specialist eye exams, cardiac exams, and DNA panels (EIC, CEA/CH, DM, PRA-prcd, and CDDY/IVDD), ensuring at least one parent is genetically Clear for each autosomal recessive disorder.
Clean and dry the ear canals thoroughly after every swim, bath, or wet field outing, and keep inner-ear hair neatly trimmed to promote airflow.
Monitor closely during warm-weather retrieving or field work and halt exercise immediately if a dog shows a wide-based stance, hindlimb dragging, or incoordinated gait.
Maintain a lean body weight and limit repetitive high-impact jumping from pickup beds or elevated docks to reduce spinal disc and joint strain.
Keep up with routine veterinary examinations, dental care, vaccinations, and year-round heartworm, tick, and flea prevention.
recommendedScreenings: Hip dysplasia radiographic evaluation (at 24 months of age or older, or validated distraction-index screening)
Patellar luxation orthopedic evaluation (at 12 months of age or older)
Annual eye examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist
Congenital cardiac examination by a veterinary specialist (at 12 months of age or older)
Exercise-Induced Collapse (EIC — DNM1 c.767G>T) DNA test
Collie Eye Anomaly / Choroidal Hypoplasia (CEA/CH — NHEJ1) DNA test
Degenerative Myelopathy (DM — SOD1) DNA test
Chondrodystrophy / Intervertebral Disc Disease risk (CDDY — 12-FGF4RG) and Progressive Rod-Cone Degeneration (PRA-prcd) DNA tests (included in comprehensive veterinary genetics panels for the breed)
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth at least two to three times per week using dog-specific toothpaste and schedule regular veterinary dental evaluations to prevent tartar accumulation and periodontal disease.
health.earCare: Flush and dry the low-set, feathered ears weekly—and after every swim—using a veterinarian-recommended ear cleanser. Seek prompt veterinary care for head shaking, redness, tenderness, or malodorous discharge.
health.skinCare: Dry the coat thoroughly after water work to prevent moisture-trapping 'hot spots,' inspect the skin and webbed feet for ticks and burrs after field outings, and consult a veterinarian if paw licking, facial rubbing, or seasonal itching occurs.

idealFor: Active individuals and families who enjoy daily hiking, running, boating, and water activities
Waterfowl, wild turkey, and upland bird hunters seeking a compact, boat-stable flushing and retrieving spaniel
Handlers interested in hunt tests, dock diving, agility, rally, or scent-detection sports
Households that welcome an affectionate indoor companion and provide consistent reward-based training
notIdealFor: Sedentary owners seeking a low-energy pet satisfied with short leash walks
Households where the dog would be left alone or kennelled outdoors for long hours every day
People unwilling to manage wet coats, muddy paws, and routine post-swim ear maintenance
Owners expecting reliable off-leash control around wildlife and water without dedicated recall training

funFacts: The breed traces back to 'Dumpy,' a small stray brown spaniel found wandering near a Methodist church in Spartanburg, South Carolina, in the early 1900s and sent to hunter Lawrence Whitaker ('Whit') Boykin near Camden.

Wateree River Swamp hunters prized the breed because it was compact enough to ride in narrow, one-person cypress 'section boats' without tipping the craft—earning its enduring motto, 'the little dog that doesn't rock the boat.'
South Carolina designated the Boykin Spaniel as its Official State Dog in 1985 and celebrates September 1 every year as Boykin Spaniel Day.
Boykin Spaniel puppies are born with milky bluish-gold eyes that gradually mature into the breed's signature shades of brilliant gold, amber, or warm brown over their first few months.

Equipped with tightly webbed toes that act like paddles, Boykin Spaniels are enthusiastic swimmers and have been trained not only on ducks, turkeys, and doves, but also to locate shed deer antlers, golf balls, and scent targets.

faq.question: Where did the Boykin Spaniel originate?
faq.answer: The Boykin Spaniel was developed in the early 1900s in South Carolina, specifically in the unincorporated community of Boykin near Camden and the Wateree River Swamp in Kershaw County.

faq.question: What was the Boykin Spaniel originally bred to do?
faq.answer: It was purpose-bred as a versatile southern gun dog to flush wild turkeys and upland game birds and retrieve waterfowl from river swamps and marshes while riding stably in small, one-person hunting boats.

faq.question: How big does a full-grown Boykin Spaniel get?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 15.5 to 18 inches at the shoulder and typically weigh 30 to 40 pounds, while females stand 14 to 16.5 inches and weigh 25 to 35 pounds. One major conformation standard specifies height and balanced substance without setting a numerical weight limit, whereas traditional hunting standards define both height and weight ranges.

faq.question: How long do Boykin Spaniels live?
faq.answer: Boykin Spaniels have a typical life expectancy of 10 to 15 years when maintained at a lean weight and supported by preventive veterinary care.

faq.question: What coat colors and textures are accepted in the Boykin Spaniel?
faq.answer: The coat is always solid rich liver, brown, or dark chocolate; no white markings are permitted other than a small white spot on the chest, though golden sun-bleaching is normal in dogs that work outdoors. Coat texture ranges from flat to slightly wavy or moderately curly with light feathering, and a short, straight coat without feathering is also recognized for warm-weather hunting.

faq.question: How much daily exercise does a Boykin Spaniel need?
faq.answer: Plan on at least 60 to 120 minutes of vigorous daily exercise—such as brisk hikes, land or water retrieving, swimming, or dog sports—paired with mental enrichment and training.

faq.question: What health tests should a responsible Boykin Spaniel breeder provide?
faq.answer: Prospective buyers should ask for documented parent clearances for hip dysplasia, patellar luxation, congenital cardiac disease (such as pulmonic stenosis), and an annual specialist eye exam, along with DNA test results for Exercise-Induced Collapse (EIC), Collie Eye Anomaly (CEA), Degenerative Myelopathy (DM), progressive retinal atrophy (PRA-prcd), and Chondrodystrophy/Intervertebral Disc Disease risk (CDDY/IVDD).

faq.question: Why do Boykin Spaniels need special ear care after swimming?
faq.answer: Their flat, feathered pendulous ears hang close to the cheeks and easily trap water and marsh debris, creating a warm environment for ear infections. Flushing and drying the ears after every swim and keeping excess inner-ear hair trimmed helps prevent chronic otitis.

overview.summary: The Braque d'Auvergne is a medium-to-large French pointing dog, known for its black-and-white ticked coat, powerful scenting ability, endurance and gentle nature with familiar people.
overview.description: Strongly built but not heavy, the Braque d'Auvergne has a balanced outline, a long head, soft pendant ears and a short, glossy coat. Its distinctive black-and-white markings may appear as dense ticking or a greying pattern, often giving the coat a blue-toned impression. Bred to search for game and point it for the hunter, this dog is designed for sustained movement over difficult ground. It is typically described as affectionate, intelligent and responsive, but its working instincts mean that an active household must provide regular exercise, scent-based enrichment and consistent training.
overview.history: The breed is associated with the Cantal area of the Auvergne region in central France, where it has been known for more than two centuries. Its precise ancestry is uncertain. The FCI historical account describes it as descending from a shared pointer ancestry and mentions a possible historical contribution from the Knights of Malta, but presents that connection as a possibility rather than a proven fact. Developed as a hunting dog, the breed retains a strong pointing instinct and the stamina needed for long days in the field.
overview.originalPurpose: A pointing gun dog developed to search for game, locate it by scent and indicate its position to the hunter.

physical.coatLength: Short and close-lying.
coatColors: Black and white, with flecked or ticked markings

distinctiveFeatures: Robust, well-boned frame without a heavy or clumsy appearance
Long head with a broad, square-ended muzzle
Soft, pendant ears
Dark hazel eyes and a typically gentle expression
Black-and-white flecked or roan coat
Enduring, supple movement suited to covering ground

Secure off-lead exercise where recall is reliable and legal
Scent work and tracking games
Retrieving and suitable gundog activities

Hiking or other suitable outdoor activities

grooming.brushing: Brush approximately once a week with a suitable dog brush to remove loose hair and dirt. Increase checks after field work.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when needed using a dog-appropriate shampoo. Avoid unnecessary frequent bathing.
notes: Check the ears after outdoor activity for grass seeds, dirt or other debris.
Inspect the paws and coat after working in fields, woodland or dense vegetation.
Trim nails when needed and maintain routine dental care.
Check the lips and skin for irritation or foreign material after outdoor exercise.

training.difficulty: Moderate; sensitive, intelligent and working-oriented
tips: Use patient, reward-based training rather than harsh corrections.
Build reliable recall gradually, starting in controlled environments.
Use scenting and retrieving activities to channel natural hunting instincts.
Practise loose-leash walking and calm behaviour around wildlife.
Keep sessions varied and engaging, especially while the dog is young.
Teach household manners consistently and reinforce desired behaviour.
training.socialization: Introduce the dog positively and gradually to different people, calm dogs, everyday environments and common household situations. Supervise interactions with children and small pets, and train carefully around wildlife because the breed has a strong hunting background.

climates: Can live in a range of climates when exercise, shelter and care are adapted to conditions.
In hot weather, provide shade, water, ventilation and exercise during cooler hours.
In cold or wet conditions, provide a dry resting area and monitor comfort after outdoor work.
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: May struggle with long periods of isolation without appropriate training and enrichment; build alone-time tolerance gradually.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced diet appropriate to the dog's life stage, body condition, activity level and health.
nutrition.guidelines: Select a complete food suitable for the dog's age and expected adult size. Measure portions, monitor body condition and adjust intake to activity and weight changes. Fresh water should always be available. A veterinarian can help determine calorie needs, particularly for dogs doing sustained field work or those with medical concerns.
considerations: Working dogs may need different energy intake on active days than on rest days.
Avoid routinely feeding excess calories when exercise decreases.
Use treats in moderation and include them in daily intake.
Introduce food changes gradually unless a veterinarian advises otherwise.
Seek veterinary advice for persistent digestive signs, appetite changes or unexpected weight loss.
nutrition.note: No universal Braque d'Auvergne-specific feeding quantity or meal schedule was established in the consulted sources. Individual needs vary with age, activity, body condition and health.

health.overview: The breed is described by some breed profiles as generally hardy, but veterinary ophthalmology references list several ocular disorders that have been reported or presumed to have an inherited component. Breed-club guidance also highlights hip scoring and attention to eyelid disorders. These sources do not provide a reliable prevalence estimate for the conditions listed below, so they should be treated as points for breeder discussion and veterinary assessment rather than predictions about an individual dog.
commonConditions: Entropion, an inward rolling of an eyelid, reported in breed-specific veterinary eye references
Distichiasis, in which extra eyelashes may irritate the eye
Other reported eyelid or third-eyelid disorders described in veterinary ophthalmology references
Hip dysplasia, for which breed-club guidance recommends attention to parental screening
preventiveCare: Arrange regular veterinary examinations and age-appropriate preventive care.
Ask breeders for documented hip-screening results for both parents.
Seek veterinary assessment for squinting, eye discharge, redness or signs of ocular pain.
Maintain dental hygiene, nail care, parasite prevention and a healthy body condition.
After field exercise, check ears, paws and coat for grass seeds, ticks, cuts or other debris.
Discuss the individual dog's lifestyle and any family history with a veterinarian.
recommendedScreenings: Hip evaluation or scoring, particularly when assessing breeding dogs
Veterinary eye examination when indicated by the dog's history, symptoms or breeding programme
Discuss breed-relevant ocular findings with the breeder and veterinarian
Confirm current recommended tests with the relevant national breed club or kennel club
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste and arrange veterinary oral checks. Ask a veterinarian about a dental-care plan if there is persistent bad breath, gum inflammation, oral pain or difficulty eating.
health.earCare: Inspect the pendant ears regularly, particularly after outdoor work. Clean only when needed with a veterinarian-approved product, and seek advice for redness, odour, discharge or persistent head shaking.
health.skinCare: Inspect the short coat and skin after outdoor activity for parasites, cuts, irritation or plant material. Seek veterinary advice for persistent itching, sores, lumps or unusual hair loss.

notIdealFor: People who prefer a low-exercise companion
Households unable to provide regular outdoor activity

funFacts: The breed has been associated with the Cantal region of France for more than two centuries.
Its coat has two recognised marking patterns, commonly described as flecked or greying.
The breed was developed for hunting and pointing, and its stamina is an important part of its traditional function.
The FCI standard mentions a possible historical contribution from the Knights of Malta, but does not present that ancestry as certain.
The breed's black-and-white coat can create a blue-toned appearance at a distance.

faq.question: How tall is a Braque d'Auvergne?
faq.answer: The FCI standard gives a height of 57–63 cm for males and 53–59 cm for females. It also specifies a tolerance of +2 cm and −1 cm around those ranges, with ideal heights of 60 cm for males and 56 cm for females.

faq.question: What colours does the Braque d'Auvergne come in?
faq.answer: The standard describes a black-and-white coat with variable white markings and two recognised patterns: flecked and greying. The head is generally black, often with a white blaze.

faq.question: Is the Braque d'Auvergne a good family dog?
faq.answer: It can be affectionate and gentle with its household, but its working background creates substantial exercise and training needs. Families should supervise all interactions between children and dogs and consider whether they can meet the breed's activity requirements.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Braque d'Auvergne need?
faq.answer: It is an active pointing breed designed for sustained work. Plan for substantial daily activity, including walks, training and scent-based enrichment. Some breed profiles recommend two hours or more of exercise a day, but individual needs depend on age, health and conditioning.

faq.question: What health checks should I discuss with a breeder?
faq.answer: Ask for the parents' hip-screening records and discuss eye health with the breeder. Veterinary ophthalmology references list several reported or presumed inherited eye disorders, but they do not establish how frequently these occur across the breed.

faq.question: Is the Braque d'Auvergne suitable for apartment living?
faq.answer: It is generally better suited to a home that can provide substantial exercise and easy access to outdoor activities. Apartment living may be difficult if the dog's daily exercise, scenting and training needs cannot be met.

overview.summary: A noble, substantial continental pointing dog native to southwestern France, prized for its chestnut-and-white coat, keen scenting ability, methodical working endurance, and docile, gentle temperament at home.
overview.description: The Braque Français (Gascogne)—also known as the French Pointing Dog of Gascogne type or Grande Taille—is a powerful, medium-to-large pointer of classic continental type. Possessing a substantial, well-muscled frame that remains athletic without coarseness, it is distinguished by a broad, rectangular muzzle, supple pendulous ears, a slight throat dewlap, and a dense, short coat of chestnut brown and white, frequently marked by extensive chestnut speckling. In the field, it is an enduring, methodical hunter that works close to the gun, points game with staunch conviction, and retrieves reliably from land and water. Indoors, it transforms into an affectionate, calm, and devoted family partner that forms close attachments with its household and thrives on patient, gentle handling.
overview.history: The Braque Français is one of the oldest continental pointing breeds, descending from ancient hunting and bird-dog stock established in the Pyrenees and southwestern France since at least the fourteenth century, when regional pointing dogs were described in Gaston Fébus's classic hunting treatises. For centuries, these dogs were selectively bred in Gascony for tracking, pointing, and retrieving partridge, woodcock, quail, and hare across rugged, brush-covered terrain. Over time, regional divergence produced two distinct types: the larger, ancestral Gascogne type and the smaller, lighter Pyrénées type. Conformation standards and dedicated club preservation began in France in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, and definitive international recognition followed in 1955. Today, the Gascogne type remains a respected, specialized hunting companion and cherished household dog that preserves the classic look and deliberate hunting style of the historic southern French pointer.

Maintain realistic expectations and exercise patience, as the breed matures at a steady, thoughtful pace.

health.overview: The Braque Français (Gascogne) is widely recognized as a robust, functional sporting dog with an average lifespan of 12 to 14 years and a low incidence of inherited genetic diseases. Because it is a medium-to-large, deep-chested hunting breed with pendulous ears and supple skin, health management focuses primarily on pre-breeding orthopedic evaluations for hip dysplasia, veterinary examination of eyelid conformation (checking for entropion or ectropion), and routine ear canal hygiene. Breed club regulations in its home country require breeding stock to undergo radiographic hip dysplasia screening and conformation confirmation.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia: a multifactorial joint development disorder monitored through pre-breeding radiographic screening in breeding programs
Conformation-related eyelid abnormalities: mild entropion (inward-turning eyelid) or ectropion (outward-sagging eyelid) can occasionally occur in dogs with looser facial skin
Otitis externa: pendulous ears restrict air circulation in the ear canal, increasing susceptibility to moisture buildup and bacterial or yeast infections
Gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat): a potential acute risk in deep-chested sporting dogs, manageable through divided meals and resting after feeding
Field-related injuries: minor cuts, torn pads, broken nails, or grass seeds encountered while hunting through dense brambles and rough cover
preventiveCare: Ensure that prospective puppies come from parents with certified pre-breeding hip dysplasia clearances and verified conformation evaluations.
Inspect, clean, and dry the pendulous ears weekly and after every swim or wet field excursion.
Check paws, coat, and skin folds for burrs, thorns, cuts, or ticks following outdoor runs.
Feed multiple smaller meals daily and avoid vigorous galloping or exercise directly before or after eating.
Maintain a lean body condition and keep core veterinary wellness visits, vaccinations, and parasite prevention up to date.
recommendedScreenings: Hip dysplasia radiographic evaluation (certified through recognized veterinary scoring schemes prior to breeding)
Ophthalmic examination by a veterinarian to ensure normal eyelid conformation (absence of entropion or ectropion)
Pre-breeding breeding soundness and conformation evaluation (confirmation), including complete dentition and bite check
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth regularly with dog-safe toothpaste and arrange veterinary dental checks as needed. Conformation standards require strong jaws with a complete, evenly spaced scissor or level bite (overshot or undershot bites are disqualifying faults).
health.earCare: Check the pendulous ears regularly for redness, discharge, foul odour, or discomfort. Use a veterinarian-recommended ear-cleaning solution when necessary, wiping gently with cotton and keeping the ear canals dry.
health.skinCare: The supple, loose skin and short coat require only periodic brushing. Inspect the throat dewlap and skin folds for moisture or chaffing, and check the skin after field outings for scrapes, ticks, or irritation.

funFacts: The Braque Français is among the oldest pointing breeds in western Europe, with historical references dating back to fourteenth-century southern French hunting manuscripts by Gaston Fébus.
The breed exists in two officially recognized types: the larger, ancestral Gascogne type (standing up to 69 cm) and the smaller, lighter Pyrénées type (standing under 58 cm).
In traditional French hunting lore, the Gascogne type was renowned for its deliberate, methodical pace, allowing hunters to follow easily on foot across rugged hills.
Unlike many modern pointing dogs that were crossed with English Pointers for speed, the Gascogne type preserved its distinctive hound-like head, pendulous ears, and throat dewlap.
Puppies often demonstrate a remarkably strong natural pointing instinct from an early age, spontaneously freezing on point at scent or moving birds without formal instruction.
Despite its imposing size and energetic hunting stamina, it is celebrated for an exceptionally docile, gentle, and affectionate nature inside the family home.

faq.question: What is a Braque Français (Gascogne)?
faq.answer: The Braque Français (Gascogne)—also called the French Pointing Dog of Gascogne type or Grande Taille—is a noble, medium-to-large continental pointing breed originating in southwestern France. It is renowned for its chestnut-and-white coat, methodical hunting style, and gentle household temperament.

faq.question: How big does a Braque Français (Gascogne) get?
faq.answer: Conformation standards specify a withers height of 58 to 69 cm (with an ideal range of 61 to 63 cm) for males and 56 to 68 cm for females. Typical adult weight ranges between 24 and 32 kg (53 to 70 pounds) for both sexes.

faq.question: What is the difference between the Gascogne type and the Pyrénées type?
faq.answer: They are two distinct varieties of the Braque Français. The Gascogne type is larger, more substantial in bone, has longer ears and a noticeable throat dewlap, and hunts at a deliberate, methodical pace. The Pyrénées type is smaller (standing under 58 cm), lighter, has shorter ears and minimal dewlap, and hunts at a faster, wider gallop.

faq.question: What coat colours are typical for the Braque Français (Gascogne)?
faq.answer: The coat is chestnut brown, either solid brown, mixed with white, or heavily speckled (ticked) with chestnut brown. Pale tan markings above the eyes, on the lips, and on the legs are also accepted.

faq.question: What is the temperament of the Braque Français (Gascogne)?
faq.answer: It is exceptionally gentle, docile, and submissive indoors, forming strong, affectionate bonds with its family. In the field, it displays keen hunting drive and steady endurance, working in close cooperation with its handler.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Braque Français (Gascogne) need?
faq.answer: As an energetic sporting breed, it requires substantial daily physical activity, including brisk leashed walks, off-leash running in secure enclosures, and mental stimulation through scent tracking, pointing drills, or retrieval games.

faq.question: Is the Braque Français (Gascogne) suitable for apartment living?
faq.answer: Generally no. Because of its large size, high exercise needs, and working heritage, it is much better suited to a home with a fenced yard in a rural or suburban environment with access to natural open spaces.

faq.question: What health tests are recommended for breeding dogs?
faq.answer: Breed-club health protocols recommend pre-breeding radiographic screening for hip dysplasia, veterinary examination of eyelid conformation (checking for entropion or ectropion), and confirmation of correct dentition and bite.

faq.question: How long does a Braque Français (Gascogne) live?
faq.answer: The typical life expectancy is 12 to 14 years when provided with appropriate exercise, balanced nutrition, and routine veterinary care.

faq.question: Is the Braque Français (Gascogne) easy to train?
faq.answer: Yes. The breed is naturally cooperative, intelligent, and eager to please, making it very responsive to reward-based training. However, it has a sensitive temperament and will shut down under harsh scolding or forceful methods.

overview.summary: A medium-to-large French pointing dog with a short white coat marked in fawn or orange, developed for energetic and cooperative game-bird hunting.
overview.description: The Braque Saint-Germain is an athletic French gun dog recognised for its white coat with orange-fawn markings, balanced proportions, and smooth, purposeful movement. Its head has a moderately defined stop and a muzzle that is parallel to, or only slightly divergent from, the skull in profile. The coat is short, and the breed's outline combines substantial bone with musculature suited to sustained work. Traditionally used to locate and point game birds, it can also work on furred game. Breed descriptions portray it as affectionate, sociable, and responsive to patient handling. Its working heritage means that exercise, outdoor exploration, scent-based activities, and considerate training are important parts of responsible ownership.
overview.history: The breed developed in France around 1830 from dogs produced by crossing an English Pointer with a continental pointing dog. It was first associated with the royal kennels at Compiègne and later became known by its connection with Saint-Germain-en-Laye when the kennels moved. The breed became prominent at early French dog shows, including the first French dog show in 1863. Its French breed club was founded in March 1913, and the FCI granted definitive recognition in 1954.

faq.question: Where does the Braque Saint-Germain originate?
faq.answer: It originates in France and was developed around 1830 from an English Pointer and a continental pointing dog. Its history is associated with Compiègne and later Saint-Germain-en-Laye.

faq.question: How tall is a Braque Saint-Germain?
faq.answer: The FCI standard gives 56–62 cm at the withers for males and 54–59 cm for females. It also describes an additional 2 cm tolerance for exceptional specimens.

faq.question: What colour is its coat?
faq.answer: The standard describes a dull white coat with orange or fawn markings. Some mottling is tolerated, but is not preferred.

faq.question: What was the breed developed to do?
faq.answer: It was developed as a pointing dog, mainly for feathered game such as pheasant, partridge, and woodcock. Breed descriptions also mention work on furred game.

faq.question: Is the Braque Saint-Germain easy to train?
faq.answer: Breed descriptions characterise it as intelligent and responsive to training. Patient, consistent, reward-based methods are appropriate; harsh handling is not recommended.

faq.question: How much does a Braque Saint-Germain weigh?
faq.answer: The FCI standard does not specify a breed-specific weight range, so this record does not provide a numerical weight estimate.

faq.question: What is its life expectancy?
faq.answer: Published breed profiles give estimates that differ. A 10–14 year range is recorded here as an approximate range, not a guarantee for an individual dog.

faq.question: Which health tests should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: A dependable breed-specific screening schedule was not established from the sources consulted. Ask the breeder for documented health information about the parents and family line, and discuss appropriate checks with a veterinarian.

faq.question: Can it live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Apartment suitability depends on the individual dog and the household's ability to provide exercise, enrichment, and training. This record rates apartment living cautiously because the breed was developed for active field work.

overview.summary: The Brittany is a medium-sized, energetic pointing dog developed in France to locate and work game birds. It combines an athletic build, a keen nose, quick movement, and a close working relationship with its handler. The breed generally suits people who enjoy outdoor activities and can provide consistent training, exercise, and mental enrichment.
overview.description: The Brittany is a compact, leggy sporting dog with an alert expression and an agile, balanced build. Its coat is relatively short to medium in appearance, usually flat or slightly wavy, with some feathering. Orange-and-white and liver-and-white patterns are familiar, while recognised colour descriptions can vary between kennel-club standards. Some Brittanys are naturally born with a very short tail or no visible tail. Bred for practical work in the field, the breed is known for its stamina, scenting ability, responsiveness, and enthusiasm for finding game. Those same qualities make structured activity and humane training important parts of life as a companion dog.
overview.history: The breed developed in the Brittany region of north-western France and became established as a versatile pointing dog. A breed-standard draft was prepared in 1907 and adopted at a breed-club meeting in 1908. The Brittany was later developed and recognised in different countries under slightly different naming and registration conventions. In the United States, the American Kennel Club registered it as the Brittany Spaniel for many years before changing the registered name to Brittany in 1982.
overview.originalPurpose: Locating and pointing game birds for hunters, with a compact and agile build suited to working across varied field terrain.
currentRoles: Agility, obedience, and other structured canine sports
Active companion for households able to provide regular exercise and training

physical.coatType: Fine, relatively short coat that lies flat or may be slightly wavy, with some feathering.
physical.coatLength: Short to medium; feathering may be present on areas such as the ears, legs, and underside.
coatColors: Roan patterns associated with recognised colour combinations
Other combinations described by particular kennel-club standards, including black-and-white or tricolour patterns under the FCI standard
distinctiveFeatures: Compact, athletic body with relatively long legs
Alert expression and high-set ears
Quick, agile movement suited to field work
Short or naturally absent tail in some individuals
Flat or slightly wavy coat with some feathering
Strong interest in scenting and finding game

traits: Energetic and enthusiastic about activity
Alert and attentive to its surroundings
Intelligent and generally responsive to reward-based training
Athletic and well suited to structured outdoor activities
Strongly motivated by scenting and hunting-related tasks
Often sociable, while individual behaviour varies with breeding, experience, and socialisation
Likely to benefit from regular mental challenges as well as physical exercise

exercise.level: High. The Brittany was developed as an active sporting dog and typically needs regular opportunities to move, explore, use its nose, and learn. The amount of activity should be adjusted to age, health, fitness, and the individual dog's behaviour.
activities: Brisk daily walks with controlled opportunities to sniff and explore
Secure-area running and play appropriate to the dog's fitness
Scent games and structured search activities
Reward-based recall practice in safe, enclosed spaces
Hiking or other outdoor activities with suitable conditioning
Agility, obedience, field work, or other supervised dog sports
Food puzzles and training games for mental enrichment

grooming.level: Low to moderate. The coat is relatively easy to maintain, but regular brushing and routine checks remain important.
grooming.brushing: Brush regularly with a suitable dog brush to remove loose hair and debris, check the skin, and maintain the coat. Pay attention to any feathering where tangles or outdoor debris can collect.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when necessary, such as after muddy outdoor activity or when the coat is dirty. Use a dog-formulated shampoo and rinse thoroughly.
notes: Check the ears regularly for dirt, redness, odour, or discharge, especially after outdoor activity.
Inspect the coat and skin for ticks, burrs, scratches, and other debris after field walks.
Trim nails as needed and check paw pads after running or walking on rough ground.
Brush the teeth regularly with dog-safe toothpaste.
Increase coat checks when the dog spends a lot of time in dense grass or woodland.

training.difficulty: Moderate. The breed is generally responsive to engaging training, but its energy and hunting interests mean that consistency and practical management are important.
tips: Use reward-based training with clear, consistent cues.
Begin recall training early and practise it in gradually more distracting environments.
Teach calm behaviour as well as active skills so the dog can settle at home.
Use scent games and appropriate retrieving activities to channel natural working interests.
Keep sessions varied and engaging, with short repetitions and clear rewards.
Use a secure area or lead where wildlife, traffic, or other hazards make off-lead activity unsafe.
training.socialization: Introduce the dog gradually and positively to different people, environments, sounds, surfaces, and other suitable dogs. Continue training throughout adolescence and adulthood, and tailor introductions to the individual dog's comfort and behaviour.

climates: Provide shade, fresh water, and rest breaks in warm weather.
Adjust exercise to temperature, humidity, age, and physical condition.
In cold or wet conditions, provide appropriate shelter and dry the coat when needed.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced dog food appropriate to the dog's life stage, body condition, activity level, and individual health needs.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Use age-appropriate puppy food and divide the daily amount into meals according to the food label and veterinary advice.
feedingFrequency.adult: Feed measured portions of an appropriate adult diet, adjusting the amount to maintain a healthy body condition and support activity.
feedingFrequency.senior: Choose a diet and feeding schedule suited to the dog's age, body condition, dental health, and any veterinary-identified needs.

nutrition.guidelines: Base feeding amounts on the dog's age, weight, body condition, activity, and the calorie content of the food rather than a single breed-wide quantity. Measure meals, account for training treats, provide clean water at all times, and adjust portions if weight changes. Consult a veterinarian when selecting a therapeutic diet or when persistent digestive, skin, or weight concerns occur.
considerations: Monitor body condition rather than relying on weight alone.
Account for treats and training rewards in the daily food allowance.
Provide fresh water, particularly after exercise and in warm weather.
Avoid sudden diet changes; transition foods gradually when practical.
Ask a veterinarian about nutrition for puppies, pregnancy, illness, or other special circumstances.
nutrition.note: Individual calorie needs vary considerably. This record does not prescribe a fixed serving size or a breed-specific supplement.

health.overview: Brittanys are often described as generally healthy, but no breed is free of inherited or age-related health problems. Breed-club recommendations emphasise hip evaluation and eye examinations, alongside an additional screening selected from several health areas. These recommendations are intended to support responsible breeding and are not a diagnosis or a statement that every Brittany will develop these conditions.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia is an inherited joint-development concern for which screening is recommended.
Eye disorders are a recognised reason for breeder screening and veterinary eye examinations.
Epilepsy or other seizure disorders have been identified as concerns in breed-club breeding guidance.
Heart, elbow, patellar, and thyroid conditions are included among the additional screening areas recommended by the breed club.
preventiveCare: Arrange routine veterinary examinations and keep vaccinations appropriate to the dog's age and lifestyle.
Use veterinarian-recommended parasite prevention.
Maintain healthy body condition and adjust activity gradually to fitness.
Discuss any repeated lameness, changes in vision, unusual episodes, or reduced exercise tolerance with a veterinarian.
Ask breeders for documented health-screening results and the relevant details for the puppy's parents.
recommendedScreenings: Hip evaluation through an accepted scheme such as OFA or PennHIP.
Eye examination by a qualified veterinary ophthalmologist; the breed-club recommendation specifies annual examinations from 2 to 8 years of age.
One additional screening submitted to OFA, selected from cardiac evaluation, elbow dysplasia, patellar luxation, or thyroid evaluation from an approved laboratory.
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with dog-safe toothpaste. Have the mouth checked during routine veterinary visits and seek advice about persistent bad breath, bleeding gums, pain, or difficulty eating.
health.earCare: Inspect the ears regularly, especially after field activity. Clean only as needed with a dog-safe product recommended by a veterinarian; seek advice for redness, discharge, odour, or repeated head shaking.
health.skinCare: Check the skin and coat during grooming for parasites, scratches, irritation, or new lumps. Seek veterinary advice for persistent itching, hair loss, sores, or changes that do not resolve.

idealFor: People who enjoy regular outdoor activity and structured training
Handlers interested in scent work, field work, or dog sports
Households prepared to provide daily exercise and mental enrichment
Owners willing to train reliable recall and manage hunting interests safely
notIdealFor: Households looking for a consistently low-energy dog with minimal activity needs
Owners who cannot provide regular exercise and enrichment
People who expect reliable off-lead behaviour without training and safe management
Homes where the dog would routinely be left without sufficient interaction or activity

funFacts: The breed takes its name from Brittany, the French region where it developed.
The Brittany is recognised as a pointing dog and is known for working closely with its handler in the field.
Some Brittanys are born with a naturally short tail or no visible tail.
The American Kennel Club changed the registered name from Brittany Spaniel to Brittany in 1982.
The breed's sporting abilities can also be channelled into activities such as agility, obedience, and scent-based games.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Brittany need?
faq.answer: Brittanys are active sporting dogs and generally need regular daily exercise plus mental enrichment. The right amount varies with age, health, fitness, and the individual dog, so this record does not prescribe a universal number of minutes.

faq.question: Is the Brittany easy to train?
faq.answer: Many Brittanys respond well to positive, engaging training. Their energy and interest in scent and wildlife make recall, lead skills, impulse control, and safe outdoor management especially useful.

faq.question: What is the typical lifespan of a Brittany?
faq.answer: The American Kennel Club lists a typical life expectancy of 12–14 years. An individual dog's lifespan depends on genetics, healthcare, lifestyle, and other factors.

faq.question: What colours can a Brittany have?
faq.answer: Orange-and-white and liver-and-white are familiar Brittany colours. Recognised colour descriptions differ between kennel-club standards, so the applicable registry standard should be checked when colour matters for registration or showing.

faq.question: What health checks should a Brittany breeder provide?
faq.answer: Breed-club recommendations include hip evaluation, eye examinations, and an additional screening chosen from cardiac, elbow, patellar, or thyroid evaluation. Ask for actual results and discuss their meaning with a veterinarian.

faq.question: Can a Brittany live in an apartment?
faq.answer: An apartment is not automatically suitable or unsuitable for every Brittany. Suitability depends on the dog's individual needs and whether the owner can provide enough exercise, enrichment, training, and opportunities to settle. The available sources do not establish a universal yes-or-no rule.

overview.summary: A commanding, heavy-boned Romanian Carpathian mountain guardian with a weatherproof pied double coat, a calm and devoted nature with its family and children, and a fearless, booming nocturnal instinct to protect flocks and property.
overview.description: The Bucovina Shepherd Dog (Ciobănesc Românesc de Bucovina)—traditionally called 'Dulău' or 'Căpău' by Carpathian shepherds—is the largest and most massively built of Romania's four native shepherd dog breeds. Standing 68 to 78 cm at the withers in males (ideally 71 to 75 cm) and 64 to 72 cm in females (ideally 66 to 68 cm), with well-marked sexual dimorphism, it combines a proud, haughty carriage with a muscular, slightly rectangular body and an effortless, ground-covering trot. Its massive head is carried slightly above the horizontal topline, featuring a skull and blunt truncated-cone muzzle of equal length, small oblique chestnut-brown almond eyes, and high-set V-shaped pendant ears carried close to the cheeks. Protected by thick dark ash-grey skin and a straight, coarse 6 to 9 cm outer coat over a dense, lighter-coloured undercoat, it carries a prominent neck mane, limb feathering, hind-leg breeches ('culottes'), and a bushy tail that rises in a sickle curve when alert. Calm, balanced, and affectionate with familiar people and children, it is deeply wary of strangers, patrols its boundaries at night, and signals approaching intruders or predators with a resonant, low-toned bark audible over long distances.
overview.history: An ancient natural landrace of the Carpathian Mountains, the breed was shaped over centuries in the Bucovina region of north-eastern Romania, where transhumant shepherds seasonally drove sheep flocks and cattle herds between lowland winter pastures and high alpine summer meadows. Selected for courage, physical power, and endurance, these dogs defended livestock against brown bears, wolves, and Eurasian lynx while also guarding rural homesteads; on open mountain pastures, working dogs traditionally wear a wooden neck stave or dangle ('jujău') suspended from a chain to signal ownership and prevent them from chasing wild game. First noted in Romanian veterinary literature in the 1930s under the local names 'Dulău' and 'Căpău', the breed received its first formal written standard in 1982, followed by national updates in 2001, March 2002, and August 2004 (at Gura Humorului). Internationally, it was granted provisional recognition on 26 March 2009 (initially known internationally as the Southeastern European Shepherd) and achieved definitive recognition on 29 April 2019, with the current international standard dated 20 August 2023 (published 1 September 2023). Between 2020 and 2024 alone, 1,984 puppies of the breed were registered in the Romanian national studbook—making it the most numerous of Romania's four native shepherd breeds in recent national registrations—and in February 2019 it was honoured on a Romanian postage stamp.
overview.originalPurpose: Guarding sheep flocks and cattle herds against large Carpathian predators (brown bears, wolves, and lynx) during seasonal transhumance, and serving as a nocturnal watchdog for rural households and estates.
currentRoles: Working livestock and flock guardian for sheep and cattle
Rural estate, farm, and property watchdog
Devoted family companion for experienced guardian-breed households with secure land
Conformation and national heritage dog-show participant

physical.coatType: Harsh, weather-resistant double coat consisting of a flat, straight, coarse outer coat (6 to 9 cm long on the body) over a shorter, very dense, supple, lighter-coloured undercoat, with short hair on the head and front of the legs, a prominent neck mane, moderate fringes on the backs of the forelegs, longer breeches ('culottes') on the backs of the hindquarters, and a bushy tail.
physical.coatLength: Long (body hair 6 to 9 cm / 2.4 to 3.5 inches; hair shorter than 6 cm or longer than 9 cm is faulted)
coatColors: Clear white with well-defined grey (sandy-charcoal / wolf-grey) patches
Clear white with well-defined black patches
Clear white with well-defined black patches showing red-fawn reflections
White-beige (yellowish-white) with well-defined black patches or black patches with red-fawn reflections (black or grey ticking may appear on the legs, whereas brindle-patterned patches are rejected)
Solid white, white-beige, ashen-grey, or black without patches (accepted, though not encouraged)
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate to heavy, particularly during spring and autumn seasonal coat changes when the dense undercoat sheds heavily.
distinctiveFeatures: Commanding, proud, and powerful mountain-molossoid build with strongly marked sexual dimorphism (males taller and heavier than females) and body length slightly exceeding withers height

Massive head carried slightly above the horizontal topline, with a moderately wide skull (16–18 cm in males, 15–17 cm in females) equal in length to the blunt, truncated-cone muzzle (1:1 ratio), slightly divergent upper craniofacial planes, and a slightly pronounced stop
Large, broad black nose, thick tight-fitting darkly pigmented lips, and strong jaws with a complete white scissor bite (level/pincer bite tolerated) and a thick, strong neck free of dewlap
Small, obliquely set almond-shaped eyes in chestnut brown or slightly lighter (never yellow, and never heterochromic/wall-eyed), framed by well-pigmented eyelids
Relatively high-set, V-shaped pendant ears with slightly rounded tips carried close to the cheeks (ear cropping is prohibited)

Broad, deep chest reaching the elbows with well-arched ribs, muscular horizontal back and loin, and strong-boned limbs with 100°–110° shoulder angulation, ~110° stifle angulation, oval compact feet with black or ash-grey nails, and unpenalized rear dewclaws

High-set bushy tail carried low to or below the hocks at rest and raised to back level or slightly higher in a sickle curve when alert or moving (never curled in a ring over the back; tail docking is prohibited)

Thick, tight-fitting dark ash-grey skin beneath a 6–9 cm coarse outer coat with a thick neck mane, foreleg fringes, and hind-leg culottes, typically in clear white or white-beige with distinct grey or black patches

Withers height of 68–78 cm (ideal 71–75 cm) for males and 64–72 cm (ideal 66–68 cm) for females with a ±4 cm tolerance (disqualifying below 64 cm or above 82 cm in males, and below 60 cm or above 78 cm in females), and weight proportionate to height (secondary working guides commonly report 50–80+ kg / 110–180+ lbs)

traits: Balanced, composed, and self-assured
Calm, loyal, and deeply devoted to its family
Fond of and patient with children in its own household
Courageous, resolute, and combative against large predators (bears, wolves, and lynx) threatening its flock
Naturally mistrustful and reserved toward strangers
Vigilant nocturnal patroller of flocks and property boundaries
Deep, powerful, low-toned warning bark that carries over long distances
Independent decision-maker bred to assess threats on its own
Never unprovokedly aggressive or overly shy (both are disqualifying faults)

exercise.level: Moderate, steady daily activity suited to an endurance patroller rather than a high-speed runner: regular country walks and room to patrol a securely fenced property, while avoiding forced high-impact exercise during the 18- to 24-month skeletal growth period.
activities: Daily leashed walks and countryside hikes suited to age, fitness, and weather
Supervised patrolling and free movement within a large, securely fenced rural yard or acreage
Active livestock-guardian work with sheep, goats, or cattle when raised and bonded for that role
Calm outdoor sniffing and environmental exploration
Short, purposeful reward-based manners and recall sessions
Low-impact mental enrichment and food puzzles

grooming.brushing: Brush thoroughly once or twice a week with a long-toothed undercoat rake, pin brush, or slicker brush—working all the way through the 6 to 9 cm outer coat and dense undercoat—and increase to daily brushing during heavy spring and autumn coat blows.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only when genuinely dirty (typically a few times a year) using a mild, dog-safe shampoo, rinsing and drying the dense double coat and undercoat thoroughly so moisture is not trapped against the dark ash-grey skin.
notes: Pay special attention to the thick neck mane, behind the ears, the foreleg fringes, the hind-leg breeches ('culottes'), and the bushy tail, where burrs, mud, and mats form first.
Never shave or clip a healthy double coat (hair shorter than 6 cm is a conformation fault), though excess hair between the paw pads may be neatened for traction and hygiene.
Inspect the high-set V-shaped pendant ears weekly for dirt, grass awns, ticks, moisture, redness, or odour.
Check the compact oval feet, black or ash-grey nails, and any rear dewclaws monthly, trimming nails if outdoor wear is insufficient.
Brush the teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste and accustom puppies early to calm grooming, dental, and veterinary handling.

training.difficulty: Challenging for novice handlers. Bred for centuries to make independent decisions while guarding flocks far from human direction, the Bucovina Shepherd quickly tires of repetitive obedience drills and requires an experienced, calm, and confident handler.
tips: Begin structured socialization and foundation manners early in puppyhood, well before adult territorial and guarding instincts mature around 12 to 18 months of age.
Use calm, fair, reward-based guidance and clear household boundaries; harsh physical punishment or intimidation can make a powerful guardian defensive and untrusting.
Keep training sessions brief, practical, and varied—focusing on loose-leash walking, recall, settling on cue, and controlled doorway/gate protocols.
Establish strict visitor-management routines so the owner—never the dog—decides who is welcomed onto the property, and never allow strangers to walk unannounced into the yard.
Enclose the property with tall, solid, gap-free physical fencing that prevents escaping and stops roaming animals or strangers from wandering into the dog's territory.
Be prepared for nocturnal patrolling and booming low-toned alert barking, which is a core working trait rather than a behavioural flaw.
training.socialization: Expose the puppy early, gradually, and positively to varied people, welcomed guests, children, calm dogs, livestock, and everyday sights and sounds. While the breed is naturally devoted to its own family and fond of children, it draws a sharp line between household members and outsiders as it matures; adult supervision around children and visitors and secure physical containment remain essential throughout life.

climates: Cool, alpine, and snowy mountain climates (for which the dense 6–9 cm double coat and thick undercoat are naturally adapted)
Temperate climates with ample outdoor space and shade
Warm weather only with abundant shade, cool resting areas, fresh water, and activity restricted to cooler morning and evening hours

nutrition.dietType: Complete and balanced, high-quality large- or giant-breed diet matched to the dog's life stage, workload (active flock guardian vs. rural companion), and lean body condition.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Several smaller measured meals daily using a large- or giant-breed puppy formula with controlled energy and calcium levels to support slow, steady skeletal growth until the growth plates close at 18 to 24 months.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two to three smaller measured meals daily rather than a single large meal, adjusted to actual physical workload and seasonal temperature.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two to three measured daily meals tailored to metabolism, mobility, dental health, and veterinary guidance.

nutrition.guidelines: Feed measured portions to keep the dog lean—especially during the first 18 to 24 months of skeletal development, when overfeeding or rapid weight gain increases mechanical stress on developing hips and elbows. Never add extra calcium, phosphorus, or vitamin supplements to a complete balanced ration unless prescribed by a veterinarian. Because the breed has a broad, deep chest reaching the elbows, help reduce the risk of life-threatening gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV or bloat) by dividing the daily ration into two or three smaller meals, ensuring calm mealtime conditions, and enforcing about an hour of rest before and after eating. Provide constant access to clean, fresh water.
considerations: Keep growing puppies lean so you can easily feel their ribs, using a controlled-growth large-breed puppy formula to help minimize hip and elbow dysplasia severity.
Do not add extra calcium or mineral supplements during growth unless specifically directed by a veterinarian.
Divide daily food into two or three smaller meals and restrict vigorous activity for an hour before and after meals to reduce bloat (GDV) risk.
Adjust adult calorie intake to actual workload—an active flock guardian patrolling mountain pastures in winter burns far more energy than a companion guarding a fenced yard.
Keep treats to no more than 10 percent of daily caloric intake, and ban cooked or poultry bones that can splinter and perforate the digestive tract.
nutrition.note: No fixed universal daily calorie or gram quota is established for the breed; tailor portion sizes with a veterinarian according to individual size, body condition, and workload.

health.overview: The Bucovina Shepherd Dog is a hardy, rustic Carpathian mountain guardian shaped by centuries of working selection (with typical longevity estimates ranging from 10 to 13 or 12 to 14 years), while population-wide epidemiological disease prevalence studies remain limited. Under conformation rules, only functionally and clinically healthy dogs with typical conformation may be used for breeding, and obesity, lack of vigour, missing teeth (other than PM1), yellow or heterochromic eyes, and physical or behavioural anomalies are penalized or disqualified. In Romania, official breeding regulations include the Bucovina Shepherd Dog on the mandatory screening table for radiographic hip dysplasia (HD, minimum age 12 months, accepted breeding grade up to C) and elbow dysplasia (ED, minimum age 12 months, accepted breeding grade up to 1) scored by accredited readers, alongside a mandatory breeding-selection examination from 15 months of age verifying body measurements, coat, pigmentation, complete dentition, balanced temperament, and movement. As with other heavy-boned, deep-chested giant guardians, attentive owners also monitor for gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat) and maintain routine dental, ear, parasite, and coat care.
preventiveCare: When acquiring a puppy, request documented parent breeding-selection approvals and official radiographic hip (HD) and elbow (ED) dysplasia clearances.
Feed a controlled-growth large-breed diet during puppyhood, keep the dog lean throughout life, and avoid forced high-impact jumping or road running before skeletal maturity (18 to 24 months).

Reduce gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat) risk by feeding two to three smaller meals daily, keeping mealtimes calm, resting the dog for an hour before and after meals, and seeking immediate emergency veterinary care for abdominal distension, unproductive retching, or sudden distress.
Part the dense double coat weekly and after outdoor work to check the dark ash-grey skin and pendant ears for ticks, burrs, grass awns, moisture, or irritation.
Maintain regular tooth brushing with dog-safe toothpaste, routine nail and dewclaw trims, and up-to-date vaccinations and parasite prevention.

Keep working and companion dogs behind secure physical fencing (and observe local legal requirements such as the traditional wooden 'jujău' neck stave on free-ranging pastoral dogs in Romania) to prevent wildlife conflicts and road trauma.
recommendedScreenings: Hip dysplasia (HD) radiographic evaluation from a minimum age of 12 months by an accredited reader (mandatory for breeding stock in Romania, with grades A, B, or C accepted for breeding).

Elbow dysplasia (ED) radiographic evaluation from a minimum age of 12 months by an accredited reader (included on the mandatory breeding screening table in Romania, with grades 0 or 1 accepted for breeding).

Pre-breeding selection and measurement examination (ADR, mandatory in Romania from 15 months of age for microchipped dogs) assessing body biometrics, coat and undercoat quality, eye/nose/mucosa pigmentation, complete dentition and scissor/level bite, normal descended testicles in males, and calm, balanced temperament.
Optional veterinary ophthalmic and cardiac evaluations prior to breeding where available.
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth several times a week with dog-specific toothpaste and schedule annual veterinary oral examinations. Conformation rules require strong jaws and a complete set of healthy, well-implanted white teeth meeting in a scissor bite (with a level/pincer bite tolerated, missing teeth other than PM1 penalized as a fault, and missing incisors or canines or overshot/undershot jaws disqualified).
health.earCare: Inspect the high-set, V-shaped pendant ears weekly—especially after work in brush, forests, or wet weather—for ticks, plant debris, excess wax, redness, or foul odour. Clean gently only as advised by a veterinarian and never insert cotton swabs deep into the ear canal.
health.skinCare: Part the 6 to 9 cm coarse outer coat and dense undercoat during weekly brushing to inspect the thick, tight-fitting dark ash-grey skin for parasites, damp undercoat mats, scratches, or hot spots, and dry the coat thoroughly if the dog has been soaked.

idealFor: Experienced owners of large livestock-guardian or molossoid working breeds
Shepherds, smallholders, and farmers needing a courageous flock or herd guardian against large predators
Rural or edge-of-town households with a large, securely fenced property to patrol
Families who include the dog in household life while providing early socialization, calm authority, and strict visitor management
Owners comfortable with a booming nocturnal warning bark and heavy seasonal undercoat shedding
notIdealFor: First-time or permissive dog owners unaccustomed to managing a 50 to 80+ kg independent guardian
Apartments, flats, or dense urban neighbourhoods with close neighbours sensitive to loud nighttime barking
Properties with low, weak, or unfenced boundaries
Owners seeking an off-leash dog-park companion, a jogging partner, or rapid sport-style obedience compliance
Households expecting a dog that automatically welcomes every unfamiliar visitor or delivery person

funFacts: In its native Carpathian Mountains, shepherds have traditionally called the Bucovina Shepherd Dog 'Dulău' or 'Căpău', relying on it for centuries to defend sheep and cattle during seasonal transhumance against brown bears, wolves, and Eurasian lynx.

Under traditional Romanian pastoral law and custom, working flock dogs on open mountain pastures wear a 'jujău'—a wooden stick or stave hung from a chain around the neck in front of the chest—to show that the dog belongs to a shepherd and to hinder it from chasing fast wild game.

It is the largest and most heavily built of Romania's four national shepherd dog breeds—alongside the Romanian Mioritic Shepherd Dog, Romanian Carpathian Shepherd Dog, and Romanian Raven Shepherd Dog (Corb)—and led all four breeds with 1,984 national studbook registrations between 2020 and 2024.
At night, the breed patrols around the sheepfold or homestead and warns of approaching strangers or predators with a remarkably deep, low-toned bark that carries over vast mountain distances.

While its classic coat is clear white or white-beige with distinct grey or black patches (and brindle patches are rejected), solid white, white-beige, ashen-grey, or black coats are also accepted—though not encouraged—and both ear cropping and tail docking are strictly prohibited.
On 22 February 2019—two months before the breed received definitive international recognition—Romania honoured the Bucovina Shepherd Dog on an official Lei 8.50 national postage stamp.

faq.question: Where does the Bucovina Shepherd Dog come from, and what are its traditional names?
faq.answer: The breed originates from the Carpathian Mountains of north-eastern Romania, particularly the historic region of Bucovina. Known officially in Romanian as the Ciobănesc Românesc de Bucovina (and internationally prior to 2019 as the Southeastern European Shepherd), it has long been called 'Dulău' or 'Căpău' by local Romanian shepherds.

faq.question: What was the Bucovina Shepherd Dog bred to do?
faq.answer: It was developed by transhumant Carpathian shepherds to protect sheep flocks and cattle herds against large predators—specifically brown bears, wolves, and lynx—while moving between lowland and alpine pastures, as well as to guard rural homes and property at night.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is an adult Bucovina Shepherd Dog?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 68 to 78 cm (27 to 31 inches) at the withers, with an ideal height of 71 to 75 cm, and adult females stand 64 to 72 cm (25 to 28 inches), with an ideal height of 66 to 68 cm (a tolerance of ±4 cm applies, with heights below 64 cm or above 82 cm in males and below 60 cm or above 78 cm in females disqualified). Conformation rules state that weight must be in proportion to height without fixing a numerical range; in working and companion populations, secondary guides typically report adult weights of 50 to 80+ kg (110 to 180+ pounds).

faq.question: How does the Bucovina Shepherd Dog differ from Romania's other native shepherd breeds?
faq.answer: Romania has four native livestock-guardian breeds: the Bucovina Shepherd Dog is the heaviest and most molossoid in build, typically white or white-beige with well-defined grey or black patches and a 6 to 9 cm body coat; the Mioritic Shepherd Dog is a long-haired sheepdog covered from head to toe in rough hair at least 10 cm long; the Carpathian Shepherd Dog is a lighter, more lupoid wolf-grey dog (65–73 cm in males); and the Raven Shepherd Dog (Corb) has a coat that is at least 80 percent black with white chest and paw markings.

faq.question: Which coat colours and patterns are accepted, and are brindle patches allowed?
faq.answer: The classical coat is a clear white or white-beige ground colour with distinct, well-defined patches of grey (wolf-grey), black, or black with red-fawn reflections, sometimes with black or grey ticking on the legs. Solid white, white-beige, ashen-grey, or black dogs without patches are accepted but not encouraged. Brindle-patterned patches are explicitly rejected.

faq.question: How long does a Bucovina Shepherd Dog live?
faq.answer: A single definitive breed-wide lifespan range has not been established, so the structured lifespan field is kept null, though typical longevity estimates range from 10 to 13 or 12 to 14 years depending on genetics, controlled puppy growth, lean body condition, and preventive care.

faq.question: Is the Bucovina Shepherd Dog good with children and family?
faq.answer: Within its own household, the breed is calm, balanced, loyal, and noted for liking children. However, because it is a massive, powerful guardian that matures into a dog deeply wary of outsiders—including unfamiliar visiting children—interactions with children should always be supervised by an adult and visitors must be introduced calmly under the owner's control.

faq.question: Can a Bucovina Shepherd Dog live in an apartment or dense city neighbourhood?
faq.answer: No. Bred to patrol wide territories and signal approaching strangers or animals at night with a booming, low-toned bark that carries over long distances, a Bucovina Shepherd confined to an apartment or small urban yard quickly becomes restless and excessively vocal. It requires a securely fenced rural or semi-rural property and an experienced handler.

faq.question: What health screenings and breeding evaluations exist for the Bucovina Shepherd Dog?
faq.answer: In its country of origin, official breeding regulations require breeding dogs to undergo radiographic screening for hip dysplasia (HD, minimum age 12 months, accepted up to grade C) and elbow dysplasia (ED, minimum age 12 months, accepted up to grade 1) scored by accredited readers, as well as a mandatory breeding-selection examination from 15 months of age assessing body measurements, coat, pigmentation, complete dentition, movement, and calm temperament. Owners should also manage puppy growth carefully and take standard precautions against bloat (GDV).
