grooming.brushing: Brush once a week with a soft-bristle brush or rubber hound glove to remove loose hair and dust and keep the short, vitreous coat sleek and gleaming.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only occasionally as needed using a mild, dog-safe shampoo, and dry thoroughly afterward so the thin-skinned, low-body-fat dog does not become chilled.
notes: The short, close-lying single coat has no feathering and requires minimal upkeep compared with long- or double-coated breeds.
During the seasonal molt, slightly lighter, undefined coat patches may temporarily appear on the shoulders, sides of the neck, or thighs.
Inspect the large, erect, open-fronted ears every week for dust, plant debris, excess wax, redness, or odour, and clean gently if needed with soft gauze and a veterinarian-recommended ear cleanser.
Trim nails frequently if they do not wear down naturally on hard ground, as overly long nails cause foot discomfort and splaying.
Check the paw pads and interdigital spaces after runs over rocky, thorny, or hot terrain.
Brush teeth frequently with dog-specific toothpaste and accustom puppies early to calm, reward-based handling.

training.difficulty: Moderate; quick to learn and often more biddable than many traditional sighthounds, yet independent-minded and powerfully motivated by hunting instincts
tips: Use patient, upbeat, reward-based positive reinforcement; harsh physical or verbal corrections are counterproductive with this sensitive, primitive-type hound.
Give the dog a purposeful outlet—such as lure coursing, nose work, tracking, agility, rally, or obedience—to satisfy its inquisitive, working mind.
Practise recall in securely fenced enclosures, and never trust off-leash reliability near roads, highways, or open wildlife areas where a fleeting scent or movement can trigger an instant chase.
Provide secure physical fencing around yards, as Cirnechi are agile jumpers built to bound from rock to rock.
Supervise carefully and introduce household cats and small furry pets gradually, recognizing that high prey drive toward squirrels, rabbits, and outdoor cats is innate.
Start puppy training classes and broad socialization early so the dog develops confident manners around unfamiliar people and environments.
training.socialization: Begin gentle, positive exposure early in puppyhood to diverse people, friendly dogs, novel sights, sounds, and surfaces. Because primitive hunting hounds raised in isolation can become wary or diffident toward strangers, consistent early socialization is essential to nurture an outgoing, confident companion.

livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate. Despite its independent working drive in the field, the Cirneco bonds closely with its family, loves to stay alongside its people indoors, and should never be left isolated alone in a backyard or kennel for long periods.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality, complete and balanced dog food appropriate for the dog's life stage (puppy, adult, or senior), activity level, and individual health needs.
nutrition.guidelines: Feed measured portions of a nutritionally complete diet suited to the dog's age, weight, and workload. Monitor body condition so the dog maintains its lean, athletic silhouette with visible musculature and a gently rising underline without excess weight. Keep clean, fresh drinking water available at all times, and consult a veterinarian or breeder regarding individual portion sizes and diet questions.
considerations: Active coursing, hunting, or agility dogs require higher caloric intake than dogs in lighter companion routines.
Count training treats within the daily calorie allowance to prevent unwanted weight gain.
Avoid feeding unsafe human foods, cooked bones, or rich table scraps.
Transition between diets gradually over several days unless directed otherwise by a veterinarian.
Consult a veterinarian if unexplained weight loss, digestive upset, or changes in appetite occur.
nutrition.note: No universal numerical daily meal schedule is prescribed for puppies, adults, or seniors; determine meal frequency and portion sizes with a veterinarian based on the individual dog and food.

health.overview: The Cirneco dell'Etna is widely regarded as a hardy, long-lived breed with a typical life expectancy of 15 to 16 years and a historically low incidence of documented hereditary disease. In North America, no routine breed-wide health test requirements are currently mandated, while in Italy selected breeding registration (Riproduzione Selezionata) from 18 months of age requires radiographic hip dysplasia grading of HD A or B. However, because the global population derives from a relatively small gene pool—with genomic studies showing higher homozygosity in self-coloured fawn lines than in tan-and-white blazed lines—responsible breeders monitor genetic diversity and emerging research closely. In February 2024, a peer-reviewed genomic study identified an autosomal recessive frameshift deletion in exon 15 of the AMPD2 gene on chromosome 6 (c.2131delG / p.D711Mfs12Stop) as the likely cause of Cirneco oculo-neurological syndrome (CONS) in two male littermates that developed episodic head tremors and forelimb dyskinesia/atypical seizures at 2 to 2.5 years of age followed by progressive retinal degeneration (PRA) and cerebral white-matter thinning by 4 years of age. Genotyping of 35 Cirnechi found the variant only in the two affected littermates and three related carriers (including their shared grandmother and a related European dog), indicating that the mutation likely originated within a specific bloodline rather than being widespread across the breed. A targeted AMPD2 DNA test is available to help breeders screen breeding stock, prevent carrier-to-carrier matings, and avoid creating a genetic bottleneck.
preventiveCare: Schedule regular veterinary wellness examinations and maintain appropriate vaccination and parasite-prevention protocols (including vector protection against Leishmania infantum in endemic Mediterranean regions).
Maintain a lean, well-muscled body condition and provide safe, enclosed exercise to prevent traffic trauma—one of the primary real-world hazards for high-prey-drive hounds.

Monitor adult dogs for any episodic head bobbing, tremors, forelimb cramping, cervical pain, or signs of dim-light vision loss, and discuss targeted AMPD2 genetic testing or specialist ophthalmic and neurological evaluation with a veterinarian if signs or family history warrant.

For breeders, utilize pedigree analysis, genomic diversity tools, hip evaluations (where required for selected breeding), and AMPD2 carrier testing thoughtfully so deleterious recessive variants are managed without narrowing the breed's small gene pool.
Inspect the upright ears weekly for dirt or wax buildup, brush the teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste, and keep nails trimmed short.
Check paw pads, nails, and thin skin for cuts, thorns, or abrasions after running on rocky or brushy terrain, and provide a warm coat in cold or wet weather.
recommendedScreenings: No routine breed-wide mandatory health test panel is currently established in North American registration programs.
Hip dysplasia radiographic screening (graded HD A or B) is required from 18 months of age for dogs entering the Italian Selected Breeding Register (Riproduzione Selezionata).

Targeted DNA testing for the AMPD2 frameshift variant (c.2131delG on chromosome 6, associated with Cirneco oculo-neurological syndrome / CONS) is recommended by veterinary geneticists and breed health foundations to monitor allele frequency and avoid carrier-to-carrier matings, particularly in related bloodlines.
Ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist and neurological assessment are advised for any dog displaying visual deficits, tremors, or paroxysmal movement episodes.
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth frequently using dog-specific toothpaste and a soft canine toothbrush, and schedule periodic veterinary dental assessments. Conformation standards require a complete, regular scissor bite with incisors set square to the jaws (absence of PM1 and M3 premolars/molars is permissible under international rules).
health.earCare: Inspect the high-set, rigid upright ears every week for dust, plant awns, excess wax, redness, or unusual odour, especially after field runs. Clean gently when needed using soft gauze and a veterinarian-recommended ear-cleaning solution, and never insert cotton swabs deep into the ear canal.
health.skinCare: Examine the fine, taut skin and short, vitreous coat during weekly brushing for scratches, ticks, or irritation, noting that minor honourable working scars are never penalized in conformation. Protect the paw pads on rough lava rock or hot pavement, and provide warm bedding and cold-weather clothing when temperatures drop.

idealFor: Active individuals and families who enjoy daily walks, hiking, lure coursing, scent work, or agility
Experienced hound or primitive-breed handlers who appreciate a lively, alert, independent-minded companion
Households with a securely fenced yard or consistent access to safe, enclosed running areas
Owners who want an affectionate, clean, low-odour indoor dog that loves cuddling under blankets after exercise
People committed to patient, gentle, reward-based training and careful management around wildlife
notIdealFor: Owners seeking reliable off-leash recall in unfenced areas near roads or wildlife
Households with cats, rabbits, or small furry pets where strong chasing instincts cannot be safely managed
Sedentary homes unable to provide daily physical exercise and mental stimulation
People who plan to leave a dog isolated outdoors or alone for long workdays without companionship
Handlers who use harsh, forceful, or punitive training methods

funFacts: Between the fifth and second centuries BC, Greek cities across Sicily minted hundreds of coin varieties bearing the image of a prick-eared hound remarkably similar to the modern Cirneco dell'Etna.

The breed takes its name from Mount Etna, Europe's largest active volcano on the east coast of Sicily, where it leaps sure-footedly across jagged volcanic lava fields in pursuit of wild rabbits; the suffix 'dell'Etna' was officially added when the first breed standard was approved in 1939.

In 1932, after Adrano veterinarian Dr. Maurizio Migneco warned that the ancient Sicilian hound was nearing extinction, Baroness Agata Paternò Castello dei Duchi di Carcaci ('Donna Aga') spent 26 years reviving the breed under her Aetnensis kennel affix.

Unlike pure sighthounds that rely mainly on vision, the Cirneco is a triple-sense hunter: it scans the landscape by sight, listens through its rigid upright ears for rabbits moving underground, and relies primarily on its keen nose to track and flush quarry.

In traditional Sicilian rabbit hunting, the Cirneco works in a classic partnership with a ferret: once the dog locates a rabbit deep inside a lava crevice or burrow and signals with excited barks, it steps aside and waits silently while the handler releases the ferret to bolt the quarry.

Every part of a Cirneco dell'Etna is meant to be monochromatic: its coat, skin, nose leather, eyelid rims, lips, paw pads, nails, and amber-to-ochre irises all harmonize in shades of fawn, tan, and flesh, and any trace of black pigment is a disqualification.

A 2021 Italian genomic study found that the Cirneco dell'Etna is genetically closest to Malta's Kelb tal-Fenek (Pharaoh Hound) and the Segugio Italiano, and identified the MITF gene as the primary locus distinguishing tan-and-white blazed Cirnechi from self-coloured fawn dogs.

faq.question: Where does the Cirneco dell'Etna originate, and what does its name mean?
faq.answer: The breed originates from the island of Sicily in southern Italy, particularly the volcanic slopes around Mount Etna. The word 'Cirneco' (pronounced 'cheer-NEK-oh', plural 'Cirnechi') is thought to derive either from ancient Cyrene in North Africa (Kyrenaikos / Cyrenaecus) or from the Latin verb cernere / cirniri ('to sift' or 'search'), while 'dell'Etna' was added in 1939 to honour its volcanic homeland.

faq.question: Is the Cirneco dell'Etna a sighthound or a scent hound?
faq.answer: Although often informally called the 'Sicilian Greyhound' and eligible for sighthound lure coursing, the Cirneco is classified internationally as a primitive-type hunting dog that hunts primarily by scent, while also using its acute hearing to detect rabbits underground and its keen sight to scan rocky terrain and course flushed game.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is an adult Cirneco dell'Etna?
faq.answer: International conformation standards specify a withers height of 46 to 50 cm for males and 44 to 48 cm for females (with a ±2 cm tolerance resulting in an overall range of 44 to 52 cm for males and 42 to 50 cm for females) and an adult weight of 10 to 13 kg for males and 8 to 11 kg for females. North American standards specify 18 to 20 inches (45.7–50.8 cm) and 20 to 28 pounds (9.1–12.7 kg) for males, and 17 to 19 inches (43.2–48.3 cm) and 19 to 25 pounds (8.6–11.3 kg) for females.

faq.question: How long does a Cirneco dell'Etna typically live?
faq.answer: The typical life expectancy is 15 to 16 years, making the Cirneco dell'Etna a notably long-lived medium-sized breed.

faq.question: What coat colours and markings are allowed in the Cirneco dell'Etna?
faq.answer: Accepted colours are self-coloured fawn or tan ranging from light wheaten, sand, or isabella to dark tan (with wheaten and honey-golden shades traditionally prized and deep mahogany less desired), as well as fawn/tan with white markings on the head (blaze), chest, throat, feet, tail tip, or belly (a white collar is less appreciated). Nose, eye rims, lips, pads, and nails must be flesh-coloured to brown; any black pigment, solid brown/liver, or brindle coat is a disqualification.

faq.question: How does a Cirneco dell'Etna differ from a Pharaoh Hound?
faq.answer: The two breeds are close Mediterranean cousins from neighbouring islands—the Cirneco from Sicily and the Pharaoh Hound (Kelb tal-Fenek) from Malta—and share an upright-eared, amber-eyed, tan-coated appearance. However, the Cirneco dell'Etna is substantially smaller and lighter (standing 44–50 cm and weighing 8–13 kg, compared with 53–63.5 cm and 20–25 kg for the Pharaoh Hound) and is built on a square 1:1 outline rather than the Pharaoh Hound's slightly longer rectangular profile.

faq.question: Does the Cirneco dell'Etna require much grooming?
faq.answer: Very little. Its short, sleek, vitreous coat stays clean with a quick weekly brushing using a soft bristle brush or hound glove and an occasional bath as needed. Weekly ear checks, frequent nail trimming, and regular tooth brushing complete its routine care.

faq.question: Can a Cirneco dell'Etna be trusted off-leash in open areas?
faq.answer: No. Because the breed was selected for millennia to pursue rabbits independently across rugged terrain, a fleeing squirrel, rabbit, or cat can instantly override recall training. Off-leash running should be restricted to securely fenced enclosures far from road traffic.

faq.question: Is the Cirneco dell'Etna good with cats and small pets?
faq.answer: Caution is essential. While some Cirnechi raised from puppyhood with an indoor cat coexist peacefully under supervision, the breed's innate drive to chase small furry animals is very strong, and outdoor cats or small pets may be viewed as quarry.

faq.question: What is Cirneco oculo-neurological syndrome (CONS), and what health tests exist for the breed?
faq.answer: Historically, the breed has had very few reported hereditary diseases and no mandatory North American screening panel (while Italian selected breeding requires HD A or B hip scores). In 2024, researchers identified an autosomal recessive frameshift deletion in the AMPD2 gene on chromosome 6 causing Cirneco oculo-neurological syndrome (CONS) in two male littermates that developed episodic head tremors and forelimb movement episodes at 2 to 2.5 years of age and progressive retinal degeneration by 4 years of age. Genotyping showed the mutation was confined to the affected family and three related carriers rather than widespread across the breed, and a targeted AMPD2 DNA test is now available to help breeders avoid carrier-to-carrier matings.

faq.question: Is the Cirneco dell'Etna suitable for apartment living?
faq.answer: Yes, provided its daily need for brisk leashed walks, enclosed running play, and mental enrichment is met. Indoors, a well-exercised Cirneco is calm, clean, affectionate, and fond of curling up under blankets next to its owners.

overview.summary: A substantial, low-set British flushing spaniel with a thoughtful expression, a dense white coat and lemon or orange markings. The Clumber Spaniel is typically steady and affectionate, with a strong nose and a purposeful working style suited to searching thick cover.
overview.description: The Clumber Spaniel is a large, heavy-boned sporting dog built with a long body, deep chest, powerful hindquarters and relatively short, strong legs. Its broad head, pronounced brows and vine-leaf-shaped hanging ears give it a distinctive appearance. The abundant, straight coat is predominantly white, often with lemon markings and sometimes orange. Despite its solid build and comparatively unhurried pace, the breed was developed to work in dense vegetation and remains capable of sustained field activity when fit. At home, many Clumbers are calm, loyal and dignified, although their size, coat care needs, tendency to shed and potential drooling should be considered before choosing one.
overview.history: The Clumber Spaniel takes its name from Clumber Park in Nottinghamshire, England, where the breed was developed in the late eighteenth century. Historical accounts associate its early development with dogs brought from France by the Duc de Noailles and maintained by the Duke of Newcastle. Bred for hunting on foot, it became valued for moving methodically through heavy cover and locating game for the guns. Its distinctive low, powerful build and predominantly white coat suited this work. The Clumber later became established as a show and companion dog as well as a sporting spaniel. It remains a comparatively uncommon and vulnerable native breed in the United Kingdom.
overview.originalPurpose: Flushing game birds from dense undergrowth for hunters working on foot.
currentRoles: Flushing and retrieving game in suitable sporting environments
Scent-based enrichment, obedience and other low-impact training activities

physical.coatType: Abundant, close, straight and silky coat, with feathering on the chest and legs.
physical.coatLength: Medium
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate to high; the dense coat sheds and needs regular brushing.
physical.droolingLevel: Can be moderate to high because of the breed's substantial lips and flews; the amount varies between individual dogs.
distinctiveFeatures: Long, low-set, rectangular body with substantial bone
Large, broad, square head with a pronounced brow and deep stop
Deep-set, dark amber eyes
Large, vine-leaf-shaped ears that hang slightly forward
Deep chest and well-sprung ribs
Short, straight, strong forelegs and powerful hindquarters
Dense, straight coat that is predominantly white with lemon or orange markings
A purposeful, ground-covering movement that should remain free and effortless

traits: Steady and composed
Kind and affectionate with familiar people
Intelligent and determined
Dignified and thoughtful in manner
Often more reserved with unfamiliar people than some other spaniels
Quiet and methodical while working
Persistent when following scent
Can be enthusiastic about play despite a calm appearance

exercise.level: Moderate. The breed profile guidance is up to about one hour per day, but the amount and intensity should be tailored to age, fitness, body condition and veterinary advice. Clumbers are substantial dogs; avoid repetitive high-impact exercise, especially while growing or if there are joint or spinal concerns.
activities: Daily walks with time to sniff and explore
Controlled scent games and food-search activities
Reward-based obedience and short training sessions
Retrieving games on suitable, safe ground
Moderate outdoor exploration once growth and health allow
Swimming only when the individual dog is comfortable, supervised and safely supported

grooming.level: Moderate to high. The dense, feathered coat benefits from brushing more than once a week, and the ears, facial folds and coat beneath the body need regular attention.
grooming.brushing: Brush and comb thoroughly at least two or three times per week, paying particular attention to feathering, the chest, belly, legs and areas that can tangle or collect debris. Increase grooming after outdoor work or when the coat is shedding heavily.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when dirty or as needed, using a dog-formulated shampoo and rinsing thoroughly. Dry the coat carefully, especially around the ears and skin folds, rather than leaving damp areas for long periods.
notes: Check and gently clean the ears as needed; hanging ears can retain moisture and debris.
Inspect the folds around the head and keep them clean and dry.
Check the eyes for discharge, irritation or changes in appearance.
Trim nails regularly and inspect the feet after walks.
Brush teeth with dog-safe toothpaste and arrange veterinary dental checks.
Check the feathering after walks for seeds, burrs and tangles.
Do not assume that a short haircut is required; routine brushing and appropriate coat maintenance are generally more useful.

training.difficulty: Moderate. The breed is intelligent and determined but can be deliberate rather than hurried. Consistent, reward-based training and clear routines usually work better than harsh or repetitive handling.
tips: Use food rewards, praise and play to reinforce desired behaviour.
Keep sessions focused and patient, and reward engagement rather than rushing the dog.
Start recall and loose-leash training early, practising around gradually increasing distractions.
Build calm handling skills for grooming, ear checks and veterinary examinations.
Use scent games to provide appropriate outlets for the breed's strong nose.
Manage food access and maintain consistent rules to help prevent unwanted scavenging.
Avoid excessive jumping and repetitive impact, particularly in puppies and dogs with joint or spinal concerns.
training.socialization: Introduce the puppy gradually and positively to a variety of people, calm dogs, household sounds, surfaces and everyday environments. Support relaxed interactions without forcing contact, and teach children to respect the dog's space.

climates: Temperate climates
Cool weather with appropriate shelter and access to warmth
Warm weather with shade, fresh water and exercise scheduled for cooler periods
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: A reliable breed-specific maximum duration was not established. Build up alone time gradually and avoid routinely leaving a companion dog alone for long stretches without appropriate care, exercise and enrichment.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced diet formulated for the dog's life stage, body condition and individual health needs.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Feed a complete puppy diet in age-appropriate meals, following the product's feeding guide and veterinary advice. Growing large-breed puppies should not be overfed.
feedingFrequency.adult: Divide the measured daily ration into two meals for many adult dogs, adjusting the amount to body condition and activity.
feedingFrequency.senior: Use a complete diet suitable for the senior dog's body condition and health needs; seek veterinary guidance if appetite, weight or mobility changes.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure food portions and reassess body condition regularly. Clumber Spaniels have a substantial frame and should not be allowed to become overweight, as excess weight can increase strain on joints and the spine. Provide clean drinking water at all times, keep treats within the overall calorie allowance and seek veterinary advice for an individual feeding plan.
considerations: Monitor body condition and weight, not just the amount recommended on packaging.
Avoid excessive calorie intake during growth.
Discuss appropriate growth rate and diet with a veterinarian for puppies.
Avoid sudden food changes; transition gradually when changing diets.
Do not give supplements or therapeutic diets without veterinary advice.
Keep toxic foods such as chocolate, grapes, raisins, onions and products containing xylitol away from the dog.
nutrition.note: No fixed calorie target or universal portion size is recorded because requirements vary with age, activity, body condition and medical status.

health.overview: Clumber Spaniels should be selected and managed with attention to their substantial build, long body and breed-specific screening recommendations. Breed-club and kennel-club guidance identifies exercise-induced collapse, PDP1 deficiency, hip and elbow dysplasia and eye screening as important topics for breeders. Other conditions have also been reported in the breed, but a reported concern is not a prediction that an individual dog will develop it. Discuss the dog's family history, screening results and symptoms with a veterinarian.
commonConditions: Exercise-induced collapse (EIC) is a recognised breed health concern and is included in current pre-breeding guidance.
Pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatase 1 deficiency (PDP1 deficiency) is a genetic condition for which DNA testing is recommended before breeding.
Hip dysplasia is reported in the breed and is a reason to review hip-screening results.
Elbow dysplasia is included in pre-breeding screening recommendations.
Entropion and ectropion are reported eye conditions; other inherited or presumed inherited ocular disorders have also been described.
Intervertebral disc disease has been reported as a concern in this long-bodied breed.
Hypothyroidism and immune-mediated haemolytic anaemia have been reported in breed health resources; prevalence is not established here.
preventiveCare: Schedule regular veterinary examinations and keep vaccinations and parasite prevention appropriate to local risks.
Maintain a lean body condition to reduce avoidable strain on joints and the spine.
Build exercise gradually and stop activity if the dog shows weakness, abnormal gait, collapse or unusual exercise intolerance.
Seek veterinary assessment for persistent lameness, back or neck pain, changes in vision, eye irritation or unusual fatigue.
Keep the ears and skin folds clean and dry, and seek advice for recurring irritation or odour.
Before breeding, review the health and genetic test results of both prospective parents with a veterinarian or relevant breed-health professional.
recommendedScreenings: Hip dysplasia assessment using an accepted hip evaluation scheme
Elbow dysplasia assessment
Ophthalmologist or recognised eye-scheme examination
DNA test for exercise-induced collapse (EIC)
DNA test for pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatase 1 deficiency (PDP1)
Discuss cardiac examination and other family-history-led screening with the veterinarian and breeder
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with dog-safe toothpaste and have the mouth checked during routine veterinary visits. Professional dental cleaning should be based on clinical need and veterinary advice.
health.earCare: The heavy, hanging ears should be inspected regularly. Keep them dry, and ask a veterinarian about safe cleaning if there is redness, odour, discharge, head shaking or persistent scratching.
health.skinCare: Inspect the facial folds and dense coat during grooming. Keep folds clean and dry, remove trapped debris and consult a veterinarian if redness, odour, itching or recurrent skin problems appear.

Owners who enjoy scent games and patient reward-based training
Homes with room for a large, heavy-bodied dog to move comfortably
Families prepared to supervise children and teach gentle handling
Prospective owners willing to review health screening and breeder records
notIdealFor: Households unable to manage regular brushing, shedding or possible drooling
People seeking a small, low-maintenance dog
Homes where the dog would routinely receive little exercise or enrichment

funFacts: The breed's name comes from Clumber Park in Nottinghamshire, where it was developed.
Its predominantly white coat helped hunters see the dog as it worked within range in dense cover.
The breed is classified internationally as a flushing spaniel rather than a retrieving or water spaniel.
The Clumber Spaniel's rolling appearance at a walk is associated with its low, broad build and characteristic movement.
It is listed as a vulnerable native breed in the United Kingdom.

faq.question: How large is a Clumber Spaniel?
faq.answer: The American breed standard gives an ideal height of 18–20 inches (about 46–51 cm) for males and 17–19 inches (about 43–48 cm) for females. Its ideal weight is substantial: around 31.8–38.6 kg for males and 24.9–31.8 kg for females under that standard. Other kennel-club standards give somewhat different weight ranges.

faq.question: What colour is a Clumber Spaniel?
faq.answer: The coat is predominantly white, with lemon markings common and orange markings also permitted. Some slight head markings and freckles on the muzzle can be acceptable under the breed standard.

faq.question: Does a Clumber Spaniel need a lot of exercise?
faq.answer: It needs regular daily activity and opportunities to use its nose. A breed-profile guide suggests up to about an hour a day, adjusted to the individual dog. Fitness, age and veterinary advice matter, and high-impact exercise should not be excessive.

faq.question: How much grooming does a Clumber Spaniel need?
faq.answer: The dense, feathered coat usually needs brushing and combing several times a week. Pay extra attention to the ears, facial folds, chest, belly and leg feathering, and check for debris after outdoor activity.

faq.question: What health tests should a Clumber Spaniel breeder discuss?
faq.answer: Important pre-breeding checks include hips, elbows, eyes, exercise-induced collapse (EIC) and PDP1 deficiency. Ask the breeder for the actual results and discuss any additional screening that fits the dog's family history with a veterinarian.

faq.question: Is a Clumber Spaniel suitable for apartment living?
faq.answer: It may adapt to different homes if its needs are met, but its large size, coat care and exercise requirements can make a spacious home more convenient. The individual dog's temperament, activity needs and access to regular walks should guide the decision.

faq.question: How long does a Clumber Spaniel live?
faq.answer: Published breed profiles commonly give a life expectancy around 10–12 years. Individual lifespan varies with genetics, health, weight, care and chance; this range is not a guarantee.

overview.summary: A graceful, long-coated herding dog known for its intelligence, sensitivity, loyalty, and close bond with its family.
overview.description: The Rough Collie is a medium-to-large, athletic herding dog distinguished by a long outer coat, dense undercoat, refined wedge-shaped head, expressive almond-shaped eyes, and an alert, balanced outline. Beneath its elegant appearance is a working dog developed to help manage livestock. Many Rough Collies are responsive to gentle instruction and enjoy participating in family activities, training, and dog sports. Their long coat needs regular attention, and they generally do best with daily companionship, exercise, and opportunities to use their minds. Individual temperament, activity needs, and grooming demands vary.
overview.history: The Rough Collie developed in Great Britain from the herding dogs associated particularly with Scotland. It was selected as a more refined version of the traditional working Collie, while retaining its herding heritage. The Rough and Smooth Collie share a common background and are distinguished primarily by coat length. The breed later became widely known as a companion and show dog as well as a working dog.
overview.originalPurpose: Herding and managing sheep and other livestock
currentRoles: Herding and farm work where suitable opportunities exist

physical.coatType: Long double coat with a dense undercoat and a longer, straight outer coat
physical.coatLength: Long and abundant on the body, with a prominent mane and frill around the neck, feathering on the legs, and a well-coated tail; the face and lower parts of the legs carry shorter, smoother hair.
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate to high, with loose undercoat requiring regular removal
distinctiveFeatures: Long, abundant coat with a dense undercoat and a pronounced neck mane and frill
Refined wedge-shaped head with a smooth outline
Almond-shaped eyes that contribute to a gentle, alert expression
Ears that are typically carried partly erect with the tips folding forward
Long, tapering muzzle and a balanced, athletic outline
Deep chest and a body built for sustained movement rather than heaviness
Long, well-coated tail
The Rough and Smooth Collie share a breed background and differ principally in coat length

traits: Intelligent and observant
Loyal and strongly attached to family
Generally responsive to gentle, consistent training
Sensitive to tone and handling
Alert to activity around the home
Often friendly and affectionate with familiar people
Active and capable of sustained outdoor activity
May bark when alerting or when under-stimulated

exercise.level: Moderate to high. Most need daily walks, active play, and mental engagement, with the amount adjusted to age, health, and the individual dog's fitness.
activities: Daily walks with time for sniffing and exploration
Fetch and interactive play in a safe area
Reward-based obedience and trick training
Agility, rally, or other suitable dog sports
Herding activities with qualified instruction where available
Food puzzles and scent games for mental enrichment

grooming.level: Moderate to high. The coat needs regular brushing, with extra attention during shedding periods and wherever tangles form.
grooming.brushing: Brush thoroughly about once a week as a starting routine, reaching through the outer coat to the undercoat. Increase frequency when shedding heavily and check behind the ears, around the elbows, feathering, and other friction areas for tangles or mats.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when needed using a dog-appropriate shampoo, then dry the dense coat thoroughly. Frequency depends on coat condition, activity, and skin health.
notes: Part the coat in sections and brush down to the undercoat rather than only smoothing the surface.
Pay particular attention behind the ears, under the legs, around the collar area, and to the feathering.
During heavier shedding, remove loose undercoat more frequently to reduce tangles and loose hair.
Check nails, paws, ears, and skin during routine grooming.
Do not shave the double coat simply to reduce routine grooming; ask a veterinarian or qualified groomer about medical or coat-specific reasons before clipping extensively.

training.difficulty: Generally moderate. The breed is often quick to learn, but sensitivity makes calm, consistent, reward-based teaching especially important.
tips: Use rewards, clear cues, and short, engaging training sessions.
Avoid harsh corrections; a sensitive dog may become worried or disengaged.
Begin socialisation early and introduce new people, places, sounds, and animals gradually and positively.
Teach a reliable recall and calm greetings from puppyhood.
Provide mental tasks as well as physical activity to reduce boredom-related behaviours.
Train barking and herding-related behaviours constructively rather than assuming they will disappear on their own.
training.socialization: Start early with positive, age-appropriate experiences. Continue throughout adulthood and let the dog approach unfamiliar people, dogs, and environments at a comfortable pace.

nutrition.dietType: Complete and balanced dog food appropriate to life stage and health
nutrition.guidelines: Choose a complete and balanced diet suitable for the dog's life stage, body condition, activity, and health. Measure meals, monitor weight and body condition, keep fresh water available, and adjust portions with veterinary guidance. Feeding amounts should follow the chosen food's instructions as a starting point, not be treated as a universal prescription.
considerations: Adjust food intake to growth, activity, neuter status, body condition, and health.
Avoid allowing excess weight to accumulate; assess body condition regularly.
Ask a veterinarian about an appropriate feeding plan for puppies, older dogs, or dogs with medical conditions.
Discuss the risk and signs of gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat) with a veterinarian, particularly if the dog has a deep chest or a relevant family history.
Do not give medication or supplements based only on breed information.
nutrition.note: No universal meal count or calorie target is specified here because requirements depend on age, food energy density, activity, body condition, and medical status.

health.overview: Rough Collies are often described as hardy, but breed-related inherited conditions and medication sensitivity deserve attention. Health risks vary among individual dogs and bloodlines. Ask for the actual screening results of the puppy's parents and discuss the dog's own screening and medication history with a veterinarian.
commonConditions: Collie Eye Anomaly (CEA), an inherited eye condition
MDR1/ABCB1 drug sensitivity, which can alter responses to certain medicines
Progressive Retinal Atrophy, rod-cone dysplasia 2 (PRA-rcd2)
Dermatomyositis (DMS)
Hip dysplasia
Degenerative myelopathy (DM)
preventiveCare: Arrange routine veterinary examinations and maintain appropriate vaccination and parasite-prevention plans.
Keep a record of genetic test results, eye examinations, and other health screening.
Discuss medication choices with the veterinarian and disclose any known MDR1/ABCB1 result before treatment.
Seek veterinary advice promptly for changes in vision, gait, skin, appetite, energy, or behaviour.
Maintain a healthy body condition and provide regular exercise suited to age and health.
recommendedScreenings: Veterinary eye examination for Collie Eye Anomaly, including the recommended examination of puppies before placement
MDR1/ABCB1 genetic testing and discussion of medication implications
PRA-rcd2 genetic testing
Dermatomyositis (DMS) genetic testing where recommended
Hip evaluation through an accepted veterinary screening programme
Discuss degenerative myelopathy testing and family history with the breeder and veterinarian
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste and arrange veterinary dental checks. Seek advice if there is persistent bad breath, gum bleeding, pain, or difficulty eating.
health.earCare: Check the ears routinely for redness, odour, discharge, or discomfort. Clean only as advised by a veterinarian and avoid inserting cotton swabs deep into the ear canal.
health.skinCare: Part the long coat periodically to check the skin for redness, parasites, sores, and mats. Ask a veterinarian about persistent itching, hair loss, lesions, or recurring skin problems.

idealFor: Households that want a close, involved companion and can provide daily company
Owners who enjoy reward-based training and mental enrichment
People prepared to maintain a long double coat
Active households interested in walks, play, obedience, or suitable dog sports
notIdealFor: People unable to provide regular coat care
Households expecting a dog to be content with little interaction or stimulation
Owners seeking a guaranteed quiet dog without training for alert barking
Anyone unwilling to discuss inherited health screening and medication sensitivity with the breeder and veterinarian

funFacts: The Rough Collie is the long-coated variety of the Collie; the Smooth Collie has a short coat.
The breed was developed for herding work, and many individuals still enjoy learning structured tasks.
Its long coat can look very heavy, but the breed's outline is intended to remain balanced and athletic rather than coarse.
Collies became widely recognised in popular culture, helping make the breed familiar to audiences far beyond the herding world.

faq.question: How long does a Rough Collie usually live?
faq.answer: The American Kennel Club lists a typical life expectancy of 12–14 years. An individual dog's lifespan depends on genetics, health, care, and other factors; this is a reference range, not a guarantee.

faq.question: Does a Rough Collie shed?
faq.answer: Yes. Its double coat sheds, and loose undercoat can become trapped in the longer outer coat. Regular brushing and more frequent coat care during heavier shedding help manage loose hair and prevent tangles.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Rough Collie need?
faq.answer: Most benefit from daily walks, play, and mental activity. The right amount varies with age, health, fitness, and temperament, so a fixed daily-minute target is not provided.

faq.question: What health tests should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Ask for documented results relevant to Collie Eye Anomaly, MDR1/ABCB1, PRA-rcd2, dermatomyositis, and hip health. The appropriate tests can depend on the programme and bloodline; review the results with a veterinarian rather than relying on verbal assurances.

faq.question: Can a Rough Collie be sensitive to medication?
faq.answer: Some Collies carry an MDR1/ABCB1 variant that can affect their response to certain medicines. Ask your veterinarian about genetic testing and medication precautions, and do not start or stop a medicine based solely on general breed information.

faq.question: Is a Rough Collie suitable for an apartment?
faq.answer: There is no universal yes-or-no answer. Exercise, barking, time spent with the household, training, and the individual dog's behaviour all matter. Evaluate the dog's needs and the building's rules before deciding.

overview.summary: A cheerful, intelligent, and deeply affectionate small companion dog from southwestern Madagascar, distinguished by its soft, cotton-textured coat, expressive dark eyes, and devoted bond with its household.
overview.description: The Coton de Tulear is a sturdy, small, long-coated companion breed built on a rectangular outline where height at the withers is roughly two-thirds of the body length. Beneath its profuse, supple white coat—which has the dry, airy feel of a natural cotton boll rather than silky or woolly hair—lies a well-muscled frame with a slightly convex topline that arches gently over a short loin to a low-set tail. Round, dark, wide-set eyes and black-pigmented lips and eyelids give the face a bright, inquisitive expression. Lively, stable, and highly sociable with people and other dogs, Cotons are renowned for their clownish antics, habit of walking on their hind legs to please their owners, and repertoire of purr-like, grunting, and trilling vocalizations. While their compact size adapts well to apartments and houses alike, their coat requires committed brushing and their people-oriented nature calls for daily companionship, positive training, and interactive play.
overview.history: Originating on the island of Madagascar off the southeastern coast of Africa, the breed takes its name from the French word coton ('cotton') and the southwestern port city of Toliara, historically known as Tuléar. Around the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, small white European Bichon-type dogs travelled aboard merchant and pirate vessels sailing around the Cape of Good Hope into the Indian Ocean, serving both as shipboard ratters and as companions to passengers. Traditional island lore recounts that survivors of a shipwreck near Tuléar swam ashore, adapted in packs, and interbred with local island dogs, though exact early ancestry narratives remain undocumented in primary historical records. By the seventeenth century, these small white dogs had been adopted by the native Malagasy and the ruling Merina tribal monarchy, which restricted ownership to nobility and royalty—earning the breed the enduring title 'Royal Dog of Madagascar'. French colonists later brought specimens to France, leading to formal international breed recognition in 1970 (with the first international standard published in 1971), organized studbook preservation in North America beginning in 1976, introduction to the United Kingdom in 1987, and subsequent national recognitions in 1996 and 2014.

grooming.brushing: Brush and comb gently all the way down to the skin 3 to 4 times per week—or daily when maintaining a full adult coat—using a quality pin brush (without balls on the pin tips, which can snag and tear the hair) and a metal comb. Mist the coat lightly with a leave-in spray conditioner before brushing to prevent hair breakage and mat formation next to the skin.
grooming.bathing: Bathe as needed using a gentle, dog-safe shampoo and conditioner formulated for long coats, rinse thoroughly, and dry the coat completely while brushing so damp hair does not felt or mat.
notes: Pay special attention to coat maintenance between 9 and 14 months of age, when the softer puppy coat transitions to the denser adult coat and matting risk is at its peak.
Inspect high-friction areas carefully during every brushing session, including behind the ears, under the collar or harness, around the elbows and armpits, in the groin, and down the legs.

Keep hair on the bottom of the feet and between the paw pads trimmed neat for traction and cleanliness; otherwise, the coat is traditionally kept in its natural, un-scissored state unless clipped into a shorter pet trim for easier upkeep.
Check the pendulous ears a couple of times each week for excess hair, wax, redness, odour, or debris to help prevent ear canal infections.
Trim nails regularly and accustom puppies early to gentle handling of their paws, face, ears, and tail.
Although low-shedding, no dog breed is completely non-allergenic; prospective owners with allergies should spend time around the breed before committing.

training.difficulty: Generally trainable and eager to please when taught with upbeat, reward-based methods
tips: Use positive reinforcement with small food rewards, play, and enthusiastic praise; Cotons are sensitive and shut down under harsh or negative corrections.
Keep training sessions short, lively, and varied so the dog stays mentally engaged and does not grow bored.
Channel their natural desire to entertain into trick training, rally, obedience, or agility.
Teach calm household manners and polite responses to doorway noises, as the breed is naturally alert and watchful of its home.
Condition puppies gradually to grooming brushes, combs, nail trims, tooth brushing, and baths as positive bonding routines.
Practice gradual alone-time conditioning early so the dog's close attachment to its people does not develop into separation distress.
training.socialization: Expose puppies early and positively to a wide variety of people, gentle children, friendly dogs, household sounds, travel, and novel environments so their naturally sociable, adaptable temperament flourishes.

livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate. Bred solely for human companionship, the Coton thrives as an indoor family member that follows its people from room to room; leaving the dog isolated for long workdays without gradual conditioning and enrichment can lead to boredom, vocalizing, or destructive behaviour.

nutrition.dietType: Complete and balanced, high-quality dog food appropriate for the dog's life stage (puppy, adult, or senior), body size, and individual health needs.
nutrition.guidelines: Feed measured portions of a nutritionally complete diet suited to the dog's age, weight, and activity level. Because some individuals are prone to gaining excess weight, monitor body condition regularly, limit high-calorie table scraps, and account for training treats within the daily calorie allowance. Provide constant access to clean, fresh water.
considerations: Watch calorie intake and body condition closely to prevent overweight and unnecessary strain on the patellas, hips, and spine.
Keep training treats small and deduct them from the daily food ration.
Avoid feeding cooked bones or high-fat table scraps that can trigger digestive upset or pancreatitis.
Transition between foods gradually over several days unless directed otherwise by a veterinarian.
Consult a veterinarian promptly if sudden weight changes, picky eating, or excessive water consumption occur.
nutrition.note: A single universal meal schedule is not assigned because optimal feeding frequency depends on age, caloric density of the diet, activity level, and individual health; confirm portion sizes and daily meal counts with a veterinarian.

health.overview: The Coton de Tulear is generally a hardy, long-lived breed with a typical life expectancy of 15 to 19 years, and documented hereditary diseases occur at a relatively low incidence (often estimated at 1% to 5% in screened populations). Health management distinguishes between clinical orthopedic, ophthalmic, and cardiac conditions monitored through pre-breeding veterinary examinations—namely patellar luxation, hip dysplasia, inherited eye anomalies, and congenital cardiac murmurs—and specific autosomal recessive mutations for which validated DNA tests allow breeders to avoid carrier-to-carrier matings. Molecularly characterized recessive disorders in the breed include Bandera's neonatal cerebellar ataxia (GRM1 mutation), canine multifocal retinopathy 2 (BEST1 mutation), and primary hyperoxaluria type 1 (AGXT mutation), alongside broader canine DNA tests for von Willebrand disease, degenerative myelopathy, hyperuricosuria, and FGF4 retrogene intervertebral disc disease predisposition.
commonConditions: Patellar luxation — a potential orthopedic issue in small breeds in which the kneecap slips out of its trochlear groove; veterinary patellar evaluation is a core pre-breeding requirement.
Hip dysplasia — reported occasionally in the breed and monitored through mandatory pre-breeding radiographic hip evaluation.

Ocular disorders and Canine Multifocal Retinopathy 2 (CMR2) — periodic veterinary ophthalmologist examinations screen for cataracts and retinal anomalies, while an autosomal recessive BEST1 gene mutation (c.482G>A) causes CMR2, producing discrete subretinal blisters around 15 weeks of age that typically stabilize by 1 year without causing blindness.

Cardiac abnormalities — congenital heart murmurs or valve defects are screened via pre-breeding veterinary cardiac evaluations; the screening requirement reflects preventive stewardship rather than high clinical prevalence.

Intervertebral disc disease (spinal disc disease) and FGF4 retrogene variants — back and disc problems are occasionally reported in the breed, and elective DNA testing is available for the chromosome 12 FGF4 retrogene (CDDY) associated with premature intervertebral disc degeneration as well as the chromosome 18 FGF4 retrogene (CDPA) associated with short-limbed chondrodysplasia.

Bandera's neonatal cerebellar ataxia (BNAt / NCA) — a severe autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxia caused by a retrotransposon insertion in exon 8 of the GRM1 gene on chromosome 1; affected puppies exhibit intention tremors, head nodding, and inability to stand or walk from about 2 weeks of age, and a separate autosomal recessive juvenile cerebellar ataxia is also under genomic investigation.

Primary hyperoxaluria type 1 (PH) — a rare, fatal neonatal autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by a missense mutation (c.996G>A / p.Gly102Ser) in the AGXT gene, leading to calcium oxalate crystal accumulation and acute renal tubular necrosis at 3 to 4 weeks of age (identified with an 8.5% carrier rate in a Finnish study cohort).

Additional conditions included in elective pre-breeding genetic or clinical panels — type 1 von Willebrand disease (vWD), degenerative myelopathy (DM / SOD1), hyperuricosuria (HU / SLC2A9), autoimmune thyroiditis, elbow dysplasia, and Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease.
preventiveCare: Request documented pre-breeding health clearances for both parents—covering veterinary ophthalmologist exams, patellar luxation, hip radiographs, cardiac evaluation, and relevant breed-appropriate DNA tests—before acquiring a puppy.
Maintain a lean body weight and healthy muscle tone through daily walks and portion control to minimize mechanical stress on the knees, hips, and spine.
Brush the coat thoroughly down to the skin several times a week to prevent painful mats that trap moisture and hide skin irritation.
Check and gently clean the drop ears a couple of times weekly to prevent wax accumulation and otitis externa.
Brush teeth regularly and schedule routine veterinary wellness and dental examinations throughout the dog's long lifespan.
Seek prompt veterinary evaluation for limping, skipping gaits, back pain, eye cloudiness or redness, coughing, or urinary changes.
recommendedScreenings: Ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (core pre-breeding requirement, performed from 6 months of age and periodically thereafter).
Patellar luxation veterinary evaluation (core pre-breeding requirement at 12 months of age or older).
Hip dysplasia radiographic evaluation (core pre-breeding requirement; preliminary radiographs before 24 months and final certification after 24 months of age).
Cardiac examination by a qualified veterinarian or veterinary cardiologist (performed at 12 months of age or older prior to breeding).

Elective genetic and clinical evaluations based on lineage and breeding program requirements: DNA tests for Bandera's neonatal cerebellar ataxia (GRM1), canine multifocal retinopathy 2 (CMR2 / BEST1), primary hyperoxaluria (PH / AGXT), type 1 von Willebrand disease (vWD), degenerative myelopathy (DM / SOD1), hyperuricosuria (HU / SLC2A9), chondrodystrophy (CDDY / FGF4), and chondrodysplasia (CDPA / FGF4), as well as laboratory thyroid profiling, elbow radiographs, and Legg-Calvé-Perthes evaluation.
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth several times a week—ideally daily—using dog-safe toothpaste and a small, soft canine toothbrush. Because small companion breeds are prone to plaque accumulation and periodontal disease over a 15- to 19-year lifespan, combine home brushing with regular veterinary dental assessments and professional cleanings when indicated.
health.earCare: Inspect the high-set, pendulous triangular ears two to three times a week and after baths. Gently remove excess hair, wax, or debris as advised by a veterinarian, keep the ear canals dry, and seek veterinary care for redness, foul odour, discharge, or head shaking.
health.skinCare: Part the dense cottony coat down to the skin during brushing to check for hidden tangles, redness, parasites, or dry skin. Use a gentle dog shampoo and leave-in conditioning spray to keep the skin and hair supple, and ensure the coat is dried completely after bathing or rain.

funFacts: The breed's name combines the French word coton ('cotton'), referring to its soft, airy cotton-boll coat texture, with Tuléar (now Toliara), the southwestern Malagasy port city associated with its early history.
In seventeenth-century Madagascar, the ruling Merina monarchy restricted ownership of these small white dogs to royalty and nobility, earning the breed the title 'Royal Dog of Madagascar'.
Madagascar has honoured the Coton de Tulear as its Official National Dog and featured the breed on national postage stamps, including a well-known 1974 stamp issue.

Cotons are famous for two endearing habits when interacting with their families: rising up to walk or hop on their hind legs and conversing through unique purr-like, grunting, or trilling vocalizations.
Unlike several other Bichon-family breeds with flat backs, the Coton de Tulear has a distinctive slightly convex topline that rises gently over a short, muscular loin to a low-set tail.

Many Coton puppies are born with noticeable yellow, tan, brown, chestnut, or grey patches on the head, ears, or body that gradually fade over their first 12 to 18 months, leaving an adult coat that is predominantly white or lightly shaded with champagne or grey on the ears.

faq.question: Where does the Coton de Tulear come from?
faq.answer: The breed originates from the island of Madagascar off the southeastern coast of Africa. Its name refers to its cotton-like coat texture and the southwestern port city of Toliara, formerly called Tuléar.

faq.question: How big is an adult Coton de Tulear?
faq.answer: International conformation standards specify an ideal withers height of 26 to 28 cm for males (with a tolerance of 25 to 30 cm) and 23 to 25 cm for females (with a tolerance of 22 to 27 cm), and an adult weight of 4 to 6 kg for males and 3.5 to 5 kg for females. North American standards list an ideal height of 10 to 11 inches (9–15 pounds) for males and 9 to 10 inches (8–13 pounds) for females, while some traditional Malagasy-type lines reach heights up to 12.5 or 13 inches (25–33 cm) and weights up to 14 or 18 pounds.

faq.question: How long does a Coton de Tulear typically live?
faq.answer: The typical life expectancy is 15 to 19 years, making the Coton de Tulear one of the longest-lived companion dog breeds.

faq.question: Does the Coton de Tulear shed, and is it hypoallergenic?
faq.answer: The breed sheds very little—primarily losing small amounts of hair during brushing or in springtime—and has hair rather than a typical fur undercoat. While many people with mild sensitivities tolerate the breed well, no dog is completely hypoallergenic because allergens are also carried in dander and saliva.

faq.question: How much grooming does a Coton de Tulear need?
faq.answer: Maintaining a full, flowing adult coat requires gentle brushing and combing all the way to the skin 3 to 4 times a week (or daily), misting lightly with a leave-in conditioner to prevent breakage and mats. Particular care is needed between 9 and 14 months of age when the puppy coat transitions to the adult coat. Owners who do not show their dogs often opt for a shorter 'puppy clip' to simplify daily maintenance.

faq.question: Is the Coton de Tulear suitable for apartment living?
faq.answer: Yes. Its small stature, moderate exercise needs, and polite indoor demeanor make it well suited to apartments as well as houses with yards, provided it receives daily walks, interactive play, and plenty of human companionship.

faq.question: Is the Coton de Tulear good with children and other pets?
faq.answer: Yes. The breed is known for a stable, cheerful, and sociable temperament toward people, children, other dogs, and household cats. As with any small breed, interactions with young children should be supervised so the dog is handled gently.

faq.question: What health screenings and DNA tests should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Prospective buyers should ask for documented results of four core clinical evaluations—board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist eye examination, patellar luxation evaluation, hip radiographs, and cardiac examination—along with relevant DNA tests used to prevent carrier-to-carrier matings, such as Bandera's neonatal cerebellar ataxia (GRM1), canine multifocal retinopathy 2 (CMR2 / BEST1), primary hyperoxaluria (PH / AGXT), von Willebrand disease (vWD), degenerative myelopathy (DM), and hyperuricosuria (HU).

faq.question: What colour is a Coton de Tulear, and why do puppies change colour?
faq.answer: In most conformation standards, the adult ground colour is white, with slight light-grey or light-tan/red-roan shading permitted on the ears and only minimal shading (up to 5% to 10%) tolerated on the body. Puppies are frequently born with darker tan, brown, chestnut, or grey patches on the head and body controlled by colour-dilution genes; these markings progressively fade into white or pale champagne by 12 to 18 months of age. Some traditional Malagasy and North American lines also recognize black-and-white and tri-colour varieties.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Coton de Tulear need?
faq.answer: The breed is moderately active and thrives on daily leashed walks at a comfortable pace combined with indoor or backyard games such as fetching a ball, trick training, or agility. Rather than following a rigid daily minute quota, tailor the duration and pace of exercise to the individual dog's age, health, and conditioning.

overview.summary: The Dalmatian is an athletic, spotted dog with a short, close coat, notable stamina and an alert, people-oriented nature. It usually thrives with daily exercise, training and company, rather than a sedentary routine.
overview.description: Dalmatians are medium-to-large, muscular dogs built for efficient movement over distance. Their distinctive coat has a white ground with clearly separated black or liver-brown spots. Many are lively, curious and eager to join family activities; their stamina and strong interest in the environment mean that exercise, recall training and enrichment should be part of everyday life. Temperament and energy vary between individuals, so socialisation and positive training matter.
overview.history: The breed is associated with Croatia and the historic region of Dalmatia. Written records and artworks from the early modern period document spotted dogs in the region. In Britain and elsewhere, Dalmatians later became well known for accompanying horse-drawn carriages, including fire-service vehicles. The breed is now kept as a companion and also participates in obedience, scent work, agility and other suitable dog sports.
overview.originalPurpose: Historically used as a hunting and carriage dog; later known for accompanying horse-drawn coaches and fire-service vehicles.
currentRoles: Running and hiking partner for appropriately conditioned adults

physical.coatType: Short, dense, hard, smooth and glossy coat that lies close to the body.
physical.coatLength: Short all over; the coat has no long feathering.
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate to high; short hairs may shed throughout the year and can be noticeable on clothing and furniture.
distinctiveFeatures: Distinct, separate spots on a white ground colour
Black or liver-brown spot varieties
Athletic, rectangular outline with strong musculature
Short, close-fitting coat and hanging ears
Long, efficient stride suited to sustained movement

traits: Lively and athletic
Generally outgoing and friendly when well socialised
Alert and observant
Often enjoys being involved in family activities
Intelligent and capable of learning varied skills
May be independent or distracted by scents and movement
Needs regular outlets for energy and mental activity

exercise.level: High
activities: Brisk walks and age-appropriate hikes
Running only after suitable maturity and conditioning
Reward-based obedience and recall practice
Scent games and food-puzzle activities
Agility or other structured dog sports when physically suitable
Safe play with regular rest and access to water

grooming.level: Low to moderate effort, with frequent shedding
grooming.brushing: Brush with a rubber grooming mitt or soft brush several times a week to remove loose hair; more frequent brushing may be useful during heavier shedding.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when dirty or needed, using a dog-appropriate shampoo and rinsing well. Avoid unnecessary frequent bathing that may dry the skin.
notes: A short coat still sheds and may leave fine hairs on fabrics.
Check ears regularly and clean only as advised by a veterinarian.
Trim nails as needed and inspect paws after exercise.
Brush teeth with dog-safe toothpaste and arrange routine oral checks.

training.difficulty: Moderate; consistent, engaging training is important for an energetic and sometimes independent dog.
tips: Use reward-based training and short, varied sessions.
Build recall gradually around distractions and use a lead or secure area until reliable.
Teach calm behaviour and settling as well as active skills.
Introduce visitors, dogs, sounds and environments positively and at the dog's pace.
Provide mental tasks as well as physical exercise.
training.socialization: Start positive, age-appropriate socialisation early and continue throughout life. Avoid forcing interactions; reward calm observation and allow the dog space to disengage.

climates: Adapt activity to temperature; provide shade and water in warm weather and suitable shelter in cold or wet conditions.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced diet appropriate to life stage, body condition and activity; urinary-health needs should be assessed individually.
nutrition.guidelines: Choose a complete diet suitable for the dog's age and workload, measure portions, monitor body condition and keep fresh water available. Because Dalmatians can be prone to urate urinary stones, discuss diet composition, hydration and urinary monitoring with a veterinarian rather than starting a restrictive diet without individual advice.
considerations: Provide constant access to fresh water and regular opportunities to urinate.
Urate-stone risk and dietary needs vary; follow veterinary advice based on the dog's history and test results.
Avoid overfeeding and adjust portions to maintain a lean, athletic body condition.
Use a veterinarian for any therapeutic or low-purine diet decision.
nutrition.note: This is general feeding information, not a prescription. Dogs with a history of urinary stones or relevant test results may need an individually planned diet and monitoring with a veterinarian.

health.overview: Dalmatians can be athletic and long-lived, but breed-associated concerns include inherited hearing impairment and urate urinary stones; copper-associated liver disease is also reported. These risks do not mean an individual dog will necessarily develop a condition. Preventive care, responsible breeding and early veterinary assessment are important.
commonConditions: Inherited hearing impairment, including unilateral or bilateral deafness
Urate urinary crystals or stones, which can sometimes cause a life-threatening urinary blockage
Copper-associated liver disease has been reported in the breed; individual risk and significance require veterinary assessment
preventiveCare: Arrange regular veterinary examinations and keep vaccinations and parasite prevention appropriate to local risk.
Provide fresh water and frequent opportunities to urinate; seek urgent veterinary care for straining, inability to pass urine, pain or blood in urine.
Discuss diet and urinary monitoring with a veterinarian, especially if there is a history of stones.
Monitor hearing and behaviour; discuss testing if hearing is uncertain.
Maintain a lean body condition and increase exercise gradually.
recommendedScreenings: BAER hearing test for puppies or breeding dogs, according to veterinary and breed-club guidance.
Hip evaluation for breeding dogs, consistent with parent-club screening recommendations.
Discuss baseline blood testing and any liver or urinary monitoring with the veterinarian based on age, family history and clinical findings.
health.dentalCare: Brush regularly with dog-safe toothpaste and arrange dental checks as part of routine veterinary care.
health.earCare: Check ears routinely for redness, odour, discharge or discomfort; seek veterinary advice for symptoms rather than inserting objects into the ear canal.
health.skinCare: Inspect the skin for irritation or unusual lesions. A short coat is easy to check, but short hairs may shed heavily; seek veterinary advice for persistent itching, redness or hair loss.

idealFor: People who can provide substantial daily activity and training
Households that enjoy outdoor activities and structured dog sports
Owners willing to manage shedding and pay attention to urinary-health guidance
notIdealFor: People seeking a low-energy dog with minimal exercise needs
Households unable to provide regular companionship, enrichment and training
Owners unwilling to plan for possible breed-associated urinary or hearing concerns

funFacts: The breed is officially associated with Croatia and the historic region of Dalmatia.
The Dalmatian became widely recognised as a coach dog, accompanying horse-drawn carriages and fire-service vehicles.
Each dog's spot pattern is individual, and puppies are born white before their spots become visible.
The breed standard recognises both black-spotted and liver-brown-spotted varieties.

faq.question: Where does the Dalmatian come from?
faq.answer: The breed is recognised as originating in Croatia and is historically associated with the region of Dalmatia.

faq.question: How tall is a Dalmatian?
faq.answer: The FCI standard gives a height of 56–62 cm for males and 54–60 cm for females, measured at the withers.

faq.question: How much does a Dalmatian weigh?
faq.answer: One kennel-club profile gives a broad breed-wide range of about 45–70 lb (20.4–31.8 kg), rather than separate male and female ranges. Individual healthy weight depends on build and body condition.

faq.question: How long does a Dalmatian live?
faq.answer: A breed foundation reports an average lifespan of about 11–13 years, although individual lifespan varies with genetics, care and health.

faq.question: Do Dalmatians need a lot of exercise?
faq.answer: Usually, yes. They are athletic dogs that benefit from regular walks, training and enrichment. Increase exercise gradually and tailor it to age, health and fitness.

faq.question: What health concerns are important for Dalmatians?
faq.answer: Inherited hearing impairment and urate urinary stones are notable breed-associated concerns. Copper-associated liver disease is also reported. A veterinarian can advise on appropriate testing and prevention for an individual dog.

faq.question: Are Dalmatians always black and white?
faq.answer: No. The recognised standard varieties are black spots on white or liver-brown spots on white.

faq.question: Do Dalmatians shed?
faq.answer: Yes. Their short coat can shed considerably, so brushing several times a week may help manage loose hair.

overview.summary: The Doberman Pinscher is a sleek, muscular German working breed known for its alert expression, close-fitting coat and strong bond with its household. Intelligent and athletic, it usually thrives with structured training, regular exercise and close involvement in family life.
overview.description: The Doberman combines a powerful, athletic frame with an elegant outline and a short, smooth coat. It was developed as a versatile working dog and is now kept as a companion, sport dog and working partner. The breed is often highly attentive to its surroundings and learns quickly, but its size, energy and guarding instincts make thoughtful training and socialisation important. Daily exercise should be paired with activities that engage its mind, such as obedience practice, scent games and structured play. Dobermans generally benefit from living closely with their people rather than being left isolated for long periods. Their short coat is relatively easy to maintain, although skin, nails, ears, teeth and overall health still need routine care.
overview.history: The Dobermann was developed in Germany in the late nineteenth century and takes its name from Friedrich Louis Dobermann, who is credited with establishing the breed. Early dogs were selected for a combination of alertness, courage, strength and usefulness as protection and working animals. They were used in police and other service roles, as well as for guarding and companionship. The breed's exact ancestry is not completely documented, so accounts that assign precise percentages or definitive contributions to particular foundation breeds should be treated cautiously.

grooming.brushing: Brush once or twice a week with a soft brush or grooming mitt to remove loose hairs and distribute skin oils. Check the skin during grooming, especially if scratching, redness or hair loss appears.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when needed with a dog-appropriate shampoo and rinse thoroughly. Avoid excessive bathing or harsh products that can irritate the skin.
notes: Check the skin for irritation, dry patches, lumps or unusual hair loss.
Trim nails regularly; active dogs do not always wear them down sufficiently.
Brush teeth with a dog-specific toothbrush and toothpaste.
Check the ears routinely for redness, odour or discharge.
Provide a comfortable resting place away from prolonged cold or wet conditions.
Introduce handling, nail care and veterinary examinations with positive reinforcement.

training.difficulty: Moderate to high: highly trainable and responsive, but powerful, energetic dogs need consistent handling, early foundations and regular practice.
tips: Use reward-based training with clear, consistent expectations.
Teach loose-leash walking and calm greetings from an early age.
Build a reliable recall in secure areas before practising around distractions.
Train impulse control, settle cues and the ability to disengage from triggers.
Socialise gradually with varied people, environments and suitable dogs.
Use structured activities to channel energy and reinforce focus.
Avoid encouraging uncontrolled aggression or relying on intimidation-based methods.
Seek a qualified, humane trainer if guarding, fear or reactivity becomes difficult to manage.
training.socialization: Provide gradual, positive exposure to everyday sounds, surfaces, people, handling and suitable dogs. Socialisation is an ongoing process rather than a single puppy-stage task. Focus on calm confidence and safe choices, not forcing the dog into overwhelming interactions.

climates: Temperate climates
Cool weather with appropriate shelter
Warm weather with shade, fresh water and exercise during cooler hours

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced diet appropriate to life stage, body condition, activity level and veterinary needs.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Feed a complete puppy diet in age-appropriate measured meals. Ask a veterinarian to guide growth, body condition and portion changes.
feedingFrequency.adult: Many adults do well with two measured meals per day. Adjust portions to activity, body condition and individual health needs.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure daily portions and monitor body condition rather than relying on a fixed amount for every dog. Keep fresh water available and include treats in the daily food allowance. Ask a veterinarian about an appropriate diet for a dog with heart, thyroid, liver or digestive concerns. Discuss meal timing and exercise with the veterinarian, particularly if the dog has a history of digestive problems.
considerations: Maintain a lean body condition to reduce unnecessary strain on joints.
Adjust portions as growth, activity and age change.
Use treats as part of the daily calorie allowance.
Provide fresh water throughout the day.
Discuss any persistent digestive symptoms or unexplained weight changes with a veterinarian.
Seek veterinary advice about diet and activity if a cardiac or other chronic condition is diagnosed.
nutrition.note: Nutritional requirements vary by individual. Use feeding guidance as a starting point and adjust according to body condition and veterinary advice.

health.overview: Doberman Pinschers have several important health considerations, particularly dilated cardiomyopathy, thyroid disease, von Willebrand disease, liver disease and cervical vertebral instability. Hip and eye evaluations are also included in breed-club screening recommendations. Some conditions can develop despite normal earlier screening, so health checks should be discussed with a veterinarian over the dog's lifetime. Breeder records, family history and appropriate testing can inform risk assessment but cannot guarantee an individual dog's future health.
commonConditions: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM): a serious heart-muscle disease associated with the breed; routine veterinary assessment and appropriate cardiac monitoring are important.
Hypothyroidism and autoimmune thyroid disease: thyroid function can be evaluated with veterinary blood testing.
Von Willebrand disease (vWD): an inherited clotting disorder for which DNA testing is available.
Chronic active hepatitis and other liver disease: veterinary assessment may include blood chemistry and additional tests when indicated.
Cervical vertebral instability, often called Wobbler syndrome: a spinal condition that can affect coordination and mobility; diagnosis requires veterinary evaluation.
Hip dysplasia: a developmental joint condition for which radiographic evaluation may be recommended.
Eye disorders: screening by a veterinary ophthalmologist is included in breed health guidance.
Gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat): a potentially life-threatening emergency involving stomach distension and rotation; urgent veterinary treatment is required if suspected.
preventiveCare: Arrange regular veterinary examinations and discuss cardiac monitoring appropriate to age, family history and risk.
Ask the breeder for documented cardiac, thyroid, eye, hip and von Willebrand disease testing where applicable.
Keep vaccination and parasite prevention current according to local veterinary guidance.
Maintain healthy body condition and build exercise gradually.
Learn the warning signs of bloat, including a swollen abdomen, repeated unproductive retching, restlessness and rapid deterioration; seek emergency care if suspected.
Seek prompt veterinary care for fainting, unexplained exercise intolerance, weakness, abnormal bleeding or changes in coordination.
Discuss ongoing screening intervals with a veterinarian because a single normal test does not exclude future disease.
recommendedScreenings: Cardiac examination by a veterinarian; breeding-dog screening may include echocardiography and Holter monitoring
Thyroid evaluation
Von Willebrand disease type I DNA test
Hip evaluation using an accepted radiographic scheme
Ophthalmologist examination
Additional liver assessment when history, symptoms or veterinary findings warrant it
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with a dog-specific toothbrush and toothpaste. Arrange veterinary dental checks and seek advice for persistent bad breath, gum redness, pain or difficulty chewing.
health.earCare: Check the ears routinely for redness, odour, discharge or discomfort. Clean only as advised by a veterinarian and seek care if signs of infection appear.
health.skinCare: The short coat makes skin checks relatively straightforward. Look for irritation, sores, unusual lumps, persistent itching or hair loss and consult a veterinarian if these persist.

idealFor: People who can provide daily exercise and mental enrichment
Owners who are willing to train consistently throughout the dog's life
