overview.summary: A miniature sighthound of exceptional grace and slender elegance, combining the speed and visual chasing instinct of a coursing hound with the affectionate, warmth-seeking devotion of a close indoor companion.
overview.description: The Italian Greyhound is the smallest of the sighthounds—a true Greyhound in miniature, built with even more slender proportions and refined bone. Its body fits into a square outline where body length is equal to or barely less than height at the withers, with a deep, narrow chest let down to the elbows, an arched loin, a pronounced abdominal tuck-up, and long, lean legs. The head is narrow and elongated with large, expressive dark eyes and small, fine-textured rose ears that fold back against the nape when relaxed and stand out horizontally ('flying' or 'propeller' ears) when alert. Lively, docile, and deeply affectionate with its immediate family—preferring to snuggle under blankets or on a lap rather than sit on the floor—it retains a true sighthound's flash-and-dash speed and strong instinct to bolt after small moving animals. Because of its fine leg bones, short satin-like coat, and minimal body fat, it requires protection from cold weather and careful management to prevent jumping injuries.
overview.history: Descended from small sighthounds kept in ancient Egypt at the court of the Pharaohs and across Greece (Laconia) and Anatolia more than 2,000 years ago, the breed reached Italy by the beginning of the fifth century BC, where it was depicted on vases, bowls, and Roman sculptures. It flourished in Renaissance Italy among aristocratic households and was immortalized in works by masters such as Giotto, Carpaccio, Sassetta, Memling, Van der Weyden, Hieronymus Bosch, and Tiepolo. Across Europe, monarchs and nobles—including Anne of Denmark, Mary Beatrice d'Este, Frederick the Great of Prussia, Catherine the Great of Russia, and Queen Victoria—kept these miniature hounds as treasured companions, and the African king Lobengula once traded 200 head of cattle for a single dog. Organized studbook registrations began in Britain in 1874 and in the United States in 1886. After the First and Second World Wars nearly extinguished European bloodlines, surviving North American and Austrian stock helped rebuild the modern population.
overview.originalPurpose: Noble companion and small-game sighthound used to course hare, rabbit, and other small, fast-moving quarry
currentRoles: Agility, rally, and reward-based obedience competitor

physical.coatType: Short, silky, fine, and glossy single coat lying smooth and close over fine, tight skin without any trace of fringing
physical.coatLength: Very short and fine all over the body
coatColors: Parti-colour (white broken with black, blue, fawn, or red markings)
physical.sheddingLevel: Low
distinctiveFeatures: Square body outline in which body length is equal to or barely less than height at the withers (32–38 cm)
Elongated, narrow head reaching up to 40% of withers height, with parallel skull and muzzle axes and skull length equal to half the total head length
Large, roundish, expressive dark eyes with pigmented rims
Very high-set, small rose ears folded back on the nape at rest and held out laterally ('flying' or 'propeller' ears) when attentive
Deep, narrow chest reaching the elbows, arched dorsal-lumbar topline, very sloping muscled croup, and accentuated sternal tuck-up
Long, straight, finely boned legs with oval hare feet where the two middle toes and nails are slightly longer than the outer ones
Low-set, fine tail tapering to the tip, carried low and straight in its first half and curved in its second half, reaching the hock
Springy, harmonious, high-stepping trot with good forward reach and a fast, sharp-springing gallop capable of bursts up to 60 km/h (35 mph)
Weight up to 5 kg maximum in international standards (ideal 3.6–4.5 kg in British standards; 3.2–6.4 kg / 7–14 lbs in North American profiles)

Coat colour rules differ by standard: international conformation standards allow only solid black, grey, and isabella (with white limited to chest and feet), whereas British and North American standards also allow red, cream, white, and parti-colour (while all standards disqualify brindle and black-and-tan markings)

Lively and vivacious
Docile and gentle

Emotionally sensitive

exercise.level: Moderate to active. Combines energetic bursts of running and play with long periods of indoor lounging and cuddling.
activities: Daily walks using a secure martingale collar or properly fitted harness and leash
Supervised sprinting and play in a safely enclosed, fenced area
Indoor interactive play (especially in multi-Italian Greyhound households)
Lure coursing and amateur racing
Age-appropriate agility, rally, and positive-reinforcement trick training

grooming.level: Low for the coat, but high priority for daily dental hygiene and frequent nail grinding.
grooming.brushing: Wipe or brush occasionally with a soft bristle brush, hound glove, or damp cloth to remove loose hair and keep the satin coat gleaming; bathe only when necessary.
grooming.bathing: Rarely required unless the dog gets dirty; use a gentle dog shampoo and dry thoroughly so the dog does not become chilled.
notes: Daily tooth brushing with canine toothpaste and yearly veterinary dental examinations/cleanings are essential because the breed is highly prone to periodontal disease.

Grind or file nails 1 to 3 times per week using an electric rotary grinder; this breed's nails and inner quicks grow rapidly, and maintaining short nails that clear the floor when standing helps preserve foot conformation and reduce leg-fracture risk.
Because the breed has a hare foot, the two middle nails naturally remain slightly longer than the outer two nails.
Dress the dog in warm sweaters, coats, or boots during cold or wet weather, as its thin coat and low body fat offer little insulation.
Inspect the fine skin regularly for scrapes, abrasions, or irritation.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging. Quick to solve problems and responsive to gentle praise and treats, yet sensitive to harsh corrections, independent-minded, and notoriously slow to house-train reliably.
tips: Use reward-based training with small, immediate food rewards and enthusiastic praise; harsh verbal or physical corrections will cause these sensitive dogs to shut down.

Commit to diligent house-training for the first 1 to 2 years: puppies only begin developing true bladder control around 14 to 16 weeks of age and need very frequent outdoor trips or a dedicated indoor paper/litter area.

Never crate a puppy for more than 2 to 3 hours at a time; for longer absences, use a secure, covered exercise pen with paper/pad area, bedding, and safe chew toys so the puppy does not learn to soil its crate.

Teach puppies how to step or jump safely off low surfaces first; young puppies often leap fearlessly off high beds, sofas, or tables before their bones mature, which is a leading cause of radius and ulna fractures.
Always use a martingale lead or escape-proof harness outdoors and never allow the dog off-leash in unfenced areas, as even obedience-trained dogs will bolt into traffic after a cat or squirrel.
Avoid unsupervised all-size dog parks; limit off-leash group play to secure areas with dogs of similar small size and gentle play style.
training.socialization: Because Italian Greyhounds bond intensely with their owners and can be aloof or timid toward unfamiliar people and children, introduce puppies early and consistently to gentle people, well-mannered children, calm dogs, and neighbourhood sights and sounds.

climates: Temperate climates
Warm climates
Cold or northern climates only as a strictly indoor dog provided with warm clothing outdoors and heated indoor living spaces
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low. Italian Greyhounds are indoor companion dogs—never kennel, backyard, or basement dogs—that thrive on physical closeness and often do best in pairs or in households where someone is home during the day.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality, energy-dense, complete and balanced small-breed dog food formulated for puppy, adult, or senior life stages, or a veterinarian-supervised home-prepared diet.

feedingFrequency.puppy: 3 meals daily until at least 6 months of age (some puppies continue needing 3 daily meals for several additional months due to their small stomach capacity and high energy demands).
feedingFrequency.adult: 2 meals daily, with clean, fresh water available at all times.

nutrition.guidelines: Because an Italian Greyhound's stomach capacity is small relative to its metabolic rate, feed a nutrient-dense, high-quality diet in measured portions. Watch calorie intake and training treats carefully to prevent excess weight, which places dangerous strain on slender legs and joints. On an Italian Greyhound in proper body condition, the tips of the hip bones should just be visible, while the ribs should not be visible but should be easily felt beneath a thin layer of flesh.
considerations: Feed puppies three times a day until at least 6 months of age so their small stomachs can meet growth and energy needs.
Keep training treats tiny and account for them in daily calories to prevent obesity.
Monitor body condition using the breed-specific visual benchmark: hip bones barely visible and ribs easily palpable but not protruding.
Combine appropriate nutrition with daily tooth brushing to manage the breed's susceptibility to gum and periodontal disease.
Consult a veterinarian promptly if digestive sensitivities, food allergies, or unexplained weight changes occur.
nutrition.note: Puppy (3 meals/day until at least 6 months) and adult (2 meals/day) schedules reflect national breed-club guidance; senior meal frequency should be individualized with a veterinarian.

health.overview: The Italian Greyhound is generally a hardy, long-lived toy sighthound that routinely reaches 14 to 15 years of age or more (and shows a 0% incidence of hip dysplasia in orthopedic registry data), but several hereditary, immune-mediated, dental, and traumatic conditions require proactive management. Peer-reviewed genetic research has established breed-specific DNA tests for three inherited disorders: autosomal recessive familial enamel hypoplasia (FEH / amelogenesis imperfecta, caused by an ENAM gene deletion with an estimated 14% affected and 30% carrier prevalence), progressive retinal atrophy (PRA-IG1, affecting 2%–4% of the breed across 5 susceptibility loci), and primary closed angle glaucoma (PCAG, associated with two linked susceptibility variants). In addition, historical population bottlenecks and homozygosity in the dog leukocyte antigen (DLA) class I and II regions predispose the breed—especially females—to autoimmune disorders including autoimmune thyroiditis, immune-mediated hemolytic anemia, and immune-mediated polyarthritis. Clinically, periodontal disease and radius/ulna leg fractures in young dogs jumping from furniture are among the most frequent everyday veterinary concerns.
commonConditions: Periodontal disease, gingivitis, and premature tooth loss (common in dogs that do not receive daily tooth brushing and regular veterinary dental cleanings)

Familial enamel hypoplasia (FEH / autosomal recessive amelogenesis imperfecta), caused by a 5-bp deletion (c.1991_1995delTTTCC) in exon 10 of the ENAM gene on chromosome 13 (estimated 14% affected and 30% carriers; causes rough, thin, brownish-mottled enamel and small pointed teeth, though not linked to periodontal disease)

Progressive retinal atrophy (PRA-IG1), a progressive photoreceptor degeneration leading to blindness that affects 2%–4% of Italian Greyhounds (average diagnosis age 6.5 years; 5-locus genetic panel identifies 90% of breed susceptibility, with aa or dd genotypes carrying a 30x risk)

Primary closed angle glaucoma (PCAG), an acute, painful intraocular pressure spike causing optic nerve damage and blindness (average diagnosis age 3.9 years, range 0.5–6 years; dogs homozygous for two linked susceptibility variants have a 60x higher risk)

Autoimmune disorders and autoimmune thyroiditis (hypothyroidism), linked in peer-reviewed studies to genome-wide and DLA class I/II homozygosity (females are 2–5 times more likely to be affected; manifestations include immune-mediated hemolytic anemia [IMHA], immune-mediated polyarthritis [IMPA], immune-mediated thrombocytopenia [IMTP], thyroiditis, pemphigus, Addison's disease, and steroid-responsive meningitis)
Traumatic forelimb fractures (particularly radius and ulna fractures), most common in puppies and young adolescents leaping off beds, sofas, stairs, or during rough play
Patellar luxation and Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (avascular necrosis of the femoral head)
Less frequent or sporadic reported conditions: idiopathic seizures/epilepsy, allergies, digestive sensitivities, congenital deafness, and cervical intervertebral disc disease
preventiveCare: Brush teeth daily with canine toothpaste starting as soon as adult teeth erupt, and schedule annual professional veterinary dental examinations and cleanings.
Grind nails 1 to 3 times weekly so they do not touch the floor when standing, supporting proper foot posture and reducing slip-and-fracture hazards.
Prevent puppies and young dogs from jumping off beds, couches, tables, or out of arms, and supervise play strictly around stairs, large dogs, and young children.

Verify that breeding stock has completed mandatory pre-breeding clinical evaluations (patellas, thyroid, and annual ophthalmologist exams) and recommended breed-specific DNA panels (PRA-IG1, PCAG glaucoma, FEH enamel hypoplasia, and genetic diversity).
Keep the dog on a martingale collar or secure harness and leash whenever outdoors in unfenced areas to prevent high-speed traffic accidents triggered by prey drive.
Protect the dog from cold and wet weather with sweaters or coats, and provide warm indoor bedding.
recommendedScreenings: Patella evaluation by a veterinarian (once after 12 months of age)
Thyroid blood evaluation (annually from ages 2 to 4 years, then biennially until age 8 years)
Ophthalmologist evaluation by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (annually until age 10 years)
Susceptibility to Progressive Retinal Atrophy (PRA-IG1) DNA test (5-locus panel; once at any age)
Susceptibility to Primary Closed Angle Glaucoma (PCAG) DNA test (once at any age)
Familial Enamel Hypoplasia (FEH / ENAM) DNA test (once at any age)
Canine Genetic Diversity DNA test (STR and DLA class I/II haplotype assessment to reduce homozygosity and autoimmune risk)
Brucellosis (Brucella canis) screening for breeding pairs prior to each mating
health.dentalCare: Daily tooth brushing with an unflavoured canine toothpaste and a soft canine toothbrush is the single most critical routine care habit for an Italian Greyhound, paired with yearly veterinary dental examinations and cleanings. Distinguish between preventable periodontal gum disease and inherited familial enamel hypoplasia (FEH), which causes congenital mottled, thin enamel and can be identified by DNA testing.
health.earCare: Inspect the delicate, folded rose ears weekly for wax buildup, redness, or odour, and clean gently only as needed with a veterinarian-approved ear cleanser.
health.skinCare: Because the skin is fine, tight, and covered only by a very short single coat with minimal subcutaneous fat, inspect regularly for scrapes, bruises, or dryness, provide soft padded bedding to protect bony prominences, and use warm clothing in cold weather.

idealFor: Adults, couples, or families with older, gentle, considerate children who respect a finely boned toy sighthound
Apartment and city dwellers as well as country homeowners who want an affectionate, clean indoor lap companion
Households where someone is home much of the day or where a second small sighthound provides companionship
Owners committed to daily tooth brushing, weekly nail grinding, patient house-training, and cold-weather clothing
People who enjoy daily leashed walks, enclosed running play, agility, or lure coursing
notIdealFor: Households with very young, boisterous, or unsupervised children, or homes with large, rough-playing dogs
Owners who expect reliable off-leash recall in unfenced areas around wildlife or traffic
People who work long hours away from home every day and would leave a single dog crated or isolated
Anyone unwilling to manage a prolonged house-training process or perform daily dental and weekly nail care
Households seeking an outdoor, kennel, or cold-hardy dog

funFacts: The Italian Greyhound is the smallest member of the sighthound (gazehound) family, yet it can sprint in bursts of up to 60 km/h (35 mph).
When the dog is alert, its high-set folded ears lift at the base and stand out horizontally to the sides—a distinctive posture known in the breed standard as 'flying ears' or 'propeller ears'.

Italian Greyhounds appear in paintings by Renaissance and early modern masters including Giotto, Vittore Carpaccio, Sassetta, Hans Memling, Rogier van der Weyden, Hieronymus Bosch, and Giambattista Tiepolo.

Royal admirers across history included Anne of Denmark, Mary Beatrice d'Este, Frederick the Great of Prussia, Catherine the Great of Russia, and Queen Victoria, while the southern African king Lobengula once traded 200 head of cattle for a single Italian Greyhound.
The breed has 'hare feet', meaning the two middle toes and their nails are naturally longer than the outer toes, creating an oval, arched foot built for sprinting.
In orthopedic registry statistics evaluating 157 dog breeds for hip dysplasia, the Italian Greyhound ranked as the least affected breed with an incidence of 0%.

faq.question: What is an Italian Greyhound?
faq.answer: The Italian Greyhound (also called the Piccolo Levriero Italiano or Italian Sighthound) is the smallest of the sighthound breeds—a true Greyhound in miniature bred for more than two millennia both as an aristocratic lap companion and as a swift courser of small game.

faq.question: How big does an Italian Greyhound get?
faq.answer: Both males and females stand 32 to 38 cm (about 12.5 to 15 inches) at the withers, with a square body outline whose length equals or is barely less than its height. International conformation standards specify a maximum weight of 5 kg (11 lbs) for both sexes, British standards list an ideal weight of 3.6 to 4.5 kg (8–10 lbs), and North American profiles describe a typical range of 3.2 to 6.4 kg (7–14 lbs).

faq.question: Why do coat colour rules differ for Italian Greyhounds in different countries?
faq.answer: European and international conformation standards allow only solid black, grey (blue/slate), and isabella (fawn/beige) in any shade, tolerating white markings solely on the chest and feet and disqualifying multi-coloured coats. By contrast, British and North American standards also accept red, cream, white, and parti-colour (white broken with coloured markings). Across all major standards, brindle markings and black-and-tan patterns are disqualifications.

faq.question: Are Italian Greyhounds good for families with young children?
faq.answer: Generally no. Because of their fine bone structure and sensitive, sometimes timid nature, national breed-club guidance advises against placing Italian Greyhounds in homes with very young or rambunctious children or large, boisterous dogs where accidental falls or rough play can easily break a leg. They do best with adults or older, gentle children.

faq.question: Why are leg fractures a concern in Italian Greyhound puppies?
faq.answer: Until skeletal maturity, an Italian Greyhound's long, slender radius and ulna bones are vulnerable to snapping from awkward landings. Young puppies often leap fearlessly from high beds, sofas, tables, or a handler's arms ('thinking they can fly'), so owners must supervise furniture access, teach controlled low steps, and keep nails ground short for traction.

faq.question: Are Italian Greyhounds difficult to house-train?
faq.answer: Yes, house-training requires patience and consistency over the first one to two years. Puppies only begin developing reliable bladder control between 14 and 16 weeks of age, cannot hold their bladder for long workdays, and dislike cold rain. Successful owners use frequent scheduled outdoor trips, positive rewards, or a dedicated indoor paper/litter area, and never crate a puppy for more than 2 to 3 hours at a stretch.

faq.question: Can an Italian Greyhound be trusted off-leash in an unfenced area?
faq.answer: No. Despite being cuddly lapdogs indoors, Italian Greyhounds retain a powerful visual sighthound prey drive and will bolt instantly after a squirrel, cat, or rabbit—ignoring recall cues and running into traffic. Outside of a securely fenced yard, they should always wear a properly fitted martingale collar or escape-proof harness and leash.

faq.question: How often should an Italian Greyhound's teeth and nails be cared for?
faq.answer: Teeth should be brushed daily with canine toothpaste and examined annually by a veterinarian, as periodontal disease is very common in the breed. Nails should be ground 1 to 3 times a week with an electric grinder so they clear the floor when the dog stands; the breed's nails and inner quicks grow rapidly, and long nails distort the hare foot and increase injury risk.

faq.question: What genetic and clinical health tests are recommended for Italian Greyhounds?
faq.answer: National breed-club guidelines recommend three clinical screenings—veterinary patella evaluation (after 12 months of age), thyroid blood testing (annually from ages 2 to 4, then biennially to age 8), and annual board-certified ophthalmologist exams (until age 10)—along with DNA tests for progressive retinal atrophy susceptibility (PRA-IG1), primary closed angle glaucoma susceptibility (PCAG), familial enamel hypoplasia (FEH / ENAM), and canine genetic diversity.

faq.question: How can you tell if an Italian Greyhound is at a healthy weight?
faq.answer: Because excess weight stresses their slender limbs, Italian Greyhounds should be kept lean. On a dog in ideal body condition, the tips of the hip bones should just be visible, and the ribs should not be visible but should be easily felt under a thin covering of flesh.

overview.summary: The Jack Russell Terrier is a small, energetic working terrier developed from English fox-working dogs and shaped into its recognised modern form in Australia. Alert, bold and quick to learn, it was bred to follow hounds and pursue quarry underground. It is usually best suited to homes that can offer daily activity, thoughtful training and safe outlets for its strong urge to chase, dig and explore.
overview.description: Compact but athletic, the Jack Russell Terrier has a body that is slightly longer than it is tall, with a flexible frame built for movement and work in tight spaces. Its coat may be smooth, rough or broken, and white should predominate with black and/or tan markings. This is not simply a small lap dog: the breed often brings a lively, persistent working temperament into everyday life. Consistent reward-based training, enrichment and secure supervision help channel its energy into appropriate activities.
overview.history: The breed traces to nineteenth-century England and Reverend John Russell, who developed fox-working terriers able to keep pace with hounds and enter dens to flush foxes and other quarry. Similar Russell-type terriers later travelled to Australia, where working dogs formed the basis of the breed developed and registered there. The Jack Russell Terrier is distinct from the taller, more squarely built Parson Russell Terrier, despite their shared historical roots.
overview.originalPurpose: A working terrier bred to accompany foxhounds and pursue foxes and other quarry into underground dens.
currentRoles: Agility and other suitable canine sports

physical.coatType: Weather-resistant coat that may be smooth, rough or broken; the coat should retain a natural working texture.
physical.coatLength: Short, with smooth, broken and rough varieties.
coatColors: Predominantly white with black and tan markings
physical.sheddingLevel: Low to moderate; regular shedding occurs.
distinctiveFeatures: Compact, flexible body slightly longer than it is tall
Lively, alert expression with small, dark, almond-shaped eyes
Button or dropped ears
Weatherproof smooth, broken or rough coat
Predominantly white coat with black and/or tan markings
Deep chest and agile frame suited to working underground

traits: Lively, alert and active
Bold and confident
Friendly and often affectionate with familiar people
Intelligent and quick to learn
Persistent and independent when following scent or movement
May chase wildlife and small animals because of its working heritage
Can bark or dig when excited, under-stimulated or pursuing an instinctive activity
Individual behaviour varies with genetics, experience, training and environment

exercise.level: High. The breed generally needs daily physical activity together with mentally engaging tasks. Tailor the amount and intensity to age, fitness, health and the individual dog.
activities: Brisk walks with opportunities to sniff and explore
Reward-based training in short, varied sessions
Scent games, food puzzles and problem-solving activities
Fetch or interactive play in a secure area
Agility, tracking or appropriate terrier activities
Recall practice in securely enclosed spaces

grooming.level: Low to moderate; rough or broken coats may need additional attention.
grooming.brushing: Brush about weekly to remove loose hair and check the skin. Rough or broken coats may need hand-stripping or help from a groomer familiar with the coat type.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when dirty or otherwise needed, using a dog-formulated shampoo and avoiding unnecessarily frequent baths.
notes: Grooming needs differ somewhat between smooth, broken and rough coats.
Check ears regularly for redness, odour or discharge and clean only as needed with an appropriate product.
Trim nails as needed to keep movement comfortable.
Brush teeth regularly with dog-safe toothpaste.
Inspect the skin and coat during grooming for parasites, irritation or wounds.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging for inexperienced handlers. The breed is capable and responsive, but can be persistent, energetic and strongly motivated to chase.
tips: Use reward-based, varied sessions to keep learning engaging.
Start recall, loose-leash walking and calm-settle training early.
Reward quiet and settled behaviour as well as active performance.
Provide safe outlets for sniffing, searching, digging and problem-solving.
Use secure fencing and a lead where wildlife or small animals may trigger chasing.
Manage introductions to children, dogs and other pets carefully.
Avoid harsh methods; seek qualified help if chasing, reactivity or barking is difficult to manage.
training.socialization: Introduce people, dogs, sounds, surfaces, transport and new settings gradually and positively. Supervise children’s interactions and use appropriate barriers around small pets; socialisation does not remove an individual dog's prey drive.

climates: Can adapt to many climates when given appropriate shelter and care.
In hot weather, provide shade, ventilation, fresh water and exercise during cooler parts of the day.
In cold or wet conditions, provide a dry, comfortable resting area and monitor the individual dog.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced dog food appropriate for life stage, body condition, activity level and health.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Feed a complete puppy diet in age-appropriate meals, following the food guidance and advice from a veterinarian.
feedingFrequency.adult: Use measured meals of a complete adult diet and adjust the amount to maintain a healthy body condition.
feedingFrequency.senior: Select a complete diet suited to activity, body condition, dental health and medical needs, with veterinary advice when appropriate.

nutrition.guidelines: Assess food needs individually rather than assuming every dog of this breed needs the same quantity. Choose a nutritionally complete diet, measure portions, include training treats in the daily allowance, provide fresh water and monitor body condition. Ask a veterinarian about persistent weight changes, digestive signs or supplements.
considerations: Adjust portions to age, activity, body condition and food energy density.
Count training treats as part of the daily intake.
Keep fresh, clean water available.
Introduce dietary changes gradually.
Discuss persistent digestive signs or unexplained weight change with a veterinarian.
Avoid supplements without a specific need and suitable veterinary advice.
nutrition.note: No universal calorie target or serving size is provided because requirements vary by individual dog, food and lifestyle.

health.overview: Jack Russell Terriers are often described as robust, but breed-specific screening guidance highlights inherited conditions that responsible breeders should consider. These include primary lens luxation and neurological disorders such as late-onset ataxia and spinocerebellar ataxia. Screening recommendations concern breeding decisions and risk management; they cannot predict with certainty whether an individual dog will become ill.
commonConditions: Primary lens luxation, an inherited eye condition that can threaten vision
Late-onset ataxia, an inherited neurological disorder
Spinocerebellar ataxia, an inherited neurological disorder
preventiveCare: Arrange routine veterinary examinations and follow locally appropriate vaccination and parasite-prevention advice.
Ask breeders for documented results from health tests relevant to the breed and the dog's lineage.
Discuss primary lens luxation and neurological DNA tests, plus eye examinations, with a veterinarian or breed specialist.
Seek prompt veterinary advice for sudden vision changes, abnormal balance, weakness, altered gait or other new neurological signs.
Maintain dental hygiene, a healthy body condition and activity suitable for the individual dog.
Remember that screening reduces uncertainty but does not guarantee future health.
recommendedScreenings: DNA test for primary lens luxation (PLL), listed as a good-practice pre-breeding test by The Royal Kennel Club.
DNA test for late-onset ataxia (LOA), listed as a best-practice test.
DNA test for spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA), listed as a best-practice test.
Eye examination using an appropriate veterinary ophthalmology screening scheme.
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth regularly with dog-safe toothpaste and arrange veterinary oral checks. Seek advice for oral pain, bleeding gums, damaged teeth, persistent bad breath or difficulty eating.
health.earCare: Check ears regularly for redness, discharge, odour or repeated scratching. Clean only as needed with a dog-safe product and seek veterinary advice for persistent or painful signs.
health.skinCare: Inspect skin and coat during grooming. Seek veterinary advice for ongoing itching, redness, sores, hair loss or recurring irritation rather than assuming the cause.

idealFor: Active households that enjoy daily outdoor activities and training
Owners willing to provide secure containment and supervise the dog around wildlife
People interested in scent games, agility, tracking or other suitable terrier activities
Households prepared for a lively dog with persistent hunting instincts
notIdealFor: People seeking a low-energy dog that needs little stimulation
Homes unable to provide safe containment or supervision around small animals
Owners expecting reliable off-leash behaviour around wildlife without training and management
Households unable to make time for daily activity, training and interaction

funFacts: The breed originated in England and was developed into its modern recognised form in Australia.
The FCI standard places the Jack Russell Terrier in Group 3, Terriers, Section 2, Small Terriers.
Its working build is slightly longer than it is tall, with a chest shaped to help it move through narrow underground spaces.
The Jack Russell Terrier is distinct from the taller, more squarely built Parson Russell Terrier.

faq.question: Where did the Jack Russell Terrier originate?
faq.answer: The breed originated in England in the nineteenth century, from terriers associated with Reverend John Russell. Australia is identified as the country of development in the FCI standard.

faq.question: How tall is a Jack Russell Terrier?
faq.answer: The FCI and Royal Kennel Club standards give an ideal height range of 25–30 cm at the withers. An individual dog's adult height can differ from the standard.

faq.question: How much should a Jack Russell Terrier weigh?
faq.answer: The FCI standard relates weight to height at approximately 1 kg for each 5 cm of height, giving about 5 kg at 25 cm and 6 kg at 30 cm. Healthy weight depends on build and body condition.

faq.question: What coat colours are accepted?
faq.answer: White should predominate, with black and/or tan markings. The coat may be smooth, rough or broken.

faq.question: Does a Jack Russell Terrier need a lot of exercise?
faq.answer: It is an energetic working terrier that benefits from daily activity and mental enrichment. The appropriate amount depends on age, health, fitness and the individual dog; no fixed minute target is specified here.

faq.question: What health tests should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Ask about primary lens luxation DNA testing, late-onset ataxia and spinocerebellar ataxia DNA testing, and appropriate eye examinations. Confirm current recommendations and results with the breeder, veterinarian or breed specialist.

faq.question: How long does a Jack Russell Terrier live?
faq.answer: A veterinary breed overview reports a lifespan of about 13–15 years. This is a general estimate, not a guarantee for an individual dog.

overview.summary: The Japanese Chin is a small companion dog with a broad face, large expressive eyes, and a long, silky coat. Often graceful and quietly amusing, it tends to enjoy close company while also showing an independent, cat-like curiosity. Its short muzzle means owners should take particular care in hot or humid weather and watch for breathing or eye discomfort.
overview.description: Compact and balanced, the Japanese Chin has a broad rounded head, short muzzle, wide-set dark eyes, feathered hanging ears, and a plume-like tail carried over the back. The coat is long, straight, and silky, with especially noticeable feathering around the neck, ears, thighs, and tail. Chin are usually kept as close household companions rather than working dogs. Many are affectionate and playful, though individual dogs differ in confidence and sociability. Gentle handling, reward-based training, routine coat care, and attention to heat tolerance support their wellbeing.
overview.history: The breed's history is closely connected with East Asian court life. The FCI standard recounts historical accounts of dogs arriving at the Japanese court from the Korean peninsula and of further exchanges with China and Korea. In Japan, the Chin became an indoor companion associated with aristocratic households, later spreading to Europe and North America. The precise early ancestry is historical rather than fully documented by modern genetic evidence.
overview.originalPurpose: A small indoor companion dog, historically kept in Japanese court and aristocratic households.
currentRoles: Participation in suitable low-impact canine activities

physical.coatType: Single-looking, silky, straight, long outer coat; the breed standard describes profuse hair over the body apart from the face.
physical.coatLength: Long, with prominent feathering on the ears, neck, thighs, and tail.
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate; loose hair is noticeable and brushing may need to increase during shedding periods.
distinctiveFeatures: Broad, rounded head and very short, broad muzzle
Large, wide-set, dark eyes
Long feathered ears
Silky coat with a neck ruff and feathered thighs
Plumed tail carried over the back
Light, elegant movement

Bright and observant
Gentle
Playful
Often quiet indoors
Curious and sometimes cat-like in movement
May be reserved when first meeting unfamiliar people

exercise.level: Low to moderate; regular gentle walks and short play sessions are generally more suitable than strenuous exercise, especially in warm weather.
activities: Short, comfortable walks
Indoor play and simple games
Reward-based trick training
Gentle sniffing and exploration in safe conditions

grooming.brushing: Brush and comb several times a week, paying attention to the ears, feathering, and areas where friction can form tangles; increase frequency when shedding.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when needed with a dog-appropriate shampoo, dry thoroughly, and avoid overheating during drying.
notes: Check behind the ears and around the trousers and tail feathering for tangles.
Keep nails trimmed and the hair under the feet neat.
Check the eyes regularly for redness, discharge, or signs of irritation.
A harness is often preferable to attaching a lead to a collar, because small dogs may have delicate necks and airways.

training.difficulty: Usually manageable with patient, gentle, consistent training; harsh methods can undermine confidence.
tips: Use short sessions and reward desired behaviour promptly.
Teach handling, grooming, and cooperative veterinary-care skills gradually.
Keep training sessions engaging and stop before the dog becomes tired.
Use secure leads and enclosed areas outdoors; do not rely on obedience alone near traffic.
training.socialization: Introduce people, calm dogs, everyday sounds, and handling gradually and positively during puppyhood, while respecting the dog's comfort and vaccination guidance.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced diet appropriate to the dog's life stage, body condition, and health needs.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Several small meals daily, following the food's feeding guide and veterinary advice.
feedingFrequency.adult: Often two measured meals daily; adjust portions to body condition, activity, and the specific food.
feedingFrequency.senior: Individualize meal size and frequency to appetite, body condition, dental health, and veterinary advice.

nutrition.guidelines: Choose a complete diet appropriate for the dog's life stage. Measure portions, keep fresh water available, and adjust feeding to maintain a lean body condition. Ask a veterinarian before making major dietary changes or adding supplements.
considerations: Small dogs can gain excess weight when treats and table scraps are not counted.
Use appropriately sized food and treats.
Monitor body condition and dental health, and seek veterinary advice if chewing or eating changes.
nutrition.note: These are general feeding principles, not a breed-specific prescription; caloric needs vary by individual.

health.overview: Japanese Chin health discussions commonly emphasize eye health, kneecaps, cardiac screening, and the inherited GM2 gangliosidosis condition. Their short muzzle and relatively prominent eyes also make heat management and eye protection important. A condition being reported in the breed does not mean every dog will develop it; individual risk depends on genetics, conformation, and other factors.
commonConditions: Patellar luxation
Eye disorders, including cataracts and corneal or eyelid-related problems
Heart murmurs or congenital heart disease concerns
GM2 gangliosidosis (a serious inherited neurological disease)
Brachycephalic airway and heat-tolerance concerns associated with a short muzzle
preventiveCare: Arrange regular veterinary examinations and keep vaccinations and parasite prevention current.
Seek prompt veterinary advice for laboured breathing, collapse, persistent coughing, eye pain, sudden vision changes, or abnormal gait.
Avoid strenuous activity and never leave the dog in a hot vehicle; provide shade, ventilation, and water in warm or humid conditions.
Maintain a healthy body condition and provide routine dental care.
recommendedScreenings: Eye examination by a qualified veterinary ophthalmologist
Patellar (kneecap) evaluation
Veterinary cardiac examination, with further testing if indicated
GM2 gangliosidosis DNA testing and informed breeding decisions
Discuss breathing and airway assessment with a veterinarian, especially for dogs with noisy or effortful breathing
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth regularly with dog-safe toothpaste and arrange veterinary dental assessment as recommended. Small dogs may need particular attention to oral health.
health.earCare: Check the hanging ears routinely for redness, odour, discharge, or discomfort. Clean only as advised by a veterinarian and do not insert cotton swabs into the ear canal.
health.skinCare: Part the long coat during grooming to check the skin for irritation, parasites, or mats. Keep facial folds and the area around the eyes clean and dry without using irritating products.

funFacts: The FCI classifies the Japanese Chin among companion and toy dogs and does not require a working trial.
Its tail is characteristically carried over the back and covered in long, profuse hair.
Owners often describe its movements and self-grooming habits as cat-like, although individual dogs vary.
The breed standard describes a white coat with black or red markings.

faq.question: Where does the Japanese Chin come from?
faq.answer: Japan is the recognised country of origin. Its early history is connected with court life in East Asia, although accounts of its earliest arrival rely partly on historical records rather than modern documentation.

faq.question: How big is a Japanese Chin?
faq.answer: The FCI standard gives males an approximate height of 25 cm at the withers and says females are slightly smaller. It does not establish a formal sex-specific weight range, so this record does not invent one.

faq.question: What coat colours are accepted?
faq.answer: The FCI standard describes a white coat with black or red markings. Markings are ideally balanced around the eyes and ears and across the body.

faq.question: How much grooming does it need?
faq.answer: Brush and comb the silky coat several times a week, paying special attention to the ears and feathering. Check the eyes and keep nails trimmed as part of routine care.

faq.question: Is the Japanese Chin suitable for apartment living?
faq.answer: Often, yes: it is a small companion breed that can do well indoors when given company, gentle activity, and regular care. Housing suitability still depends on the individual dog's needs and daily routine.

faq.question: What health issues should I discuss with a breeder?
faq.answer: Ask for documented eye, patella, and cardiac evaluations and discuss GM2 gangliosidosis DNA testing. A veterinarian can also assess breathing, particularly if the dog snores loudly or shows effort when breathing.

faq.question: Does the Japanese Chin tolerate hot weather?
faq.answer: Its short muzzle can make heat and humidity harder to manage. Provide shade, ventilation, and fresh water, avoid strenuous activity in hot conditions, and seek veterinary help for signs of heat stress or breathing difficulty.

faq.question: How long does a Japanese Chin live?
faq.answer: The breed club gives a typical life expectancy of about 10–12 years, though individual lifespan varies with genetics, health, and care.

overview.summary: A medium-sized, loyal, and adaptable German companion and house dog, celebrated for its spirited personality, deep devotion to its family, agile jumping ability, and two distinct coat varieties: rough-haired with a signature beard and smooth-haired with flowing furnishings.
overview.description: The Kromfohrländer is an athletic, medium-sized companion dog originating in Germany, characterized by a slightly rectangular silhouette in which body length slightly exceeds height at the withers. The breed is bred in two distinct coat varieties: a rough-haired (wirehaired) variety defined by a characteristic beard, longer facial hair, and a harsh, wiry outer coat across the back and limbs; and a smooth-haired variety distinguished by a clean-shaven face without a beard, close-lying body hair, longer feathering on the ears, chest, and legs, and a well-plumed tail. Both varieties display a white ground colour adorned with light brown to very dark brown patches or saddle markings, centered around a distinctive head mask split by a symmetrical, uninterrupted white blaze reaching the forehead or nape. Spirited, docile, and highly adaptable, the breed combines lively indoor affection with a sensitive, thoughtful nature. It forms an exceptionally intense bond with its household—often choosing a favourite person—while maintaining a natural, polite reserve around unfamiliar people and strange dogs. Its keen intelligence and desire for companionship make patient, reward-based training essential.
overview.history: The Kromfohrländer is one of the youngest recognized German dog breeds, originating in 1945 in the aftermath of the Second World War near the town of Siegen in southern North Rhine-Westphalia. The breed was established by Ilse Schleifenbaum, who took in a scruffy, wirehaired stray terrier-type dog named Peter that had been found in northern France by American soldiers and served as their military troop mascot. When Peter mated with a local black-and-white female terrier named Fiffi, the resulting puppies exhibited a remarkably uniform, appealing appearance and loving character. Recognized ancestors in the breed's foundation include the wirehaired Fox Terrier and the Grand Griffon Vendéen. The breed takes its name from the local geographical district 'krom Fohr' (Low German for 'crooked furrow') near Hilchenbach and Siegen where Schleifenbaum lived. Formal breed club stewardship began with the establishment of the national breed club in 1955, the same year the breed gained definitive international recognition. The breed subsequently expanded to North America, where dedicated fanciers established national club representation and studbook recording in the early twenty-first century.
overview.originalPurpose: Companion and house dog

physical.coatType: Dense double coat occurring in two distinct varieties: rough-haired with a beard and harsh outer coat, or smooth-haired without a beard and with soft feathering, both over a short, soft undercoat
physical.coatLength: Medium length, measuring not longer than 7 cm at the withers and along the back, and about 3 cm on the sides. In the rough-haired variety, the coat is harsh and thick with longer hair on the face forming a beard, and harsher hair along the back and limbs. In the smooth-haired variety, the coat lies close to the body without a beard, featuring short facial hair, longer hair on the ears, lower neck, and chest, distinct feathering along the backs of the legs and thighs, and a plumed tail.

physical.sheddingLevel: Low to moderate seasonal shedding occurring primarily once or twice a year, varying slightly between the rough and smooth coat varieties
distinctiveFeatures: Medium-sized, harmonious build with body length slightly greater than height at the withers in an approximate 1.1:1 ratio
Two distinct coat varieties: rough-haired (featuring a harsh wiry texture and a beard) and smooth-haired (close-lying without a beard, with leg feathering and a plumed tail)
Elongated head with parallel planes between the muzzle and skull in an equal 1:1 length ratio, with a clearly defined stop and strong scissor bite
High-set, triangular semi-drop ears with rounded tips that fold forward close to the cheeks and move expressively with the dog's mood
Medium-sized, oval dark brown eyes with dark-pigmented rims, conveying an alert, intelligent expression
Striking symmetrical facial mask in tan to dark brown, neatly divided by an uninterrupted white blaze that extends to the forehead or nape
Un-docked, medium-length sabre tail carried hanging with an upward curve at rest and raised as a sickle over the back during action
Flowing, active gait with forward-reaching strides and strong drive, accompanied by a natural love for jumping and climbing
Shoulder height of 38 to 46 cm for both sexes, with adult weights of 11 to 16 kg for males and 9 to 14 kg for females (or 15 to 18 inches and 20 to 35 pounds)

Deeply affectionate with family

exercise.level: Active. Requires regular daily outdoor walks, vigorous interactive play, and purposeful mental challenges to satisfy its lively intelligence and athletic agility.
activities: Long daily walks and nature hikes suited to the dog's endurance
Interactive fetch and retrieving games with balls and toys
Agility courses, climbing, and hurdle jumping (waiting until skeletal maturity around age three for high-impact disc jumping)

grooming.level: Low to moderate. Straightforward routine upkeep for both coat types, though the rough-haired variety requires periodic hand-stripping to maintain its proper harsh texture.
grooming.brushing: Brush weekly with a firm bristle brush or pin brush to remove loose hair and prevent tangles in the feathering. The rough-haired coat requires regular hand-stripping or plucking with a stripping knife several times a year to remove dead wire hair and preserve coat texture; electric clipping or shaving should be avoided as it destroys the wiry texture.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only occasionally as needed. The coat naturally repels dirt, dries quickly, and carries virtually no typical doggy odour, even after outdoor play or when damp.
notes: The rough-haired coat should be hand-stripped periodically rather than clipped or shaved, which softens the wire and alters colour.
The smooth-haired variety requires routine brushing through the longer feathering on the ears, neck, chest, tail, and back of the legs to prevent knots.
The coat naturally repels mud and dirt and has little to no doggy odour even when wet.
Begin gentle nail trimming in early puppyhood and maintain it consistently, as the breed's natural sensitivity can make foot handling challenging if neglected.
Inspect the semi-drop ears weekly for dirt, wax, or redness, and brush teeth regularly to support oral hygiene.

training.difficulty: Moderate. Highly intelligent, intuitive, and quick to learn commands, but its emotional sensitivity requires gentle, patient guidance rather than heavy-handed pressure.
tips: Use upbeat, reward-based positive reinforcement with treats, gentle praise, and play.
Avoid harsh verbal scolding or physical corrections, as sensitive dogs easily become inhibited or timid under pressure.
Keep training sessions engaging, short, and varied to channel the breed's problem-solving intelligence.
Gradually build confidence for independent activities such as competitive agility.
Introduce novel people, animals, and environments slowly at the dog's own pace, keeping in mind that the breed prefers familiar companions over crowded dog parks.
Provide plenty of mental enrichment through trick training, puzzle solving, and agility games.
training.socialization: Begin gentle, comprehensive socialization during early puppyhood and continue throughout adolescence. Expose the puppy positively to varied people, calm dogs, novel surfaces, and household sounds. Because the breed is naturally reserved with strangers and selective with unfamiliar dogs, allow the dog to assess new acquaintances at its own pace rather than forcing immediate physical interactions.

livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate. Strongly attached to its household and particularly to its primary caregiver, the breed thrives on constant family inclusion. It does not tolerate prolonged isolation or outdoor kennel living well, and can become anxious or unhappy if left alone for extended periods.

nutrition.dietType: Complete and balanced, high-quality dog food formulated for active medium-sized dogs, tailored to the individual's life stage, body condition, and energy output.
nutrition.guidelines: Provide a high-quality, balanced diet suited to the dog's age, weight, and activity level. Individual appetites vary considerably: some individuals are finicky or selective eaters, while others consume meals with enthusiasm. Because the breed is naturally active and rarely overeats, portions should be measured to maintain lean muscle mass and an ideal body condition. Consult a veterinarian or breeder to determine customized puppy and adult feeding amounts, and ensure clean, fresh water is available at all times.
considerations: Appetite varies between individuals, ranging from selective eaters to enthusiastic feeders.
High-quality, nutrient-dense nutrition supports steady energy for this active breed.
Monitor body condition regularly and adjust portions to avoid unwanted weight fluctuations.
Collaborate with a veterinarian or breeder to establish appropriate feeding schedules for puppies and adults.
Ensure continuous access to fresh drinking water, and seek professional advice before adding dietary supplements.
nutrition.note: Consult a veterinarian or experienced breeder to establish tailored feeding schedules, portion sizes, and nutrient profiles matched to the individual dog's life stage and metabolism.

health.overview: The Kromfohrländer is a relatively rare breed developed from a small foundation stock, making genetic surveillance and responsible breeding practices essential. Scientifically validated DNA screening has identified an autosomal recessive missense mutation in the FAM83G gene (c.155G>C, p.R52P) on canine chromosome 5 responsible for hereditary footpad hyperkeratosis (HFH), also known as digital hyperkeratosis or 'corny feet'. An inherited bleeding disorder, von Willebrand disease (vWD Type I), is also recognized in the breed, and pre-breeding DNA testing allows breeders to identify carriers and prevent affected litters. Other conditions reported within breed populations include autoimmune disorders, idiopathic epilepsy, cystinuria, patellar luxation, and spondylosis. Pre-breeding health protocols in its country of origin require general veterinary fitness certification, dental charting, and mandatory genetic testing for digital hyperkeratosis alongside DNA archival for ongoing scientific research.
commonConditions: Hereditary footpad hyperkeratosis (HFH / digital hyperkeratosis), an autosomal recessive dermatological disorder caused by a missense mutation in the FAM83G gene (c.155G>C, p.R52P) leading to severely thickened, hardened paw pads with painful fissures, abnormal nail growth, and coat texture changes beginning around 4 to 5 months of age
Von Willebrand disease (vWD Type I), an inherited blood-clotting deficiency causing prolonged bleeding from mucosal surfaces or surgical wounds, manageable through pre-breeding DNA testing
Autoimmune disorders, documented as an immune-mediated health concern in the breed population
Idiopathic epilepsy, a neurological seizure disorder reported in breed health surveillance
Cystinuria, an inherited metabolic condition predisposing dogs to the formation of cystine urinary bladder stones
Patellar luxation, an orthopedic condition involving kneecap instability or dislocation
Spondylosis, a degenerative spinal condition characterized by bony spurs along the vertebrae in maturing dogs
preventiveCare: Ensure breeding stock undergoes DNA testing for hereditary footpad hyperkeratosis (FAM83G) and von Willebrand disease to avoid carrier-to-carrier matings and prevent affected offspring.
Review family health histories with a veterinarian, paying close attention to autoimmune, neurological, urinary, and orthopedic backgrounds.
Inspect paw pads, interdigital spaces, and nails regularly for signs of thickening, hardening, painful cracks, or lameness, seeking prompt veterinary care if lesions develop.
Maintain routine veterinary wellness visits, dental cleanings, parasite preventives, and core vaccinations.
Support joint health and longevity with regular moderate exercise, gradual positive nail care, and maintaining a lean, athletic body condition.
recommendedScreenings: Canine Footpad Hyperkeratosis (HFH) DNA Test (FAM83G c.155G>C variant)
Von Willebrand Disease Type I (vWD Type I) DNA Test
Pre-breeding general veterinary clinical examination and dental charting
Patellar luxation clinical veterinary evaluation
health.dentalCare: Establish a routine dental care program early in life, including regular tooth brushing with dog-safe toothpaste and periodic professional veterinary cleanings. Conformation standards require strong jaws with a complete, regular scissor bite of 42 teeth (a pincer bite is permitted, and absence of more than two molars or more than three premolars is disqualified). Adults generally maintain sound dentition, though occasional tooth loss can occur with advancing age.
health.earCare: Inspect the semi-drop ears weekly during regular grooming for signs of wax buildup, redness, debris, or foul odour. Clean the outer ear gently using a veterinarian-recommended ear cleaner when necessary, and seek veterinary advice if persistent head shaking or discharge occurs.
health.skinCare: Examine the paw pads and skin regularly for signs of excessive keratinization, cracking, or tenderness. In dogs affected by hereditary footpad hyperkeratosis, clinical signs typically emerge between 4 and 5 months of age with hardened, cracked footpads, rapid-growing hard nails, and duller coat texture. Routine inspection and genetic testing provide the most reliable safeguards.

idealFor: Households seeking a devoted, people-oriented companion that forms an intensely close bond with its family
Active individuals and families who enjoy regular outdoor walks, hiking, fetching, agility, and trick training
Owners committed to patient, reward-based training and gentle, positive guidance
Handlers willing to provide regular grooming, including hand-stripping the rough coat or maintaining smooth coat feathering
notIdealFor: Households where a dog would be left alone or crated for long workdays without companionship
Owners looking for an aloof, independent dog or an off-leash dog-park dog that immediately welcomes all unfamiliar dogs and strangers
Homes unable to provide daily outdoor exercise, mental stimulation, and thoughtful, considerate handling

funFacts: The breed was established in 1945 and is one of Germany's youngest recognized companion breeds.

The entire breed descends from a stray wirehaired terrier mix named Peter, who was discovered by American troops in northern France during the Second World War and served as their beloved troop mascot before being adopted by the breed's founder.
The breed name honors the historical geographical district 'krom Fohr' (Low German for 'crooked furrow') near Siegen in North Rhine-Westphalia, where the original kennel was located.
A distinctive breed trait is the famous greeting grin, where happy dogs curl their lips into a toothy 'smile' and may sneeze when enthusiastically welcoming their owners.
Puppies are born in two distinct coat types—rough-haired with a charming beard and smooth-haired without a beard—both of which share the same clean, dirt-shedding qualities.
Despite its medium size and companion role, the breed possesses extraordinary jumping agility and springiness, often leaping effortlessly over obstacles.

faq.question: How big does an adult Kromfohrländer get?
faq.answer: Conformation standards specify a height at the withers of 38 to 46 cm (approximately 15 to 18 inches) for both males and females. Typical adult weight ranges between 11 and 16 kg (24 to 35 pounds) for males and 9 to 14 kg (20 to 31 pounds) for females.

faq.question: What are the two coat varieties of the Kromfohrländer?
faq.answer: The breed exists in rough-haired and smooth-haired varieties. The rough-haired variety features a harsh outer coat and a distinctive beard, while the smooth-haired variety has a smooth face without a beard, close-lying body hair, longer feathering on the ears, neck, chest, and legs, and a plumed tail.

faq.question: What colours and markings are standard for the breed?
faq.answer: The ground colour is white, marked with light brown, tan, to very dark brown patches or a saddle pattern. The head features symmetrical brown-to-tan markings across the cheeks, over the eyes, and on the ears, neatly divided by an unbroken central white blaze extending to the forehead or nape.

faq.question: What inherited health conditions affect the Kromfohrländer?
faq.answer: Key genetic concerns include hereditary footpad hyperkeratosis (HFH / 'corny feet'), caused by a mutation in the FAM83G gene, and von Willebrand disease Type I. Both conditions can be identified through DNA screening. Additional health concerns monitored in the breed include autoimmune disorders, idiopathic epilepsy, cystinuria, patellar luxation, and spondylosis.

faq.question: What pre-breeding health screenings should prospective puppy owners look for?
faq.answer: Responsible breeding programs require DNA testing for hereditary footpad hyperkeratosis (FAM83G) and von Willebrand disease, along with general clinical veterinary examinations, dental evaluations, and patellar assessments to ensure sound breeding stock.

faq.question: How much exercise and mental stimulation does a Kromfohrländer need?
faq.answer: As an active and spirited companion, the breed requires daily outdoor exercise, such as long nature walks, interactive fetch, and scent games, paired with mental challenges like trick training or agility. High-impact jumping should be deferred until joints are fully mature around three years of age.

faq.question: How does a Kromfohrländer typically behave around strangers and other dogs?
faq.answer: The breed is naturally devoted to its immediate family but tends to be reserved and observant with unfamiliar people, preferring to make introductions at its own pace. It is generally polite with dogs it knows well, but it is not typically suited to bustling dog parks where strange dogs crowd its space.

overview.summary: The Löwchen, whose name means 'little lion' in German, is a small companion dog known for its lively expression, affectionate nature, and confident personality. It combines a sturdy build with an elegant outline and is often recognised by its traditional lion clip. It generally enjoys being involved in family life and benefits from positive training, play, and regular companionship.
overview.description: The Löwchen is a compact, well-proportioned dog with a proud head carriage, dark expressive eyes, and pendant ears with long fringes. Its long, silky, wavy coat has no undercoat and can appear in many colours and combinations. The traditional lion clip leaves a mane around the front of the body while the hindquarters are clipped short; the unclipped coat should remain natural rather than sculpted. Despite its decorative appearance, the breed is robust and lively, and enjoys walks, games, and learning with its people.
overview.history: The Löwchen has a long history as a European companion dog. Images resembling the breed appear in medieval and Renaissance art, including carvings and tapestries, and historical accounts describe its popularity among European court circles. Its early geographical origin has been debated, but the modern breed standard identifies France as its country of origin. By the twentieth century, numbers had become very low. Dedicated breeders, especially in Europe, worked to preserve and rebuild the breed population, and it later spread to the United Kingdom and North America.

grooming.bathing: Bathe when needed with a dog-appropriate shampoo, rinse thoroughly, and gently dry and comb the coat to reduce tangling. A long coat or show-style lion clip may need more regular professional maintenance.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Puppies usually need several small, measured meals each day. Adjust the schedule to age, growth, the food's directions, and veterinary advice.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals per day can be a practical routine; portion size should reflect body condition, activity, and food energy density.
feedingFrequency.senior: Adjust the diet and portions to activity, body condition, dental health, appetite, and medical needs with veterinary guidance.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure food portions and monitor body condition rather than relying only on package estimates. Small dogs can gain excess weight when treats are frequent or portions are not adjusted. Provide fresh water at all times, count training treats in the daily allowance, and ask a veterinarian for individual guidance if weight or digestion changes.

Screening recommendations identify risks worth managing; they do not mean that every dog will develop these conditions or establish their prevalence in the population.

Eye examination by a qualified veterinary ophthalmologist

health.dentalCare: Brush teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste. Small dogs can develop dental problems, so have the mouth checked during veterinary visits and seek advice for persistent bad breath, pain, bleeding, or difficulty eating.
health.earCare: Check the pendant ears and fringes regularly for tangles, dirt, redness, odour, or discharge. Clean only when needed with a dog-safe product, and consult a veterinarian if discomfort or persistent signs occur.
health.skinCare: Inspect the skin while brushing, especially beneath long hair and around the ears, legs, and tail. Persistent itching, sores, unusual hair loss, or recurrent irritation should be assessed by a veterinarian rather than treated as a normal coat issue.

idealFor: People seeking a small, affectionate companion dog
Households that can provide daily walks, play, and interaction
Owners willing to maintain a long coat or arrange professional grooming
People interested in reward-based training and small-dog activities
Households that can teach alert barking appropriate limits
notIdealFor: People unwilling to maintain a long coat or pay for regular grooming
Households expecting a dog that never barks to alert
People unable to provide regular companionship and interaction
Owners who rely on harsh corrections rather than patient training

funFacts: The name Löwchen means 'little lion' in German.
The traditional lion clip is a defining part of the breed's show presentation.
The FCI standard describes the coat as long, silky, wavy, and without an undercoat.
Historical depictions of dogs resembling the Löwchen appear in European art dating back several centuries.
The breed is classified as a companion dog rather than a working dog.

faq.question: Where does the Löwchen come from?
faq.answer: The FCI lists France as the breed's country of origin. Its early history has been debated, and historical depictions of similar dogs appear in several parts of Europe.

faq.question: How big does a Löwchen get?
faq.answer: The FCI standard gives a height of 26–32 cm at the withers, with a tolerance of 1 cm above or below that range. The standard describes weight as approximately 6 kg rather than providing separate male and female ranges.

faq.question: Why is the Löwchen called a Little Lion Dog?
faq.answer: The name means 'little lion' in German and refers to the traditional lion clip, which leaves a mane-like coat around the front of the body while the hindquarters are clipped short.

faq.question: How long does a Löwchen live?
faq.answer: The American Kennel Club lists a life expectancy of 13–15 years. This is a population-level estimate, not a guarantee for an individual dog.

faq.question: Does a Löwchen shed?
faq.answer: The breed is often described as low-shedding, but loose hair can still occur. Regular brushing is important because the long coat can tangle or mat.

faq.question: Is the Löwchen easy to train?
faq.answer: It is intelligent and often responsive to positive training. Early work on recall, calm greetings, and barking helps establish good household habits.

faq.question: What health checks should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Ask for documented hip and patellar evaluations and an eye examination by a qualified veterinary ophthalmologist. Discuss family health history and any additional tests with the breeder and veterinarian.

faq.question: Does a Löwchen need the lion clip?
faq.answer: The FCI standard requires the lion clip for showing under that standard. A companion dog can be kept in a practical pet trim, provided its coat is cared for properly.
