overview.summary: The Parson Russell Terrier is a small, athletic working terrier developed for fox hunting. It combines a lively, confident nature with stamina, agility, and a strong instinct to investigate and pursue moving animals. It generally suits people who can provide regular activity, training, supervision, and mental enrichment.
overview.description: This terrier has a balanced, flexible body, relatively long legs, a narrow chest, and an alert expression. Its coat can be smooth, broken, or rough, with a dense, weather-resistant texture. White is the dominant colour, usually with black, tan, or lemon markings depending on the standard being followed. The breed is energetic and clever, but its hunting instincts and independent problem-solving can make secure containment and consistent training especially important.
overview.history: The breed developed in southern England during the nineteenth century from fox-working terriers associated with Reverend John Russell. These dogs were expected to keep pace with hounds and horses, then enter underground dens to locate and flush foxes. The Parson Russell Terrier became a distinct recognised breed after a long period in which different working terriers were often grouped under overlapping Russell or Jack Russell names.
overview.originalPurpose: A working terrier bred to accompany foxhounds and pursue foxes both above ground and into underground dens.
currentRoles: Earthdog and other suitable terrier activities
Tracking and other structured canine sports

physical.coatType: Double coat that may be smooth, broken, or rough; the coat is naturally harsh, dense, close-fitting, and weather-resistant.
physical.coatLength: Short to medium, depending on the smooth, broken, or rough coat variety.
coatColors: Predominantly white with lemon markings under the FCI standard
White with a combination of permitted markings
physical.sheddingLevel: Low to moderate: shedding occurs throughout the year but is described as not excessive.
distinctiveFeatures: Compact, athletic body built for stamina
Relatively long legs and a narrow, flexible chest
Alert expression with dark, almond-shaped eyes
Forward-folding V-shaped ears
Predominantly white coat with permitted coloured markings
Smooth, broken, or rough coat varieties
Strong hunting instinct and ability to work underground

traits: Energetic and athletic
Bold and confident
Clever and inquisitive
Playful and often affectionate with familiar people
Independent and persistent when pursuing an interesting scent or target
May chase small animals because of its working heritage
Benefits from early socialisation and consistent, reward-based training
Individual temperament varies with genetics, experience, health, and training

exercise.level: High. This active working terrier needs daily physical activity and purposeful mental enrichment. Adapt activity to age, fitness, health, weather, and the individual dog's behaviour.
activities: Brisk walks with opportunities to sniff and explore
Reward-based training and short learning sessions
Securely supervised fetch or interactive play
Food puzzles and scent games
Agility, tracking, or suitable terrier activities
Recall practice in securely enclosed areas

grooming.level: Low to moderate. The coat is intended to retain a natural appearance; rough or broken coats may need additional maintenance.
grooming.brushing: Brush regularly with a suitable dog brush or comb to remove loose hair and check the skin. Rough and broken coats may require hand-stripping or help from a groomer familiar with the breed.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when necessary with a dog-formulated shampoo. Frequent bathing is usually unnecessary unless the dog becomes dirty or a veterinarian recommends it.
notes: Keep the coat looking natural rather than excessively sculpted.
Check the ears regularly and clean only as needed with appropriate products.
Trim nails as needed to maintain comfortable movement.
Brush teeth regularly with dog-safe toothpaste.
Inspect the skin and coat during routine grooming for irritation, parasites, or wounds.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging for inexperienced handlers. The breed is intelligent and can learn quickly, but its energy, persistence, and hunting instincts require consistent management.
tips: Use short, varied, reward-based sessions to maintain engagement.
Train recall and loose-leash walking early, while recognising that prey drive can remain strong.
Reward calm behaviour and teach a reliable settle cue.
Provide safe outlets for sniffing, searching, and problem-solving.
Use secure fencing and a lead in open areas where wildlife or small animals may trigger chasing.
Introduce children, dogs, people, and new environments gradually and positively.
Avoid harsh or frightening methods; seek a qualified trainer if reactivity or chasing becomes difficult to manage.
training.socialization: Introduce the dog to people, dogs, household sounds, surfaces, transport, and new places gradually and positively. Supervise interactions with children and other animals, and do not assume that socialisation will eliminate the breed's natural hunting drive.

climates: A range of ordinary climates can be managed with suitable shelter and care.
In hot weather, provide shade, ventilation, fresh water, and cooler times for exercise.
In cold or wet conditions, provide a dry, comfortable resting area.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced dog food appropriate for the dog's life stage, body condition, activity level, and health.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Feed a complete puppy diet in portions and at a frequency appropriate for the puppy's age, growth, and the food's feeding instructions. Ask a veterinarian for individual guidance.
feedingFrequency.adult: Use measured meals of a complete adult diet. Adjust portions to maintain a healthy body condition and account for treats used during training.
feedingFrequency.senior: Choose a complete diet suited to the dog's body condition, activity, dental health, and medical needs. Ask a veterinarian before making major dietary changes.

nutrition.guidelines: Choose a nutritionally complete diet and monitor body condition rather than relying on a universal portion size. Food requirements vary with age, activity, health, and the energy density of the food. Keep fresh water available, introduce dietary changes gradually, and discuss persistent weight changes, digestive problems, or supplement use with a veterinarian.
considerations: Measure portions and adjust them to maintain a healthy body condition.
Include training treats in the overall daily food allowance.
Provide fresh, clean water at all times.
Use a life-stage-appropriate complete diet.
Discuss suspected food intolerance, persistent digestive signs, or unexplained weight change with a veterinarian.
Do not add supplements unless there is a clear need and suitable veterinary advice.
nutrition.note: No universal calorie target or serving size is specified because individual requirements depend on body condition, activity, age, food composition, and health.

health.overview: The breed is generally described as robust, but breed-health resources identify concerns that responsible breeders may screen for, including patellar luxation, congenital deafness, certain inherited neurological conditions, and eye disorders. Primary lens luxation and inherited dental enamel disease also appear in breed-specific DNA-testing resources. These are potential concerns, not a prediction that an individual dog will develop them.
commonConditions: Patellar luxation, in which the kneecap moves out of its normal position
Congenital deafness
Late-onset ataxia, an inherited neurological condition
Spinocerebellar ataxia and related inherited neurological conditions
Eye disorders, including primary lens luxation
Amelogenesis imperfecta, an inherited disorder affecting tooth enamel
preventiveCare: Arrange routine veterinary examinations and keep vaccinations and parasite prevention appropriate to local veterinary advice.
Ask the breeder for documented health-screening results for both parents.
Discuss breed-relevant eye, patella, hearing, and DNA tests with a veterinarian or knowledgeable breed specialist.
Seek veterinary advice promptly for sudden vision changes, unusual gait or balance, hearing concerns, or signs of pain.
Maintain dental hygiene, healthy body condition, and regular activity suited to the individual dog.
Remember that a screening result can inform risk but cannot guarantee that a dog will remain free of disease.
recommendedScreenings: Patella evaluation for breeding dogs.
Examination by a veterinary ophthalmologist.
BAER hearing assessment where recommended.
Discuss DNA testing for primary lens luxation and breed-relevant ataxia variants with a veterinarian or breed specialist.
Ask whether testing for other documented breed-associated inherited conditions is appropriate for the individual dog's lineage.
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with dog-safe toothpaste and arrange veterinary dental checks. Seek veterinary advice for persistent bad breath, oral pain, bleeding gums, damaged teeth, or difficulty eating.
health.earCare: Check the ears regularly for redness, discharge, odour, or repeated scratching. Clean only when needed with a dog-safe product, and ask a veterinarian about persistent or painful signs.
health.skinCare: Inspect the skin and coat during grooming. Seek veterinary advice for persistent itching, redness, sores, hair loss, or recurring skin problems rather than assuming the cause.

idealFor: People who enjoy regular outdoor activity and interactive training
Owners able to provide secure containment and supervised exercise
Households interested in scent games, agility, tracking, or suitable terrier sports
People prepared to manage a lively dog with strong hunting instincts
notIdealFor: People seeking a low-energy dog that needs little activity or engagement
Households unable to provide safe containment or supervision around small animals
Owners expecting reliable off-leash behaviour around wildlife without substantial training and management
People who cannot commit to ongoing training, enrichment, and daily interaction

funFacts: The breed was developed to work with foxhounds and horses and to pursue foxes underground.
The FCI standard describes male and female ideal heights separately: 36 cm for males and 33 cm for females.
The coat can be smooth, broken, or rough, and is intended to remain natural-looking rather than heavily sculpted.
The breed's hunting heritage helps explain why secure containment and recall training are important.

faq.question: How tall is a Parson Russell Terrier?
faq.answer: The FCI standard gives ideal heights of 36 cm for males and 33 cm for females. The AKC standard gives ideal heights of 14 inches for males and 13 inches for females, and disqualifies dogs under 12 or over 15 inches. These are standard-specific measurements, not a guarantee of an individual dog's adult size.

faq.question: How much does a Parson Russell Terrier weigh?
faq.answer: The AKC standard describes 13–17 pounds as the usual weight for a terrier in hard working condition, approximately 5.9–7.7 kg. Healthy weight depends on the individual dog's frame, condition, and activity.

faq.question: What colours can a Parson Russell Terrier be?
faq.answer: The FCI standard describes a white or predominantly white coat with tan, lemon, or black markings, or a combination of these. Colour rules can differ between kennel-club standards.

faq.question: Does a Parson Russell Terrier need a lot of exercise?
faq.answer: It is an active working terrier that generally needs regular exercise, training, and mental enrichment. No single daily minute target is provided here because needs vary by age, fitness, health, and the individual dog.

faq.question: Can a Parson Russell Terrier live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Apartment suitability cannot be determined from breed alone. The dog's exercise, enrichment, noise, training, access to safe outdoor activity, and the household's circumstances all matter.

faq.question: What health checks should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Ask for documented results relevant to the breed, including patella, eye, and hearing assessments, and discuss appropriate DNA tests for inherited conditions with a veterinarian or breed specialist. Testing recommendations can change and should be confirmed before breeding.

faq.question: How long does a Parson Russell Terrier live?
faq.answer: A reliable, consistently supported lifespan range was not established from the sources used for this record, so no numerical range is supplied. Individual lifespan varies with genetics, healthcare, environment, and chance.

overview.summary: The Petit Brabançon is a small, short-coated Belgian companion dog with a sturdy, nearly square build, a short muzzle, and an alert, expressive face. It is closely related to the rough-coated Brussels Griffon and Belgian Griffon; the smooth coat distinguishes this variety. Typically people-focused and watchful, it thrives with kind training, close companionship, and care that takes its compact size and short face into account.
overview.description: Compact but not delicate in build, the Petit Brabançon has a broad head, large dark eyes, a short nose, and a smooth coat that lies close to the body. The breed standard describes a confident, attentive dog strongly attached to its owner, without timidity or aggression. Many enjoy being involved in household routines and short play or training sessions. Because the muzzle is short and the body is small, owners should watch for breathing difficulty in heat, avoid rough handling, and protect the dog from falls or play that could cause injury.
overview.history: The Petit Brabançon shares its origins with the Brussels Griffon and Belgian Griffon. The FCI breed history traces the three varieties to small rough-coated dogs known as Smousje in the Brussels area. In the nineteenth century, crosses involving King Charles Spaniels and Pugs helped shape the modern type, including the short-coated variety. These small dogs were used around stables and carriages, including for alerting people and controlling rodents, and later became companion dogs.
overview.originalPurpose: A small alert companion and watchdog, historically kept around Brussels stables and carriages and used to help control rodents.

physical.coatType: Short, smooth, close-lying coat.
physical.coatLength: Short and close to the body, without the longer facial furnishings of the rough-coated Griffon varieties.
physical.sheddingLevel: Low to moderate; some seasonal loose hair is possible.
distinctiveFeatures: Compact, nearly square body
Large, broad head relative to the body
Very short muzzle and black nose
Large, round, dark eyes
Short, smooth coat
Slightly undershot jaw is characteristic of the breed standard

traits: Strongly attached to familiar people
Alert and watchful
Confident and proud in carriage
Intelligent and responsive
Can be sensitive to harsh handling
May be reserved with unfamiliar people
Often playful and people-oriented

exercise.level: Low to moderate
activities: Daily walks adapted to age and breathing comfort
Short reward-based training sessions
Indoor play and food-puzzle games
Supervised sniffing and exploration
Low-impact play in safe, temperate conditions

grooming.brushing: Brush the short coat once or twice a week with a soft brush or grooming mitt to remove loose hair and check the skin.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when needed using a dog-appropriate shampoo, and dry thoroughly. Avoid getting shampoo or water into the eyes and ears.
notes: Wipe facial folds gently when needed and dry them to reduce moisture build-up.
Check eyes regularly because prominent eyes can be vulnerable to irritation or injury.
Trim nails routinely and inspect paws.
Brush teeth with dog-safe toothpaste; small companion breeds can need particular attention to dental health.

training.difficulty: Moderate; generally responsive to gentle, consistent training, though house-training may take patience.
tips: Use short, upbeat, reward-based sessions.
Keep house-training routines predictable and provide frequent toilet breaks, especially for puppies.
Teach calm handling and cooperative care early.
Avoid harsh corrections, which can undermine confidence.
Use secure equipment and supervise around larger dogs because of the breed's small size.
training.socialization: Introduce the dog gradually and positively to people, calm dogs, handling, sounds, and everyday environments during puppyhood and continue throughout life.

climates: Temperate conditions are generally easier to manage
Use extra caution in hot or humid weather because of the short muzzle
Provide warmth and shelter in cold weather
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Often companionship-oriented; build alone time gradually and avoid routinely leaving the dog alone for long periods.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced dog food appropriate to life stage, body condition, and veterinary needs.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Usually 3–4 small meals daily, adjusted to age and the food's directions.
feedingFrequency.adult: Usually 2 measured meals daily.
feedingFrequency.senior: Often 2 measured meals daily; adjust energy intake and diet to health, appetite, and body condition.

nutrition.guidelines: Choose a complete diet appropriate for the dog's age and condition. Measure portions, account for treats, provide fresh water, and adjust intake to maintain a lean body condition. Ask a veterinarian to advise on individual calorie needs, dental issues, or medical diets.
considerations: Small dogs can gain excess weight when treats and portions are not measured.
Use small, appropriately sized treats during training.
Monitor eating comfort and dental health; consult a veterinarian if chewing or swallowing changes.
nutrition.note: Feeding amounts vary with age, activity, metabolism, body condition, and food energy density; no single gram amount is appropriate for every dog.

health.overview: The breed's very short face and prominent eyes deserve particular attention. Related Brussels Griffon health programmes identify patellar luxation, eye disorders, cardiac concerns, hip dysplasia, and respiratory function among issues that may be screened in breeding dogs. These are potential concerns, not a diagnosis or a statement that every Petit Brabançon will develop them. Seek veterinary assessment for noisy or laboured breathing, exercise intolerance, eye pain, limping, or fainting.
commonConditions: Brachycephalic airway or heat-intolerance concerns associated with a short muzzle
Patellar luxation
Eye disorders, including cataracts or other inherited eye defects
Cardiac conditions
Hip dysplasia
Potential spinal or neurological conditions reported in the related Brussels Griffon population; breed-specific prevalence is uncertain
preventiveCare: Arrange routine veterinary wellness examinations and keep vaccinations and parasite prevention current.
Maintain a lean body condition and avoid strenuous exercise in hot or humid weather.
Seek prompt veterinary advice for noisy breathing, open-mouth breathing at rest, blue or pale gums, collapse, eye squinting, or sudden lameness.
Use a harness that does not put pressure on the neck, and supervise jumping from furniture.
Maintain regular dental care and monitor the eyes for redness, discharge, cloudiness, or injury.
recommendedScreenings: Veterinary patellar luxation assessment
Ophthalmologist eye examination
Cardiac examination as advised by the veterinarian or breeding programme
Hip evaluation where recommended
Respiratory function assessment for breeding dogs where an appropriate scheme is available
Discuss relevant family history and any additional tests with a breed-informed veterinarian
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth regularly with dog-safe toothpaste and arrange veterinary dental checks. Ask a veterinarian to assess retained teeth, crowding, bad breath, oral pain, or difficulty chewing.
health.earCare: Check the ears regularly and clean only when needed with a veterinary-recommended product. Seek advice for persistent odour, redness, discharge, or head-shaking.
health.skinCare: Inspect the short coat and skin during grooming. Keep facial folds clean and dry, and consult a veterinarian about persistent itching, redness, sores, or unusual hair loss.

funFacts: The Petit Brabançon is the smooth-coated variety among three closely related Belgian breeds described together in the FCI standard.
Its name refers to Brabant, the historical region associated with the breed name.
The breed's ancestors were used around stables and carriages before becoming popular companion dogs.

faq.question: What is a Petit Brabançon?
faq.answer: It is a small Belgian companion breed and the short-coated variety among the Petit Brabançon, Brussels Griffon, and Belgian Griffon group described by the FCI.

faq.question: How much does a Petit Brabançon weigh?
faq.answer: The FCI standard gives a weight range of 3.5–6 kg. Individual dogs should be assessed by body condition and veterinary advice rather than weight alone.

faq.question: What colours can it have?
faq.answer: The standard accepts red, black, black-and-tan, and belge colouring, with a dark facial mask. The exact wording and acceptance of colours should be checked against the registry standard being used.

faq.question: Is the Petit Brabançon good for apartment living?
faq.answer: Its small size can suit apartment life when it receives daily walks, enrichment, companionship, and training. The owner must also manage its short-muzzle sensitivity to heat.

faq.question: Does it need a lot of grooming?
faq.answer: Its short, smooth coat usually needs less grooming than the rough-coated related varieties. Regular brushing, nail care, dental care, and attention to facial hygiene are still important.

faq.question: What health checks should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Ask for documented eye and patella screening, discuss cardiac and hip evaluation where appropriate, and ask what respiratory or other tests are advised for the family line. A veterinarian can help interpret results.

faq.question: Can it tolerate hot weather?
faq.answer: A short muzzle can make heat and humidity harder to manage. Keep activity gentle in warm weather, provide shade and water, and seek urgent veterinary help for distress or laboured breathing.

overview.summary: An athletic, clean-lined Maltese warren hound (Kelb tal-Fenek) that hunts by sight, scent, and hearing across rocky limestone terrain, celebrated for its amber eyes, mobile erect ears, tan-to-chestnut coat, and habit of blushing rose-pink when happy or excited.
overview.description: The Pharaoh Hound—known natively in Malta as the Kelb tal-Fenek ('rabbit dog')—is a medium-sized, graceful yet powerful hound with hard, clean-cut lines and a noble bearing. Slightly longer in body from breastbone to haunch than tall at the withers, it combines a long, lean, blunt-wedge head with parallel skull and foreface planes, oval amber eyes, and large, broad-based erect ears that pivot attentively to pinpoint sounds when working close. Its short, glossy, odourless coat ranges from tan and rich tan to chestnut, harmonized with flesh-coloured nose, lip, and eye-rim pigment that flushes a deep rose colour ('blushing') when the dog is excited or pleased. Unlike pure sighthounds, it is a versatile triple-sense hunter that locates quarry by scent, tracks underground movement by hearing, and courses at high speed by sight. Indoors, a well-exercised Pharaoh Hound is affectionate, comical, and playful well into old age, while remaining vocal, independent-minded, and unsuitable for off-leash freedom in unenclosed areas.
overview.history: For centuries, rural hunters and farmers across the Maltese archipelago of Malta and Gozo bred the Kelb tal-Fenek to hunt wild rabbits at night among steep, rocky hills and dry-stone rubble walls, often working alongside belled ferrets. Popular accounts long proposed that Phoenician traders brought ancient Egyptian 'Tesem' hunting dogs to Malta, inspired by the breed's striking visual similarity to hounds depicted in Egyptian tomb chapels (such as those of Mereruka and Senbi) and to the jackal-headed god Anubis. However, the earliest written record in Malta dates to 1647, when Maltese historian Giovanni Francesco Abela wrote in 'Della Descrittione di Malta' of local rabbit-hunting hounds ('Cernechi') prized as far away as France for rocky mountain terrain. Modern canine genomic and phylogeographic studies (including microsatellite and mitochondrial analyses in 2004 and 2023) indicate that the Kelb tal-Fenek is not a direct unchanged survivor of ancient Egypt, but rather a member of the Mediterranean warren-hound family—closely related to the Sicilian Cirneco dell'Etna and Iberian Podencos—showing low inbreeding and high genetic divergence from modern Egyptian street dogs. First imported to Britain in the 1920s and early 1960s, the breed produced its first litter outside Malta in the United Kingdom in 1963 and its first litter in the United States in 1970. After British fanciers adopted the name 'Pharaoh Hound' (a name originally used on the continent in 1963 for Mediterranean prick-eared hounds), Britain approved a dedicated standard for the Maltese breed in 1974—the same year Malta honoured the Kelb tal-Fenek as its National Dog (commemorated on a 1977 one-Maltese-lira silver coin)—followed by updated international adoption in 1977 and North American recognition in 1983–1984.
overview.originalPurpose: Nighttime and daytime hunting and coursing of wild rabbits and small game across rocky limestone terrain and dry-stone rubble walls using scent, hearing, and sight (traditionally in tandem with ferrets)
currentRoles: Working rabbit-hunting warren hound in Malta
Lure coursing and amateur racing competitor
Agility, obedience, rally, nose work, and tracking participant
Therapy dog and alert household watchdog

physical.coatType: Short, glossy single coat ranging in texture from fine and close-lying to slightly harsh, with no feathering and no undercoat
physical.coatLength: Short
coatColors: Tan (from yellowish-tan 'isfar' to rich golden tan)

Tan, rich tan, or chestnut with permitted white markings: white tail tip (strongly desired), white chest patch ('the Star'), white on the toes, and a slim white blaze or snip on the centre line of the face
physical.sheddingLevel: Low to moderate
distinctiveFeatures: Long, lean, well-chiselled head shaped like a blunt wedge from above and in profile, with a slight stop and parallel skull and foreface planes (foreface slightly longer than the skull)
Flesh-coloured nose, lips, and eye rims that blend with the coat colour (no other nose colour is permitted) and visibly 'blush' a deep rose-pink when the dog is happy or excited

Oval, moderately deep-set amber eyes that harmonize with the coat colour and give a keen, intelligent expression (puppies are born with blue eyes that transition through blue-grey to amber by 3 to 4 months of age)
Large, fine, broad-based ears set medium high, carried erect when alert, laid flat back for minimal wind resistance when sprinting, and remarkably mobile when listening for quarry

Lithe, slightly rectangular body (length from breastbone to haunch bone slightly greater than withers height) with an almost straight topline, deep brisket reaching the elbows, moderate tuck-up, and strong, well-knuckled feet that are neither cat nor hare feet
Medium-set, whip-like tail that is fairly thick at the base and tapers below the point of the hock in repose, carried high and curved like a rudder in action (a screw tail is a fault)

Strict coat-marking rules: a white tail tip is strongly desired, white on the chest ('the Star'), white toes, and a slim central facial snip/blaze are permitted, flecking is undesirable, and any solid white patch on the back of the neck, shoulder, back, or sides is a disqualification in North American standards

Withers height of 56–63.5 cm (22–25 in) for males and 53–61 cm (21–24 in) for females in international and British standards (58.42–63.5 cm [23–25 in] for males and 53.34–60.96 cm [21–24 in] for females in American standards) and typical adult weight of 20.4–24.9 kg (45–55 lbs)

traits: Alert, observant, and keen
Friendly, affectionate, and people-oriented with family
Playful and comical throughout adulthood and senior years
Intelligent and quick to learn, yet an independent thinker
Sensitive to harsh handling or heavy-handed corrections
Can be aloof or reserved with strangers, preferring to initiate greetings on its own terms
Vocal and expressive, using barks and a wide variety of pack-hound sounds
Intense hunting and chasing drive triggered by both sight and scent
Good alert watchdog that announces visitors, but non-aggressive and unsuited as a guard dog

exercise.level: High. Requires a consistent daily schedule: either 15 to 20 minutes twice daily of free sprinting for a 'self-runner' inside a minimum 50 × 50 foot (15 × 15 m) enclosure with a 6-foot-high (1.8 m) fence, or at least 20 minutes twice daily of brisk leashed walking and structured exercise.
activities: Free sprinting in a securely fenced enclosure (minimum 50 × 50 feet with a 6-foot fence)
Brisk daily leashed walks and jogging with an active handler
Lure coursing and amateur straight or oval racing
Agility, rally, and positive-reinforcement obedience
Tracking, nose work, and scent-detection games that engage the breed's keen nose
Interactive toy play (which most Pharaoh Hounds enjoy well into their senior years)

grooming.brushing: Light daily brushing or a thorough weekly going-over with a hound glove, rubber curry brush, or damp cloth to remove loose hair and keep the short coat gleaming.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only as needed with a gentle dog-safe shampoo; the breed naturally lacks a 'doggy odour' even when wet, so any noticeable body odour warrants a veterinary check.
notes: Keep toenails trimmed or ground short enough that they do not make a tapping sound when the dog walks across a hard floor.
Pay particular attention to keeping the large, erect ears clean and free of dust or debris after outdoor runs.
Inspect the thin skin and short coat after field runs for minor bramble or rock scratches (which are never penalized as conformation faults).
Provide a warm dog coat outdoors in cold, wet, or snowy weather and a soft, warm indoor bed.
Brush teeth regularly at home and have them checked at annual veterinary exams.

training.difficulty: Moderate
tips: Use creative, upbeat positive reinforcement ('praise, patience, and provisions'); Pharaoh Hounds are quick learners when convinced that the task is their own idea, but shut down or balk under harsh corrections.

Never trust any amount of obedience training to override the breed's hunting instinct in an unenclosed area: off-leash Pharaoh Hounds that catch a sight or scent trail will bolt oblivious to traffic and can be lost for days or struck by vehicles.
Enclose yards with a stout, minimum 6-foot-high (1.8 m) physical fence, and always use a strong leash and secure martingale collar or harness on walks.
Gently redirect or distract alert barking from puppyhood onward; the breed is naturally vocal and a household with a Pharaoh Hound is rarely completely bark-free.
Provide daily mental enrichment—such as tracking, nose work, agility, or puzzle toys—because a bored Pharaoh Hound quickly invents destructive entertainment.
training.socialization: Expose puppies early and positively to varied people, gentle children, friendly dogs, and novel sights. Because Pharaoh Hounds can be aloof with strangers, allow them the courtesy of making the first overture when meeting new people rather than forcing contact, and supervise carefully around cats and small furry pets.

climates: Warm and sunny Mediterranean climates (for which the short coat and large heat-dissipating ears are naturally adapted)
Temperate climates
Cool or cold climates only as a strictly indoor family dog provided with warm outdoor coats during exercise and cosy indoor bedding
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate. Because of its lack of insulating undercoat and strong need for human companionship, the Pharaoh Hound must be an indoor family dog rather than a backyard or outdoor kennel dog, and needs ample exercise before being left alone.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality, complete and balanced commercial dog food or veterinarian-supervised and approved home-prepared diet appropriate for the dog's life stage (puppy, adult, or senior) and activity level
nutrition.guidelines: Feed a nutritionally complete diet suited to the dog's age and workload, monitoring calorie intake and body condition so the dog stays lithe and lean without excess weight on its joints. Deduct training treats from the daily food allowance to prevent obesity, and keep clean, fresh water available at all times.
considerations: Watch calorie consumption and treat intake closely, as some individuals are prone to gaining excess weight when not actively coursing or running.
Prepare home-cooked diets only under the supervision and approval of a veterinarian.
Avoid vigorous sprinting immediately before or after meals.
Consult your breeder or veterinarian to establish individualized daily meal schedules for puppies, adults, and seniors.
nutrition.note: Consulted kennel-club and parent-club sources do not prescribe fixed numerical meal counts per day for puppies, adults, or seniors; tailor meal frequency and portion sizes with a veterinarian or breeder.

health.overview: The Pharaoh Hound is widely regarded by veterinary and breed-club health committees as a hardy, long-lived breed (typical lifespan 12 to 14 years) with low inbreeding and no widespread breed-specific genetic syndromes. Parent-club breeding ethics require all breeding dogs to be at least 24 months of age and to complete pre-breeding health certification screenings for hip dysplasia, patellar luxation, autoimmune thyroiditis (thyroid function), and inheritable eye diseases (via a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist), with elbow dysplasia also evaluated in health registries; the vast majority of screened dogs test normal. Like other lean coursing hounds, Pharaoh Hounds can be sensitive to certain anesthetics (such as barbiturates) and chemical insecticides due to their low body-fat percentage. In senior dogs, the most commonly reported cancers are hemangiosarcoma, mast cell tumours, and mammary tumours in unspayed females, which reflect general age-related canine risks rather than breed-specific defects.
commonConditions: Orthopedic screening targets: hip dysplasia, patellar luxation, and elbow dysplasia (screened prior to breeding under parent-club health protocols, with the majority of tested dogs scoring normal)
Autoimmune thyroiditis / hypothyroidism: monitored via mandatory pre-breeding thyroid blood panels in parent-club health programs
Hereditary ocular disorders: screened via periodic examinations by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist
Age-related cancers in older dogs: hemangiosarcoma, mast cell tumours, and mammary gland tumours in intact females (spaying companion females reduces mammary cancer risk)
Sighthound-type sensitivity to certain anaesthetic agents (such as thiobarbiturates) and chemical compounds/insecticides, linked to the breed's lean, low-body-fat build
Traumatic skin lacerations, torn nails, or sprains incurred while sprinting across rough or rocky terrain
preventiveCare: Verify that both parents of any prospective puppy are at least 24 months of age at breeding and hold documented health clearances for hips, patellas, thyroid function, and veterinary ophthalmologist eye exams (as well as elbow evaluations where performed).

Ensure every puppy is permanently identified via microchip before placement, and keep secure 6-foot fencing and leashes in place to prevent traffic trauma—one of the greatest real-world threats to the breed.
Inform your veterinarian about coursing-hound anaesthetic and chemical sensitivities prior to dental cleanings or surgery.
Keep nails trimmed short enough that they never tap on hard floors to prevent toe and foot splaying or high-speed running injuries.
Maintain a lean, athletic body weight and inspect the skin, ears, and paw pads after outdoor runs.
recommendedScreenings: Hip dysplasia evaluation (radiographic screening at 24 months of age or older, or distraction-index evaluation; required prior to breeding under parent-club ethics rules)
Patellar luxation veterinary evaluation (required prior to breeding under parent-club ethics rules)
Ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (required prior to breeding under parent-club ethics rules)
Thyroid panel / autoimmune thyroiditis blood evaluation (recommended by the national breed club and included in parent-club health screening)
Elbow dysplasia radiographic evaluation (included in parent-club health committee screening)
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth regularly at home with dog-safe toothpaste and have the teeth and gums examined at every annual veterinary checkup. Conformation standards require powerful jaws with a complete, strong scissor bite set square to the jaws.
health.earCare: Pay close attention to keeping the large, upright, mobile ears clean and free of dust, seeds, or wax buildup, wiping gently with a veterinarian-approved ear cleaner when needed.
health.skinCare: Because the short, fine single coat lacks an undercoat, inspect the skin regularly for scrapes after runs, provide a warm coat during cold or wet weather, and note that a healthy Pharaoh Hound has virtually no doggy odour (any strong skin or coat odour should be investigated by a veterinarian).

idealFor: Active individuals and families who want an affectionate, playful, clean indoor companion
Homes with a securely enclosed yard (at least 50 × 50 feet with a 6-foot fence) or owners committed to brisk twice-daily leashed walks and safe running outlets
Enthusiasts of lure coursing, racing, agility, rally, obedience, tracking, or nose work
Owners who use gentle, creative, reward-based training and appreciate a dog with a sense of humour
Households seeking a low-odour, short-coated breed with minimal coat grooming needs
notIdealFor: Anyone who wants an off-leash hiking or walking companion in unenclosed areas
Households with cats, rabbits, or small furry pets that cannot be safely separated or managed
People who plan to keep a dog outdoors in a kennel or backyard away from the family
Noise-sensitive households expecting a completely silent, bark-free home
Heavy-handed trainers who demand instant, robotic obedience without patience

funFacts: Known natively in Malta as the Kelb tal-Fenek ('rabbit dog'), the breed was declared the National Dog of Malta in 1974 and featured on the reverse of the 1977 one-Maltese-lira silver coin.

When a Pharaoh Hound is happy or excited, increased blood flow causes its flesh-coloured nose, ears, and eye rims to 'blush' a deep rose-pink, and many dogs also curl their lips into a toothy 'smile'.
Puppies are born with bright blue eyes that gradually turn blue-grey and deepen to the adult golden-amber colour at around 3 to 4 months of age.

In traditional Maltese rabbit hunting ('kaċċa tal-fenek') at night among limestone rubble walls, hunters use a belled ferret ('nemes') to flush rabbits from deep burrows; the Kelb tal-Fenek can hear the ferret's tiny bell up to 3 metres (10 feet) underground through solid rock crevices.

Although the breed bears a striking visual resemblance to ancient Egyptian tomb reliefs and the jackal-headed god Anubis, modern DNA studies show that it is an indigenous Mediterranean warren hound closely related to the Sicilian Cirneco dell'Etna rather than a direct survivor from pharaonic Egypt.

The first documented historical mention of Malta's rabbit-hunting hounds appears in 1647, when Maltese historian Giovanni Francesco Abela wrote that the island's 'Cernechi' were sought after as far away as France for hunting in steep, stony terrain.
A healthy Pharaoh Hound has virtually no 'doggy odour'—even when soaking wet.

faq.question: What is a Pharaoh Hound?
faq.answer: The Pharaoh Hound—traditionally called the Kelb tal-Fenek ('rabbit dog') in its native Malta—is a medium-sized, athletic Mediterranean hunting hound that pursues quarry using scent, hearing, and sight. It is famous for its amber eyes, large erect ears, short tan-to-chestnut coat, and ability to 'blush' rose-pink on its nose and ears when excited.

faq.question: Did the Pharaoh Hound really come from ancient Egypt?
faq.answer: Despite popular lore linking the breed to ancient Egyptian tomb art and Phoenician traders, genomic and mitochondrial studies published in 2004 and 2023 show that the modern Kelb tal-Fenek is not a direct unchanged descendant of ancient Egyptian dogs. Instead, it developed on the islands of Malta and Gozo (where rabbit-hunting hounds were recorded by Giovanni Francesco Abela in 1647) as part of the Mediterranean warren-hound group alongside Sicily's Cirneco dell'Etna and Spain's Podencos. The English name 'Pharaoh Hound' was applied in the twentieth century when the breed was exported to Britain.

faq.question: How big does a Pharaoh Hound get?
faq.answer: International and British conformation standards specify a withers height of 56 to 63.5 cm (22–25 inches) for males and 53 to 61 cm (21–24 inches) for females, while American standards specify 23 to 25 inches (58.42–63.5 cm) for males and 21 to 24 inches (53.34–60.96 cm) for females. Typical adult weight is 20.4 to 24.9 kg (45–55 pounds) for both sexes.

faq.question: What coat colours and white markings are allowed on a Pharaoh Hound?
faq.answer: The coat ranges from tan and rich tan to chestnut (with flesh-coloured nose, lip, and eye-rim pigment that blends with the coat). Permitted white markings are a strongly desired white tip on the tail, a white patch on the chest called 'the Star', white on the toes, and a slim white blaze or snip on the centre line of the face. Flecking is undesirable, and any solid white spot on the back of the neck, shoulder, back, or sides is a disqualification in North American standards.

faq.question: Why does a Pharaoh Hound blush and smile?
faq.answer: Because the breed carries recessive dilution pigment that gives it a flesh-coloured nose, eye rims, and inner ears rather than black pigment, increased blood flow when the dog is happy, affectionate, or excited turns its nose and ears a vivid rose-pink. Many Pharaoh Hounds also pull back their lips in a toothy 'smile' to greet their owners.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Pharaoh Hound need, and what fencing is required?
faq.answer: For a dog that naturally runs on its own ('a self-runner'), 15 to 20 minutes of free sprinting twice a day in a securely enclosed area of at least 50 by 50 feet surrounded by a 6-foot-high fence is ideal. If such an enclosure is unavailable or the dog does not self-exercise, owners should provide at least 20 minutes of brisk leashed walking twice daily alongside regular opportunities for lure coursing, agility, tracking, or enclosed running.

faq.question: Can a Pharaoh Hound ever be trusted off-leash in an unfenced area?
faq.answer: No. Unlike pure sighthounds that hunt only by vision, the Pharaoh Hound hunts by both sight and scent. Once it spots or scents a rabbit, squirrel, or cat in an open area, its hunting instinct overrides obedience training; off-leash dogs frequently run for miles oblivious to road traffic.

faq.question: Are Pharaoh Hounds quiet or vocal indoors?
faq.answer: Because they were bred to hunt in pairs or packs and bark to signal when quarry is located, Pharaoh Hounds are naturally vocal. They make excellent alert watchdogs that announce visitors and use a wide repertoire of barks and expressive sounds at home, though early gentle redirection helps keep barking manageable.

faq.question: What health tests are required or recommended for Pharaoh Hound breeding stock?
faq.answer: The breed is generally very healthy with low rates of hereditary disease. Parent-club breeding ethics require breeding dogs to be at least 24 months old and to complete screenings for hip dysplasia, patellar luxation, autoimmune thyroiditis (thyroid blood panel), and inheritable eye diseases (board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist exam), with elbow dysplasia also evaluated in health registries.

faq.question: Are there special veterinary precautions for Pharaoh Hounds?
faq.answer: Yes. Like other lean coursing hounds with very low body fat, Pharaoh Hounds can be sensitive to certain anaesthetic drugs (such as thiobarbiturates) and chemical insecticides, so owners should remind their veterinarian before any surgery or dental procedure.

overview.summary: An athletic Portuguese water dog developed to assist fishermen, known for its intelligence, stamina, webbed feet and distinctive curly or wavy coat.
overview.description: The Portuguese Water Dog is a strong, medium-sized working breed with a nearly square outline, a broad head, a muscular body and a thick tail that helps it manoeuvre in water. Its single coat may be curly or wavy and is usually low-shedding, but it continues to grow and requires consistent grooming. Alert, spirited and quick to learn, the breed often enjoys retrieving games, swimming, training and activities that involve working closely with people. Its energy and intelligence are best channelled through regular exercise, structured training and mental enrichment.
overview.history: The breed was historically found along Portugal's Atlantic coast, where fishermen used dogs of this type for a range of tasks connected with boats and fishing. These included retrieving objects, recovering escaped fish or loose equipment, and carrying messages between boats and shore. As fishing practices changed, the population became more associated with the Algarve region. The breed is recognised as a native Portuguese dog, although the exact beginnings of its history are not documented with certainty.
overview.originalPurpose: Fishermen's working dog used for retrieving, water work, carrying messages between boats and shore, and guarding boats and property.
currentRoles: Dock-diving and other suitable water sports

physical.coatType: Single coat without an undercoat; either curly or long and wavy, with strong hair that continues to grow.
physical.coatLength: Variable with grooming and coat variety. The wavy variety has longer, slightly shiny hair; the curly variety has shorter, dense curls. The head may develop a topknot, and the ears can carry longer hair in the wavy variety.
physical.sheddingLevel: Low compared with many double-coated breeds, but not zero. Loose hair may remain trapped in the coat, making regular combing and clipping important.

Thick-based tail that tapers towards the tip and assists movement in water

grooming.level: High. Low shedding does not mean low maintenance; the continuously growing coat needs regular detangling and periodic clipping.
grooming.brushing: Comb and brush regularly, working through the coat to prevent mats close to the skin. Frequency depends on coat length, curl, activity and the individual dog's coat condition.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when needed with a dog-appropriate shampoo, rinse thoroughly and dry the coat carefully. Arrange regular professional or competent home clipping according to the chosen coat style.
notes: Check the skin while combing, especially where mats can form.
Keep the coat around the eyes and other areas at a practical, comfortable length.
Check ears after swimming and dry them gently when wet.
Inspect paws and webbing for debris, irritation or small injuries after outdoor activity.
The traditional lion clip and the retriever clip are recognised grooming styles.
Do not assume a low-shedding coat is allergy-free; individual people can still react to this breed.

training.difficulty: Moderate to demanding. Intelligence and eagerness to work can make learning rewarding, but high energy and persistence call for consistent boundaries and regular practice.
tips: Use reward-based training and short, engaging sessions.
Teach recall, loose-leash walking and calm greeting behaviour early.
Provide appropriate outlets for retrieving and carrying objects.
Introduce water gradually and never force a dog to swim.
Practise settling and relaxation as well as active tasks.
Use food puzzles and problem-solving games to reduce boredom.
Keep rules consistent across household members.
training.socialization: Introduce the puppy gradually and positively to a range of people, dogs, environments, sounds and handling experiences. Continue practising calm, appropriate behaviour as the dog matures.

climates: Temperate climates with appropriate exercise and shelter
Warm weather with shade, fresh water and activity scheduled for cooler periods
Cooler conditions with suitable protection, supervision and coat care
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Often prefers company and purposeful interaction. Build alone-time tolerance gradually; avoid routinely leaving the dog isolated for long periods without exercise and enrichment.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced diet appropriate to the dog's life stage, body condition, activity and health.
nutrition.guidelines: Choose a nutritionally complete food suited to the dog's age and workload, measure portions, monitor body condition and keep fresh water available. Adjust portions with veterinary guidance if activity, weight or health changes.
considerations: Match energy intake to activity level and body condition rather than assuming every working-type dog needs the same portion.
Use treats in moderation and account for them within daily intake.
Provide fresh water at all times, particularly after exercise or swimming.
Introduce dietary changes gradually.
Ask a veterinarian about diet if the dog develops persistent digestive signs, itching or unexplained weight change.

health.overview: Portuguese Water Dogs can develop inherited and general canine health conditions. Breed-club guidance highlights the value of screening breeding dogs and checking the documented results of both parents. Screening reduces avoidable risk but does not guarantee that an individual dog will remain free of disease.

Maintain a healthy body condition and regular, age-appropriate activity.
Brush teeth regularly with dog-specific dental products.

Discuss breed-relevant screening and family history with a veterinarian or responsible breeder.
Seek veterinary assessment for persistent changes in vision, exercise tolerance, appetite, digestion or behaviour.

health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with toothpaste made for dogs. Ask a veterinarian about dental checks and professional cleaning when indicated.
health.earCare: Inspect the ears regularly, especially after swimming. Keep them clean and dry without inserting cotton swabs deeply into the ear canal. Seek veterinary advice for redness, odour, discharge or repeated head-shaking.
health.skinCare: Part the coat during grooming to check the skin for irritation, parasites, wounds and mats. Address persistent itching, redness or hair loss with a veterinarian.

funFacts: The breed's webbed feet are a useful adaptation for swimming.
Its traditional work included retrieving items and helping fishermen communicate between boats and shore.
The FCI standard recognises both curly and wavy coat varieties.
A traditional lion clip leaves the hindquarters and parts of the muzzle and tail clipped, with a plume at the tail tip.
Despite its reputation as a low-shedding breed, the Portuguese Water Dog still needs extensive grooming.

faq.question: Where did the Portuguese Water Dog originate?
faq.answer: It originated in Portugal and has a long association with the country's Atlantic coast, particularly the Algarve region.

faq.question: How large does a Portuguese Water Dog get?
faq.answer: The FCI standard gives a height of 50–57 cm for males and 43–52 cm for females. Its listed weight ranges are 19–25 kg for males and 16–22 kg for females.

faq.question: Does the Portuguese Water Dog shed?
faq.answer: It generally sheds less than many double-coated breeds, but shedding is not zero. Its coat continues to grow and requires regular combing and clipping.

faq.question: Is the Portuguese Water Dog hypoallergenic?
faq.answer: No dog breed is guaranteed to be allergy-free. Some people may react less to this low-shedding coat, but people with allergies should spend time around the breed before bringing one home.

faq.question: Does this breed need a lot of exercise?
faq.answer: Yes. It is an athletic working breed that benefits from daily physical activity, training and mental enrichment. The precise amount should be adapted to the individual dog.

faq.question: Is it suitable for families with children?
faq.answer: It can be a good family companion in a household that teaches children respectful handling and supervises interactions. Its enthusiasm and strength mean young children should not be left unsupervised with it.

faq.question: What grooming does it need?
faq.answer: Regular brushing and combing, mat prevention, bathing when needed, and periodic clipping are important. The required effort depends on coat type, length and lifestyle.

faq.question: Which health tests should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Ask for documented hip and eye evaluations and breed-relevant genetic screening, including tests for GM-1 gangliosidosis, PRA, EOPRA, microphthalmia syndrome and juvenile dilated cardiomyopathy. Check the results for both parents and confirm current recommendations with the breed club or veterinarian.

overview.summary: The Puli is a lively Hungarian herding dog best known for its distinctive coat, which naturally forms dense cords as it matures. Compact, agile and quick to learn, it was developed to work closely with people and manage livestock. It often forms a close bond with its household and benefits from regular activity, mental challenges and a consistent routine. Its unusual coat needs dedicated maintenance, especially when kept corded.
overview.description: Beneath its unmistakable coat, the Puli is a medium-sized, muscular dog with a square outline and light, agile movement. The coat combines a woolly undercoat with a coarser outer coat; as it develops, the hair can form round cords or flatter, ribbon-like locks. Its appearance should not obscure the needs of the dog underneath: regular movement, training, social contact and careful health checks remain important. Pulik were bred to work with herders, so many enjoy learning tasks and taking part in activities with their people. They can be alert and reserved around unfamiliar visitors, making early positive socialisation and thoughtful introductions valuable. Owners should plan for the practical demands of whichever coat style they choose, since a corded coat takes time to wash and dry thoroughly.
overview.history: The Puli is an old Hungarian herding breed with historical links to the livestock-keeping communities of the Carpathian Basin. The FCI standard describes it as a Hungarian breed of Asian origin and says its ancestors most probably arrived with migrating Magyar groups who practised nomadic animal husbandry. The Puli worked with flocks and helped people manage livestock in the Hungarian countryside. Although the breed's history reaches back many centuries, precise claims about individual ancestral breeds or a single date of origin are not established by the reviewed standards.

grooming.brushing: Grooming depends on the chosen coat style. For a corded coat, check the skin and separate developing cords by hand so that they form evenly without becoming one large, compact mat. For a brushed-out coat, frequent thorough brushing is needed to prevent tangles. Check the coat down to the skin rather than only grooming its surface.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when necessary with dog-appropriate shampoo. A corded coat can take a long time to rinse and dry completely, so allow ample time and ensure the coat is fully dry to help prevent dampness remaining close to the skin.
notes: Choose and maintain a coat style deliberately; corded, brushed and clipped coats have different upkeep needs.
Inspect the skin regularly because a dense coat can conceal irritation or debris.
Check the coat after outdoor activity for leaves, burrs and other material.
Trim nails as needed and introduce paw handling gradually.
Keep ears clean and dry, and seek veterinary advice for persistent odour, redness or discharge.
Maintain routine dental care.

training.difficulty: Moderate
tips: Start reward-based training early and keep sessions engaging.
Teach recall, leash manners and calm greetings before allowing more freedom.
Use games and short training sessions to make use of the breed's learning ability.
Provide mental work as well as physical exercise.
Reward quiet, settled behaviour rather than reinforcing demand barking.
Use consistent rules and avoid harsh or intimidating methods.
training.socialization: Introduce the puppy gradually to a variety of people, friendly dogs, handling, sounds and everyday environments. Keep experiences positive and controlled, especially around unfamiliar visitors. Continue socialisation through adulthood and allow the dog to observe new situations at a comfortable distance instead of forcing contact.

climates: Cool and temperate conditions
Warm conditions when shade, fresh water and heat management are provided

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced diet appropriate to the dog's life stage, body condition, activity and individual veterinary needs.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Usually 3–4 measured meals daily, adjusted for age, growth and veterinary advice.
feedingFrequency.adult: Often 2 measured meals daily; adjust the total amount to maintain a healthy body condition.
feedingFrequency.senior: Adjust meal size, calorie intake and diet to health, appetite, mobility and veterinary advice.

nutrition.guidelines: Use a nutritionally complete diet and measure portions instead of relying on guesswork. Adjust intake as the dog grows or its activity and body condition change. Provide fresh water at all times. Introduce dietary changes gradually and consult a veterinarian for an individual plan, particularly during growth, illness or older age.
considerations: Monitor body condition rather than using a generic weight target.
Count treats as part of the daily intake.
Avoid adding supplements without a specific need and veterinary guidance.
Choose a diet suitable for the dog's age, activity and any diagnosed medical conditions.

health.overview: The reviewed breed-club and kennel-club materials recommend health screening for breeding Pulik, including evaluation of hips and patellae, an eye examination and a DNA test for the common variant associated with degenerative myelopathy. These are screening recommendations intended to support responsible breeding; they do not mean that every Puli will develop these conditions. Ask a breeder for the parents' relevant test results, and discuss any screening or diagnostic concerns for an individual dog with a veterinarian.
preventiveCare: Keep routine veterinary examinations and vaccinations up to date according to local veterinary advice.
Discuss age-appropriate hip, patella and eye assessment with a veterinarian.
Ask the breeder about documented screening results for the puppy's parents, including degenerative myelopathy DNA testing.
Maintain a healthy body condition and regular physical activity.
Inspect the skin and coat routinely, particularly under cords and around areas where debris can collect.
Seek veterinary advice for persistent changes in movement, vision, appetite, energy or behaviour.

Patella evaluation
Ophthalmologist eye examination
Degenerative myelopathy (DM) DNA test for the common variant
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with dog-safe toothpaste and introduce oral handling gradually. Seek veterinary advice for gum bleeding, persistent bad breath, oral pain or difficulty eating.
health.earCare: Inspect the ears routinely and keep them clean and dry when needed. Avoid inserting cotton swabs deeply into the ear canal. Persistent scratching, odour, discharge or redness should be assessed by a veterinarian.
health.skinCare: Check the skin beneath the coat regularly for irritation, parasites, wounds or unusual lumps. Keep the coat clean and ensure it dries fully after bathing, especially when corded. Persistent itching, redness, hair loss or sores need veterinary assessment.

funFacts: Puli is the singular name; Pulik is the Hungarian plural.
The breed's country of origin is Hungary.

faq.question: Where does the Puli come from?
faq.answer: The Puli originates in Hungary and has a long history associated with Hungarian livestock herding.

faq.question: What was the Puli bred to do?
faq.answer: It was developed as a herding dog that worked alongside people managing livestock, particularly sheep.

faq.question: How tall is a Puli?
faq.answer: The FCI standard gives a permitted height range of 39–45 cm for males and 36–42 cm for females. These are standard ranges, not a prediction of an individual dog's exact size.

faq.question: What colours can a Puli have?
faq.answer: The FCI standard lists pearl white, black, black shaded with rust-red or grey, fawn with a pronounced black mask, and grey in any shade. Colour terminology can differ between registries.

faq.question: How long does a Puli usually live?
faq.answer: A breed-club FAQ gives an average lifespan of around 10–15 years. Individual lifespan varies with genetics, health, environment and veterinary care.

faq.question: Does every Puli have a corded coat?
faq.answer: The coat is naturally inclined to form cords as it matures, but owners may maintain it corded, brushed out or clipped. Each style has its own upkeep requirements.

faq.question: Is the Puli easy to groom?
faq.answer: No. Its coat requires a substantial time commitment. Cords need to be separated and checked, while a brushed-out coat needs frequent brushing. A corded coat can also take a long time to wash and dry fully.

faq.question: Which health tests should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Breed-club recommendations include hip and patella evaluations, an eye examination and DNA testing for the common variant associated with degenerative myelopathy. Ask for documented results and discuss their interpretation with your veterinarian.
