overview.summary: A giant, noble Spanish livestock guardian from the Pyrenees of Aragon and Navarre, distinguished by its thick snow-white coat with a clearly defined facial mask and body patches, double dewlap, deep chest bark, and calm, fearless devotion to its flock and family.
overview.description: The Pyrenean Mastiff (Mastín del Pirineo) is a giant, powerfully muscled Molosser developed in the southern Pyrenees of Spain to defend transhumant sheep flocks against wolves, bears, and thieves. Built on a slightly rectangular frame (about a 9:10 height-to-length ratio, with chest girth roughly 10:7 relative to withers height and chest depth reaching at least 50% of withers height), it combines massive bone and strength with agile, harmonious movement that is never heavy or sluggish. Its thick, coarse, bristly coat—6 to 9 cm (2.5 to 3.5 inches) along the midline of the back—is snow-white with a mandatory dark mask covering the eyes and spotted ears, irregular sharp-edged body patches of matching colour, and always-white lower legs and tail tip. Calm, gentle, and affectionate with its family and children, and possessed of a very low prey drive toward livestock and small animals, it remains proud, discerning, and unyielding when confronting a genuine threat.
overview.history: Ancestral mastiff-type flock guardians are thought to have arrived in the Iberian Peninsula around 3,000 years ago with Phoenician and eastern Mediterranean traders, evolving in the Aragonese and Navarrese Pyrenees (where the breed was also historically known as the Navarra Mastiff). For centuries, these dogs accompanied shepherds and massive sheep flocks along seasonal transhumance routes between high summer mountain pastures and winter valleys, wearing heavy spiked iron collars (carlancas) to protect their throats while fighting wolves and bears. Following the Spanish Civil War and the mid-twentieth-century decline of large predators by the 1940s, keeping such giant working dogs became economically difficult and purebred numbers fell critically low, even though international recognition had been granted on 13 November 1954. In the 1970s, Rafael Malo Alcrudo and a dedicated group of Spanish breeders surveyed the region, locating about 100 surviving dogs and selecting the top 30 specimens as the foundation of the modern breed. They established the dedicated Spanish preservation society in 1977 and published the modern conformation standard on 26 May 1982. The breed subsequently spread across Europe—establishing a major population in Finland—reached the United States in 1996, entered the British Imported Breed Register in 2001, and gained further North American registry recognitions in 2006 and 2014.
overview.originalPurpose: Guarding and defending transhumant sheep flocks, livestock, and rural estates against wolves, bears, and thieves across the Spanish Pyrenees.
currentRoles: Country estate, farm, and property guardian
Calm, devoted family companion in a spacious, securely fenced home
Conformation, obedience, and low-impact hiking companion

physical.coatType: Dense, thick, moderately long double coat with a coarse, bristly (never woolly) outer texture; longer and fuller around the neck and shoulders (forming a pronounced ruff or mane, especially in males), under the belly, down the backs of the legs, and on the softer plumed tail.
physical.coatLength: Medium to long (ideal length 6 to 9 cm / 2.5 to 3.5 inches along the middle of the topline; coat 4 cm / 1.5 inches or shorter, or longer than 13 cm / 5 inches, is a disqualification)
coatColors: Snow-white base coat with a clearly defined dark facial mask, spotted ears, white lower legs and tail tip, and medium grey patches
White with intensive golden-yellow or gold patches
White with light beige or sandy patches
White with marbled, agouti, sable (with or without black tipping), or badger markings

White with brindled patch markings (accepted in North American conformation rules; solid white without a mask, white on the ears or over the eyes, tricolour / tan-point markings, red patches, or a yellowish-white base coat are serious or disqualifying faults)
physical.sheddingLevel: High; sheds moderately year-round and blows its dense undercoat heavily twice a year in spring and autumn over a period of several weeks.
physical.droolingLevel: High; like most giant mastiff breeds with a double dewlap, it drools noticeably—especially after drinking, eating, or in warm weather.
distinctiveFeatures: Giant, powerful, slightly rectangular frame (ideal height-to-length ratio of 9:10 and height-to-chest-girth ratio of 7:10) with minimum withers heights of 77 cm (30 inches) for males and 72 cm (28 inches) for females, no upper height limit, and preferred heights above 81 cm (32 inches) for males and 75 cm (29.5 inches) for females
Snow-white coat with white hair roots, a mandatory symmetrical dark mask covering the eyes and spotted ears, clearly outlined body patches, and always-white lower legs and tail tip
Large, strong, moderately long head with a 5:4 skull-to-muzzle ratio, broad subconvex skull, gentle stop, black nose, and black mucous membranes with ridged black gums
Small, almond-shaped hazel to dark brown eyes with black-pigmented rims (tight when alert, showing a slight stripe of conjunctiva in repose)
Broad, muscular, blunt-cone neck with thick, elastic skin and a well-defined double dewlap that is never exaggerated
Medium-high-set, thick-rooted plumed tail reaching the hocks with a curved final third, carried in a sabre curve with a terminal hook when moving
Cat feet (slightly more oval on the hind legs) with single or double hind dewclaws (double dewclaws preferred when quality is equal)

traits: Calm, composed, and gentle indoors
Noble, affectionate, and deeply devoted to family and children
Very intelligent and observant
Courageous, proud, and self-assured around strangers—never backing down from a real threat
Benevolent and aware of its superior strength around other dogs
Very low prey drive toward livestock and small animals
Independent thinker that conserves energy until needed
Deep, resonant chest bark used to alert when something is amiss rather than incessant barking

exercise.level: Moderate; conserves energy indoors on cool tile or a couch, but requires daily leisurely walks, safe yard patrolling, and careful joint protection during growth.
activities: Leisurely daily walks and age-appropriate hikes on unpaved, low-impact surfaces
Supervised patrolling and free movement in a large, securely fenced yard or pasture
Positive-reinforcement obedience and household manners training
Working livestock or property guardianship with appropriate supervision
Low-impact swimming or water activities when thoroughly dried afterward

grooming.brushing: Brush thoroughly once a week to once every two weeks with a pin brush, slicker brush, or high-velocity dryer to clear dust and dander, focusing on the feathering behind the forelegs, underbelly, elbows, hindquarters, tail plume, and behind the ears; increase to daily brushing during the twice-yearly spring and autumn coat blows.
grooming.bathing: Bathe every three months or as needed when dirty, as the coarse outer coat is largely self-cleaning; always dry the dense undercoat completely to the skin—especially in humid climates—to prevent moisture-induced hot spots.
notes: Wipe and clean the double dewlap and neck folds regularly, as drool and dirt easily collect under the chin.
Trim toenails regularly, paying close attention to the front dewclaws and the single or double rear dewclaws so they do not overgrow.
Inspect and flush the folded, triangular hanging ears monthly (or more often if needed) with a veterinarian-approved ear cleanser to prevent debris buildup and infection.
Examine the eyes during grooming for redness, cloudiness, or irritation from eyelid slackness or stray eyelashes.
Never shave the double coat, which insulates the dog against both cold mountain weather and summer solar heat.

training.difficulty: Moderate; intelligent and eager to please when motivated early with rewards, though independent-minded and capable of testing boundaries if training is delayed.
tips: Start daily positive-reinforcement training with high-value food rewards during the critical first year of puppyhood so the dog learns to communicate and cooperate willingly before reaching 54 to 86 kg.
Establish clear, calm, and consistent household boundaries early, as adolescent and adult dogs can try to manipulate permissive handlers.
Limit forced or extended repetitive exercise while the giant-breed growth plates remain open (up to 18–24 months), favouring unpaved surfaces over hard pavement.
Provide a sturdy, secure physical fence around the property;guardian instinct and territorial awareness require reliable containment.
Teach polite leash walking, calm doorway greetings, and a reliable settle cue when welcomed guests arrive.
training.socialization: Socialize puppies immediately and consistently with varied people, children, calm dogs, veterinary handling, and new environments outside the property so their natural guardian discernment develops into steady confidence rather than over-suspicion.

climates: Cool and temperate climates
Cold and snowy mountain climates with appropriate shelter
Warm or humid climates only when provided with air-conditioned indoor rest areas, cool tile floors, shade, fresh water, and thorough coat drying to prevent hot spots
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate; having been bred to travel alongside shepherds and flocks rather than in complete isolation, the Pyrenean Mastiff thrives on daily human interaction and a sense of purpose.

nutrition.dietType: A complete, balanced large- or giant-breed diet formulated for steady skeletal growth in puppies (up to 18–24 months) and lean weight maintenance in adults.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Feed three measured meals per day using a balanced large- or giant-breed puppy formula until skeletal maturity—typically until 18 months of age for females and 24 months (2 years) of age for males.
feedingFrequency.adult: Feed two measured meals per day rather than free-feeding or offering a single large daily meal.

nutrition.guidelines: Because Pyrenean Mastiffs are prone to weight gain that places damaging stress on giant-breed hips, elbows, and spines, avoid free-feeding and adjust daily portions using the dog's body condition score (palpating and viewing the ribcage). Take strict mealtime precautions against gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat): divide daily rations into two to three smaller meals, use a slow-feeder bowl if the dog eats rapidly, avoid elevated food bowls, and restrict vigorous exercise immediately before and after eating. Keep clean, fresh water available at all times.
considerations: Keep female puppies on a balanced giant/large-breed puppy diet until 18 months of age and males until 24 months of age to prevent overly rapid bone growth.
Feed two to three smaller daily meals, use slow-feeder bowls, avoid raised bowls, and rest before and after meals to help reduce bloat (GDV) risk.
Monitor body condition score closely so excess weight does not accelerate hip, elbow, or spinal arthritis.
Discuss joint-support nutrients—such as glucosamine, chondroitin, and fish or salmon oil—with a veterinarian before supplementing.
Account for high-value training treats within the daily caloric budget.
nutrition.note: Caloric needs vary by age, sex, metabolism, and workload; refine portion sizes with veterinary guidance based on body condition scoring.

health.overview: The Pyrenean Mastiff is generally a hardy giant breed with an average lifespan of 10 to 12 years (8 to 12 years across veterinary guides), though its massive frame and historical 1970s population bottleneck require proactive orthopedic, cardiac, and genetic screening. Pre-breeding health certification protocols prioritize four core evaluations performed at 24 months of age or older: radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation, radiographic elbow dysplasia evaluation, veterinary cardiac evaluation, and DNA testing for degenerative myelopathy (SOD1). Optional pre-breeding evaluations include spine radiographs (at 24 months or older) and veterinary ophthalmologist examinations (after 12 months of age). Owners must also guard against life-threatening gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat), osteosarcoma, and moisture-related hot spots in humid climates.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia: a polygenic developmental malformation of the coxofemoral joint influenced by genetics, growth rate, and weight; international screening data across Finland (291 dogs), Spain (82 dogs), and the United States/Canada (81 dogs) show over 50% of radiographed dogs achieving passing normal (A/B or Excellent/Good/Fair) hip grades, with pre-breeding certification required at 24 months of age or older.

Elbow dysplasia: developmental abnormalities of the elbow joint; international screening data show over 90% of evaluated Pyrenean Mastiffs achieving normal (Grade 0) elbows, with pre-breeding radiographic certification required at 24 months of age or older.

Cardiac disease (including dilated cardiomyopathy): giant breeds carry an elevated risk of heart disease; in Finnish registry mortality records from 1990 to 2025, cardiac disease accounted for 46 reported deaths (6.25% of reported deaths, at an average age of 6 years 10 months, and 6.61% over the last 15 years at an average age of 5 years 10 months), prompting mandatory pre-breeding cardiac auscultation or echocardiography at 24 months of age or older.

Degenerative myelopathy (DM): a late-onset, progressive autosomal recessive spinal cord neuropathy associated with the SOD1 gene; because DM carriers have been identified in certain bloodlines, mandatory pre-breeding DNA screening ensures carriers are only mated to clear dogs so at-risk offspring are never produced.

Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat): an acute, life-threatening emergency in deep-chested giant dogs in which the stomach distends with gas and twists on its axis, cutting off blood supply to the stomach and spleen.
Osteosarcoma and other cancers: an aggressive bone tumour seen more frequently in large and giant breeds, typically presenting with sudden lameness or localized limb swelling.

Ophthalmic conditions: iris-to-iris persistent pupillary membranes (PPM, fairly common in the breed and usually not affecting vision unless strands attach to the cornea or lens), entropion (inward-rolling eyelid), ectropion (outward-drooping lower eyelid), and distichiasis or trichiasis (extra or misdirected eyelashes).

Spinal anomalies and spondylosis: spondylosis deformans (vertebral bone spurs), lumbosacral transitional vertebrae (LTV), and congenital vertebral anomalies reported in European and North American screening, monitored via optional spine radiographs from 24 months of age.

Additional sporadically reported conditions under breed monitoring: Addison's disease, autoimmune disorders, allergies, idiopathic epilepsy, hock instability or subluxation, idiopathic rear-leg trembling, and acute moist dermatitis (hot spots) when the dense undercoat remains damp.
preventiveCare: Verify that both parents of any prospective puppy are at least 24 months old and have publicly recorded results for hip radiographs, elbow radiographs, cardiac evaluation, and degenerative myelopathy (SOD1) DNA testing, as well as optional eye and spine evaluations where performed.

Protect developing joints by keeping female puppies on large/giant-breed puppy food until 18 months and males until 24 months, maintaining a lean body condition, and avoiding forced running or high-impact jumping before growth plates close.

Reduce bloat (GDV) risk by feeding two to three smaller meals daily, using a slow-feeder bowl, avoiding elevated food bowls, and restricting exercise right before and after meals; seek immediate emergency veterinary care for abdominal distension, dry heaving, or sudden distress.
Dry the dense double coat completely to the skin after baths, swimming, or rain—especially in humid regions—to prevent hot spots, and clean the folded ears monthly.
Schedule regular veterinary wellness and cardiac checkups and have any new lameness or limb swelling evaluated promptly.
recommendedScreenings: Hip dysplasia radiographic evaluation (at 24 months of age or older; required for pre-breeding health certification)
Elbow dysplasia radiographic evaluation (at 24 months of age or older; required for pre-breeding health certification)

Cardiac evaluation—auscultation by a veterinarian or board-certified veterinary cardiologist at 24 months of age or older, followed by an echocardiogram if abnormal (required for pre-breeding health certification)
Degenerative myelopathy (DM / SOD1) DNA test (required for pre-breeding health certification)
Ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist after 12 months of age (optional pre-breeding screening)
Spine radiographs at 24 months of age or older (optional pre-breeding screening for spondylosis and transitional vertebrae)
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with canine-specific toothpaste and schedule routine veterinary dental assessments; conformation standards require a complete, strong scissor bite with large canines and molars and black-pigmented gums with pronounced transverse ridges.
health.earCare: Inspect the medium-sized, triangular hanging ears regularly and clean them monthly with a veterinarian-approved ear-cleaning solution, as folded ears can trap dirt, moisture, and debris.
health.skinCare: Clean drool and debris from the double dewlap as needed, inspect the thick pink-and-dark-patched skin during biweekly brushing, and always dry the undercoat thoroughly to the skin in humid or wet weather to prevent acute moist dermatitis (hot spots).

idealFor: Families with a spacious home and securely fenced yard or acreage seeking a calm, affectionate, and protective giant companion
Ranchers, farmers, and rural estate owners needing a dependable livestock or property guardian with a very low prey drive
Experienced dog owners who use positive-reinforcement motivation early in puppyhood and maintain clear, consistent boundaries
Households prepared for giant-breed food and veterinary budgets, heavy seasonal shedding twice a year, and mastiff drool
notIdealFor: Apartment dwellers or small urban homes without sufficient indoor and securely fenced outdoor space
First-time or physically frail owners unable to manage a 54 to 86 kg guardian dog
Neat freaks bothered by drool on the dewlap or heavy spring and autumn coat blows
Owners seeking a high-speed running partner or a dog that welcomes unannounced strangers onto the property without supervision

funFacts: In its native Spain, the Pyrenean Mastiff is called the Mastín del Pirineo (and was also historically known as the Navarra Mastiff); when defending transhumant sheep flocks against wolves and bears, working dogs wore a heavy iron spiked collar called a 'carlanca' to protect their throats.

After the Spanish Civil War and the 1940s decline of wolves and bears nearly drove the breed to extinction, Rafael Malo Alcrudo and fellow Spanish breeders searched Aragon in the 1970s, locating about 100 surviving dogs and selecting the top 30 to rebuild the modern breed.

Unlike the solid-white Great Pyrenees from the French side of the mountains, a Pyrenean Mastiff must never be solid white: it always has a snow-white base coat with a dark facial mask, spotted ears, and white lower legs and tail tip.

There is no upper height limit for the breed: males must stand at least 77 cm (30 inches) and females at least 72 cm (28 inches), with males over 81 cm (32 inches) and females over 75 cm (29.5 inches) preferred when quality is equal.
Because it was bred for millennia as a flock guardian with a very low prey drive, the Pyrenean Mastiff is famously gentle and protective toward children, livestock, and small household animals alike.

faq.question: How does the Pyrenean Mastiff differ from the Great Pyrenees (Pyrenean Mountain Dog)?
faq.answer: Although both breeds originated in the Pyrenees mountains as flock guardians and share distant Molosser roots, they are separate breeds from opposite sides of the border. The Pyrenean Mastiff (Mastín del Pirineo) developed in Aragon and Navarre in Spain, is taller and heavier (standing at least 77 cm for males and 72 cm for females, and weighing 54 to 86 kg / 120 to 190 lbs), and must always have a snow-white coat with a dark facial mask, spotted ears, and distinct body patches—whereas the French Great Pyrenees is predominantly solid white or lightly badger-marked.

faq.question: How big does a Pyrenean Mastiff get?
faq.answer: Minimum withers height is 77 cm (30 inches) for males and 72 cm (28 inches) for females, with no upper height limit; males exceeding 81 cm (32 inches) and females exceeding 75 cm (29.5 inches) are preferred when conformation quality is equal. Full-grown adults typically weigh between 54.4 and 86.2 kg (120 to 190 pounds).

faq.question: Are Pyrenean Mastiffs good family dogs?
faq.answer: Yes. Having been bred to travel closely with shepherds and protect vulnerable lambs, Pyrenean Mastiffs have a very low prey drive and a calm, gentle, and affectionate nature with their family and children. Because of their giant size and natural guardian instincts toward strangers, early socialization, reward-based puppy training, and adult supervision around young children are essential.

faq.question: What coat colours and markings are required on a Pyrenean Mastiff?
faq.answer: The base coat is snow-white with white hair roots, always accompanied by a clearly defined facial mask covering the eyes and spotted ears, while the tip of the tail and lower parts of the legs must always be white. Body patches match the head colour and may be medium grey, golden yellow, brown, black, silver-grey, light beige, sandy, marbled, agouti, sable, badger, or brindled. Solid white dogs lacking a mask, white on the ears or over the eyes, tricolour (tan-point) patterns, or red patches are faulted or disqualified.

faq.question: How much grooming and exercise does a Pyrenean Mastiff need?
faq.answer: Despite its size, the Pyrenean Mastiff is a calm, energy-conserving dog that needs moderate daily activity—such as 45 to 90 minutes of leisurely walks on soft or unpaved surfaces and time in a fenced yard—while avoiding high-impact exercise until growth plates close around 18 to 24 months of age. Its coarse double coat is largely self-cleaning, needing thorough brushing once every one to two weeks, daily brushing during its twice-yearly spring and autumn coat blows, regular dewlap wiping, and baths every three months (always drying the undercoat completely to the skin).

faq.question: What health screenings should I ask a Pyrenean Mastiff breeder about?
faq.answer: Prospective buyers should ask for publicly recorded pre-breeding clearances performed at 24 months of age or older for hip dysplasia, elbow dysplasia, and cardiac health (auscultation or echocardiogram), along with DNA test results for degenerative myelopathy (SOD1). Breeders are also encouraged to perform optional veterinary ophthalmologist eye exams (after 12 months of age) and spine radiographs (at 24 months or older).

faq.question: How should a Pyrenean Mastiff puppy and adult be fed to protect joints and prevent bloat?
faq.answer: Feed a balanced large- or giant-breed puppy diet three times daily until skeletal maturity—18 months of age for females and 24 months for males—before transitioning to two measured adult meals per day. To reduce the risk of life-threatening bloat (gastric dilatation-volvulus), avoid free-feeding, use a slow-feeder bowl, avoid elevated food bowls, and restrict exercise immediately before and after meals.

overview.summary: A diminutive, long-legged, finely boned Russian companion breed developed in smooth-haired and long-haired varieties, combining lively intelligence and cheerful athleticism with intense devotion to its household.
overview.description: The Russian Toy (Russkiy Toy) is one of the world's smallest dog breeds—an elegant, lively, high-stationed toy dog with fine bone, lean musculature, and a square body outline in which height at the withers equals body length. Its chest reaches the elbows, the height at the elbows is slightly more than half the withers height, and sexual dimorphism is only slightly defined. The breed exists in two coat varieties that can appear in the same litter: a sleek, shiny, close-lying smooth coat without undercoat, and a long-haired variety featuring a 3 to 5 cm body coat, feathered limbs and tail, and dramatic, butterfly-like ear fringes covering large, high-set triangular ears. Active, cheerful, curious, and keenly intelligent, the Russian Toy bonds closely with its family, loves both energetic play and lap snuggling, and may be slightly reserved with strangers while remaining neither timid nor aggressive.
overview.history: The Russian Toy traces its ancestry to English Toy Terriers imported into Russia as early as the eighteenth century—evidenced by a preserved short-haired terrier dated 1716–1725 in the Zoological Museum in Saint Petersburg that belonged to Emperor Peter the Great—and became a fashionable companion of the Russian aristocracy by the early twentieth century. Following the 1917 revolution and between 1920 and 1950, breeding of purebred toy terriers nearly ceased and numbers fell to a critical level. When Soviet breeders began reviving the stock in the mid-1950s in isolation, most surviving dogs lacked pedigrees and were not purebred, resulting in a distinct Russian type with a higher, rounder skull, flatter cheeks, and rounder eyes than the English Toy Terrier. On 12 October 1958, two smooth-coated dogs (one with slightly longer hair) produced a male puppy named Chikki with striking fringes on his ears and limbs. Acquired and bred in Moscow by Yevgueniya Fominichna Zharova—who mated him to a slightly long-coated female named Irma—this line became known as the Moscow Longhaired Toy Terrier. A first Russian standard for the two varieties was approved in 1966, and in 1988 both the smooth-haired Russian Toy Terrier and the Moscow Longhaired Toy Terrier were unified under a single breed standard, later dropping the word 'Terrier' to become the Russian Toy.
overview.originalPurpose: Aristocratic companion dog (historically also used as an alert household watchdog and ratter)
currentRoles: Agility, obedience, rally, and trick-dog competitor

physical.coatType: Two coat varieties: smooth-haired (short, close-lying, glossy single coat without undercoat) and long-haired (straight or slightly wavy close-lying coat with ear fringes and limb/tail feathering)
physical.coatLength: Smooth-haired: short and close-lying all over. Long-haired: moderately long (3–5 cm / 1–3 in) on the body and neck, short and close-lying on the head and front of the legs, with long silky hair on the feet hiding the nails, distinct feathering on the backs of the legs and tail, and thick ear fringes that completely cover the outer edges and tips of the ears by three years of age
physical.sheddingLevel: Low to moderate
distinctiveFeatures: Diminutive, high-legged, square-proportioned build with fine bone and lean muscle, where height at the elbows is slightly more than half the height at the withers
Small, light, wedge-shaped head with a high, slightly rounded skull, clearly pronounced stop, and lean pointed muzzle measuring one-third to two-fifths of head length
Large, thin, high-set erect ears shaped like a high isosceles triangle—dramatically fringed in the long-haired variety once mature (by about 3 years of age)
Large, rounded, dark, expressive eyes set well apart and looking straight ahead, with pigment matching the coat colour
Two interbreedable coat varieties (smooth-haired and long-haired) that can be born in the same litter when smooth-coated parents carry the recessive long-coat allele
Moderately high-set sickle or sabre tail carried at or above back level when moving (or docked to 2–4 vertebrae where legal)
Light, straightforward, fast, energetic gait with the head held proudly high and no change in the topline

Preferred height of 25 cm (range 22–27 cm internationally, 20–28 cm ± 1 cm in Britain, and 8–11 in / 20.3–27.9 cm in North America) and preferred weight of 2.3 kg (up to 3 kg internationally, with weight under 1.5 kg or over 3 kg disqualifying; up to 6–6.5 lbs in North America)

Very cheerful

exercise.level: Moderate (up to 1 hour per day). Energetic and playful indoors and outdoors, yet small enough that daily walks, yard runs, and interactive indoor play readily meet its physical needs.
activities: Daily walks on a harness and leash with its owner
Romping and chasing toys in a safely enclosed yard or indoor space
Agility, obedience, rally, and trick-dog training
Nose-work and scent-detection games
Lure coursing for toy breeds

grooming.level: Low to moderate. Simple routine upkeep for both varieties, with extra brushing required for the long-haired variety's ear fringes and feathering.
grooming.brushing: Long-haired variety: brush or comb 2 to 3 times per week, paying special attention to the ear fringes and leg feathering. Smooth-haired variety: brush weekly with a soft bristle brush and wipe daily with a chamois cloth to maintain shine and minimize loose hair.
grooming.bathing: Bathe monthly (or every 1 to 2 weeks for show/companion maintenance) using a gentle, high-quality dog shampoo and conditioner or creme rinse; smooth-coated dogs can also be bathed occasionally as needed.
notes: Both varieties shed minimally, with noticeably less visible hair from the short smooth coat.
On long-haired dogs, comb out ear fringes and feathering gently to prevent tangles and keep them free of debris.
Long-coated puppies typically shed much of their puppy coat between 5 and 12 months of age; full adult coat develops after 1 year and full ear fringing may take until 2 to 3 years of age.
Keep nails clipped short and trim excess hair beneath the feet on long-coated dogs; no other coat trimming is needed (and trimmed coats are penalized in conformation).
Brush teeth regularly and inspect ears, eyes, and skin during routine grooming.

training.difficulty: Moderate. Keenly intelligent, agreeable, and eager to please, though capable of a terrier-like stubborn streak and trying to take charge if boundaries are inconsistent.
tips: Use upbeat, reward-based training with tiny treats and praise; keep sessions fun and engaging.
Enrol in puppy kindergarten and obedience classes early to channel the breed's intelligence and prevent bossy behaviour.
Take advantage of the breed's athleticism and nose by introducing agility, trick training, rally, or nose work.
Always walk the dog on a well-fitted harness rather than attaching a leash to a collar, protecting the delicate neck and trachea.
Remove collars and harnesses while the dog is inside the home so they cannot snag on household objects and cause injury.
Because of the breed's fine bone structure, prevent jumping from heights above 40 cm (such as high sofas or beds) and supervise interactions around large dogs.
training.socialization: Begin early, positive socialization in puppyhood with varied people, gentle handling, puppy kindergarten classes, and calm, size-appropriate dogs so natural reserve toward strangers does not turn into timidity or reactivity.

climates: Temperate climates
Indoor living with cold-weather protection (coats/sweaters or indoor litter/pad options during severe winter weather)
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low. Deeply attached to its human companions, the Russian Toy thrives on closeness and will quickly vocalize or become stressed if left isolated or neglected for long periods.

nutrition.dietType: Complete, balanced, high-quality small-breed dog food (with extra-small kibble) or a veterinarian-supervised and approved home-prepared diet appropriate to life stage (puppy, adult, or senior).
nutrition.guidelines: Feed a nutritionally complete diet suited to the dog's age and activity level, selecting very small kibble that suits a miniature jaw. Because some Russian Toys have a poor sense of satiety and can easily become overweight—placing extra stress on delicate bones and patellas—measure daily portions carefully, limit training treats, avoid free-feeding, and keep fresh water available at all times.
considerations: Choose extra-small kibble sized for a toy breed weighing under 3 kg.
Monitor body condition and calorie intake closely, as excess weight strains slender legs and kneecaps.
Keep training treats tiny and deduct them from the daily food allowance.
Prepare home-cooked diets only with veterinary supervision and nutritional balancing.
Consult a veterinarian or breeder to set appropriate daily meal counts for puppies, adults, and seniors.
nutrition.note: Consulted kennel-club and breed-club sources do not prescribe fixed daily meal counts for puppies, adults, or seniors; feeding schedules should be tailored with a veterinarian.

health.overview: The Russian Toy is generally a healthy, long-lived toy breed with a typical life expectancy of 12 to 14 years (and some individuals reaching 15 years or more). As in many diminutive breeds, dental issues are the most frequent everyday veterinary concern: most puppies retain deciduous (baby) teeth that require veterinary extraction by about nine months of age to prevent malocclusion, and tartar buildup with periodontal disease can begin by one year of age. Because of its fine bone structure, the breed is also vulnerable to limb fractures from falls or rough play and to tracheal injury if walked on a neck collar rather than a harness. For breeding stock, national breed-club and kennel-club health programs prioritize clinical screening for patellar luxation, inherited eye diseases (such as progressive retinal atrophy), and cardiac abnormalities, with optional evaluations for Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, hip and elbow dysplasia, and congenital liver shunts.
commonConditions: Retained deciduous (puppy) teeth: most puppies fail to shed all baby teeth naturally as adult teeth erupt around 6 months of age, frequently requiring surgical extraction under anaesthesia by 9 months of age to prevent double rows of teeth, misalignment, and periodontal disease
Periodontal disease, plaque, and tartar buildup: can begin as early as 1 year of age without regular tooth brushing and routine veterinary dental care
Patellar luxation: a potentially inherited kneecap instability common to toy breeds and included in mandatory pre-breeding orthopedic screening

Inherited and traumatic eye conditions: progressive retinal atrophy (PRA, screened via ophthalmic exams and biobank research) as well as corneal ulcers and surface eye injuries due to large, prominent eyes
Cardiac conditions: monitored through pre-breeding veterinary cardiology evaluations

Traumatic bone fractures and open fontanel: fine limb bones can fracture from jumping off furniture or rough contact with large dogs, and an open fontanel (unclosed skull soft spot) past 9 months of age is a disqualifying developmental defect

Additional conditions monitored via optional breed-club screening: Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (avascular necrosis of the femoral head), hip and elbow dysplasia, and congenital portosystemic (liver) shunts
preventiveCare: Brush the teeth regularly and have a veterinarian monitor tooth eruption between 6 and 9 months of age so retained baby teeth can be removed before they cause misalignment or gum disease.
Schedule routine veterinary dental examinations and professional cleanings as needed starting in young adulthood.
Walk the dog using a well-fitted harness rather than a neck collar to protect the fragile neck and trachea, and remove collars and harnesses indoors to prevent snagging accidents.
Prevent jumps from furniture or heights over 40 cm and supervise all interactions with large dogs or young children to avoid bone fractures.
Verify that breeding dogs have completed recommended orthopedic (patellar luxation), ophthalmic, and cardiac evaluations.
recommendedScreenings: Patellar luxation veterinary evaluation for breeding dogs
Annual ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (or accredited national eye-scheme examiner) for breeding dogs
Basic cardiac evaluation by a qualified veterinarian or veterinary cardiologist for breeding dogs

Optional additional breed-club evaluations: radiographic screening for Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, hip dysplasia, and elbow dysplasia; paired serum bile acid testing for congenital liver shunts; and DNA biobank/panel participation
health.dentalCare: Most Russian Toy puppies retain deciduous (baby) teeth when their permanent teeth erupt, often requiring veterinary extraction by nine months of age so the jaw and bite develop normally. Because tartar and periodontal disease can start by one year of age, daily or frequent tooth brushing and regular veterinary dental checks are essential.
health.earCare: Inspect the thin, erect triangular ears during weekly grooming for wax, debris, or irritation. On long-haired dogs, comb the thick ear fringes two to three times a week to keep them tangle- and debris-free.
health.skinCare: The skin is thin and tight-fitting. On smooth-coated dogs, brush weekly with a soft brush and wipe daily with a chamois cloth to remove dead hair and prevent flaky skin; on both varieties, use a gentle dog shampoo and conditioner or creme rinse when bathing.

idealFor: Apartment, flat, or house dwellers seeking a tiny, clean, devoted indoor companion
Owners who spend plenty of time at home and enjoy both lap snuggling and lively daily play
Active handlers interested in small-dog agility, obedience, rally, trick training, or nose work
Careful, attentive households willing to brush teeth regularly, use a harness, and protect a finely boned toy dog from falls
notIdealFor: Households that leave a dog alone for long workdays without companionship
Homes with boisterous, loud, or unsupervised young children or large, rough-playing dogs
Owners unwilling to manage puppy dental care (including possible deciduous tooth extraction) and routine tooth brushing

funFacts: A preserved short-haired terrier named Lizetta dating from 1716–1725, which personally belonged to Russian Emperor Peter the Great, is displayed at the Zoological Museum in Saint Petersburg as early evidence of the breed's English-type ancestors in Russia.

The long-haired variety traces back to a single male puppy named Chikki, born on 12 October 1958 to two smooth-coated parents with slightly longer hair and developed in Moscow by breeder Yevgueniya Fominichna Zharova.
Both smooth-haired and long-haired puppies can be born in the same litter when two smooth-coated parents carry the recessive gene for long hair.
In long-haired Russian Toys, the signature butterfly-like ear fringes and full adult coat take two to three years to reach their full length.

Originally known separately as the Russian Toy Terrier (smooth-coated) and the Moscow Longhaired Toy Terrier (long-coated), the two varieties were united under one standard in 1988 and later had the word 'Terrier' dropped from the official breed name.

Despite standing only 22 to 27 cm tall (with 25 cm and 2.3 kg considered ideal in international standards), the Russian Toy competes enthusiastically in agility, rally, obedience, lure coursing, and nose work.

faq.question: How tall is a Russian Toy?
faq.answer: International conformation standards specify a withers height of 22 to 27 cm for both males and females, with 25 cm preferred (and heights under 18 cm or over 29 cm disqualified). British standards list 20 to 28 cm (with a ±1 cm tolerance), and North American standards specify 8 to 11 inches (about 20.3 to 27.9 cm, with dogs under 7 inches or over 12 inches disqualified).

faq.question: How much does a Russian Toy weigh?
faq.answer: International standards specify a weight of up to 3 kg (6.6 lbs) for both sexes, with 2.3 kg (about 5 lbs) preferred, and disqualify dogs weighing under 1.5 kg or over 3 kg. North American standards specify a weight of up to 6 to 6.5 pounds (about 2.7 to 2.95 kg), with a preferred weight of 5 pounds and a disqualifying minimum of 2 pounds.

faq.question: What is the difference between the smooth-haired and long-haired Russian Toy?
faq.answer: The smooth-haired variety has a short, glossy, close-lying coat with no undercoat or feathering, and is often described as slightly more terrier-like in attitude. The long-haired variety has a 3 to 5 cm (1 to 3 inch) straight or slightly wavy body coat, distinct feathering on the legs and tail, and long, thick fringes on the ears that completely cover the ear edges and tips by three years of age. Both varieties share the same anatomy and can even be born in the same litter.

faq.question: Why do Russian Toy puppies often need baby teeth removed by a veterinarian?
faq.answer: Like several other tiny toy breeds, most Russian Toy puppies do not shed all of their deciduous (baby) teeth naturally when their permanent teeth erupt around six months of age. If retained baby teeth are not surgically extracted by about nine months of age, two teeth occupy the same socket, leading to bite misalignment, trapped food, rapid tartar buildup, and early periodontal disease.

faq.question: Why should a Russian Toy wear a harness instead of a collar on walks?
faq.answer: Because very small dogs have delicate necks and tracheas, pulling against a neck collar can cause throat or tracheal injury. Walking the dog on a well-fitted harness distributes pressure safely across the chest. Indoors, collars and harnesses should be removed so they cannot catch on furniture or vents.

faq.question: When does a long-haired Russian Toy get its full coat and ear fringes?
faq.answer: Puppies typically shed much of their puppy coat between 5 and 12 months of age. An adult coat does not develop until the dog is over a year old, and the full, dramatic ear fringing is often not complete until two to three years of age.

faq.question: What health screenings are recommended for Russian Toy breeding dogs?
faq.answer: Pre-breeding health programs recommend three core clinical evaluations—patellar luxation screening, an annual examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (or accredited eye-scheme examiner), and a basic cardiac evaluation—along with optional screenings for Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, hip and elbow dysplasia, and paired serum bile acid testing for congenital liver shunts.

overview.summary: The Samoyed is a sturdy, sociable Arctic spitz breed known for its thick double coat, upright ears, curled tail, and characteristic friendly expression. Originally developed among peoples of northern Russia and Siberia, it worked alongside families in demanding cold environments. It usually thrives with companionship, regular activity, patient training, and substantial coat care.
overview.description: Samoyeds are medium-sized, strong dogs with a dense undercoat and a longer, weather-resistant outer coat. Their expression is often described as a 'Samoyed smile', formed by the shape of the eyes and slightly upturned corners of the mouth. They are generally outgoing and alert, and tend to enjoy being involved in family routines. Their thick coat sheds heavily, and their social nature means that long periods without interaction may be difficult for many individuals. Each dog still has its own temperament, activity level, and needs.
overview.history: The breed takes its name from Samoyedic peoples of northern Russia and Siberia. Historical accounts describe dogs used for sled pulling, hunting, and helping manage reindeer, with close contact between dogs and the families they lived with. Dogs brought to western Europe by explorers and travellers helped establish the modern western breed. The first written breed standard was produced in England in the early twentieth century.

grooming.brushing: Brush thoroughly several times per week and more frequently during heavy shedding. Work through the coat in sections so the dense undercoat is reached, paying attention to areas behind the ears, under the legs, around the trousers, and beneath the tail. Use suitable brushes and combs without scraping or irritating the skin.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when necessary using dog-appropriate products and rinse the dense coat thoroughly. Ensure the undercoat is completely dried after bathing to reduce dampness trapped close to the skin.
notes: Expect substantial loose hair, particularly during seasonal coat changes.
Check for mats, debris, skin irritation, and parasites during grooming.
Avoid shaving the double coat as a routine response to warm weather; discuss coat or skin problems with a veterinarian or qualified groomer.
Trim nails regularly and check paws after outdoor activity.
Brush teeth with dog-safe toothpaste and arrange routine dental checks.
Provide shade, fresh water, ventilation, and cooler exercise periods during hot weather.

training.difficulty: Moderate; consistency, motivation, and patience are important.
tips: Use reward-based training and keep sessions varied and engaging.
Teach recall and loose-lead walking early; practise in secure areas before adding distractions.
Reward calm behaviour as well as active responses.
Use enrichment games to provide mental activity.
Manage barking by identifying its cause and reinforcing alternative behaviours rather than relying on punishment.
Use secure fencing and supervision because some dogs may roam if given the opportunity.
training.socialization: Introduce the dog gradually and positively to people, dogs, handling, transport, household sounds, and different environments. Continue training and social learning into adulthood. Supervise interactions with children and unfamiliar dogs; early socialization helps build confidence but does not guarantee that every dog will enjoy every situation.

climates: Cold weather is generally more comfortable for this Arctic-adapted breed.
Hot and humid conditions require extra precautions because of the dense double coat.
In warm climates, provide shade, fresh water, good ventilation, and exercise during cooler parts of the day.
Never leave a dog in a parked vehicle or an inadequately ventilated hot space.
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Often low; many Samoyeds prefer company and may become bored or vocal if left alone for long periods. Build alone-time skills gradually and provide suitable enrichment.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced dog food appropriate to the dog's life stage, body condition, activity, and individual health needs.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Usually several small meals daily; follow the food manufacturer's age-specific guidance and your veterinarian's advice.
feedingFrequency.adult: Often fed in two meals per day, with portions adjusted to body condition and activity.
feedingFrequency.senior: Choose a suitable diet and feeding schedule according to body condition, activity, dental health, and veterinary guidance.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure meals rather than feeding by guesswork. Monitor body weight and body condition, adjust portions as activity or life stage changes, and include treats in the daily calorie total. Keep clean drinking water available at all times. A veterinarian can help choose an appropriate diet if the dog has a medical condition or persistent weight or digestive concerns.
considerations: Avoid overfeeding and monitor body condition regularly.
Adjust portions for age, activity, neuter status, and individual metabolism.
Introduce food changes gradually when practical.
Do not add supplements or prescribe restrictive diets without veterinary advice.
Ask a veterinarian about persistent itching, gastrointestinal signs, weight changes, or changes in appetite.
nutrition.note: These are general feeding principles, not an individual calorie prescription. Food choice and quantity should be tailored to the dog's condition and veterinary needs.

health.overview: Responsible Samoyed breeding programmes commonly recommend screening for hip, eye, and cardiac disorders, along with DNA testing for specified inherited eye conditions. Screening helps breeders assess risk but cannot guarantee that a dog will never develop disease. Individual symptoms and health decisions should be assessed by a veterinarian.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia, for which screening is recommended in breeding dogs
Inherited eye disorders, including X-linked progressive retinal atrophy
Retinal dysplasia and oculoskeletal dysplasia associated with the RD/OSD testing programme
Cardiac disorders for which examination is included in recommended breeder screening
preventiveCare: Schedule routine veterinary examinations and keep vaccinations and parasite prevention appropriate to local risks.
Maintain a healthy body condition and provide age-appropriate activity.
Ask breeders for documented health-screening results and relevant family history.
Seek veterinary assessment for persistent lameness, vision changes, fainting, breathing difficulty, or sustained changes in appetite or behaviour.
Keep the coat clean and dry and check the skin during brushing.
recommendedScreenings: Hip evaluation through a recognised programme such as OFA or an equivalent in the breeder's country
Annual eye examination by a veterinary ophthalmologist for breeding dogs
Cardiac examination by an appropriately qualified veterinary cardiologist
DNA test for X-linked progressive retinal atrophy (XLPRA1)
DNA test for retinal dysplasia/oculoskeletal dysplasia (RD/OSD)
Ask the breeder and veterinarian whether additional tests are appropriate for the dog's family line
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste and arrange veterinary dental checks. Seek advice for persistent bad breath, oral pain, bleeding, or difficulty eating.
health.earCare: Inspect the ears regularly and after outdoor activity. Clean only when needed with a dog-safe product. Redness, odour, discharge, pain, or repeated head-shaking should be assessed by a veterinarian.
health.skinCare: Check the skin while brushing, especially beneath dense coat and feathering. Persistent itching, sores, unusual hair loss, or recurrent irritation warrants veterinary assessment.

funFacts: The breed's name comes from Samoyedic peoples of northern Russia and Siberia.
Historically, Samoyeds worked as sled dogs and also supported families in other tasks.
The familiar Samoyed smile is associated with the shape of the eyes and slightly upturned mouth corners.
The breed's dense double coat includes a soft insulating undercoat and a harsher outer coat.
Samoyeds are classified by the FCI among Nordic sledge dogs.

faq.question: Where does the Samoyed originate?
faq.answer: The breed originates from northern Russia and Siberia, where it lived and worked closely with Arctic communities.

faq.question: How big does a Samoyed get?
faq.answer: The FCI standard gives ideal heights of about 57 cm for males and 53 cm for females, each with a tolerance of 3 cm. The American Kennel Club lists typical male weights of 45–65 lb and female weights of 35–50 lb.

faq.question: How long does a Samoyed live?
faq.answer: The American Kennel Club lists a typical life expectancy of 12–14 years. Individual lifespan varies with genetics, health, care, and environment.

faq.question: Do Samoyeds shed a lot?
faq.answer: Yes. Their dense double coat sheds throughout the year, often with heavier seasonal shedding. Regular brushing helps remove loose hair and reduce tangles.

faq.question: Are Samoyeds suitable for hot climates?
faq.answer: They are adapted to cold conditions and need careful heat management in warm or humid weather. Provide shade, water, ventilation, and exercise during cooler hours, and watch for signs of overheating.

faq.question: Are Samoyeds easy to train?
faq.answer: They are intelligent and can learn well with reward-based training, but may also be independent or easily distracted. Short, varied sessions and consistent practice are helpful.

faq.question: Can Samoyeds be left alone all day?
faq.answer: Many Samoyeds are strongly social and may struggle with long periods of isolation. Build alone-time skills gradually and arrange companionship and enrichment suited to the individual dog.

faq.question: What health tests should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Ask for documented hip, eye, and cardiac evaluations, plus DNA test results for X-linked progressive retinal atrophy and retinal dysplasia/oculoskeletal dysplasia. A CHIC number means required results have been submitted for publication; it does not itself mean every result is normal.

faq.question: How much grooming does a Samoyed need?
faq.answer: Frequent, thorough brushing is important because the double coat sheds heavily and can tangle. Grooming needs often increase during seasonal coat changes.

overview.summary: The Schipperke is a small, sturdy Belgian dog with a dense black coat, a distinctive neck ruff, a lively personality and a strong instinct to watch over its surroundings.
overview.description: Compact and nearly square in outline, the Schipperke combines the build of a small working sheepdog with the alert expression and energetic manner of a keen watchdog. Its pointed ears, wedge-shaped head, thick double coat and prominent ruff give it a recognisable silhouette. It is curious, quick to react to movement and often vocal when something unusual happens. Although small enough to fit many homes, it is an active dog that benefits from daily physical exercise, training and tasks that engage its mind.
overview.history: The breed developed in Belgium and has documented roots reaching back to the seventeenth century. Historical accounts associate it with working people in Brussels and describe its usefulness in catching rats and other vermin. It was exhibited in Spa in 1882, reached Britain and the United States in 1887, and had a breed standard drawn up in 1888. Its history connects small-scale guarding and vermin control with its later role as a household companion.
overview.originalPurpose: Small watchdog and companion, with a longstanding reputation for catching rats and other vermin.

physical.coatType: Dense double coat with a straight, firm outer coat and a thick, soft undercoat.
physical.coatLength: Short on the head and ears; medium and close-lying on the body, with longer hair forming a ruff, mane, frill and breeches.
physical.sheddingLevel: Seasonal shedding; shedding can become heavy once or twice a year.
distinctiveFeatures: Small, upright, triangular ears
Wedge-shaped head and alert expression
Compact, sturdy, nearly square body
Prominent ruff, mane and frill around the neck and chest
Longer coat over the hindquarters forming breeches
Natural tails may vary; some dogs are born with a short or absent tail

traits: Alert and watchful
Curious and inquisitive
Lively and energetic
Confident and independent-minded
Reserved with unfamiliar people
Often vocal when alerting to activity
Affectionate with familiar household members
May chase small animals because of its vermin-hunting background

exercise.level: Moderate to high for a small breed
activities: Daily walks with opportunities to explore
Short training sessions and reward-based games
Agility or other suitable dog sports
Scent work and supervised search games
Trick training and interactive enrichment
Secure, supervised play

grooming.level: Moderate; easy to maintain between seasonal sheds
grooming.brushing: Brush at least weekly and more often when seasonal shedding increases. Check the ruff, breeches and undercoat for loose hair or tangles.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when needed rather than on a rigid schedule, using a dog-appropriate shampoo and rinsing thoroughly.
notes: The coat's natural texture should be maintained; routine brushing is preferable to unnecessary trimming.
Check nails regularly and trim them when needed.
Inspect ears, teeth, skin and paw pads during routine grooming.
Expect more loose coat during seasonal shedding periods.

training.difficulty: Moderate; the breed can be clever but independent
tips: Use short, consistent, reward-based sessions.
Teach recall early and practise it in controlled environments before allowing greater freedom.
Train a reliable quiet or settle cue to help manage alert barking.
Provide puzzle games and tasks so the dog has appropriate outlets for its curiosity.
Use secure fencing and a leash where small-animal chasing could create a risk.
Avoid harsh handling; build cooperation through predictable, positive training.
training.socialization: Introduce the dog gradually and positively to different people, calm dogs, household sounds and everyday environments. Supervise interactions with children and small animals, and allow the dog space when it appears uncomfortable.

climates: Can live in a range of climates with suitable shelter and care.
In hot weather, provide shade, fresh water, ventilation and exercise during cooler parts of the day.
In cold weather, provide a dry, sheltered resting place and monitor comfort during outdoor activity.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced dog food appropriate to the dog's life stage, body condition and individual health needs.
nutrition.guidelines: Choose food labelled complete and balanced for the appropriate life stage. Measure portions, monitor body condition and adjust intake to maintain a healthy weight. Fresh water should always be available. Ask a veterinarian for individual guidance if the dog has a medical condition, changes weight unexpectedly or needs a therapeutic diet.
considerations: Adjust portions to activity level, age and body condition rather than relying on a generic amount.
Use treats in moderation and account for them in daily intake.
Introduce diet changes gradually unless a veterinarian advises otherwise.
Discuss any persistent digestive problems, appetite changes or weight changes with a veterinarian.
nutrition.note: The sources consulted do not establish a unique Schipperke-specific feeding formula or universal meal schedule. Individual calorie needs vary.

health.overview: Schipperkes can live into their teens, but breed health resources identify several inherited or monitored conditions. These include mucopolysaccharidosis type IIIB (MPS IIIB), epilepsy and Legg-Calve-Perthes disease; breed-club resources also discuss von Willebrand disease type 1 and the bobtail-associated mutation. Listing a condition does not mean it is common in every line or that an individual dog is affected. Ask for relevant health records and consult a veterinarian about screening appropriate to the dog's age and family history.
commonConditions: Mucopolysaccharidosis type IIIB (MPS IIIB), a serious inherited condition for which DNA testing is available
Epilepsy, reported in breed health resources
Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, a hip-joint condition discussed in breed health resources
Patellar luxation, a condition for which screening is recommended
Eye and thyroid disorders, addressed by breed screening guidance
Von Willebrand disease type 1, discussed in breed-club health information
Brachyury or bobtail-associated genetic variation, relevant to some breeding decisions
preventiveCare: Arrange routine veterinary examinations and age-appropriate preventive care.
Discuss breed-relevant eye, patella, thyroid and hip screening with the breeder and veterinarian.
Ask about MPS IIIB testing and the parents' results when considering a puppy or breeding dog.
Maintain dental hygiene, nail care, parasite prevention and a healthy body condition.
Seek veterinary advice promptly for changes in coordination, recurrent seizures, persistent lameness or unusual bleeding.
recommendedScreenings: Eye examination by a qualified veterinary eye specialist
Patella evaluation
Thyroid evaluation
Hip evaluation
MPS IIIB DNA testing, particularly for breeding decisions
Discuss cardiac evaluation and broader genetic testing with the breeder and veterinarian where appropriate
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste and arrange veterinary dental checks. Ask a veterinarian for a dental-care plan if there is persistent bad breath, gum redness, pain or difficulty eating.
health.earCare: Check the ears regularly for redness, odour, discharge or irritation. Clean only when needed with a veterinarian-approved product, and seek advice if signs of discomfort or infection appear.
health.skinCare: During brushing, check the skin and coat for irritation, parasites, lumps, debris or unusual hair loss. Seek veterinary advice for persistent itching, sores or changes in the coat.

idealFor: People who enjoy an alert, interactive and energetic small dog
Households able to provide daily walks, training and mental enrichment
Owners interested in agility, scent games or trick training
People who appreciate a watchdog and can manage alert barking
Homes prepared to manage a small dog's interest in chasing vermin
notIdealFor: People who require a consistently quiet dog and cannot work on barking
Households expecting a highly compliant dog without consistent training
Owners who cannot provide regular activity or mental stimulation
Homes where small pets cannot be safely separated from a dog with chasing instincts
People who plan to leave a dog alone for long periods without suitable care

funFacts: The breed's history reaches back to seventeenth-century Belgium.
Schipperkes were historically valued for catching rats and other vermin as well as guarding.
The characteristic neck ruff, mane, frill and breeches create much of the breed's distinctive outline.
Some Schipperkes are naturally born with a short or absent tail.
The FCI standard classifies the Schipperke as a sheepdog, even though it is small in stature.

faq.question: How big does a Schipperke get?
faq.answer: The AKC lists typical heights of 11–13 inches for males and 10–12 inches for females, equivalent to approximately 27.9–33.0 cm and 25.4–30.5 cm. The FCI standard gives an overall weight range of 3–9 kg, with 4–7 kg sought after, but does not provide separate male and female weight ranges.

faq.question: Are Schipperkes good family dogs?
faq.answer: They can be affectionate and engaging with their household, and the FCI standard describes them as gentle with children. As with any breed, children and dogs should be supervised together, children should be taught respectful handling, and the individual dog's temperament should guide introductions.

faq.question: Do Schipperkes bark a lot?
faq.answer: They are naturally alert watchdogs and can bark readily when they notice movement or unfamiliar activity. Early training, appropriate enrichment and teaching a calm response to triggers can help, but prospective owners should be comfortable living with a vocal dog.

faq.question: How much grooming does a Schipperke need?
faq.answer: Regular brushing, at least weekly, helps remove loose hair and maintain the double coat. Brushing more frequently during seasonal shedding can help manage the extra hair. Bathe when needed and check nails, ears, teeth and skin routinely.

faq.question: What health tests should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Ask for documented eye, patella, thyroid and hip screening, and discuss MPS IIIB DNA testing. Breed-club health resources also discuss other inherited concerns. Recommendations can change, so confirm current requirements with the relevant breed club and your veterinarian.

faq.question: Can a Schipperke live in an apartment?
faq.answer: It can adapt to apartment life if its exercise, training and enrichment needs are met. Alert barking may be challenging in shared buildings, so work on calm behaviour and consider neighbours when deciding whether this environment is suitable.
