funFacts: The Welsh Terrier developed in Wales and has a long history as a working hunting terrier.
The breed was used to hunt foxes, badgers and otters.
Its traditional coat combines a hard, wiry outer layer with a softer undercoat.
Welsh Terriers have been shown in dog shows since the nineteenth century.
The breed's familiar black-and-tan look is also reflected in its historical name, the Welsh Black and Tan Rough-Coated Terrier.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Welsh Terrier need?
faq.answer: A healthy adult may benefit from roughly 45–75 minutes of daily activity, adjusted for age, health and temperament. Combine walks with play, training and sniffing opportunities rather than relying on exercise alone.

faq.question: Do Welsh Terriers shed?
faq.answer: They tend to have low visible shedding when their wiry coat is properly maintained, but they can still release loose hair. Brushing and suitable professional grooming help keep the coat tidy.

faq.question: Are Welsh Terriers easy to train?
faq.answer: They are intelligent and capable learners, but their terrier curiosity and persistence can make training challenging around distractions. Short, varied, reward-based sessions and consistent recall practice are useful.

faq.question: Are Welsh Terriers good with children?
faq.answer: An individual Welsh Terrier may live successfully with children when introductions, training and supervision are appropriate. Suitability depends on the dog and the household; supervise interactions and teach children to respect the dog's space.

faq.question: What grooming does a Welsh Terrier need?
faq.answer: Brush and comb the coat once or twice a week, paying attention to the beard and furnishings. Traditional coats may need hand-stripping, while clipping is a common pet-grooming option. A groomer familiar with wire-coated terriers can help establish a suitable routine.

faq.question: What health test should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Ask about Primary Lens Luxation (PLL) DNA testing, which is recommended by the breed club. Discuss family history and any other appropriate screening with a veterinarian.

faq.question: What colours does a Welsh Terrier have?
faq.answer: The recognised standard colours are black and tan or black grizzle and tan. The darker jacket covers much of the body, while tan appears on the head, legs and underside.

faq.question: How long does a Welsh Terrier live?
faq.answer: The American Kennel Club lists a life expectancy of 12–15 years. Individual lifespan varies with genetics, health, preventive care and living conditions.

faq.question: Can a Welsh Terrier live in an apartment?
faq.answer: It depends on the individual dog and the household's ability to provide exercise, enrichment and appropriate noise management. A yard can be useful but does not replace walks, training or interaction.

overview.summary: A versatile, medium-sized Hungarian pointing and retrieving dog bred for field, forest, and icy water, distinguished from the smooth-coated Vizsla by its heavier bone, weather-resistant russet-gold wire coat, pronounced eyebrows, and harsh beard.
overview.description: The Wirehaired Vizsla (Drótszőrű Magyar Vizsla) is a lean yet robust, medium-sized multi-purpose gun dog that stands slightly taller and carries more substance than its smooth-coated relative while remaining a completely separate breed. Its close-lying, non-glossy wiry outer coat (about 2 to 3 cm long) and dense water-repellent undercoat protect the dog against rough cover and winter cold without hiding its athletic outline. Characteristic facial furnishings—pronounced eyebrows that highlight the stop and a harsh 2 to 3 cm beard on both sides of a blunt, muscular muzzle—combine with V-shaped neck brushes and self-coloured brown pigment on the nose, lips, and eye rims to create a clever, determined expression. Passionate, staunch on point, and determined to stay on a scent even while swimming, the breed is calm, gentle, loyal, and affectionate indoors, thriving on close handler contact and positive, varied training.
overview.history: Developed in the 1930s after the First World War by Hungarian and Austrian hunters and falconers—led initially by Vizsla breeder József Vasas of the Csabai kennel and German Wirehaired Pointer breeder László Gresznárik of the de Selle kennel—the breed was created to combine the golden-rust colour and close-working biddability of the smooth Hungarian Vizsla with a heavier frame and a dense, weatherproof wire coat suited to harsh winters and cold-water retrieving. Foundation crosses mated two working Vizsla females (Zsuzsi and Csibi) with a solid liver German Wirehaired Pointer sire (Astor von Potat), producing Dia de Selle, the first three-generation Wirehaired Vizsla ever exhibited, shown in Hungary on 6 June 1943. Stabilized in Hungary by 1950 and granted international recognition in 1963, the breed held its first dedicated Hungarian field trials in 1976 with 26 entries, reached North America in the 1970s (earning Canadian recognition in 1978 and North American field recognition in 1986 with female Palotásmenti Jutka), and achieved full conformation recognition in the United States in 2014.
overview.originalPurpose: Versatile gun and falconry dog bred to point, track, and retrieve feathered and furred game across field, dense forest, and cold water, including European deerstalking
currentRoles: Versatile hunting companion for upland game birds, waterfowl, furred game, and deerstalking
Pointing, retrieving, water-test, and blood-tracking competitor
Agility, obedience, rally, tracking, nose work, dock diving, barn hunt, and lure coursing participant
Therapy dog and active household companion

physical.coatType: Close-lying, strong, dense, non-glossy wiry outer coat over a dense, water-repellent undercoat, with shorter, softer hair on the lower legs, chest, and belly and characteristic facial and neck furnishings
physical.coatLength: Outer coat 2 to 3 cm (0.75–1.25 in; about 2.5 cm / 1 in in American standards and 3–4 cm / 1.25–1.5 in in Canadian standards) on the body, with a harsh 2 to 3 cm beard on the muzzle, pronounced eyebrows, V-shaped brushes on both sides of the neck, and feathering brushes along the backs of the legs
coatColors: Dark sandy gold (semmelgelb / dark sandy yellow)
Golden rust (with or without a white forechest/throat patch up to 5 cm / 2 in in diameter and white toe markings)
physical.sheddingLevel: Low to moderate
distinctiveFeatures: Dense, close-lying wiry outer coat (2–3 cm) and water-repellent undercoat that protect against briars and icy water without obscuring the body outline
Pronounced bushy eyebrows accentuating the stop and a harsh 2 to 3 cm beard on both sides of the blunt, muscular muzzle
V-shaped coat brushes on both sides of the neck and distinct hair brushes along the backs of the forelegs (absence of undercoat or leg brushes is a disqualifying or eliminating fault)
Self-coloured dark brown nose, lip, and eye-rim pigment that harmonizes with the russet-gold coat (any black on the nose or a spotted butterfly nose is a disqualification)
Rounded V-shaped pendulous ears set at medium height and hanging close to the cheeks, slightly shorter than those of the smooth Vizsla

Slightly rectangular body (length from breastbone to buttocks exceeding withers height in roughly a 10:9 ratio) with brisket depth slightly less than half the withers height and elbows level with the sternum
Complete, regular scissor bite of 42 teeth; slightly oval feet with tough slate-grey or dark pads; rear dewclaws are a disqualification

Withers height of 58–64 cm for males and 54–60 cm for females internationally (58.4–63.5 cm [23–25 in] and 54.6–58.4 cm [21.5–23 in] in the United States; 57–64 cm and 53–60 cm in Canada), and typical adult weights of 25–29.5 kg (55–65 lbs) for males and 20–25 kg (45–55 lbs) for females (or 22–30 kg / 48.5–66.25 lbs across both sexes in Canadian standards)

traits: Affectionate, loyal, and closely bonded to its handler and family
Calm, gentle, and tractable indoors
Intelligent, self-confident, and eager to learn
Sensitive and intolerant of harsh handling or physical punishment
Passionate, determined, and staunch on point in the field and water
Can display a stubborn streak or bore easily with repetitive drills
Outgoing and friendly, though occasionally reserved with strangers
Possesses a well-developed protective and watchdog instinct

exercise.level: High
activities: Field hunting, pointing, tracking, and land or water retrieving
Swimming and dock diving (a natural, low-impact outlet for puppies and adults)
Hiking, jogging, and cycling with an active owner once skeletally mature
Off-leash running in a securely fenced area (essential due to strong prey drive)
Nose work, blood tracking, barn hunt, agility, rally, obedience, and lure coursing
Interactive puppy games such as 'wing on a string', toy retrieving, and hidden-treat scent searches

grooming.brushing: Routine brushing with a slicker brush or grooming mitt removes dirt and loose hair; wiping with a damp cloth suffices between baths. Dogs with longer wire coats benefit from periodic hand-stripping (by hand or stripping knife, working small sections at a time) to pull dead hairs and stimulate coarse wire regrowth.
grooming.bathing: Monthly or only as needed using a mild dog-safe shampoo; excessive bathing softens the harsh wire texture.
notes: Never clip or shave a correct wire coat; clipping damages the weather-resistant wire texture and is penalized as a fault in conformation.

Coat expression varies genetically within the breed: alongside the ideal rough wire coat (up to about 2–5 cm), some puppies inherit almost no furnishings ('smooth' wires requiring minimal upkeep), while others develop a long, soft, woolly coat that does not strip out and requires specialized care.
Use a grooming mitt or shedding blade during seasonal shedding to reduce loose hair indoors.
Trim toenails every four weeks (many owners do this during the dog's monthly bath).
Clean and dry the hanging ears regularly—especially after swimming—and wipe the beard after meals.
Begin regular tooth brushing early in puppyhood.

training.difficulty: Moderate
tips: Enrol in puppy kindergarten early and use upbeat, reward-based positive reinforcement; because the breed has a soft, sensitive temperament, harsh words or physical corrections are counterproductive and damaging.
Keep training lessons short, varied, and engaging—always ending on a positive note—as these clever dogs bore quickly with repetitive drills and can show a stubborn streak.
Provide calm, consistent household boundaries and gradually condition puppies to alone time so their close attachment to family does not develop into separation anxiety.

Avoid strenuous forced exercise—such as long-distance running, high-impact jumping, or excessive stair climbing—until the growth plates close at skeletal maturity; let puppies regulate their own play and rest after training lessons.
Ensure off-leash running takes place in a securely fenced area until field conditioning and recall are solid, as natural prey drive is strong.
training.socialization: Provide early, ongoing positive exposure to diverse people, children, dogs, surfaces, and field environments. Properly socialized adults are outgoing, steady, and adaptable in the home and field, neither timid nor aggressive.

climates: Cold and snowy winter climates (for which the dense wire coat and undercoat were specifically bred)
Cool and temperate climates
Warm climates when provided with shade, fresh water, and exercise during cooler hours
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low. Deeply people-oriented and bred to maintain close contact with its handler, the Wirehaired Vizsla thrives as an indoor family member and can develop separation anxiety, restlessness, or destructive habits if isolated for long periods.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality, complete and balanced commercial dog food or veterinarian-supervised home-prepared diet matched to life stage (puppy, adult, or senior) and workload
nutrition.guidelines: Active hunting and sporting dogs require a nutrient-dense ration during working seasons that differs substantially from the diet needed by a growing puppy or a less active companion. Because Wirehaired Vizslas are strongly food-motivated, measure daily portions carefully, deduct training treats from the daily calorie allowance to prevent obesity, and keep clean, fresh water available at all times.
considerations: Adjust caloric density and portion sizes to match seasonal hunting, training, or companion activity levels.
Watch treat consumption closely during reward-based training, as the breed is food-oriented and can gain excess weight if overfed.
Prepare home-cooked diets only with veterinary supervision and approval.
Ensure constant access to fresh water—especially important for dogs carrying or at risk for hyperuricosuria.
Consult a veterinarian to establish individualized meal schedules for puppies, adults, and seniors.
nutrition.note: Authoritative kennel-club and parent-club sources do not prescribe fixed numerical meal counts per day for puppies, adults, or seniors; consult a veterinarian for life-stage feeding frequency.

health.overview: The Wirehaired Vizsla is generally a sturdy, long-lived hunting breed with a typical lifespan of 12 to 14 years, supported by parent-club health surveillance and mandatory pre-breeding screening. Under the national breed club's Code of Ethics (amended October 2025), all breeding parents must hold hip dysplasia clearances (radiographic certification at 24 months or older and/or a hip distraction-index score of 0.70 or better without degenerative joint disease), a current annual board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist eye clearance, and documented DNA testing for Exfoliative Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus (ECLE, requiring at least one parent of every litter to test Clear/Normal). A second autosomal recessive disorder with a validated DNA test in the breed is canine hyperuricosuria (HUU, caused by an SLC2A9 mutation), which predisposes affected dogs to urate bladder and kidney stones. Breeders also screen for elbow dysplasia and cardiac disease (such as subaortic stenosis), and monitor for inherited eye conditions, cancer, hypothyroidism, idiopathic epilepsy, and reported breed sensitivities to anaesthesia and combined vaccine/flea-medication protocols.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia: a primary orthopedic screening focus required prior to breeding (in 2025 orthopedic registry testing of 19 dogs, 21% scored Excellent/Normal, 68% Good, and 11% Fair)

Exfoliative Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus (ECLE): an autosomal recessive chronic cutaneous lupus caused by a missense variant in the UNC93B1 gene (c.1438C>A / p.Pro480Thr on chromosome 18), recently confirmed by biopsy and DNA testing in Wirehaired Vizslas; causes scaling, crusting, and hair loss beginning on the ears, muzzle, and back and spreading to the limbs and ventrum, along with joint pain/lameness, intermittent fever, lymphadenopathy, and possible proteinuria (often presenting around age 3 in this breed with symptoms that require lifelong management)

Hyperuricosuria (HUU): an autosomal recessive purine metabolism defect caused by a missense mutation in exon 5 of the SLC2A9 gene (c.563G>T / p.Cys188Phe on chromosome 3), leading to elevated urinary uric acid and predisposition to urate bladder and kidney stones that often require surgical removal

Ophthalmic disorders: hereditary cataracts, progressive retinal atrophy (PRA), glaucoma, persistent pupillary membranes (PPM), entropion, ectropion, and distichiasis (double row of eyelashes; both entropion/ectropion and distichiasis are disqualifying or eliminating faults in conformation standards)
Elbow dysplasia and subaortic stenosis (SAS): orthopedic and congenital cardiac conditions included in parent-club elective pre-breeding screening

Additional conditions tracked in breed health surveys and advisories: cancer, autoimmune diseases, hypothyroidism, idiopathic epilepsy, moisture-related outer ear infections in swimming dogs, sensitivity to vaccines or combined vaccine/flea-medication administration, and delayed recovery from anaesthesia
preventiveCare: Verify that both parents of any prospective puppy hold hip clearances (at ≥24 months or distraction index ≤0.70), current annual board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist certificates, and ECLE DNA test documentation showing at least one Clear/Normal parent, along with recommended HUU, elbow, and cardiac results.

Discuss vaccination schedules, parasite preventives, and anaesthetic protocols with your veterinarian in advance, as sensitivity to combined vaccine/flea-medication treatments and slow recovery from anaesthesia have been reported in the breed.

Protect growing joints by avoiding forced long-distance running, repetitive jumping, or excessive stairs until skeletal maturity, and consult your veterinarian regarding the timing of spaying or neutering.
Clean and thoroughly dry the pendulous ears after swimming or wet field work to prevent otitis externa.
Monitor urinary habits (straining, hematuria, or frequent small voids), especially in dogs not cleared of hyperuricosuria.
recommendedScreenings: Hip dysplasia evaluation (radiographic certification at 24 months of age or older and/or hip distraction-index score of 0.70 or better; mandatory under parent-club Code of Ethics)
Annual ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (mandatory under parent-club Code of Ethics)
Exfoliative Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus (ECLE / UNC93B1 c.1438C>A) DNA test (mandatory under parent-club Code of Ethics that at least one parent of a litter be tested Clear/Normal)
Hyperuricosuria (HUU / SLC2A9) DNA test via buccal swab or blood sample (recommended by the parent club)
Elbow dysplasia radiographic evaluation and veterinary cardiac evaluation (recommended by the parent club)
Optional coat-genetics DNA testing (furnishings and coat length) for breeding planning
health.dentalCare: Begin a regular tooth-brushing routine with dog-safe toothpaste at an early age and schedule routine veterinary dental checks. Conformation standards require strong jaws with a complete, regular scissor bite of 42 teeth.
health.earCare: Inspect the rounded V-shaped hanging ears weekly for redness, debris, or odour, and dry them carefully after every swim or bath to prevent moisture-related ear canal infections.
health.skinCare: Maintain the wiry coat and skin through regular brushing and periodic hand-stripping rather than clipping. Watch for uncharacteristic scaling, crusting, or hair loss on the ears, muzzle, and back (which warrant veterinary evaluation for ECLE or other dermatoses), and discuss separated timing for vaccines and flea/tick medications with your veterinarian.

idealFor: Upland bird, waterfowl, and deerstalking hunters or falconers seeking a cold-hardy, versatile pointing and retrieving dog
Active families and outdoor enthusiasts who hike, jog, swim, or cycle and want their dog closely involved in daily life
Handlers interested in hunt tests, field trials, water tests, nose work, tracking, agility, rally, obedience, or dock diving
Owners who use gentle, reward-based training and can provide daily physical and mental stimulation
notIdealFor: Sedentary households or owners unable to provide vigorous daily exercise and mental work
Homes where the dog would be left isolated for long workdays or kept in an outdoor kennel away from the family
Heavy-handed trainers who rely on harsh verbal or physical corrections
Owners unwilling to manage a strong hunting prey drive around small animals or provide secure fencing

funFacts: Created in the 1930s by Hungarian Vizsla breeder József Vasas (Csabai kennel) and German Wirehaired Pointer breeder László Gresznárik (de Selle kennel), the breed was designed for hunters and falconers who needed a heavier-boned, cold-hardy dog for winter field and icy water work.
The first three-generation Wirehaired Vizsla ever exhibited at a dog show was a female named Dia de Selle, shown in Hungary on 6 June 1943.
In 1976, the first dedicated field tests exclusively for Wirehaired Vizslas were held in Hungary, drawing 26 entries.

The first Wirehaired Vizsla recorded in North American versatile hunting dog testing (#WV-000001) was a female named Palotásmenti Jutka, owned by Sándor Arany, who earned the breed's first Utility Prize II in 1986.

Although closely related to the smooth-coated Vizsla, the Wirehaired Vizsla is a completely separate breed that stands slightly taller and heavier, and cross-breeding between the two is not permitted by any major registry.

Because of the breed's natural affinity for water and determination to stay on a scent while swimming, it is eligible to compete not only in pointing breed hunt tests and water tests, but also in retriever hunt tests.

Conformation standards prize a natural working dog: a Wirehaired Vizsla is shown with minimal stripping and is explicitly never penalized in the show ring for sinewy working muscle or 'honorable scars' earned in the field.

faq.question: What is a Wirehaired Vizsla, and is it just a coat variety of the smooth Vizsla?
faq.answer: No. Although developed in the 1930s by crossing smooth-coated Hungarian Vizslas with German Wirehaired Pointers, the Wirehaired Vizsla (Drótszőrű Magyar Vizsla) is a completely separate breed with its own conformation standard and studbook. It is slightly taller, heavier-boned, and more robust than the smooth Vizsla, and cross-matings between the two breeds cannot be registered.

faq.question: How big does a Wirehaired Vizsla get?
faq.answer: International conformation standards specify a withers height of 58 to 64 cm (22.75–25.25 in) for males and 54 to 60 cm (21.25–23.75 in) for females. American standards specify 23 to 25 inches (58.4–63.5 cm) for males and 21.5 to 23 inches (54.6–58.4 cm) for females, while Canadian standards allow 57 to 64 cm for males and 53 to 60 cm for females. Typical adult weights are 25 to 29.5 kg (55–65 lbs) for males and 20 to 25 kg (45–55 lbs) for females, or 22 to 30 kg (48.5–66.25 lbs) across both sexes in Canadian standards.

faq.question: How long does a Wirehaired Vizsla live?
faq.answer: The typical lifespan is 12 to 14 years.

faq.question: Why do some Wirehaired Vizslas have smooth or woolly coats?
faq.answer: Coat texture and length vary within the breed due to coat-furnishing and coat-length genetics. While the ideal coat is a harsh, close-lying wire topcoat (about 2–4 cm long) with a dense undercoat, beard, and eyebrows, some puppies inherit almost no wire furnishings and appear nearly smooth, whereas others inherit a longer, soft, woolly coat that cannot be hand-stripped and is faulted in the show ring.

faq.question: How should a Wirehaired Vizsla's coat be groomed?
faq.answer: For everyday care, the coat is nearly 'wash and wear': routine brushing with a slicker brush or grooming mitt and wiping with a damp cloth between occasional baths keep it clean. Dogs with longer wire hair benefit from periodic hand-stripping—pulling dead outer hairs by hand or with a stripping knife in small sections—to encourage coarse new growth. A correct wire coat should never be clipped with electric clippers.

faq.question: What health screenings and DNA tests are required for Wirehaired Vizsla breeding dogs?
faq.answer: Under the national breed club's Code of Ethics, breeding dogs must have hip dysplasia clearance (radiographic certification at 24 months or older and/or a hip distraction-index score of 0.70 or better), a current annual board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist eye exam, and DNA testing confirming that at least one parent of the litter is Clear/Normal for Exfoliative Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus (ECLE / UNC93B1). Breeders are also encouraged to test for Hyperuricosuria (HUU / SLC2A9), elbow dysplasia, and cardiac health.

faq.question: What is Exfoliative Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus (ECLE) in the Wirehaired Vizsla?
faq.answer: ECLE is an autosomal recessive autoimmune skin and systemic disorder caused by a missense mutation in the UNC93B1 gene. It causes scaling, crusting, and hair loss starting on the ears, muzzle, and back and spreading to the legs and underside, sometimes accompanied by joint pain, lameness, fever, and proteinuria. Although cases identified in Wirehaired Vizslas have often appeared later (around age 3) and been less severe than in German Shorthaired Pointers, it is a painful, life-altering condition that breeders prevent through mandatory DNA screening.

faq.question: Are there any special veterinary precautions for Wirehaired Vizslas?
faq.answer: Yes. The national breed club's health statement notes that Wirehaired Vizslas have been reported to be sensitive to vaccines and combined vaccine/flea-medication treatments, and some dogs have experienced difficulty or slow recovery when waking from anaesthesia. Owners should discuss these sensitivities with their veterinarian before procedures.

faq.question: How much exercise should a Wirehaired Vizsla puppy get?
faq.answer: Puppies have abundant energy and need daily play and mental stimulation—such as retrieving games, 'wing on a string', hidden-treat scent games, and swimming—but they should not be taken on forced long-distance runs, high-impact jumps, or excessive stairs until their growth plates close at maturity. Let puppies self-regulate their activity and rest after training sessions.

faq.question: Are Wirehaired Vizslas easy to train?
faq.answer: They are intelligent, intuitive, and eager to please, but they have a sensitive ('soft') temperament and bore quickly with repetitive drills. Short, fun, reward-based sessions with clear, calm boundaries work best, whereas harsh verbal or physical punishment should never be used.

overview.summary: The Yorkshire Terrier is a tiny, confident terrier with a long, silky coat and an alert, lively personality. Although now widely kept as a companion, it retains the curiosity, determination, and quick responses associated with its working-terrier ancestry.
overview.description: Yorkshire Terriers have a compact frame, upright V-shaped ears, dark expressive eyes, and a long coat that is traditionally parted along the back. The adult coat is typically steel blue over the body with rich tan on the head and legs; puppies are generally born darker and change as they mature. Their small size makes them adaptable to many homes, but they still need daily activity, mental engagement, patient training, and careful handling. Regular grooming and dental care are important parts of responsible ownership.
overview.history: The breed developed in nineteenth-century northern England, especially around Yorkshire, where small terriers were used to control rats in mills and other working environments. Several small terrier types contributed to its development. Over time, the Yorkshire Terrier became increasingly popular as a companion and show dog. Its appearance became more refined, but the lively and determined character associated with terriers remains evident.
overview.originalPurpose: Small working terrier used primarily for controlling rats and other vermin in mills and similar settings.
currentRoles: Small-dog sports participant where suitable for the individual dog

physical.coatType: Long, fine, glossy, silky coat; the standard describes a straight outer coat and does not specify a dense woolly undercoat.
physical.coatLength: The coat can grow long and hang evenly down both sides of the body, with a long fall on the head. Many companion dogs have a shorter practical trim.
coatColors: Black and tan in puppies before the adult coat develops
Black and gold in puppies before the adult coat develops
physical.sheddingLevel: Often described as low-shedding, but loose hair and coat-care needs vary between individuals and grooming styles.
distinctiveFeatures: Very small, compact body with an alert, confident carriage.
Small V-shaped ears that are carried erect.
Dark, alert eyes and a black nose.
Long, fine, silky coat parted along the back.
Adult coat usually combines steel blue on the body with tan or gold on the head and legs.
Puppy coat is generally darker and changes during maturation.

traits: Alert and observant.
Lively and playful.
Confident despite small size.
Affectionate with familiar people.
Intelligent and capable of learning routines.
May be vocal when excited or alerting to sounds.
Can show independence and persistent terrier instincts.

exercise.level: Moderate for a toy breed. Daily walks, play, and short training activities are useful; activity should be adjusted for age, health, weather, and individual stamina.
activities: Short daily walks on a well-fitted harness or leash.
Indoor games and supervised play.
Reward-based obedience and trick training.
Scent games and food puzzles.
Age-appropriate activities in a secure area.

grooming.level: Moderate to high, especially when the coat is kept long.
grooming.brushing: Brush and comb frequently, ideally daily for a long show-style coat, to reduce tangles and mats. Work gently through the coat and pay attention to friction areas such as behind the ears, under the legs, and around the harness.
grooming.bathing: Bathe as needed with a dog-appropriate shampoo and dry the coat thoroughly. Long coats need careful detangling before and after bathing to avoid tightening knots.
notes: A shorter companion trim can reduce day-to-day coat maintenance.
Inspect the skin while parting the coat, since long hair can conceal irritation or debris.
Keep hair around the eyes clean and avoid letting tangles pull at the skin.
Check ears, nails, and paws regularly.
Introduce brushing and handling early with short, positive sessions.

training.difficulty: Moderate. The breed is intelligent and responsive but may be persistent or distracted by interesting sounds and movement.
tips: Use reward-based training with small treats and clear cues.
Keep sessions brief and engaging.
Teach calm behaviour and a reliable response to attention cues.
Reward quiet behaviour rather than reinforcing alert barking.
Practise recall in secure areas before adding distractions.
Teach cooperative handling for brushing, tooth care, and veterinary checks.
training.socialization: Provide gradual, positive exposure to different people, sounds, surfaces, and calm dogs. Supervise interactions with children and larger dogs because the Yorkshire Terrier's small size makes accidental injury possible.

climates: Temperate climates.
Warm weather with shade, fresh water, and activity scheduled around cooler periods.
Cool weather with appropriate protection when needed.
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Variable. Gradually teach comfortable alone time and provide safe enrichment; do not assume that every individual will tolerate long periods without company.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced diet appropriate to the dog's life stage, size, activity, and health. Home-prepared diets should be formulated with veterinary nutritional guidance.
nutrition.guidelines: Measure portions and adjust them according to growth, body condition, and veterinary advice. Toy breeds have small energy reserves, so young puppies may need especially careful meal scheduling. Keep fresh water available and avoid excessive treats.
considerations: Choose food appropriate to the dog's life stage and small size.
Monitor body condition rather than relying only on package feeding charts.
Keep treats small and count them toward the daily food allowance.
Ask a veterinarian about feeding schedules for very young or underweight puppies.
Avoid starting supplements or restrictive diets without professional advice.
nutrition.note: The consulted sources do not establish one universally appropriate number of meals or calorie target for all Yorkshire Terriers; requirements vary with age, weight, activity, and health.

health.overview: Yorkshire Terriers can live long lives, but some conditions deserve attention when choosing a puppy and planning preventive care. Breed-club recommendations include patella and eye evaluations for breeding dogs. Other conditions reported in veterinary and breed-health resources include dental disease, tracheal collapse, bladder stones, progressive retinal atrophy, lens luxation, liver shunt, and certain gastrointestinal or neurologic disorders. These conditions vary in evidence and frequency; this list is not a prediction about an individual dog.
commonConditions: Patellar luxation: displacement of the kneecap, which may cause intermittent lameness or altered movement.
Dental disease: small jaws and crowded teeth can make regular home dental care and veterinary checks especially important.
Tracheal collapse: a disorder affecting the windpipe that may cause coughing or breathing difficulty and requires veterinary assessment.
Bladder stones: mineral stones can cause urinary signs and need veterinary diagnosis and treatment.
Progressive retinal atrophy: an inherited retinal condition that can lead to progressive vision loss.
Lens luxation and other eye disorders: eye symptoms should be assessed promptly by a veterinarian.
Liver shunt and microvascular dysplasia: vascular liver conditions discussed in breed health resources.
Other reported concerns include protein-losing enteropathy, encephalitis, degenerative myelopathy, and Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease; evidence and risk differ by condition.
preventiveCare: Schedule routine veterinary examinations and discuss any changes in movement, coughing, urination, vision, appetite, or energy.
Brush teeth regularly with dog-appropriate products and arrange veterinary dental checks.
Avoid encouraging repeated high jumps, especially in puppies, and handle the dog carefully.
Maintain a healthy body condition and age-appropriate exercise.
Ask breeders for documented health information on the parents and close relatives.
Discuss breed-relevant screening with a veterinarian before breeding or when evaluating a puppy.
recommendedScreenings: Patella evaluation for breeding dogs, following the breed club's recommended protocol.
Ophthalmologist evaluation for breeding dogs, following the breed club's recommended protocol.
Discuss optional genetic testing for progressive retinal atrophy (PRA-prcd) and primary lens luxation with the breeder and veterinarian.
Discuss liver shunt, microvascular dysplasia, and other family-history concerns when relevant; testing decisions should be based on veterinary advice.
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth frequently using dog-safe toothpaste and a suitable brush. Small breeds can develop dental problems, so schedule veterinary oral checks and follow recommendations for professional cleaning.
health.earCare: Inspect the ears routinely for redness, odour, discharge, or persistent scratching. Clean only with appropriate products and seek veterinary advice if irritation develops.
health.skinCare: Part the coat during grooming to check for redness, parasites, sores, or mats. Persistent itching, hair loss, or recurring skin changes should be assessed by a veterinarian.

idealFor: Owners looking for a small, lively companion.
Households able to provide regular grooming and dental care.
People who enjoy short training sessions and interactive play.
Homes that can supervise interactions with young children and larger animals.
notIdealFor: Owners wanting a coat that needs little maintenance.
Households unable to provide gentle handling and supervision.
People expecting a small dog to need no training or exercise.
Owners who cannot arrange veterinary care when small-dog health concerns arise.

funFacts: The breed developed in nineteenth-century northern England, where small terriers worked in mills and similar settings.
The Yorkshire Terrier's adult coat typically changes substantially from the darker puppy coat.
The long coat is traditionally parted along the back.
Despite its toy size, the breed retains the alertness and determination associated with terriers.

faq.question: How big does a Yorkshire Terrier get?
faq.answer: The AKC standard sets a maximum weight of seven pounds, approximately 3.18 kg. The AKC breed profile lists a typical height of about 7–8 inches. Individual dogs can vary, and these profile figures should not replace veterinary assessment of healthy growth.

faq.question: How long does a Yorkshire Terrier live?
faq.answer: The AKC profile lists a life expectancy of 11–15 years. Longevity varies with genetics, preventive care, body condition, and the dog's individual health.

faq.question: Does a Yorkshire Terrier need daily grooming?
faq.answer: A long coat benefits from frequent, often daily, brushing to prevent tangles and mats. A shorter companion trim can reduce the time required, but regular coat, skin, ear, nail, and dental care are still needed.

faq.question: Are Yorkshire Terriers good with children?
faq.answer: They can live with considerate children, but their small size makes them vulnerable to accidental injury. Teach children to handle the dog gently and supervise all interactions, especially with very young children.

faq.question: What health checks should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Ask for patella and eye screening information for the parents, and discuss family history of inherited eye disease and other conditions with the breeder and veterinarian. Screening reduces uncertainty but cannot guarantee that a puppy will never develop a health problem.

faq.question: Can a Yorkshire Terrier live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Yes, apartment living can suit the breed when daily walks, indoor play, training, grooming, and toilet routines are provided. The individual dog's needs and the household routine still matter.
